Give 15-20g rapid-acting carbohydrate of the person with diabetes in hospital's choice where possible." https://abcd.care/sites/default/files/site_uploads/JBDS_Guidelines_Current/JBDS_01_Hypo_Guideline_with_QR_code_January_2023.pdf
- Pass: The treatment given for a conscious, swallowing-safe patient with hypoglycaemia is documented as 15-20g of a recognised rapid-acting carbohydrate (e.g. Dextrosol tablets, GlucoTabs, pure fruit juice, sugar in water). Target: ≥90%. Sample: 30 consecutive qualifying hypoglycaemic episodes over the last 3-6 months
- Change: Stock a standard, pre-measured hypo box (containing 15-20g rapid-acting carbohydrate items) on every ward, with a location known to all staff, replacing ad hoc use of whatever is available.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-420.csv`
- Pitfalls: Staff give whatever sugary item is to hand rather than a measured 15-20g dose → stock a standard hypo box.; Treatment given but not documented in detail (just 'hypo treated') → add a structured field naming the treatment and estimated carbohydrate content.; Patients on a low-potassium or fluid-restricted diet given an unsuitable treatment → audit for this as a specific error type.; Under-reporting of hypo episodes overall → cross-check against glucose meter downloads.
- Pearls: Introduction of standard hypo boxes has been shown elsewhere to raise correctly-managed episodes substantially; cite this local evidence when presenting.; Ask the diabetes specialist nurse team to restock and check hypo boxes on a fixed schedule.; Provide a laminated JBDS algorithm card inside each hypo box.; Report the proportion of episodes needing more than the initial treatment, as a marker of undertreatment.

**NNA-421. What proportion of scheduled doses of levodopa-containing Parkinson's medicine for adult inpatients on general wards are given within 30 minutes of the prescribed time?** (under-audited)
- Standard: NHS Specialist Pharmacy Service, Defining time critical medicines (reviewed 2024/2025), citing the Institute for Safe Medication Practices definition: "Those where early or delayed administration of maintenance doses of greater than 30 minutes before or after the scheduled dose may cause harm or result in substantial sub-optimal therapy." https://sps.nhs.uk/articles/defining-time-critical-medicines/
- Pass: The administration time recorded on the electronic medicines administration record is within 30 minutes of the scheduled time for that dose. Target: ≥90%. Sample: 40 consecutive doses across 10 patients over the last 4 weeks
- Change: Flag Parkinson's medicines as 'time-critical' in the e-prescribing system with exact-time (not round-time) dosing and an automatic alert to nursing staff when a dose is 30 minutes late.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-421.csv`
- Pitfalls: Drug rounds are organised by ward routine rather than individual medicine timing → flag time-critical medicines so they are given outside the standard round if needed.; Patient admitted without their usual medicines brought in from home, causing delay while a supply is found → audit whether self-administration or 'own drugs' policies are used.; Nil-by-mouth patients have no alternative route considered → include a dispersible or patch alternative in the ward's Parkinson's toolkit.; eMAR times are rounded to the nearest 15 or 30 minutes by the system, masking small delays → confirm the system records exact times before relying on it.
- Pearls: Identify every inpatient with Parkinson's disease at the daily board round so nursing staff know who needs time-critical dosing.; Provide a 'Parkinson's disease: time-critical medicines' alert sticker for the drug chart or bedside.; Involve the Parkinson's disease specialist nurse in reviewing every admission with the condition.; Audit the reasons for delay as well as the headline rate, to target the fix at the real cause.

**NNA-422. What proportion of scheduled short-acting insulin doses for adult inpatients are given within 30 minutes of the prescribed or meal time?** (new)
- Standard: NHS Specialist Pharmacy Service, Defining time critical medicines (reviewed 2024/2025), citing the Institute for Safe Medication Practices definition: "Those where early or delayed administration of maintenance doses of greater than 30 minutes before or after the scheduled dose may cause harm or result in substantial sub-optimal therapy. [Insulin (short-acting)] ... used in diabetes management." https://sps.nhs.uk/articles/defining-time-critical-medicines/
- Pass: The administration time recorded on the eMAR is within 30 minutes of the scheduled or meal time for that dose. Target: ≥90%. Sample: 40 consecutive doses across 10 patients over the last 4 weeks
- Change: Align meal service and insulin drug round times, and flag insulin as time-critical in e-prescribing with an alert when a dose is 30 minutes late.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-422.csv`
- Pitfalls: Meal trays arrive before the drug round reaches the patient → realign the round or use a 'give with meal' nurse-led protocol.; Patients who miss meals (off the ward for a scan) have insulin given at the wrong time → audit whether these are flagged and rescheduled.; eMAR times are rounded, masking real delays → confirm exact-time recording before relying on the system.; Sliding-scale corrections are confused with meal-time bolus insulin in the data → record dose type clearly.
- Pearls: Involve catering and nursing together in redesigning meal/drug round timing.; Use ward pharmacists to spot-check timing accuracy weekly during the collection period.; Provide point-of-care glucose meters on the drug trolley so checks and dosing happen together.; Share results with the ward as 'doses on time' rather than only 'doses missed', to keep the message positive.

**NNA-423. What proportion of adults having elective surgery are fasted from food for no longer than 8 hours and from clear fluids for no longer than 3 hours before their scheduled procedure?** (new)
- Standard: Association of Anaesthetists of Great Britain and Ireland recommended fasting times, cited in the PIER Network Peri-operative Fasting Policy (October 2020): "The Association of Anaesthetists Great Britain and Ireland (AAGBI) states that recommended fasting times are six hours for food, four hours for breast milk and two hours for clear fluids." https://www.piernetwork.org/uploads/4/7/8/1/47810883/enc_g_pier_fasting_guideline_oct2.pdf
- Pass: Local standard: the recorded time from last food to induction is 8 hours or less and from last clear fluid to induction is 3 hours or less, allowing a practical margin over the AAGBI minimums for list scheduling. Target: ≥80%. Sample: 40 consecutive elective surgical patients over the last 4 weeks
- Change: Replace a fixed 'nil by mouth from midnight' instruction with a staggered sip-til-send protocol and clear fluids allowed up to the pre-operative assessment team's confirmed call time.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-423.csv`
- Pitfalls: List order changes on the day so a fixed fasting instruction becomes inaccurate → use a rolling sip-til-send system tied to the actual call time.; Ward staff default to 'nil by mouth from midnight' out of habit → replace the printed instruction on the pre-op leaflet and drug chart.; Patients over-restrict themselves beyond what is prescribed → give clear written instructions on what and when they may drink.; Definition of 'induction time' varies by data source → use the anaesthetic chart time consistently.
- Pearls: Involve theatre coordinators in agreeing a realistic call-time process before cycle 1.; Use patient information leaflets that state the sip-til-send instructions clearly.; Track cancellations and delays as a balancing measure to show the change has not caused new problems.; Re-audit after a full list cycle (including list re-ordering on the day) to test robustness.

**NNA-424. What proportion of blood component transfusions have a documented bedside positive patient identification check (patient asked to state their name and date of birth, checked against the identity band, prescription and compatibility label) before the unit is started?** (new)
- Standard: British Society for Haematology, Guideline on the administration of blood components (2018, review ongoing): "The Serious Hazards of Transfusion (SHOT) scheme has repeatedly identified that patients are harmed, and some die, as a result of being given the incorrect type of blood. SHOT therefore recommends a structured process with a bedside checklist." https://b-s-h.org.uk/guidelines/guidelines/administration-of-blood-components/
- Pass: The bedside checklist is documented as completed, with the patient (or two staff members if the patient cannot confirm) checking name, date of birth and a unique identifier against the identity band, prescription and unit compatibility label immediately before starting the unit. Target: 100%. Sample: 40 consecutive transfused units over the last 4 weeks
- Change: Introduce an electronic bedside scanning system (or a mandatory paper bedside checklist) that will not release the unit for administration until the identification steps are recorded.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-424.csv`
- Pitfalls: Confused or unconscious patients cannot confirm their own identity → define the two-staff-member check as the alternative in the protocol.; Bedside check rushed when a unit is urgently needed → build the check into the electronic unit-release process so it cannot be bypassed.; Checklist completed on paper but filed separately from the prescription → keep it with the transfusion record.; 100% target may feel unrealistic to staff → frame this explicitly as a zero-tolerance patient-identification safety step, distinct from other, more negotiable targets.
- Pearls: Involve the hospital transfusion practitioner in designing and auditing the checklist.; Use electronic bedside scanning where available, since it makes the check harder to skip.; Report any near-misses found during the audit directly to the transfusion committee, not just the percentage.; Re-audit unannounced, since a scheduled re-audit may prompt a temporary improvement.

**NNA-425. What proportion of blood component units have the blood group and expiry date checked against the compatibility report and prescription immediately before transfusion is started?** (new)
- Standard: British Society for Haematology, Guideline on the administration of blood components (2018, review ongoing): "SHOT therefore recommends a structured process with a bedside checklist; an alert from the Chief Medical Officer 9th November 2017 provides information against which organisations should assess their bedside systems." https://b-s-h.org.uk/guidelines/guidelines/administration-of-blood-components/
- Pass: The unit's blood group, expiry date and unique donation number are documented as checked against the compatibility report and the prescription before the unit is connected. Target: 100%. Sample: 40 consecutive transfused units over the last 4 weeks
- Change: Add a structured 'unit check' section, separate from the patient-identification section, to the bedside transfusion checklist so both checks are recorded distinctly.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-425.csv`
- Pitfalls: Unit check and patient check are recorded as a single tick, hiding which part was actually done → separate them on the form.; Expired units are occasionally still in fridge stock → report any near-misses found to the blood bank immediately.; Staff assume the laboratory has already checked everything → reinforce that the bedside check is an independent final safeguard.; Rushed urgent transfusions skip the documented check → provide a rapid but complete checklist version for emergencies.
- Pearls: Combine with the patient-identification audit as one transfusion safety audit, reported as two separate results.; Use the hospital transfusion practitioner's existing spot-check programme as a data source where one exists.; Report any discrepancies found as a serious incident review trigger, not just an audit finding.; Keep the checklist short so it is actually used under time pressure.

**NNA-426. What proportion of adult inpatients' identity bands contain the correct four identifiers (surname, forename, date of birth and NHS number) with no additions or omissions?** (new)
- Standard: NHS patient identifiers for identity bands standard (ISB 0099), cited in Leicestershire Partnership NHS Trust Positive Patient Identification Policy (October 2023): "All identity bands must be applied as part of the initial admission process and contain the following information, with no additions or omissions: Last name, First name, Date of birth, NHS Number or unique hospital number if NHS Number unknown." https://www.leicspart.nhs.uk/wp-content/uploads/2023/10/Positive-Patient-Identification-Policy-Exp-April-2027.pdf
- Pass: The identity band worn by the patient at the time of the spot-check shows all four required identifiers, correctly spelled/formatted, with no other information added. Target: ≥98%. Sample: 40 inpatients checked across 4 wards on the same day
- Change: Standardise identity band printing through the EPR admission process (auto-populated, printed band) instead of hand-written bands, removing the main source of transcription error.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-426.csv`
- Pitfalls: Hand-written bands have transcription errors → move to printed bands generated from the EPR.; Bands not replaced after a name or NHS number correction on the EPR → add a prompt to reprint the band whenever demographics are amended.; Auditors themselves misread small print → use a standard checklist and, where possible, compare to a second printed source (e.g. wristband label copy).; Sensitive to Hawthorne effect if staff know the audit is happening → do the spot-check without prior ward announcement.
- Pearls: Combine this with the transfusion identification audit so both use the same observation visit.; Involve ward clerks, who often apply bands on admission, in the change process.; Feed back errors found immediately to the ward so they can be corrected on the spot, in addition to the aggregate report.; Repeat the spot-check on different wards and shifts to get a representative picture.

**NNA-427. What proportion of adult inpatients with a documented drug or other allergy are wearing a red allergy identity band?** (new)
- Standard: NHS patient identifiers for identity bands standard (ISB 0099), cited in Leicestershire Partnership NHS Trust Positive Patient Identification Policy (October 2023): "5.2.1 All inpatients should have a white identity band unless they have an identified allergy. 5.2.2 All inpatients with an identified allergy must have either a red identity band with black text." https://www.leicspart.nhs.uk/wp-content/uploads/2023/10/Positive-Patient-Identification-Policy-Exp-April-2027.pdf
- Pass: A patient with a documented allergy on their drug chart or EPR allergy field is wearing a red (not white) identity band at the time of the spot-check. Target: ≥98%. Sample: 40 inpatients with a documented allergy, checked across 4 wards on the same day
- Change: Add an EPR rule that prints a red band automatically, and flags an alert to nursing staff, whenever an allergy is entered on the drug chart or admission assessment.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-427.csv`
- Pitfalls: Allergy identified after the white band is already applied and the band is not changed → add an automatic reminder when a new allergy is documented.; Red bands not stocked on the ward when needed → confirm supply as part of the change.; Allergy status disputed or uncertain (e.g. intolerance vs true allergy) → use the trust's existing allergy documentation policy to decide what counts.; Patients transferred from another ward keep an old band that was never updated → include a band check in the transfer checklist.
- Pearls: Combine this spot-check with the general identity band accuracy audit.; Involve pharmacy in reviewing any mismatches found, since these are medicines safety incidents.; Make sure red bands are as freely available as white ones on every ward.; Report mismatches found as safety learning at ward level, not just an aggregate percentage.

**NNA-428. What proportion of adult inpatients who are unable or unwilling to wear an identity band have a documented alternative means of identification?** (new)
- Standard: Leicestershire Partnership NHS Trust Positive Patient Identification Policy (October 2023), based on the NHS identity band standard: "Patients in inpatient areas should wear identity bands, it is however recognised that patients with acute mental health needs or confusion may not agree to wearing an identity band. In these cases, and where there are documented efforts to explain to patients the purpose in relation to their safety, a patient photograph should be taken with the consent of the patient to provide an alternative means of identification." https://www.leicspart.nhs.uk/wp-content/uploads/2023/10/Positive-Patient-Identification-Policy-Exp-April-2027.pdf
- Pass: For a patient not wearing an identity band, the notes document the reason, the attempt made to explain its purpose, and an agreed alternative (e.g. a consented photograph, or a documented process) is in place. Target: ≥90%. Sample: All patients found without a band during 4 ward spot-checks over 4 weeks (expected around 20-30 cases; extend the period if fewer)
- Change: Add a mandatory 'alternative identification' care plan entry, triggered whenever a nurse records that a patient is not wearing a band, prompting the photograph-with-consent process.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-428.csv`
- Pitfalls: Small numbers, since most patients do wear a band → extend the audit period or pool wards with higher rates of confusion/mental health needs.; Staff avoid raising the issue with the patient again once refused once → make re-attempting the explanation part of the daily care plan review.; Photograph consent process is unfamiliar to staff → provide a simple one-page guide at the nursing station.; Confusion between 'refused' and 'clinically unable' (e.g. skin condition) is not distinguished → record the specific reason, not just 'no band'.
- Pearls: Focus data collection on wards with higher numbers of patients with dementia, delirium or acute mental health needs.; Involve the safeguarding and dementia teams in designing the alternative-identification process.; Review with patients and carers, where possible, whether the alternative process felt respectful.; Re-audit on the same wards after staff turnover to check the process has bedded in.

**NNA-429. What proportion of adult inpatients transferred between wards have their identity band checked against their notes for accuracy at the point of transfer?** (new)
- Standard: Leicestershire Partnership NHS Trust Positive Patient Identification Policy (October 2023), based on the NHS identity band standard: "In the event of a patient being transferred between wards, the identity band should be checked with the patient and/or case notes for accuracy. This may be from ward to ward, ward to department, or between hospitals." https://www.leicspart.nhs.uk/wp-content/uploads/2023/10/Positive-Patient-Identification-Policy-Exp-April-2027.pdf
- Pass: The transfer checklist or handover documentation records that the identity band was checked against the patient and/or case notes at the point of transfer. Target: ≥90%. Sample: 40 consecutive ward-to-ward transfers over the last 4 weeks
- Change: Add an identity band check as a mandatory item on the ward-to-ward transfer/handover checklist, to be signed by the receiving nurse.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-429.csv`
- Pitfalls: Transfer checklists are completed retrospectively rather than at the time → make the identity check the first item, ahead of clinical handover.; Verbal handover replaces the written checklist → require the checklist to travel with the patient's notes.; Bed pressures lead to rushed transfers where the checklist is skipped → audit out-of-hours and high-occupancy periods specifically.; Discrepancies found are not escalated → add a clear 'what to do if a discrepancy is found' step to the checklist.
- Pearls: Use the same transfer checklist already required for other information (e.g. VTE status, allergies) so this is one extra line, not a new form.; Train bed managers and site teams on the importance of this final identity check.; Report any discrepancies found as safety learning, in addition to the completion rate.; Re-audit at a different time of year to check winter bed-pressure periods are not worse.

**NNA-430. What proportion of adult inpatients who have bed rails fitted have an individual written risk assessment completed before the bed rails are used?** (new)
- Standard: Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency, Bed rails: management and safe use (updated 2023): "Chest or neck entrapment in bed rails is listed (number 11) as a 'Never Event' according to the NHS in 2018... Risk assessments should account for any characteristics which might put the bed user at greater risk from use of bed rails." https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/government/uploads/system/uploads/attachment_data/file/1181044/Bed_rails_guidance.pdf
- Pass: A documented, individualised bed rail risk assessment (considering the patient's size, mobility, confusion or agitation, and bed/mattress configuration) is completed and filed before the bed rails are fitted. Target: ≥95%. Sample: 40 inpatients with bed rails in use, identified across 4 wards on the same day
- Change: Make the bed rail risk assessment a mandatory EPR step that must be completed before a 'bed rails in use' order can be entered, using a standard entrapment-risk checklist.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-430.csv`
- Pitfalls: Bed rails put up as a default without individual assessment → make the assessment a prerequisite in the EPR order.; Risk assessment done once on admission and not reviewed when the patient's condition changes → audit whether it is reviewed after any relevant change.; Staff underestimate entrapment risk because they see bed rails as routine → include Never Event learning in ward teaching.; Assessment completed but not accessible to night staff → keep it in a single, easy-to-find EPR location.
- Pearls: Use the MHRA's example adult entrapment risk assessment checklist as the basis for the EPR form.; Involve the moving and handling/tissue viability team in reviewing findings.; Report any Never Event near-misses found during the audit immediately through the incident system.; Repeat the spot-check on wards with higher rates of confusion or frailty.

**NNA-431. What proportion of decisions to use bed rails are documented with the reasoning, and evidence that this was explained to the patient or their family?** (new)
- Standard: Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency, Bed rails: management and safe use (updated 2023): "Every effort should be made to explain to the person being cared for why their bed has or is likely to have bed rails fitted. The potential risks, as identified by their individual risk assessment should also be explained to the person, as appropriate... The decision to use bed rails should be made with the person's consent, wherever possible." https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/government/uploads/system/uploads/attachment_data/file/1181044/Bed_rails_guidance.pdf
- Pass: The notes record the reason bed rails were prescribed, that this was explained to the patient (or their family/representative if the patient lacks capacity), and whether consent was given. Target: ≥90%. Sample: 40 inpatients with bed rails in use, identified across 4 wards on the same day
- Change: Add 'reason explained to patient/family' and 'consent/best interests' as mandatory fields on the bed rail risk assessment form, alongside the risk assessment itself.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-431.csv`
- Pitfalls: Explanation given verbally but not recorded → add a specific field rather than relying on general nursing notes.; Patients who lack capacity are not covered by a best-interests decision → link the field to the trust's Mental Capacity Act documentation.; Family not contactable at the time bed rails are first used → record this and require follow-up documentation once contact is made.; Staff see this as extra paperwork → combine it with the risk assessment form so it is one document, not two.
- Pearls: Combine this audit with the risk-assessment-before-use audit as one bed rails safety audit.; Provide a simple patient/family information leaflet on bed rails to support the conversation.; Involve the mental capacity/best interests lead where patients lack capacity.; Share good-practice examples of clear documentation at ward teaching sessions.

**NNA-432. What proportion of beds with bed rails fitted are checked each shift for gaps or configuration changes that could increase the risk of entrapment?** (new)
- Standard: Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency, Bed rails: management and safe use (updated 2023): "What configuration of bed, mattress and rail system is being used?... Our adverse incident investigations have shown that the physical or clinical condition of bed occupants means that some are at greater risk of entrapment in bed rails." https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/government/uploads/system/uploads/attachment_data/file/1181044/Bed_rails_guidance.pdf
- Pass: A documented shift check confirms the bed, mattress and rail configuration matches what was risk-assessed, with no new gaps, and flags any change for a repeat risk assessment. Target: ≥90%. Sample: 30 patients with bed rails, checked over 3 consecutive shifts each, over 2-4 weeks
- Change: Add a bed rail configuration check to the twice-daily intentional rounding checklist, prompting a repeat risk assessment whenever the bed, mattress or rail is changed.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-432.csv`
- Pitfalls: Mattress replaced (e.g. for pressure relief) without repeating the bed rail check → link mattress ordering to an automatic bed rail re-check prompt.; Checks become a tick-box exercise without real inspection → include a photo-based training aid on what to look for.; Night shift checks are less thorough → include night shifts explicitly in the sample.; Staff unfamiliar with entrapment zones → provide the MHRA entrapment-area diagram at the nursing station.
- Pearls: Combine with other intentional rounding items (pressure area care, hydration) so it is one round.; Use the MHRA entrapment risk-area diagram for staff training.; Involve estates/equipment teams when a mismatched bed and mattress combination is found.; Report any hazards found immediately, not only in the aggregate audit result.

**NNA-433. What proportion of safeguarding concerns identified for adult inpatients with care and support needs have a safeguarding referral made and documented on the day the concern is identified?** (new)
- Standard: Department of Health and Social Care, Care and support statutory guidance (Care Act 2014), paragraph 14.7: "Safeguarding means protecting an adult's right to live in safety, free from abuse and neglect. It is about people and organisations working together to prevent and stop both the risks and experience of abuse or neglect." https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/care-act-statutory-guidance/care-and-support-statutory-guidance
- Pass: A safeguarding concern/referral form is completed and submitted to the local authority safeguarding team on the same calendar day the concern is identified and documented by staff. Target: ≥90%. Sample: 30 consecutive safeguarding concerns identified on adult wards over the last 3-6 months
- Change: Add a same-day safeguarding referral task to the EPR whenever a safeguarding concern is documented, with an automatic reminder to the named nurse or ward manager if the referral has not been submitted by the end of the shift.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-433.csv`
- Pitfalls: Staff are unsure whether a concern meets the referral threshold and delay while seeking advice → provide a same-day advice line staffed by the trust safeguarding team.; Concerns identified out of hours wait until the next working day → confirm an out-of-hours referral route exists and is used.; Small numbers of qualifying concerns on general wards → extend sampling to 6 months or pool several wards.; Referral made verbally to a colleague but not formally submitted → audit only formal referrals recorded in the safeguarding log.
- Pearls: Work with the trust safeguarding adults lead to define what counts as 'identified' versus 'referred'.; Provide a laminated safeguarding referral pathway card on every ward.; Report both the same-day rate and the reasons for any delay found.; Re-audit after staff safeguarding training to see if the change has had an effect.

**NNA-434. What proportion of adult inpatients who receive rapid tranquillisation have their pulse, blood pressure, respiratory rate, temperature, hydration and level of consciousness monitored at least hourly afterwards?** (new)
- Standard: NICE guideline NG10 Violence and aggression: short-term management in mental health, health and community settings, recommendation 1.4.45 (2015): "After rapid tranquillisation, monitor side effects and the service user's pulse, blood pressure, respiratory rate, temperature, level of hydration and level of consciousness at least every hour until there are no further concerns about their physical health status. Monitor every 15 minutes if the BNF maximum dose has been exceeded or the service user..." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng10/chapter/Recommendations
- Pass: All six parameters (pulse, blood pressure, respiratory rate, temperature, hydration status, level of consciousness) are documented at least hourly for the period following rapid tranquillisation until concerns have resolved. Target: ≥90%. Sample: 30 consecutive episodes of rapid tranquillisation on general wards over the last 6-12 months
- Change: Build a dedicated post-rapid-tranquillisation monitoring chart (paper or electronic) that pre-populates the six required parameters and the hourly (or 15-minute) schedule automatically when the drug is recorded as given.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-434.csv`
- Pitfalls: Rapid tranquillisation episodes are uncommon on general wards, giving small numbers → extend the sampling period to 6-12 months across the whole trust.; Standard NEWS2 charts do not capture hydration or consciousness in the way needed → use a dedicated chart rather than the routine observation chart.; Staff are focused on managing the acute behavioural disturbance and monitoring is deprioritised → assign a named member of staff to monitoring at the time the drug is given.; Episodes are not all captured on the incident system → cross-check against pharmacy records of parenteral sedatives given.
- Pearls: Involve the mental health liaison team, who are often called to these episodes on general wards.; Use a pre-printed sticker or EPR order set that starts the monitoring schedule automatically.; Review every episode with a debrief involving the nurse in charge, not only the aggregate percentage.; Track any adverse events (oversedation, respiratory depression) alongside the audit as an outcome measure.

**NNA-435. What proportion of documented episodes of manual restraint on adult wards record that the least restrictive intervention was used and the reasons for the level of restriction chosen?** (under-audited)
- Standard: NICE guideline NG10 Violence and aggression: short-term management in mental health, health and community settings, recommendation 1.1.9 (2015): "Ensure that service users understand that during any restrictive intervention their human rights will be respected and the least restrictive intervention will be used to enable them to exercise their rights... Identify and reduce any barriers to a service user exercising their rights and, if this is not possible, record the reasons in their notes." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng10/chapter/Recommendations
- Pass: The restraint incident record documents that a less restrictive option was considered, and states the reason the level of restriction used was chosen. Target: ≥90%. Sample: 30 consecutive restraint episodes over the last 6-12 months
- Change: Add mandatory fields to the restraint incident form for 'less restrictive options considered' and 'reason for level of restriction used', which must be completed before the form can be closed.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-435.csv`
- Pitfalls: Incident forms focus on what happened rather than why that level of restriction was chosen → add specific fields rather than free text alone.; Staff under time pressure after an incident complete the form minimally → allow the form to be completed in two stages (immediate facts, then reflection within 24 hours).; Small numbers of restraint episodes on general wards → extend the sampling period.; Different staff have different thresholds for what counts as 'least restrictive' → provide training and examples.
- Pearls: Run this alongside the existing post-incident debrief audit so the whole NG10 documentation standard is reviewed together.; Involve service user representatives in reviewing what good documentation looks like.; Use restrictive intervention reduction programme data (already required by NG10) as a source of episodes.; Share themes from the reasons documented, not just the completion rate, to guide training.

**NNA-436. What proportion of adult inpatients have an oral health/mouth care assessment completed within 24 hours of admission?** (new)
- Standard: Health Education England, Mouth Care Matters (2019), cited in a hospital Trust Mouthcare Policy CLP157: "It is suggested by (NHS Health Education Mouth Care Matters 2019) a mouth care assessment should be undertaken on admission or within 24 hours of admission and should be reviewed weekly." https://foi.ghc.nhs.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/a-CLP157-Mouthcare-Policy-V2-issued-21.7.25_Redacted.pdf
- Pass: A mouth care assessment screening tool is completed and documented within 24 hours of admission. Target: ≥90%. Sample: 40 consecutive adult admissions over the last 4 weeks
- Change: Add a mandatory mouth care assessment field to the electronic nursing admission assessment for every adult inpatient.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-436.csv`
- Pitfalls: Mouth care assessment seen as a low priority compared with other admission tasks → make it part of the same mandatory admission bundle as pressure ulcer and falls risk assessment.; Staff lack confidence assessing the mouth without dental training → provide short Mouth Care Matters training and a simple visual guide.; Assessment done but not reviewed weekly as required → track weekly review as a separate, later measure.; Patients with dentures or dysphagia need a modified approach not captured by a simple tool → add a free-text note field for these cases.
- Pearls: Use the trust's existing Mouth Care Matters-based assessment tool rather than creating a new one.; Provide a basic mouth care kit at every bedside so assessment leads straight into action.; Involve speech and language therapy for patients with dysphagia identified through the assessment.; Report results alongside pressure ulcer and falls assessment rates, since all three are part of the same admission bundle.

**NNA-437. What proportion of adult inpatients assessed as needing help with mouth care (amber or red on the mouth care assessment) receive documented mouth care at least twice daily?** (new)
- Standard: Hospital Trust Mouthcare Policy CLP157, applying Health Education England's Mouth Care Matters standard: "Independent (Green), promote good oral mouth health care as a minimum of twice daily; Needs supervision/help to clean teeth (Amber)... Needs mouth care (Red), assist with mouth care." https://foi.ghc.nhs.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/a-CLP157-Mouthcare-Policy-V2-issued-21.7.25_Redacted.pdf
- Pass: For a patient scored amber or red on the mouth care assessment, documented mouth care is recorded at least twice in each 24-hour period. Target: ≥85%. Sample: 30 consecutive amber/red patients, reviewed over 3 days each, over the last 4-8 weeks
- Change: Add mouth care to the twice-daily intentional rounding checklist for every patient scored amber or red, with a signature box for each round.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-437.csv`
- Pitfalls: Mouth care given but not recorded → build recording into the same electronic round as repositioning and hydration.; Staff shortages mean mouth care is deprioritised against other tasks → make it an explicit, named item on the intentional rounding chart rather than assumed.; Patients who are nil by mouth are wrongly assumed not to need mouth care → clarify that NBM patients need mouth care even more, not less.; Reduced consciousness or intubated patients need a different technique not distinguished on a simple chart → add a note field for special techniques used.
- Pearls: Stock basic mouth care kits (sponge sticks, non-foaming toothpaste) on every bed bay.; Train healthcare assistants specifically, since they often deliver most mouth care.; Combine this audit with the mouth care assessment audit to review the full pathway.; Report results by ward, since dependency levels vary a great deal between specialties.

**NNA-438. What proportion of omitted or delayed doses of a medicine flagged as time-critical are documented with a reason on the drug chart or eMAR?** (new)
- Standard: NHS Specialist Pharmacy Service, Defining time critical medicines (reviewed 2024/2025): "Those where early or delayed administration of maintenance doses of greater than 30 minutes before or after the scheduled dose may cause harm or result in substantial sub-optimal therapy." https://sps.nhs.uk/articles/defining-time-critical-medicines/
- Pass: Every omitted or more-than-30-minutes-delayed dose of a medicine on the ward's time-critical medicines list has a coded or documented reason entered on the eMAR. Target: ≥95%. Sample: 40 consecutive omitted or delayed time-critical doses identified from the eMAR over the last 4-8 weeks
- Change: Make the omission/delay reason a mandatory coded field in the eMAR (rather than optional free text) whenever a time-critical medicine is recorded as omitted or given late.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-438.csv`
- Pitfalls: Reason entered as vague free text ('N/A') that does not explain the cause → use a fixed drop-down list of reason categories.; Staff do not know which medicines on the chart are time-critical → flag them visually on the eMAR.; Doses omitted overnight are under-documented due to lower staffing → include night shifts in the sample.; Reason coding varies between wards using paper versus electronic charts → restrict the audit to wards on the same eMAR system for consistency.
- Pearls: Agree the trust's time-critical medicines list with pharmacy before starting data collection.; Use the coded reasons to run a monthly pharmacy-led review of recurring causes.; Pair this audit with the specific Parkinson's and insulin timing audits to build a full picture.; Feed back common reasons (e.g. 'medicine not available') to procurement or ward stock processes.

**NNA-439. What proportion of elective surgical patients who are cancelled or delayed on the day of surgery are offered food or drink within 1 hour of being told they will not have surgery that day?** (new)
- Standard: Association of Anaesthetists of Great Britain and Ireland recommended fasting times, cited in the PIER Network Peri-operative Fasting Policy (October 2020): "Excessive fasting can cause a great deal of stress for children and their carers... Excessive fasting leads to irritability and agitation whilst waiting for surgery." https://www.piernetwork.org/uploads/4/7/8/1/47810883/enc_g_pier_fasting_guideline_oct2.pdf
- Pass: A documented offer of food or drink (or a stated clinical reason why this is not yet possible) is recorded within 1 hour of the patient being informed their operation will not go ahead that day. Target: ≥90%. Sample: 30 consecutive cancelled or significantly delayed elective patients over the last 4-8 weeks
- Change: Add a 'cancelled: may eat and drink now?' step to the theatre coordinator's cancellation process, with a scripted phone call to the ward and a timed nursing task to offer food and drink.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-439.csv`
- Pitfalls: Communication delay between theatres and the ward means the ward is unaware of the cancellation → use a direct phone call, not just an electronic list update.; Patient still due to be rescheduled later the same day so remains fasted appropriately → record this as a valid reason, not a failure.; Cancellations late in the day are under-recorded because staff focus on other tasks → include all times of day in the sample.; No consistent record of when the patient was actually told → agree a single point of documentation (nursing notes) for this time.
- Pearls: Give the theatre coordinator a one-line script to use when phoning the ward.; Track patient-reported experience of cancellation alongside the audit as a balancing measure.; Share cancellation and fasting-related complaints with the theatres team to reinforce the case for change.; Re-audit during a busy winter period to test the process under pressure.

**NNA-440. What proportion of restrictive intervention decisions for patients who lack capacity involve documented consultation with a carer or family member, in line with the Mental Capacity Act 2005?** (new)
- Standard: NICE guideline NG10 Violence and aggression: short-term management in mental health, health and community settings, recommendation 1.1.10 (2015): "Ensure that carers are involved in decision-making whenever possible, if the service user agrees, and that carers are involved in decision-making for all service users who lack mental capacity, in accordance with the Mental Capacity Act 2005." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng10/chapter/Recommendations
- Pass: For a patient who lacks capacity at the time of a restrictive intervention decision, the notes document that a carer or family member was consulted, or record why this was not possible. Target: ≥85%. Sample: 30 consecutive qualifying restrictive intervention episodes over the last 6-12 months
- Change: Add a mandatory 'carer/family consulted (or reason why not)' field to the restrictive intervention incident form, linked to the Mental Capacity Act assessment section.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-440.csv`
- Pitfalls: Urgent situations mean consultation happens after, not before, the intervention → accept and record retrospective consultation as long as it is documented promptly.; No carer or family member is contactable → record this explicitly rather than leaving the field blank.; Capacity assessment itself is not documented, making the population hard to define → run this audit alongside a capacity-documentation check.; Staff conflate 'informing' a family member after the event with 'involving' them in the decision → clarify the distinction in training.
- Pearls: Link this audit to the trust's existing Mental Capacity Act training programme.; Involve the safeguarding and mental capacity leads in reviewing findings.; Provide a quick-reference card on when and how to contact carers out of hours.; Report findings alongside the least-restrictive-intervention audit for a fuller picture of NG10 compliance.

**NNA-441. What proportion of adult inpatients on a variable-rate intravenous insulin infusion have their capillary blood glucose measured at least hourly?** (new)
- Standard: Joint British Diabetes Societies for Inpatient Care, JBDS 01: The Hospital Management of Hypoglycaemia in Adults with Diabetes Mellitus (revised January 2023): "If the person was on IV insulin, continue to check blood glucose every 15 minutes until..." https://abcd.care/sites/default/files/site_uploads/JBDS_Guidelines_Current/JBDS_01_Hypo_Guideline_with_QR_code_January_2023.pdf
- Pass: Local standard, applying the JBDS principle of frequent glucose monitoring during IV insulin therapy: capillary blood glucose is documented at least once every hour while the variable-rate insulin infusion is running. Target: ≥90%. Sample: 30 consecutive patients on a variable-rate insulin infusion, reviewed over their first 12 hours on the infusion, over the last 3 months
- Change: Set the EPR insulin infusion order to automatically schedule and prompt hourly glucose-check tasks for the duration of the infusion.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-441.csv`
- Pitfalls: Glucose checks recorded on a separate paper chart not linked to the EPR infusion order → move monitoring into the same electronic system as the infusion.; Checks clustered together after a gap rather than genuinely hourly → measure the longest gap, not just the total number of checks.; Ward staffing pressure causes delays overnight → include night hours specifically in the sample.; Infusion stopped and restarted multiple times, complicating the 12-hour window → record only the first continuous run.
- Pearls: Use networked glucose meters that time-stamp readings automatically to reduce data collection effort.; Involve the diabetes inpatient specialist nurse team in reviewing outlying cases.; Track hypoglycaemia and severe hyperglycaemia rates on infusions as an outcome measure alongside monitoring frequency.; Re-audit on wards less familiar with insulin infusions, such as surgical wards, separately from specialist diabetes wards.

## General practice and community care

**NNA-442. What proportion of adults newly registering with a GP practice have their MMR vaccination history checked and, if unvaccinated or partially vaccinated, are offered catch-up MMR?** (new)
- Standard: UKHSA Green Book, Measles chapter (updated 2 April 2026): "MMR vaccine can be given to individuals of any age and should be offered opportunistically and promoted to unvaccinated or partially vaccinated younger adults. New GP registration, and entry into college, university or other higher education institutions, prison or military service also provides an opportunity to check an individual's immunisation history. Those who have not received MMR should be offered appropriate MMR immunisation." https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/measles-the-green-book-chapter
- Pass: The new patient health check or registration template records MMR status (two doses, one dose, none or unknown) and, where the patient has had fewer than two documented doses, an offer of catch-up MMR is recorded within 8 weeks of registration.. Target: ≥90%. Sample: 40 consecutive new adult registrations over the last 3 months, from the practice registration list.
- Change: Add a mandatory 'MMR history: 0/1/2/unknown' field to the new patient health check template in the EPR, with an automatic task to the practice nurse to offer catch-up MMR whenever fewer than 2 doses are recorded.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-442.csv`
- Pitfalls: Immunisation history from other countries is often unavailable → record as 'unknown after checking' rather than assuming fully vaccinated, and offer catch-up unless clear written evidence of 2 doses exists.; Reception staff may not prompt the MMR question at registration → build it into the mandatory new-patient questionnaire, not a free-text box.; Small numbers of eligible unvaccinated adults in some practices → extend the sampling window to 6 months if fewer than 40 new registrations are found.; Staff may worry about vaccine hesitancy conversations taking appointment time → agree a short scripted offer and a nurse-led catch-up clinic slot before cycle 1.; Gains fade once the new-patient template reverts to a free-text field after a system upgrade → re-check the template build after any EPR update.
- Pearls: Recruit the practice nurse who runs new-patient checks as the change champion before cycle 1.; Agree the catch-up MMR offer script and consent process with the whole team before starting data collection.; Use the same registration list report each cycle so the sample is reproducible.; Link the audit to the practice's outbreak-preparedness discussion to keep it a clinical priority after the lead rotates.

**NNA-443. What proportion of severely immunosuppressed adults under 80 who are eligible for shingles vaccination have been offered Shingrix in the last 12 months?** (new)
- Standard: UKHSA Green Book, Shingles (herpes zoster) chapter (12 August 2025): "From September 2025, Shingrix® should be offered to all severely immunosuppressed individuals aged 18 years and over (with no upper age limit). Previously this was offered to immunosuppressed individuals aged 70 to 79 years and then those aged 50 years and over. Eligible individuals should be offered two doses of Shingrix®." https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/shingles-herpes-zoster-the-green-book-chapter-28a
- Pass: The patient's GP record shows a documented offer of Shingrix in the last 12 months (accepted, declined with reason, or already fully vaccinated with 2 doses).. Target: ≥85%. Sample: All patients on the immunosuppression register aged under 80, or 40 consecutive patients if the register is larger, checked over the last 3 months.
- Change: Add a rule-based search that cross-references the immunosuppression/DMARD register against the shingles vaccination record, run monthly by a named administrator, generating a recall letter for anyone not yet offered Shingrix.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-443.csv`
- Pitfalls: Age-based call/recall systems will not flag immunosuppressed patients under 50 or 60 → build a separate immunosuppression-register search rather than relying on the age search.; Defining 'severely immunosuppressed' consistently is hard → agree the practice's operational definition (drug list and doses) with a GP before starting.; Small numbers per practice → consider a PCN-level audit pooling several practices.; Clinicians may be unsure about timing relative to chemotherapy cycles → agree a simple rule (for example, avoid the week of chemotherapy) with a specialist in advance.; The immunosuppression register itself may be incomplete → cross-check against recent hospital letters and repeat prescriptions for biologics or high-dose steroids.
- Pearls: Ask the practice pharmacist to build and run the register cross-reference; they already handle DMARD/biologic searches.; Agree with hospital specialists a simple safe-timing rule for vaccination around treatment before cycle 1.; Use the same immunosuppression register definition at re-audit so the sample is comparable.; Keep the monthly search running after the audit team rotates by assigning it a named permanent owner, not an individual GP.

**NNA-444. What proportion of adults newly added to a pneumococcal at-risk clinical group have been offered pneumococcal vaccination within 3 months of the risk factor being coded?** (new)
- Standard: UKHSA Green Book, Pneumococcal chapter (29 July 2026): "Adults aged 65 years and over, and clinical risk groups aged 2 years or over: a single dose of 0.5ml of PPV23 or PCV20 ... Antibody levels are likely to decline rapidly in individuals with asplenia, splenic dysfunction (including sickle cell disease) or chronic kidney disease ... and, therefore, re-immunisation with PPV23 or PCV20 is recommended every five years in these groups." https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/pneumococcal-the-green-book-chapter-25
- Pass: Pneumococcal vaccine is offered (given, declined with reason, or already up to date) within 3 months of the date the qualifying clinical risk group code (for example, chronic respiratory disease, chronic heart disease, diabetes on medication, chronic kidney disease, chronic liver disease, or immunosuppression) is first entered in the record.. Target: ≥85%. Sample: 40 consecutive adults with a new qualifying risk-group code over the last 6 months.
- Change: Build an EPR alert that fires when a qualifying risk-group code is entered, creating a task for the practice nurse to check and offer pneumococcal vaccination at the same or next contact.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-444.csv`
- Pitfalls: Risk-group coding is often incomplete or inconsistent between clinicians → agree a fixed code list with the coding lead before starting.; Diagnoses made in secondary care may not be coded in primary care promptly → include a check of recent discharge summaries and clinic letters in the search.; Patients may decline vaccination → count a documented, informed decline as meeting the standard.; The 3-month window may be too tight for patients seen infrequently → confirm the window with the team before cycle 1 rather than changing it after seeing the results.; Alert fatigue if too many pop-ups are added to the EPR → restrict the new alert to the specific risk-group codes being audited.
- Pearls: Ask the practice's data quality lead to build the risk-group code search; it can be reused for other opportunistic vaccination audits.; Agree with the nursing team who owns the task list generated by the alert before go-live.; Use the same code list at re-audit to keep the sample comparable.; Fold the alert into the standard new-diagnosis workflow so it survives staff turnover.

**NNA-445. What proportion of adults in a pneumococcal high-risk group (asplenia, splenic dysfunction or chronic kidney disease) who are due 5-yearly revaccination receive it within 3 months of the due date?** (new)
- Standard: UKHSA Green Book, Pneumococcal chapter (29 July 2026): "Antibody levels are likely to decline rapidly in individuals with asplenia, splenic dysfunction (including sickle cell disease) or chronic kidney disease ... and, therefore, re-immunisation with PPV23 or PCV20 is recommended every five years in these groups." https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/pneumococcal-the-green-book-chapter-25
- Pass: Revaccination is given, or a documented offer and decline is recorded, within 3 months of the 5-year due date calculated from the last dose.. Target: ≥85%. Sample: All eligible patients identified by a practice search, or 40 consecutive patients if the register is larger.
- Change: Add a 5-year pneumococcal revaccination recall to the practice's existing asplenia/CKD register searches, run quarterly, generating an invitation letter automatically.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-445.csv`
- Pitfalls: Immunisation records may show the vaccine name but not clearly flag it as needing a 5-year recall → use a dedicated recall date field rather than relying on staff remembering the rule.; Patients may have moved practices since their first dose, losing the vaccination date → request records from PCSE/previous practice where the date is missing.; Small numbers at individual practice level → combine data across a PCN if needed to reach 30-40 cases.; Confusing PPV23 with the routine over-65 dose → clarify in the template that this audit is only about the 5-yearly at-risk revaccination.; Recall lists not reviewed once built → assign a named administrator to run and act on the quarterly search.
- Pearls: Ask the practice's long-term conditions nurse to lead, since they already run the asplenia/CKD annual review.; Agree the exact due-date calculation (last dose + 5 years) with the whole team before cycle 1.; Use the same register definitions at re-audit for a fair comparison.; Hand the quarterly search to the practice's routine search rota so it continues after the lead moves on.

**NNA-446. What proportion of adult smokers identified in general practice consultations are told about the range of stop-smoking support available and referred if they wish to quit?** (new)
- Standard: NICE NG209 Tobacco: preventing uptake, promoting quitting and treating dependence, rec 1.12.1 (2021, amended 2025): "Tell people who smoke that a range of interventions is available to help them stop smoking. Explain how to access them and refer people to stop-smoking support if appropriate." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng209/chapter/Promoting-quitting
- Pass: The consultation record shows smoking status was checked, the patient (if a current smoker) was told about the range of stop-smoking options, and, if the patient expressed interest, a referral to stop-smoking support (in-house, pharmacy or specialist service) was made or offered.. Target: ≥80%. Sample: 40 consecutive current-smoker consultations over the last 4 weeks, from a search of coded smoking status.
- Change: Add a one-click 'discussed stop-smoking support / referred' template item to the consultation screen that pops up whenever the smoking status is 'current smoker', linked directly to the local stop-smoking service referral form.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-446.csv`
- Pitfalls: Smoking status may be out of date → include a rule to re-check status if it has not been updated in 12 months.; Staff may feel repeated advice annoys patients → agree brief, non-judgemental wording in advance, as NICE recommends.; Recording bias: 'discussed' may be ticked without a genuine conversation → spot-check a sample of consultation free text alongside the coded box.; Referral pathways to external stop-smoking services vary by area and may be confusing → print the local referral route on the consultation template before cycle 1.; Improvement may fade once the prompt becomes routine and is dismissed automatically → review click-through rates at re-audit, not just referral numbers.
- Pearls: Recruit the practice's health promotion or long-term conditions lead to champion the template change.; Agree the referral pathway and paperwork with the local stop-smoking service before cycle 1.; Keep the same coded smoking-status search for both cycles so results are comparable.; Report referral numbers back to reception and nursing staff regularly to sustain motivation after the lead moves on.

**NNA-447. What proportion of adults who screen positive for hazardous or harmful drinking on AUDIT/AUDIT-C in general practice receive a structured brief alcohol intervention at the same or next contact?** (new)
- Standard: NICE PH24 Alcohol-use disorders: prevention, Recommendation 10: brief advice for adults (2010): "Offer a session of structured brief advice on alcohol. If this cannot be offered immediately, offer an appointment as soon as possible thereafter. Use a recognised, evidence-based resource that is based on FRAMES principles (feedback, responsibility, advice, menu, empathy, self-efficacy). It should take 5–15 minutes." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ph24/chapter/Recommendations
- Pass: A structured brief alcohol intervention (using a FRAMES-based resource, taking 5-15 minutes) is delivered at the same appointment, or an appointment for one is offered within 2 weeks, for every patient scoring in the hazardous or harmful range on AUDIT or AUDIT-C.. Target: ≥80%. Sample: 40 consecutive patients with a new hazardous/harmful AUDIT or AUDIT-C score over the last 3 months.
- Change: Add a mandatory 'brief intervention delivered / appointment offered' field to the AUDIT/AUDIT-C template, which cannot be closed until completed, and give staff a standard FRAMES-based script card.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-447.csv`
- Pitfalls: Screening and brief intervention may both be ticked as done without a genuine 5-15 minute conversation → spot-check free-text notes against the coded box.; Appointment time pressure may push staff to skip the intervention → build a 10-minute brief-intervention slot into nurse or HCA clinics.; Patients scoring in the possible-dependence range need a different pathway (full assessment, not brief intervention) → exclude them from this audit and route separately.; Staff training in FRAMES-based brief advice varies → agree and circulate one resource before cycle 1.; Improvement may fade if the template field becomes a routine tick-box → review free-text quality at re-audit.
- Pearls: Recruit a practice nurse or HCA trained in alcohol brief intervention to champion the change.; Agree the FRAMES-based resource and script with the whole team before starting data collection.; Use the same AUDIT/AUDIT-C threshold definitions at re-audit for a fair comparison.; Keep the mandatory template field live after the audit team rotates by building it into new-starter induction.

**NNA-448. What proportion of women reaching the 20-week screening scan in pregnancy have been offered pertussis vaccination, and what proportion have received it before 32 weeks?** (new)
- Standard: UKHSA Green Book, Pertussis chapter (19 December 2025): "Pregnant women should be offered a single 0.5 ml dose of pertussis containing vaccine in every pregnancy. Women should normally receive pertussis vaccine around the time of the mid-pregnancy scan (usually 20 weeks) but can receive it from 16 weeks gestation. To maximise the likelihood that the baby will be protected from birth, the vaccine should be given before 32 weeks." https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/pertussis-the-green-book-chapter-24
- Pass: Pertussis vaccination is offered at or before the 20-week scan appointment and, where accepted, is given before 32 weeks of gestation.. Target: ≥90% offered by 20 weeks; ≥85% vaccinated before 32 weeks. Sample: 40 consecutive women reaching 20 weeks over the last 3 months, from the practice maternity register.
- Change: Add an automatic 'pertussis vaccine due' task to the GP maternity template at the point the 16-week booking bloods are recorded, with a reminder if not given by the time the 20-week scan result is filed.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-448.csv`
- Pitfalls: Vaccination may be delivered by the maternity unit rather than the GP practice, so records can be incomplete in the GP system → cross-check with the hand-held maternity notes or shared care record.; Some women decline vaccination → record a documented, informed decline as distinct from a missed offer.; Late bookers may reach 20 weeks with little time before 32 weeks → flag these women for an earlier offer at booking.; Coding of pregnancy stage may be inconsistent → agree a standard gestation-recording method before starting.; Improvement may not persist if midwifery and GP records are not integrated → confirm information-sharing arrangements with the maternity unit before cycle 1.
- Pearls: Recruit the practice's maternity liaison midwife or lead GP to champion the reminder task.; Agree with the local maternity unit how vaccination given there will be recorded back in the GP system.; Use the same maternity register extraction method at re-audit.; Keep the reminder task linked to the booking bloods step so it continues automatically after the audit lead moves on.

**NNA-449. What proportion of patients on the practice's non-responder list for cervical screening have a documented follow-up action recorded within 8 weeks of appearing on the list?** (new)
- Standard: NHS Cervical Screening: guidance for call and recall administration best practice, section 10 (updated 2024): "Individuals join the non-responder list (NRL) if they have been sent an invitation and a reminder but have not attended for a test within 26 weeks of their NTDD (or 32 weeks of invite). GP practices will be prompted to check their NRL on CSMS." https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/cervical-screening-call-and-recall-administration-best-practice/cervical-screening-call-and-recall
- Pass: Within 8 weeks of a patient appearing on the practice's cervical screening non-responder list, the record shows a documented follow-up action: a further invitation, a phone call, a discussion opportunistically flagged for the next appointment, or a recorded reason for ceasing recall.. Target: ≥90%. Sample: 40 consecutive patients added to the non-responder list over the last 3 months, or all if fewer.
- Change: Assign a named administrator to review the CSMS non-responder list monthly and action every entry within 2 weeks, using an agreed local script for calls and opportunistic flags.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-449.csv`
- Pitfalls: The non-responder list may not be checked regularly if no one owns the task → name a specific administrator and add it to their job plan before cycle 1.; Opportunistic flags may be added but never actioned at the next visit → audit whether the flag led to a discussion, not just whether it was added.; Patients who have valid reasons for non-attendance (for example, no cervix, pregnancy) should be excluded or ceased, not repeatedly chased → build a clear ceasing pathway.; Data protection and consent must be respected for phone calls → confirm the practice's telephone contact policy before starting.; Improvement may fade if the CSMS list is not checked after the administrator changes role → document the process in a standard operating procedure.
- Pearls: Recruit the practice's screening administrator as the audit lead, since they already access CSMS.; Agree a short call script and letter template addressing common barriers (fear, embarrassment, cultural sensitivity) before cycle 1.; Use the same CSMS extraction method at re-audit for a fair comparison.; Write the monthly review into a standard operating procedure so it survives staff changes.

**NNA-450. What proportion of patients eligible for an NHS Health Check who do not attend their first invited appointment are re-invited using a different contact method within 12 weeks?** (new)
- Standard: NHS Health Check generic service specification for general practice (NHS Health Check programme, Public Health England template): "The check is offered once every five years. The Department of Health expects 20% of the eligible population to be invited each year over the 5 year rolling programme with an uptake moving from an initial 50% towards 75%... The practice will ensure that the most appropriate mix of invitation methods are used to encourage uptake of the programme... All attempts to contact patients will be recorded using the agreed local template. DNAs should be managed in line with the practice's own local DNA policy." https://www.healthcheck.nhs.uk/seecmsfile/?id=718
- Pass: A patient who does not attend their first invited NHS Health Check appointment is re-invited using a different contact method (for example, phone call or text after a letter) within 12 weeks, with the attempt recorded on the practice's invitation log.. Target: ≥85%. Sample: 40 consecutive DNAs to a first NHS Health Check invitation over the last 6 months.
- Change: Build a 12-week DNA recall rule into the NHS Health Check invitation system that automatically triggers a second invitation by a different method (text after a letter, or a phone call after a text).
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-450.csv`
- Pitfalls: DNA management is often left to individual staff discretion → write a single agreed local DNA policy before cycle 1.; Contact details may be out of date, especially for less engaged groups → verify phone numbers at the point of first invitation.; Practices may deprioritise Health Checks against same-day clinical demand → protect specific appointment slots for the programme.; Equity: some groups (deprived, hard-to-reach) DNA more often and need tailored, not just repeated, invitations → review DNA rates by deprivation decile if data allow.; Improvement may fade once the automatic rule is switched off after a system change → check the rule is still active at re-audit.
- Pearls: Recruit the healthcare assistant or nurse who runs the Health Check clinic to lead the audit.; Agree the second-contact method and script with reception before cycle 1.; Use the same invitation log extraction method at re-audit for a fair comparison.; Report DNA and re-invitation rates to the practice manager regularly to keep the recall rule prioritised after the lead rotates.

**NNA-451. What proportion of people entering prison have a first-stage health assessment completed, before allocation to a cell, that documents any prescribed medicines and immediate health and safety issues?** (new)
- Standard: NICE NG57 Physical health of people in prison, rec 1.1.1 (2016): "At first reception into prison, a healthcare professional (or trained healthcare assistant under the supervision of a registered nurse) should carry out a health assessment for every person. Do this before the person is allocated to their cell. As part of the assessment, identify: any issues that may affect the person's immediate health and safety before the second-stage health assessment; priority health needs to be addressed at the next clinical opportunity." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng57/chapter/Recommendations
- Pass: The first-stage health assessment (Table 1 of NG57) is completed and documented before the person is recorded as allocated to a cell, including the prescribed-medicines question and identification of any immediate health and safety issues.. Target: ≥95%. Sample: 40 consecutive new receptions over the last 4 weeks, from the reception log.
- Change: Make cell allocation on the prison IT system dependent on the first-stage health assessment record being saved first, so custodial staff cannot allocate a cell before healthcare confirms the assessment is complete.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-451.csv`
- Pitfalls: Late-night or high-volume receptions create time pressure that can push assessment after cell allocation → agree an escalation process for surge nights before cycle 1.; Custody and healthcare IT systems may not talk to each other, making the sequencing hard to verify → use manual timestamp checks if systems are not linked.; Staff may complete the assessment but backdate or forget to timestamp it → audit against the reception log time, not just presence of a record.; Reduced staffing at weekends and bank holidays → review results by day of week to check for a pattern.; The IT dependency change needs governor and healthcare provider sign-off together → secure both before cycle 1, not after.
- Pearls: Recruit the reception nurse lead and the prison's head of residence together, since this crosses healthcare and custodial systems.; Agree the IT change with both the healthcare records supplier and the prison establishment before cycle 1.; Use the same reception log extraction at re-audit for a fair comparison.; Report results at the joint health and justice partnership board so the change survives staff and contract rotation.

**NNA-452. What proportion of people in prison have a second-stage health assessment completed within 7 days of their first-stage assessment?** (new)
- Standard: NICE NG57 Physical health of people in prison, rec 1.1.13 (2016): "A healthcare professional (for example, a registered general nurse) should carry out a second-stage health assessment for every person in prison. Do this within 7 days of the first-stage health assessment." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng57/chapter/Recommendations
- Pass: The second-stage health assessment is completed and documented within 7 days (168 hours) of the recorded date and time of the first-stage assessment.. Target: ≥90%. Sample: 40 consecutive receptions with a completed first-stage assessment over the last 6 weeks.
- Change: Add an automatic 'second-stage assessment due' task to the prison health record, created on completion of the first-stage assessment with a 7-day countdown visible on the nursing team's daily worklist.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-452.csv`
- Pitfalls: Staff shortages on the nursing team can push second-stage assessments beyond 7 days → review staffing rotas alongside the audit results.; People released or transferred within 7 days will not have a completed second-stage assessment for a valid reason → exclude them rather than counting as a failure.; IT worklists may not be checked if not part of the daily routine → build the check into the nursing handover, not a separate report.; Assessment quality may drop if teams rush to hit the 7-day target → spot-check a sample of second-stage assessments for completeness alongside timeliness.; Improvement may fade if the worklist task is not maintained after an IT upgrade → confirm it is still functioning at re-audit.
- Pearls: Recruit the prison's senior nurse for reception healthcare as the audit lead.; Agree the worklist design with the nursing team before cycle 1 so it fits their existing handover process.; Use the same reception log extraction method at re-audit.; Review the worklist task list at the weekly clinical governance meeting so it stays visible after the audit team changes.

**NNA-453. What proportion of people entering prison who were taking prescribed medicines in the community have their next dose confirmed as given, or a prescriber referral made, before the second-stage health assessment?** (new)
- Standard: NICE NG57 Physical health of people in prison, recs 1.1.4 (table 1, item 2) and 1.7.10 (2016): "[Prescribed medicines] Yes: document any current medicines being taken and generate a medicine chart. Refer the person to the prescriber for appropriate medicines to be prescribed, to ensure continuity of medicines. If medicines are being taken, ensure that the next dose has been provided... Let the person know that medicines reconciliation will take place before the second-stage health assessment. [1.7.10] Ensure the person can keep taking their medicines after coming into prison." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng57/chapter/Recommendations
- Pass: For a person who reports taking prescribed medicines at first-stage assessment, the record shows either the next dose was given/provided, or a same-day referral to the prescriber was made, and full medicines reconciliation is completed before or at the second-stage assessment.. Target: ≥95%. Sample: 40 consecutive receptions reporting prescribed medicines over the last 4 weeks.
- Change: Build a same-day electronic referral from the reception nurse's medicines question directly to the prison pharmacist/prescriber worklist, with a flag that clears only once the next dose is confirmed given.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-453.csv`
- Pitfalls: Community medication lists brought in by the person may be incomplete or unverifiable → agree a process for contacting the community pharmacy or GP the same day.; Critical medicines (for example, anticonvulsants, insulin, opioid substitution therapy) need faster action than routine ones → prioritise these using the NG57 table 2 critical medicines list.; Reception nights with high volume may overwhelm the pharmacist worklist → agree an escalation and cover plan before cycle 1.; Paper-based medicine charts can be lost between reception and the wing → track the chart alongside the person, not as a separate document.; Improvement may fade if the electronic referral is bypassed during IT downtime → have a clear paper backup process and check it is used correctly at re-audit.
- Pearls: Recruit the prison pharmacist and reception nurse lead jointly, since this spans both roles.; Agree escalation routes for out-of-hours prescribing before starting data collection.; Use the same critical-medicines definition (NG57 table 2) at re-audit.; Report near misses as well as full audit results to keep the pathway prioritised after the lead rotates.

**NNA-454. What proportion of people in prison who were on community opioid substitution treatment have their opioid substitution medicine continued, at a confirmed dose, within 24 hours of reception?** (new)
- Standard: NICE NG57 Physical health of people in prison, recs 1.1.4 (table 1, item 14) and 1.7.10-1.7.11 (2016): "[Alcohol and substance misuse] Has the person used street drugs in the last month?... heroin, methadone... Yes: refer the person to substance misuse services if there are concerns about their immediate clinical management and they need immediate support... [1.7.10] Ensure the person can keep taking their medicines after coming into prison. [1.7.11] Give critical medicines in a timely way to prevent harm from missed or delayed doses [including] drugs used to treat substance misuse." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng57/chapter/Recommendations
- Pass: For a person confirmed to be on community methadone or buprenorphine, the substance misuse team confirms the dose and last dispensing with the community pharmacy/prescriber, and a dose is prescribed and given within 24 hours of reception.. Target: ≥90%. Sample: 40 consecutive receptions reporting current OST over the last 6 weeks, or all if fewer.
- Change: Add a same-day electronic confirmation pathway between the prison substance misuse team and community pharmacies (or the national controlled drug database where available), with a target of confirming dose and pharmacy within 4 hours of reception.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-454.csv`
- Pitfalls: Community pharmacies or prescribers may be unreachable out of hours or at weekends → agree an escalation and interim-dose protocol with clinical leadership before cycle 1.; Self-reported doses may be inaccurate or exaggerated → always attempt independent confirmation before prescribing the full dose.; Reception at night or on Fridays increases delay risk → review results by day/time of reception.; Prescribers may be reluctant to prescribe without full confirmation, causing safe but slow practice → agree a documented interim bridging protocol for uncertain cases.; Improvement may fade if the confirmation pathway relies on one enthusiastic clinician → build it into the substance misuse team's standard operating procedure.
- Pearls: Recruit the prison substance misuse lead clinician and the reception nurse team together.; Agree the interim bridging protocol and escalation contacts with the substance misuse service before cycle 1.; Use the same OST-reporting definition at re-audit.; Report near-miss delays as well as completed audits at the substance misuse governance meeting to sustain the pathway after staff turnover.

**NNA-455. What proportion of people entering prison are offered confidential testing for hepatitis B and hepatitis C, and what proportion of those tested receive their result regardless of location?** (new)
- Standard: NICE NG57 Physical health of people in prison, recs 1.1.23 (2016), adapted from the NICE guideline on hepatitis B and C testing: "Prison healthcare services (working with the NHS lead for hepatitis) should ensure that: all people are offered a hepatitis B vaccination when entering prison... all people are offered access to confidential testing for hepatitis B and C when entering prison and during their detention; people who test for hepatitis B or C receive the results of the test, regardless of their location, when they become available." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng57/chapter/Recommendations
- Pass: The record shows hepatitis B and C testing was offered at reception, and, where the person accepted and was tested, the result was documented as communicated to the person regardless of their current location (including segregation or transfer).. Target: ≥90% offered; ≥95% of those tested given their result. Sample: 40 consecutive new receptions over the last 4 weeks.
- Change: Add hepatitis B/C testing as a default opt-out item on the first-stage reception assessment template, with an electronic result-tracking flag that stays open (and is checked at every wing move or segregation transfer) until the result is confirmed given to the patient.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-455.csv`
