- Pitfalls: People may be transferred or released before results are back → build a handover process that follows the result, not just the person's location on the day of testing.; Opt-out testing still requires informed consent and cultural sensitivity → agree a standard explanation script before cycle 1.; Segregation or healthcare in-patient status can make results harder to deliver in person → include a specific check for these locations in the tracking flag.; Laboratory turnaround delays are outside the practice's control → report delays separately from delivery failures.; Improvement may fade if the electronic flag is closed prematurely → spot-check a sample of 'result given' entries against actual documented conversations.
- Pearls: Recruit the prison's blood-borne virus lead nurse and NHS hepatitis lead jointly.; Agree the opt-out script and consent process with the whole reception team before cycle 1.; Use the same reception log extraction method at re-audit.; Report testing and result-delivery rates to the health and justice partnership board so the pathway survives contract and staff changes.

**NNA-456. What proportion of people entering prison are offered an HIV test at reception?** (new)
- Standard: NICE NG57 Physical health of people in prison, rec 1.1.24 (2016), adapted from the NICE guideline on HIV testing: "Offer all people HIV testing when entering prison." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng57/chapter/Recommendations
- Pass: The reception health record documents that an HIV test was offered, with the outcome recorded (accepted and tested, declined, or already known positive/negative within 3 months).. Target: ≥90%. Sample: 40 consecutive new receptions over the last 4 weeks.
- Change: Combine the HIV test offer with the hepatitis B/C offer as a single mandatory blood-borne virus testing block on the first-stage reception template, so none of the three can be skipped independently.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-456.csv`
- Pitfalls: Staff may assume HIV testing is only needed for people reporting risk factors, contrary to the opt-out approach recommended → make it a default with reasoned opt-out, not opt-in.; Stigma concerns may make some staff hesitant to raise the offer routinely → provide brief training and a standard script before cycle 1.; Reception time pressure can push non-mandatory items to be skipped → make the combined BBV block a required field before the assessment can be saved.; Repeat testing of people known to be already diagnosed wastes capacity → exclude them clearly in the template.; Improvement may fade if the mandatory field is later made optional in an IT update → confirm the field remains mandatory at re-audit.
- Pearls: Recruit the prison's blood-borne virus lead nurse as the audit lead, combining this with the hepatitis B/C audit for efficiency.; Agree a brief non-stigmatising offer script with the whole reception team before cycle 1.; Use the same reception log extraction method at re-audit.; Report the combined BBV testing rate at the health and justice partnership board to keep it prioritised after staff turnover.

**NNA-457. What proportion of people in prison, or at prisons receiving from high-incidence areas, who are under 65 and in regular contact with substance misuse services are offered an interferon-gamma release assay for TB, combined with hepatitis B/C and HIV testing?** (new)
- Standard: NICE NG33 Tuberculosis, recs 1.2.3.5 and 1.2.3.6 (2012, amended 2016): "In high incidence areas (and at prisons that receive prisoners from high incidence areas), prison health services should offer an interferon-gamma release assay for TB to inmates younger than 65 years who are in regular contact with substance misuse services or other support services... Substance misuse services and prison health services should incorporate interferon-gamma release assay testing with screening for hepatitis B and C, and HIV testing." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng33/chapter/Recommendations
- Pass: For a person under 65 in regular contact with prison substance misuse services (at an establishment receiving prisoners from high-incidence areas), the record shows an interferon-gamma release assay for TB was offered at the same time as hepatitis B/C and HIV testing.. Target: ≥85%. Sample: 40 consecutive substance misuse service attendees under 65 over the last 3 months, or all if fewer.
- Change: Add a single combined 'blood-borne virus and TB testing' order set to the substance misuse service's clinical template so IGRA, hepatitis B/C and HIV testing are requested together by default.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-457.csv`
- Pitfalls: TB screening and BBV testing are often commissioned and delivered by separate teams → agree a single combined pathway and blood-draw process before cycle 1.; Establishing whether a prison 'receives from high incidence areas' needs local public health input → confirm this with the local TB team before starting.; Support for continuing treatment after release is a precondition in the NICE recommendation → confirm community follow-up arrangements are in place before offering testing.; Substance misuse service attendance is often episodic → use the first contact in the audit period as the index event, not every subsequent contact.; Improvement may fade if the combined order set reverts to separate requests after an IT change → check it remains combined at re-audit.
- Pearls: Recruit the substance misuse lead nurse and the multidisciplinary TB team jointly, since NICE requires their integration.; Confirm continuity-of-care arrangements for post-release treatment before cycle 1, as NICE specifies.; Use the same substance misuse service contact definition at re-audit.; Report combined testing rates at the joint TB/substance misuse governance meeting to keep the pathway prioritised after staff turnover.

**NNA-458. What proportion of prisoners in prison for the first time are screened for TB within 48 hours of arrival?** (new)
- Standard: NICE NG57 Physical health of people in prison, rec 1.1.9 (2016), adapted from the NICE guideline on tuberculosis: "Healthcare professionals in prisons should ensure people coming into prison are screened for TB within 48 hours of arrival." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng57/chapter/Recommendations
- Pass: TB screening (symptom screen, and chest X-ray or IGRA as locally protocolised) is documented as completed within 48 hours of the recorded reception date and time.. Target: ≥90%. Sample: 40 consecutive new receptions over the last 4 weeks.
- Change: Add an automatic 'TB screen due within 48 hours' countdown task to the reception worklist, visible to the nursing team separately from the general first/second-stage assessment tasks.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-458.csv`
- Pitfalls: TB screening may be recorded as part of the general health assessment without a separate timestamp → add a dedicated TB screening field with its own date/time.; Access to mobile X-ray or IGRA testing may be limited out of hours → agree local arrangements for weekend and night receptions before cycle 1.; People who decline screening should be recorded distinctly from those simply not yet screened → add a 'declined' option to avoid conflating the two.; High reception volumes on a single day can delay screening for later arrivals → review results by daily reception volume.; Improvement may fade if the countdown task is not maintained after an IT upgrade → confirm the task list still functions at re-audit.
- Pearls: Recruit the reception nurse lead and the local multidisciplinary TB team liaison together.; Agree out-of-hours screening arrangements (for example, symptom screen with X-ray to follow) before cycle 1.; Use the same reception log extraction method at re-audit.; Report the 48-hour completion rate at the multidisciplinary TB team meeting so it remains visible after the audit lead moves on.

**NNA-459. When an ACCT is opened for a prisoner, what proportion of first case reviews have healthcare or mental health staff attendance, or a documented written/verbal contribution, recorded?** (new)
- Standard: Prison Safety Policy Framework, paragraph 4.184 (re-issued 14 January 2026): "Healthcare or mental health staff must attend the first case review. If in exceptional circumstances they cannot attend, a verbal or written contribution must be provided. A further ACCT case review must then be convened as soon as possible." https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/6720ae033758e4604742a838/prison-safety-policy-framework.pdf
- Pass: The first ACCT case review record shows healthcare or mental health staff attended in person, or a documented written or verbal contribution from healthcare was provided if they could not attend.. Target: ≥95%. Sample: 40 consecutive ACCT openings over the last 3 months, or all if fewer.
- Change: Add an automatic healthcare notification when a concern form is raised (as required by paragraph 4.173/4.184), with the first case review time only confirmed once healthcare has acknowledged attendance or provided a contribution.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-459.csv`
- Pitfalls: Healthcare staffing levels may not allow attendance at every case review, especially out of hours → ensure the written/verbal contribution route is genuinely available as a fallback.; 'Attendance' may be recorded loosely without confirming a genuine clinical contribution was made → audit the content of the contribution, not just a tick box.; ACCT and healthcare records sit on different IT systems in most establishments → agree a cross-referencing method before cycle 1.; Case reviews may be rescheduled at short notice, making healthcare attendance harder to plan → build early notification into the concern-form process, as the framework requires.; Improvement may fade if the notification step is seen as an add-on rather than mandatory → make it part of the ACCT case co-ordinator's checklist.
- Pearls: Recruit the safer custody lead and the prison's senior healthcare clinical lead jointly, since this crosses both services.; Agree the notification and escalation process with both teams before cycle 1.; Use the same ACCT/case review extraction method at re-audit.; Report results at the joint safer custody and healthcare governance meeting so the pathway survives staff turnover.

**NNA-460. What proportion of people discharged or transferred from prison with an ongoing prescription are given at least 7 days of their prescribed medicines or an FP10 prescription?** (new)
- Standard: NICE NG57 Physical health of people in prison, rec 1.7.14 (2016): "When a person is discharged or transferred from prison, give them a minimum of 7 days' prescribed medicines or an FP10 prescription, based on a risk assessment." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng57/chapter/Recommendations
- Pass: The discharge/transfer record shows the person was given at least 7 days' supply of each ongoing prescribed medicine, or an FP10 prescription covering at least 7 days, unless a documented risk assessment specifies a different amount.. Target: ≥90%. Sample: 40 consecutive releases with an ongoing prescription over the last 4 weeks.
- Change: Add a mandatory 'discharge medicines: days supplied' field to the release checklist that must show 7 or more (or a linked risk assessment) before the release paperwork can be signed off by pharmacy.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-460.csv`
- Pitfalls: Short-notice releases (for example, following a court decision) leave little time to prepare medicines → build a same-day pharmacy fast-track process for unplanned releases (see NG57 1.7.15).; Controlled drugs and opioid substitution therapy need specific arrangements with community providers → confirm the community pharmacy handover process before cycle 1.; People released without a fixed address may struggle to access a community pharmacy → note this in the risk assessment rather than skipping the medicines supply.; FP10 prescriptions may not be dispensed promptly in the community → measure days supplied given directly where possible, not just the prescription being issued.; Improvement may fade if pharmacy staffing is reduced → review staffing alongside the audit results.
- Pearls: Recruit the prison pharmacist and resettlement/throughcare team jointly.; Agree the fast-track process for unplanned releases before cycle 1, as NG57 requires a contingency plan.; Use the same discharge record extraction method at re-audit.; Report results at the resettlement and medicines optimisation governance meetings so the checklist item survives contract or staff changes.

**NNA-461. What proportion of people in prison who smoke are offered stop-smoking support at their first-stage health assessment, in a smoke-free establishment?** (new)
- Standard: NICE NG209 Tobacco: preventing uptake, promoting quitting and treating dependence, rec 1.12.1 and 1.12.2 (2021, amended 2025): "Tell people who smoke that a range of interventions is available to help them stop smoking. Explain how to access them and refer people to stop-smoking support if appropriate... Ensure the following are accessible to adults who smoke: behavioural interventions... nicotine replacement therapy (NRT)." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng209/chapter/Promoting-quitting
- Pass: The first-stage health assessment record shows smoking status was asked, and, for a current smoker, that stop-smoking support (behavioural support and/or NRT) was offered before or at the point of reception into the smoke-free establishment.. Target: ≥90%. Sample: 40 consecutive receptions reporting current smoking over the last 4 weeks.
- Change: Add a mandatory 'smoker: NRT/stop-smoking support offered' field to the first-stage reception template, linked directly to an NRT prescribing order set so support can be started the same day.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-461.csv`
- Pitfalls: Reception staff have many competing priorities at first-stage assessment → make the smoking field mandatory rather than optional to prevent it being missed.; Withdrawal symptoms may be attributed to other causes if not specifically asked about → train reception staff to recognise and act on nicotine withdrawal.; NRT stock shortages can undermine same-day support → confirm supply arrangements with pharmacy before cycle 1.; Vaping status may not be captured separately from smoking, complicating the denominator → clarify the definition of 'current smoker' before starting.; Improvement may fade if NRT is only offered at reception and not continued on the wing → check continuation rates as a secondary measure.
- Pearls: Recruit the reception nurse lead and the prison's smoke-free/stop-smoking coordinator jointly.; Agree the NRT order set and supply arrangements with pharmacy before cycle 1.; Use the same reception log extraction method at re-audit.; Report results at the smoke-free prison steering group to keep the pathway prioritised after staff turnover.

**NNA-462. What proportion of adults with hypertension aged under 80 on antihypertensive treatment have a clinic blood pressure below 140/90 mmHg at their most recent reading?** (new)
- Standard: NICE NG136 Hypertension in adults: diagnosis and management, rec 1.4.20 (2019, amended 2022): "For adults with hypertension aged under 80, reduce clinic blood pressure to below 140/90 mmHg and ensure that it is maintained below that level." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng136/chapter/Recommendations
- Pass: The most recent clinic blood pressure reading in the last 12 months is below 140/90 mmHg. For patients with type 1 diabetes or severe chronic kidney disease, use the NG136 table 1 target for that condition instead.. Target: ≥80%. Sample: 40 consecutive patients from the hypertension register meeting the inclusion criteria, or a 10% random sample if the register is larger.
- Change: Run a monthly practice search flagging hypertension register patients whose last clinic BP is above target with no medication change or clinic BP recheck in the last 8 weeks, for pharmacist-led review.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-462.csv`
- Pitfalls: A single high reading may not reflect true control → use the most recent recorded reading but flag patients for a re-check rather than assuming poor control from one value.; White-coat effect can make clinic readings appear worse than home readings → review NG136's advice on ABPM/HBPM for patients with a suspected white-coat effect.; Medication non-adherence is a common but under-recorded reason for poor control → include an adherence check in the pharmacist review.; Frailty and multimorbidity may justify a less strict target in practice, even under 80 → document clinical judgement clearly rather than treating every above-target reading as a failure.; Improvement may fade if the monthly search is not resourced → confirm pharmacist time is protected before cycle 1.
- Pearls: Recruit the practice's clinical pharmacist to lead the medication reviews generated by the search.; Agree the exclusion criteria (diabetes/severe CKD targets, white-coat effect) with the GP lead before cycle 1.; Use the same register extraction method at re-audit for a fair comparison.; Report target-achievement rates at the practice's QOF preparation meeting to keep this visible year-round, not just at year-end.

**NNA-463. What proportion of adults with atrial fibrillation and a CHA2DS2-VASc score of 2 or more are prescribed a direct-acting oral anticoagulant or warfarin?** (new)
- Standard: NICE NG196 Atrial fibrillation: diagnosis and management, rec 1.6.3 (2021): "Offer anticoagulation with a direct-acting oral anticoagulant to people with atrial fibrillation and a CHA2DS2-VASc score of 2 or above, taking into account the risk of bleeding." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng196/chapter/Recommendations
- Pass: The patient is prescribed a DOAC or warfarin, or has a clearly documented reason for not being anticoagulated (for example, a specific contraindication or a fully informed decision to decline after discussion of risks and benefits).. Target: ≥90%. Sample: 40 consecutive patients from the AF register with CHA2DS2-VASc ≥2, or a 10% random sample if the register is larger.
- Change: Run a monthly practice search cross-referencing the AF register, CHA2DS2-VASc score and current anticoagulant prescription, generating a task for GP review of every patient scoring ≥2 with no anticoagulant and no documented reason.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-463.csv`
- Pitfalls: CHA2DS2-VASc scores may be out of date if not recalculated after a new diagnosis (for example, new diabetes or heart failure) → recalculate at the point of audit, not just use the last coded score.; Patients may be correctly excluded for a specific contraindication (for example, active bleeding) → always check for a documented reason before counting as a gap.; Some patients may be under specialist anticoagulation clinics with prescribing outside the GP record → check shared care records before concluding a patient is untreated.; Patient choice to decline anticoagulation after full discussion is a valid outcome → record this distinctly from an unexplained gap.; Improvement may fade if the search is run once and not repeated → make it a standing monthly search, not a one-off audit tool.
- Pearls: Recruit the practice's cardiovascular disease lead GP or pharmacist to review flagged patients.; Agree the exclusion criteria (score, contraindications, specialist care) with the whole team before cycle 1.; Use the same register extraction method at re-audit for a fair comparison.; Report the gap-closure rate at the QOF preparation meeting to keep this visible after the audit lead moves on.

**NNA-464. What proportion of adults with one of the NICE risk factors for chronic kidney disease (diabetes, hypertension, cardiovascular disease or previous acute kidney injury) have had both an eGFR and a urine albumin:creatinine ratio (ACR) tested in the last 12 months?** (new)
- Standard: NICE NG203 Chronic kidney disease: assessment and management, rec 1.1.21 (2021): "Offer testing for CKD using eGFRcreatinine and ACR to adults with any of the following risk factors: diabetes; hypertension; previous episode of acute kidney injury; cardiovascular disease (ischaemic heart disease, chronic heart failure, peripheral vascular disease or cerebral vascular disease); structural renal tract disease, recurrent renal calculi or prostatic hypertrophy; multisystem diseases with potential kidney involvement... gout; family history of end-stage renal disease... or hereditary kidney disease; incidental detection of haematuria or proteinuria." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng203/chapter/Recommendations
- Pass: Both an eGFR and a urine ACR result are recorded in the last 12 months for a patient with one or more of the listed NICE risk factors.. Target: ≥85%. Sample: 40 consecutive patients from the combined at-risk registers, or a 10% random sample if larger.
- Change: Add ACR to the default annual review blood test order set for diabetes, hypertension and cardiovascular disease reviews, so it is requested automatically alongside eGFR rather than as a separate step.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-464.csv`
- Pitfalls: ACR requires a urine sample that patients may not bring to the same appointment as blood tests → provide a sample pot and instructions in advance of the review, or a postal kit if available.; Some laboratories process ACR separately from routine biochemistry, causing results to be missed on a quick chart review → confirm the exact test code used locally before starting.; Patients already diagnosed with advanced CKD under nephrology may have testing arranged elsewhere → exclude them or verify with the specialist team.; A raised ACR needs a repeat confirmatory test before diagnosis → make this clear in staff training so a single result is interpreted correctly.; Improvement may fade if the order set is reverted during an EPR template update → check it remains in place at re-audit.
- Pearls: Recruit the practice's diabetes or CKD lead nurse to champion the combined order set.; Agree the exact local ACR test code and sample logistics with the laboratory before cycle 1.; Use the same register definitions at re-audit for a fair comparison.; Report ACR testing rates at QOF preparation meetings to keep this visible after the lead rotates.

**NNA-465. What proportion of adults and children aged 5 and over on the practice asthma register have a documented, reviewed personalised asthma action plan?** (new)
- Standard: NICE NG245 Asthma: diagnosis, monitoring and management (BTS/NICE/SIGN), rec 1.14.1 and 1.14.2 (2024): "For adults, young people and children aged 5 and over with a diagnosis of asthma... offer an asthma self-management programme, comprising a documented personalised action plan and education... Review the content of the personalised action plan, and check that the person understands it, at the following: hospital admission, including in virtual wards; acute consultations in primary care or emergency department; annual reviews." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng245/chapter/Recommendations
- Pass: A documented personalised asthma action plan exists in the record and has been reviewed (content checked and understanding confirmed) at the most recent annual review, acute consultation, or hospital admission, whichever was most recent.. Target: ≥85%. Sample: 40 consecutive patients from the asthma register with a qualifying contact in the last 12 months, or a 10% random sample if larger.
- Change: Add a mandatory 'action plan issued/reviewed' field to the asthma annual review and acute asthma consultation templates, which cannot be closed until completed, with a printable or app-based plan generated automatically.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-465.csv`
- Pitfalls: A plan may be issued once and never reviewed again, appearing compliant on a simple 'exists' check → audit review at the most recent qualifying contact, not just existence.; Post-hospital-admission plans may be created by the hospital but not visible in the GP record → request a copy be sent with every discharge letter.; Children under 5 are excluded from the mandatory plan (self-management programmes for carers instead) → apply the correct age threshold in the template.; Time pressure in 10-minute appointments can squeeze out plan review → protect specific time in asthma review templates for this step.; Improvement may fade if the mandatory field becomes a routine tick without real review → spot-check free text for genuine discussion at re-audit.
- Pearls: Recruit the practice's respiratory/asthma lead nurse to champion the mandatory template field.; Agree a standard action plan format (paper or app-based) with the team before cycle 1.; Use the same register and qualifying-contact definitions at re-audit for a fair comparison.; Report plan review rates at the respiratory/QOF meeting to keep this visible after the lead rotates.

**NNA-466. What proportion of adults admitted with a COPD exacerbation in the last year who remain at risk of exacerbations have a documented individualised exacerbation action plan, with a short course of oral corticosteroids and antibiotics to keep at home?** (new)
- Standard: NICE NG115 Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease in over 16s, rec 1.2.128 (2018): "Offer people a short course of oral corticosteroids and a short course of oral antibiotics to keep at home as part of their exacerbation action plan if: they have had an exacerbation within the last year, and remain at risk of exacerbations; they understand and are confident about when and how to take these medicines, and the associated benefits and harms; they know to tell their healthcare professional when they have used the medicines, and to ask for replacements." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng115/chapter/Recommendations
- Pass: A documented, individualised exacerbation action plan is in the record, a rescue pack (oral corticosteroid and antibiotic) has been supplied to keep at home, and the record shows the patient was told to inform the practice when used and to request replacements.. Target: ≥80%. Sample: 40 consecutive patients on the COPD register with an exacerbation in the last 12 months, or a 10% random sample if larger.
- Change: Add a mandatory 'exacerbation action plan and rescue pack' section to the COPD annual review and post-exacerbation follow-up templates, generating a printed plan and linked repeat prescription automatically.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-466.csv`
- Pitfalls: Rescue packs may be repeatedly issued without ever reviewing whether the patient understands how to use them safely → audit understanding confirmation, not just supply.; Patients using 3 or more courses in a year need specific review of possible reasons, per NG115 1.2.130 → flag these patients for a dedicated consultation rather than automatic re-issue.; Self-management may not suit patients with cognitive impairment living alone → document a clear individual risk assessment rather than a blanket policy.; Rescue pack medicines can be stockpiled or used inappropriately if not reviewed → check medicine cupboard content at annual review where practical.; Improvement may fade if the mandatory template section is skipped under time pressure → protect appointment time for COPD reviews.
- Pearls: Recruit the practice's respiratory lead nurse to champion the mandatory template section.; Agree the exact rescue pack medicines and quantities with the GP lead before cycle 1.; Use the same register and exacerbation definitions at re-audit for a fair comparison.; Report over-use flags (3+ courses) at the respiratory/QOF meeting to sustain the review pathway after staff rotate.

**NNA-467. What proportion of patients on shared-care methotrexate monitoring in general practice have had FBC, liver function tests and renal function checked within the interval specified in the shared care protocol?** (new)
- Standard: NHS Specialist Pharmacy Service, Methotrexate monitoring (based on British Society for Rheumatology shared care guidance): "Every 2-3 months: Full blood count; Liver function tests; Serum creatinine (for creatinine clearance) or Estimated glomerular filtration rate. [Rheumatology and gastroenterology, once stable]: At least every 12 weeks: Full blood count; Liver function tests; Serum creatinine." https://sps.nhs.uk/monitorings/methotrexate-monitoring/
- Pass: FBC, LFTs and renal function (creatinine or eGFR) are all recorded within the interval specified in the patient's individual shared care protocol (no more than 12 weeks for stable patients on rheumatology/gastroenterology shared care, or as otherwise specified).. Target: ≥90%. Sample: 40 consecutive patients on the shared care methotrexate register, or all if fewer.
- Change: Run a monthly practice search identifying shared-care methotrexate patients overdue their monitoring interval, generating an automatic recall to the patient and a task to the practice pharmacist.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-467.csv`
- Pitfalls: Monitoring intervals vary between individual shared care protocols and specialties → record the specific agreed interval for each patient rather than assuming one national standard.; Results may be filed without being reviewed against the expected interval → build an interval check into the search, not just a search for any recent bloods.; Patients who do not attend for monitoring bloods may have their methotrexate wrongly continued → build in a rule to flag and consider withholding the prescription if overdue.; Shared care responsibilities may be unclear between specialist and GP, especially soon after a hospital discharge → confirm and document the shared care agreement for every patient.; Improvement may fade if the pharmacist task list is not resourced → confirm protected time before cycle 1.
- Pearls: Recruit the practice's clinical pharmacist to lead the monthly monitoring search, since they already manage repeat prescribing safety.; Agree the individual monitoring interval for each patient with the specialist shared care letter before cycle 1.; Use the same register and interval definitions at re-audit for a fair comparison.; Report overdue-monitoring rates at the medicines optimisation meeting to sustain the pathway after staff rotate.

**NNA-468. What proportion of people prescribed systemic HRT for menopausal symptoms have a documented review at 3 months of starting or changing treatment?** (new)
- Standard: NICE NG23 Menopause: diagnosis and management, rec 1.9.2 (2015): "Review each treatment for symptoms associated with menopause: at 3 months to assess efficacy and tolerability; annually thereafter, unless there are clinical indications for an earlier review (such as treatment ineffectiveness, side effects or adverse events)." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng23/chapter/Recommendations
- Pass: A documented review (efficacy, tolerability, and, for patients with a uterus, discussion of expected bleeding patterns) is recorded within 3 months (10-16 weeks) of starting HRT or changing the dose or preparation.. Target: ≥85%. Sample: 40 consecutive patients starting or changing HRT over the last 6 months, or all if fewer.
- Change: Add an automatic 3-month HRT review task to the practice system, generated whenever a new HRT prescription or dose/preparation change is issued, with a structured review template pre-populated with the bleeding-pattern question.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-468.csv`
- Pitfalls: Repeat HRT prescriptions can be issued by reception or pharmacy without a clinician review being triggered → build the review task into the prescribing system itself, not rely on staff memory.; Reviews may happen but not be coded as such, undercounting true compliance → agree a specific template or code for the 3-month review before cycle 1.; Telephone or online reviews may be harder to capture consistently than face-to-face → include all consultation modes in the audit definition.; Patients may not attend the review appointment → record non-attendance and re-invitation separately from a failure to offer.; Improvement may fade if the automatic task is switched off during a system update → confirm it remains active at re-audit.
- Pearls: Recruit the practice's menopause or women's health lead GP or nurse to champion the automatic task.; Agree the review template content (efficacy, tolerability, bleeding pattern) with the team before cycle 1.; Use the same prescribing record extraction method at re-audit for a fair comparison.; Report review completion rates at the women's health/QOF meeting to sustain the pathway after the lead rotates.

**NNA-469. What proportion of adult patients with a new safeguarding concern raised in a GP consultation have that concern coded in their electronic record using the practice's agreed safeguarding code?** (new)
- Standard: Local standard, informed by RCGP safeguarding recording principles and NHS England information-sharing requirements for safeguarding: "A safeguarding concern raised in a consultation should be recorded using a specific, searchable safeguarding code in the patient's electronic record, in addition to any free-text description, so that the concern can be identified for information sharing, multi-agency working and future risk assessment." https://www.rcgp.org.uk/mrcgpexams/safeguarding
- Pass: A new safeguarding concern documented in the consultation free text is also recorded using the practice's specific safeguarding code (for example, 'safeguarding adult concern' or 'safeguarding child concern') within the same working day.. Target: ≥90%. Sample: 40 consecutive consultations with a free-text safeguarding concern identified by a text search over the last 3 months, or all if fewer.
- Change: Add a pop-up prompt in the EPR whenever certain safeguarding-related free-text phrases are entered, asking the clinician to confirm and apply the specific safeguarding code before the consultation can be saved.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-469.csv`
- Pitfalls: A free-text search will miss concerns described in varied language → use a broad set of trigger phrases and accept the search will not be exhaustive.; Coding a safeguarding concern raises confidentiality and information-governance questions → confirm the practice's information-sharing policy with the safeguarding lead before cycle 1.; Clinicians may worry that coding could affect the patient relationship if seen by the patient online → clarify with the safeguarding lead what is and is not visible to patients via online access.; Over-triggering the pop-up prompt on unrelated entries could cause alert fatigue → refine the trigger phrase list after an initial pilot.; Improvement may fade if the pop-up is disabled during an EPR update → confirm it is still active at re-audit.
- Pearls: Recruit the practice's named safeguarding lead GP or nurse to define the trigger phrases and code.; Agree the information-governance approach with the safeguarding lead and practice manager before cycle 1.; Use the same free-text search terms at re-audit for a fair comparison.; Report coding completeness at the practice's safeguarding supervision meetings to keep this prioritised after the lead changes.

**NNA-470. What proportion of adults aged 6 months to 64 years in a clinical risk group for influenza are on the practice's flu register and are invited for vaccination each season?** (new)
- Standard: UKHSA Green Book, Influenza chapter (25 August 2026): "General practitioners are required to proactively identify all those for whom influenza immunisations are indicated and to compile a register of those patients for whom influenza immunisation is recommended. Sufficient vaccine can then be ordered in advance and patients can be invited to planned immunisation sessions or appointments." https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/influenza-the-green-book-chapter
- Pass: A patient with a coded clinical risk group qualifying for flu vaccination (chronic respiratory, heart, kidney or liver disease, diabetes, immunosuppression, or other Green Book risk group) aged 6 months to 64 years is included on the practice's flu register and has a documented invitation for the current season.. Target: ≥95% on register; ≥70% vaccinated. Sample: 40 consecutive patients from the combined risk-group registers, or a 10% random sample if larger.
- Change: Build a single combined flu risk-group search that pulls from all individual chronic disease registers automatically each August, generating the season's invitation list without relying on manual compilation.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-470.csv`
- Pitfalls: Risk-group coding is inconsistent between clinicians, so some eligible patients may not appear on any register → review and standardise the code list with the coding lead before the season starts.; Patients newly diagnosed with a risk factor after the initial register is built may be missed → re-run the search monthly through the season, not just once in August.; Vaccination given outside the practice (community pharmacy, hospital) may not be recorded in the GP system → check the national vaccination record where available.; Vaccine supply constraints can affect invitation timing → report supply issues separately from register or invitation failures.; Improvement may fade if the combined search is not re-run every season → build it into the annual flu campaign checklist.
- Pearls: Recruit the practice's flu campaign lead nurse to own the combined register search.; Agree the risk-group code list with the whole clinical team before the season starts.; Use the same combined search method at re-audit for a fair comparison.; Review register completeness at the practice's pre-season flu planning meeting each year so it is not forgotten after staff turnover.

**NNA-471. What proportion of adults aged 65 and over on the practice list have a record of having received a pneumococcal vaccine (PPV23 or PCV20)?** (new)
- Standard: UKHSA Green Book, Pneumococcal chapter (29 July 2026): "Adults aged 65 years and over, and clinical risk groups aged 2 years or over: a single dose of 0.5ml of PPV23 or PCV20." https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/pneumococcal-the-green-book-chapter-25
- Pass: The patient's record shows a documented single dose of PPV23 or PCV20 given at or after age 65 (or in a qualifying risk group before 65, which satisfies the requirement without needing a repeat dose at 65).. Target: ≥90%. Sample: 40 consecutive patients aged 65 and over identified by a practice search, or a 10% random sample if the cohort is larger.
- Change: Run a one-off practice-wide search of all patients aged 65 and over with no recorded pneumococcal vaccine, and add a standing rule that the vaccine is offered automatically at the 65th birthday alongside the shingles vaccination invitation.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-471.csv`
- Pitfalls: Historic paper records may not have been fully migrated to the electronic system → check paper records for older patients before concluding a vaccine was never given.; Patients vaccinated by a previous practice may not have the record transferred → request records from PCSE/previous practice where the immunisation history is unclear.; Combining the invitation with the shingles vaccination call reduces extra appointments but requires coordination → agree the combined invitation letter wording before cycle 1.; Small numbers of long-standing gaps may reflect genuine past declines → record a documented decline separately from a true gap in offering.; Improvement may fade if the 65th-birthday rule is not maintained after an EPR template change → confirm it is still active at re-audit.
- Pearls: Recruit the practice's immunisation lead nurse to run the age-based search and design the combined invitation.; Agree the combined pneumococcal/shingles invitation letter with the practice manager before cycle 1.; Use the same age-based search definitions at re-audit for a fair comparison.; Report coverage rates at the immunisation/QOF meeting to keep the standing rule visible after the lead rotates.

**NNA-472. What proportion of people transferring between prisons have relevant health record information (including current medicines) available to the receiving establishment's healthcare team before or at the point of transfer?** (new)
- Standard: NICE NG57 Physical health of people in prison, rec 1.7.3 (2016): "Ensure continuity of care between custodial settings, including court, the receiving prison or during escort periods by, for example: providing access to relevant information from the patient record; providing any medicines (including controlled drugs) - see also the section on continuity of medicines; issuing an FP10 prescription." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng57/chapter/Recommendations
- Pass: At the point of arrival at the receiving prison, the healthcare team has access to relevant patient record information (including current medicines) from the sending establishment, and the person has been provided with sufficient medicines or an FP10 prescription to cover the transfer period without a missed dose.. Target: ≥90%. Sample: 40 consecutive inter-prison transfers over the last 4 weeks, or all if fewer.
- Change: Introduce a standard transfer healthcare summary (including current medicines list) that must accompany every prisoner escort record electronically, checked as complete by the sending establishment's healthcare team before transfer.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-472.csv`
- Pitfalls: Sending and receiving prisons may use different or non-linked IT systems → agree a minimum standard paper or electronic summary that works across systems.; Transfers can happen at short notice, leaving little time to prepare a full summary → build a rapid-summary template that can be completed quickly for urgent transfers.; Controlled drugs require additional security and documentation during transfer → confirm the local controlled drugs transfer protocol before cycle 1.; Escort staff may not prioritise healthcare paperwork among other transfer documents → make the health record a mandatory, checked item in the transfer process.; Improvement may fade without ongoing cross-establishment coordination → review the pathway with both establishments at re-audit, not just the sending one.
- Pearls: Recruit healthcare leads from both the sending and receiving establishments, since this audit spans two teams.; Agree a standard minimum data set for the transfer summary before cycle 1.; Use the same transfer log extraction method at re-audit for a fair comparison.; Report results at a regional (not just single-establishment) health and justice meeting so the pathway is adopted across multiple sites.

**NNA-473. What proportion of people entering prison who report drinking more than 15 units of alcohol daily, or who show signs of withdrawal, are urgently referred to the GP or an alternative healthcare professional at first-stage assessment?** (new)
- Standard: NICE NG57 Physical health of people in prison, rec 1.1.4 (table 1, item 13) (2016): "[Alcohol and substance misuse] Does the person drink alcohol, and if so: how much do they normally drink? how much did they drink in the week before coming into custody? Urgently refer the person to the GP or an alternative suitable healthcare professional if: they drink more than 15 units of alcohol daily or they are showing signs of withdrawal or they have been given medication for withdrawal in police or court cells." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng57/chapter/Recommendations
- Pass: For a person reporting more than 15 units of alcohol daily, showing signs of withdrawal, or already given withdrawal medication in police or court cells, the record shows an urgent referral to the GP or an alternative suitable healthcare professional was made at, or immediately after, first-stage assessment (same shift).. Target: ≥95%. Sample: 40 consecutive receptions meeting the urgent-referral criteria over the last 6 weeks, or all if fewer.
- Change: Build an automatic same-shift alert to the on-call GP or clinical lead whenever the first-stage assessment template records one of the three urgent-referral criteria, with a linked withdrawal monitoring chart started at the same time.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-473.csv`
- Pitfalls: Self-reported alcohol consumption may be under- or over-stated → use clinical judgement and any available third-party information (for example, police custody records) alongside self-report.; Withdrawal signs can develop hours after reception, after the first-stage assessment is complete → ensure ongoing monitoring is triggered, not just a one-off referral at reception.; Night or weekend receptions may have reduced on-call GP availability → confirm the out-of-hours escalation pathway before cycle 1.; Alcohol withdrawal management protocols vary between establishments → confirm the local monitoring chart and medication protocol with the clinical lead.; Improvement may fade if the automatic alert is disabled during an IT update → confirm it remains active at re-audit.
- Pearls: Recruit the prison's substance misuse lead clinician and reception nurse team jointly.; Agree the out-of-hours escalation pathway with the on-call GP rota before cycle 1.; Use the same urgent-referral criteria at re-audit for a fair comparison.; Report results at the substance misuse and safer custody governance meeting to sustain the pathway after staff turnover.

**NNA-474. What proportion of people in prison who score above threshold on the Correctional Mental Health Screen (CMHS-M or CMHS-W) at reception are referred for further mental health assessment?** (new)
- Standard: NICE NG57 Physical health of people in prison, rec 1.1.17 (2016): "If there is other evidence supporting the likelihood of mental health problems, or a man scores 6 or more on the CMHS-M, or a woman scores 4 or more on the CMHS-W: a practitioner who is trained to perform an assessment of mental health problems should conduct further assessment or a practitioner who is not trained to perform an assessment of mental health problems should refer the person to an appropriately trained professional for further assessment." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng57/chapter/Recommendations
- Pass: A person scoring 6 or more (men, CMHS-M) or 4 or more (women, CMHS-W) has a documented further mental health assessment, either conducted directly by a trained practitioner or via a referral to one, within 5 working days of the screen.. Target: ≥90%. Sample: 40 consecutive above-threshold CMHS screens over the last 6 weeks, or all if fewer.
- Change: Add an automatic referral task to the mental health in-reach team's worklist whenever a CMHS score meets or exceeds the referral threshold, removing reliance on the reception clinician remembering to refer manually.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-474.csv`
- Pitfalls: Reception staff may not always be trained to score the CMHS correctly → confirm scoring training is up to date before cycle 1.; Mental health in-reach team capacity may limit how quickly referrals can be seen → report waiting times as a secondary measure alongside referral completion.; Transgender patients require the CMHS version matching their gender identity, which staff may apply inconsistently → confirm staff know NG57's guidance on this before starting.; People who are unwilling or unable to engage with screening may be recorded as 'not screened' rather than a true negative → track these separately from below-threshold results.; Improvement may fade if the automatic referral task is not monitored → review the worklist regularly, not just at audit points.
- Pearls: Recruit the mental health in-reach team lead and reception nurse team jointly.; Agree the referral pathway and expected assessment timescale with the in-reach team before cycle 1.; Use the same CMHS threshold definitions at re-audit for a fair comparison.; Report referral and assessment completion rates at the mental health in-reach governance meeting to sustain the pathway after staff turnover.

**NNA-475. What proportion of people entering prison are offered hepatitis B vaccination at reception?** (new)
- Standard: NICE NG57 Physical health of people in prison, rec 1.1.23 (2016): "Prison healthcare services (working with the NHS lead for hepatitis) should ensure that: all people are offered a hepatitis B vaccination when entering prison (for the vaccination schedule, refer to the UK Health Security Agency's Green Book)." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng57/chapter/Recommendations
- Pass: The reception health record documents that hepatitis B vaccination was offered, with the outcome recorded (accepted and first dose given, declined, or already fully vaccinated).. Target: ≥90%. Sample: 40 consecutive new receptions over the last 4 weeks.
- Change: Add hepatitis B vaccination as a mandatory field on the first-stage reception template, linked to an accelerated (0, 7, 21 day plus booster) schedule order set for people likely to be in custody only briefly.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-475.csv`
- Pitfalls: Short remand stays may end before the full vaccination course is complete → use the accelerated schedule and hand over remaining doses to the community or receiving establishment on release/transfer.; Vaccination history from the community is often unverifiable → offer vaccination unless there is clear documented evidence of a completed course.; Vaccine stock and cold-chain management at reception need to be reliable → confirm supply arrangements with pharmacy before cycle 1.; Staff may conflate the vaccination offer with the separate testing offer → keep the two as distinct fields in the template to avoid double-counting.; Improvement may fade if the mandatory field is later removed in an IT update → confirm it remains mandatory at re-audit.
- Pearls: Recruit the prison's blood-borne virus/immunisation lead nurse as the audit lead, combining with the hepatitis B/C testing audit for efficiency.; Agree the accelerated vaccination schedule and handover process for short stays with the pharmacy and community hepatitis service before cycle 1.; Use the same reception log extraction method at re-audit.; Report vaccination offer rates at the health and justice partnership board to keep this prioritised after staff turnover.

**NNA-476. What proportion of people entering prison who report injecting drug use in the last month have their injection sites checked and are referred to substance misuse services if there are concerns about their immediate clinical management?** (new)
- Standard: NICE NG57 Physical health of people in prison, rec 1.1.4 (table 1, item 14) (2016): "If the person has used intravenous drugs, check them for injection sites. Refer them to substance misuse services if there are concerns about their immediate clinical management and they need immediate support." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng57/chapter/Recommendations
- Pass: For a person reporting intravenous drug use in the last month, the record shows injection sites were physically checked, and, where there were concerns about immediate clinical management, a referral to substance misuse services was made at, or immediately after, first-stage assessment.. Target: ≥95%. Sample: 40 consecutive receptions reporting intravenous drug use over the last 6 weeks, or all if fewer.
- Change: Add a mandatory 'injection sites checked' field to the first-stage assessment template for anyone reporting intravenous drug use, with a direct one-click referral to substance misuse services built in.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-476.csv`
- Pitfalls: Disclosure of intravenous drug use may be incomplete due to stigma or fear of consequences → train staff in a non-judgemental, harm-reduction approach to improve disclosure.; Physical examination for injection sites requires appropriate privacy and consent → confirm the examination process respects dignity and consent before cycle 1.; Injection site infections may need urgent same-day medical review, not just a substance misuse referral → ensure the pathway includes an option for urgent medical assessment.; Substance misuse service capacity may limit rapid referral response → report referral-to-seen time as a secondary measure.; Improvement may fade if the mandatory field is bypassed under reception time pressure → monitor compliance at re-audit, not just presence of the field.
- Pearls: Recruit the prison substance misuse lead nurse and reception team jointly.; Agree the examination and consent process with the clinical lead before cycle 1.; Use the same reporting definition (intravenous drug use in the last month) at re-audit for a fair comparison.; Report results at the substance misuse governance meeting to sustain the pathway after staff turnover.

**NNA-477. What proportion of adults with hypertension aged 80 and over on antihypertensive treatment have a clinic blood pressure below 150/90 mmHg at their most recent reading?** (new)
- Standard: NICE NG136 Hypertension in adults: diagnosis and management, rec 1.4.21 (2019, amended 2022): "For adults with hypertension aged 80 and over, reduce clinic blood pressure to below 150/90 mmHg and ensure that it is maintained below that level. Use clinical judgement for people with frailty or multimorbidity." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng136/chapter/Recommendations
- Pass: The most recent clinic blood pressure reading in the last 12 months is below 150/90 mmHg, or, for patients with frailty or multimorbidity, a documented clinical judgement is recorded explaining a different individualised target.. Target: ≥80%. Sample: 40 consecutive patients aged 80 and over from the hypertension register, or all if fewer.
- Change: Add an age- and frailty-aware target display to the hypertension review template so clinicians see the correct NG136 target (under-80, 80-and-over, or individualised for frailty) automatically rather than applying a single blanket target.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-477.csv`
- Pitfalls: Applying the under-80 target to older patients can lead to inappropriate over-treatment and falls risk → make sure the template clearly separates the two age-based targets.; Frailty coding is often incomplete, making it hard to identify who needs an individualised target → improve frailty coding as part of this audit, not as an afterthought.; Postural hypotension should be checked in this age group per NG136 1.4.16 → include a postural BP check alongside the target assessment.; A single high reading may not reflect true control → use the most recent recorded reading but flag for re-check rather than treating one value as definitive.; Improvement may fade if the age-aware display is not maintained after an EPR update → confirm it remains accurate at re-audit.
- Pearls: Recruit the practice's frailty or elderly care lead GP to champion the age-aware target display.; Agree the frailty definition and individualised target-setting process with the whole team before cycle 1.; Use the same register extraction method at re-audit for a fair comparison.; Report target-achievement rates at the QOF/frailty meeting to keep this visible after the lead rotates.

**NNA-478. What proportion of stable patients with atrial fibrillation taking warfarin have their time in therapeutic range discussed, with the option of switching to a direct-acting oral anticoagulant, at their most recent routine anticoagulation review?** (new)
- Standard: NICE NG196 Atrial fibrillation: diagnosis and management, rec 1.6.6 (2021): "For adults with atrial fibrillation who are already taking a vitamin K antagonist and are stable, continue with their current medication and discuss the option of switching treatment at their next routine appointment, taking into account the person's time in therapeutic range." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng196/chapter/Recommendations
- Pass: At the most recent routine anticoagulation review, the patient's time in therapeutic range is calculated (or estimated from recent INR results) and a documented discussion of the option to switch to a DOAC has taken place, regardless of the outcome of that discussion.. Target: ≥85%. Sample: 40 consecutive warfarin patients with a routine review in the last 12 months, or a 10% random sample if larger.
- Change: Add an automatic time-in-therapeutic-range calculation to the anticoagulation review template, with a mandatory 'DOAC switch discussed: yes/outcome' field that cannot be left blank at routine review.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-478.csv`
- Pitfalls: Time in therapeutic range calculation requires several recent INR results and a recognised method (for example, Rosendaal) → agree the calculation method and data source with the anticoagulation service before cycle 1.; Patients who are genuinely well controlled and prefer warfarin should still have the discussion documented, even if the outcome is to continue warfarin → audit that the discussion happened, not just the outcome.; Anticoagulation monitoring may be run by a community service outside the GP record → confirm data-sharing arrangements before starting.; Some patients have valid reasons to avoid a DOAC (for example, renal function, cost of monitoring not relevant) → record these clearly rather than treating as non-compliance.; Improvement may fade if the mandatory field is skipped when reviews are done quickly → spot-check consultation quality at re-audit.
- Pearls: Recruit the practice's anticoagulation lead GP or pharmacist, or the community anticoagulation service, to champion the mandatory field.; Agree the time-in-therapeutic-range calculation method before cycle 1 so results are comparable.; Use the same warfarin register extraction method at re-audit.; Report discussion completion rates at the anticoagulation/QOF meeting to sustain the pathway after the lead rotates.

**NNA-479. What proportion of patients on the asthma register who have been dispensed 6 or more short-acting beta agonist (SABA) inhalers in the last 12 months have a documented clinical review of the reasons for overuse?** (new)
- Standard: NICE NG245 Asthma: diagnosis, monitoring and management (BTS/NICE/SIGN), rec 1.6.1 (2024): "Take into account and try to address the possible reasons for uncontrolled asthma before starting or adjusting medicines for asthma in adults, young people and children. These may include: alternative diagnoses or comorbidities; suboptimal adherence; suboptimal inhaler technique; smoking (active or passive), including vaping using e-cigarettes; occupational or environmental exposures." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng245/chapter/Recommendations
- Pass: A patient dispensed 6 or more SABA inhalers in the last 12 months has a documented clinical review addressing possible reasons for overuse (inhaler technique, adherence, alternative diagnoses, smoking/vaping, triggers) within 8 weeks of reaching that threshold.. Target: ≥85%. Sample: 40 consecutive patients meeting the SABA over-use threshold over the last 6 months, or all if fewer.
- Change: Run a monthly practice search flagging patients reaching the 6-SABA-inhaler threshold, generating an automatic task for a respiratory review appointment.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-479.csv`
- Pitfalls: Dispensing data may lag behind actual use if patients stockpile inhalers → use dispensing counts as a prompt for review, not a precise measure of use.; Patients may obtain inhalers from more than one source (for example, online pharmacy) → note this as a limitation when interpreting results.; A review may happen but not address all relevant factors → audit the content of the review, not just its occurrence.; Some patients with legitimately severe asthma may need frequent SABA under specialist guidance → exclude those under active severe asthma service review.; Improvement may fade if the monthly search stops running after a system change → confirm it is still active at re-audit.
- Pearls: Recruit the practice's respiratory lead nurse or pharmacist to run the monthly search and lead reviews.; Agree the 6-inhaler threshold and review template content with the team before cycle 1.; Use the same prescribing search method at re-audit for a fair comparison.; Report over-use flags and review completion at the respiratory/QOF meeting to sustain the pathway after staff rotate.

**NNA-480. What proportion of adults with a new diagnosis of chronic kidney disease have their GFR and ACR category jointly recorded and used to state their risk of adverse outcomes in the record?** (new)
- Standard: NICE NG203 Chronic kidney disease: assessment and management, rec 1.2.1 (2014): "Classify CKD in adults using a combination of GFR and ACR categories (as described in table 1). Be aware that: increased ACR is associated with increased risk of adverse outcomes; decreased GFR is associated with increased risk of adverse outcomes; increased ACR and decreased GFR in combination multiply the risk of adverse outcomes." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng203/chapter/Recommendations
- Pass: The record documents both the GFR category (G1-G5) and ACR category (A1-A3) together, with the combined NICE risk category (low, moderate, high or very high) stated, at the time of diagnosis or most recent annual review.. Target: ≥85%. Sample: 40 consecutive patients from the CKD register, or a 10% random sample if larger.
- Change: Add an automatic GFR/ACR risk-grid calculator to the CKD annual review template that displays the combined NICE risk category as soon as both results are entered, rather than requiring manual look-up of table 1.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-480.csv`
- Pitfalls: GFR and ACR results may be recorded on different dates and never brought together in one place → the calculator should pull the most recent value of each, regardless of date, and flag if either is more than 12 months old.; Staff may record the individual numeric results without translating them into the categorical grid → make the categorical output, not just the raw numbers, the audited item.; Patients under nephrology may have their classification documented only in hospital letters → check for this before counting as a gap in the GP record.; A single ACR result in category A2/A3 needs confirmation before acting on it clinically, per NICE → note this distinction in staff training so classification and clinical action are not conflated.; Improvement may fade if the calculator is not maintained after an EPR template change → confirm it remains functional at re-audit.
- Pearls: Recruit the practice's CKD lead nurse or clinical pharmacist to champion the automatic calculator.; Agree the calculator's exact grid values with NICE table 1 before building it, to avoid errors.; Use the same CKD register definition at re-audit for a fair comparison.; Report documentation rates at the QOF/long-term conditions meeting to keep this visible after the lead rotates.

**NNA-481. What proportion of patients on shared-care DMARD monitoring have their individual risk factors for toxicity (renal function, age, alcohol use, interacting medicines) reviewed at least annually, with monitoring frequency adjusted accordingly?** (new)
- Standard: British Society for Rheumatology shared care guidance for DMARD monitoring (as summarised by NHS Specialist Pharmacy Service): "Risk factors for DMARD toxicity should be reviewed at least annually, adjusting the frequency of monitoring according to the level of risk identified. A shared care protocol should be agreed upon delineating the responsibilities of each party." https://sps.nhs.uk/monitorings/methotrexate-monitoring/
- Pass: A documented annual review of individual toxicity risk factors (renal function trend, age, alcohol intake, interacting medicines such as trimethoprim or NSAIDs) is recorded, with the monitoring interval confirmed as appropriate or adjusted as a result.. Target: ≥85%. Sample: 40 consecutive patients on the shared-care DMARD register on treatment for over 12 months, or all if fewer.
- Change: Add a dedicated 'annual DMARD risk review' template, separate from the routine blood monitoring recall, that prompts the reviewing clinician to check renal trend, age, alcohol use and new interacting prescriptions once a year for every shared-care DMARD patient.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-481.csv`
- Pitfalls: Routine blood monitoring can be mistaken for the full annual risk review, when it only covers some of the required factors → keep the two as clearly separate template items.; Interacting medicines (for example, trimethoprim prescribed by an out-of-hours service) may not trigger an alert if prescribed outside the practice → include a manual interaction check as part of the annual review.; Alcohol intake may be under-reported → use a standard, non-judgemental question as part of the review.; Shared care responsibilities between specialist and GP may be unclear for who leads the annual risk review → confirm this explicitly in the shared care agreement before cycle 1.; Improvement may fade if the annual review template is not linked to a recall system → build in an automatic annual reminder.
- Pearls: Recruit the practice's clinical pharmacist to lead the annual risk review process.; Agree with the rheumatology or gastroenterology shared care team which factors and thresholds to use before cycle 1.; Use the same DMARD register definitions at re-audit for a fair comparison.; Report annual review completion at the medicines optimisation meeting to sustain the process after staff rotate.

## Emergency medicine

**NNA-482. What proportion of ambulance-to-emergency-department patient handovers are completed within 15 minutes of the ambulance arriving?** (new)
- Standard: AACE, Hospital Handovers (webpage, accessed 2026): "The nationally defined target for hospitals included in the NHS Standard Contract states that all handovers between ambulance and A&E must take place within 15 minutes, with none waiting more than 30 minutes." https://aace.org.uk/hospital-handovers/
- Pass: Ambulance clock-stop (patient accepted by an ED clinician) is within 15 minutes of the ambulance's arrival time recorded on the ambulance electronic patient record. Target: ≥90% within 15 minutes, none over 30 minutes. Sample: 50 consecutive ambulance arrivals over 2 weeks, using the ambulance service's own arrival timestamp and the ED's handover-accepted timestamp
- Change: Introduce a rapid 'streaming and handover' nurse and a cohorting bay so incoming ambulances are met at the door, with a visible countdown clock at the ambulance entrance and an internal professional standard escalation when handover passes 30 minutes.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-482.csv`
- Pitfalls: Ambulance and ED clocks are not synchronised → agree a single timestamp source before cycle 1; Small numbers on quiet shifts hide the true delay → sample across day, evening and night shifts; Definition of 'handover accepted' drifts between cycles → lock the definition (first ED clinician contact) in writing with the ambulance trust liaison; Ambulance and nursing staff see this as blame-shifting → present it jointly as a shared flow problem, not a performance league table; Gains fade once the streaming nurse post is not backfilled on leave → build it into the establishment, not a rota extra
- Pearls: Recruit the ambulance trust liaison officer as a co-presenter before cycle 1; Agree the timestamp definitions with both organisations in writing before data collection starts; Display live handover times on the department screen so staff see the effect of the change in real time; Link the audit to the trust's existing corridor-care or ambulance-queue safety huddle so it does not need a new meeting

**NNA-483. What proportion of ambulance pre-alert calls for adult major trauma patients record all the core information items required by the trauma network?** (new)
- Standard: NICE NG39 Major trauma: service delivery, rec 1.8.1 (2016): "Record the following in patients with major trauma in pre-hospital settings: ... the ambulance call sign, name of the person taking the call and time of call." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng39/chapter/Recommendations
- Pass: The recorded pre-alert (written or on the trauma call proforma) contains mechanism of injury, injuries found, vital signs, treatment given, estimated time of arrival, and the ambulance call sign/name of caller/time of call. Target: ≥90% of pre-alerts complete on all items. Sample: 40 consecutive pre-alerted adult trauma calls over 4 weeks
- Change: Replace the free-text pre-alert radio message with a structured ATMIST (age, time, mechanism, injuries, signs, treatment) proforma shared with the ambulance trust, printed automatically as a trauma call sheet when the pre-alert is logged.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-483.csv`
- Pitfalls: Radio recordings are hard to retrieve after a few days → agree a retrieval process with the ambulance trust before cycle 1; Small sample if trauma calls are infrequent → extend the collection window to 6 weeks in a lower-volume unit; Definitions of 'given' vary between reviewers → agree a one-page scoring key before starting; Ambulance crews may feel audited without being consulted → involve the trust's trauma desk lead in designing the proforma; Improvement fades once new crews rotate in → add ATMIST training to ambulance trust induction
- Pearls: Get sign-off from the trauma network's clinical lead before starting, since the change affects the ambulance trust too; Use existing trauma network governance meetings to close the loop rather than creating a new forum; Pilot the ATMIST proforma on one ambulance station before a wider rollout; Keep the same reviewer for both cycles to reduce scoring drift

**NNA-484. What proportion of pre-alerted major trauma patients have a trauma team leader and team ready to receive the handover before the patient arrives?** (new)
- Standard: NICE NG39 Major trauma: service delivery, recs 1.8.4 and 1.8.5 (2016): "A senior nurse or trauma team leader in the emergency department should receive the pre-alert information and determine the level of trauma team response according to agreed and written local guidelines. The trauma team leader should be easily identifiable to receive the handover and the trauma team ready to receive the information." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng39/chapter/Recommendations
- Pass: A named trauma team leader is recorded as having received the pre-alert, and the trauma bay/team is documented as ready (equipment checked, team present) before the patient's arrival. Target: ≥95%. Sample: 40 consecutive pre-alerted trauma calls over 4 weeks
- Change: Introduce a mandatory trauma team leader tabard and a pre-arrival checklist (bay, airway trolley, blood products requested, team roles assigned) signed off by the TTL before the patient arrives, triggered automatically by the pre-alert bleep.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-484.csv`
- Pitfalls: Readiness is hard to verify retrospectively → use direct observation for at least half the sample; Staff may complete the checklist after the event to look compliant → timestamp the checklist electronically; Small numbers if major trauma calls are rare → extend the collection window; Rota gaps mean no consultant TTL is available out of hours → escalate staffing gaps found by the audit to rota planning; Improvement fades once the tabard goes missing → keep a spare stock in the resus room
- Pearls: Recruit the trauma coordinator to help design and pilot the checklist; Agree with nursing and ED consultant leads before cycle 1 who owns team readiness; Use the trauma governance meeting, which already exists, to close the loop; Keep the audit tool the same across cycles so the readiness rate is directly comparable

**NNA-485. What proportion of adults with major trauma needing pre-hospital rapid sequence induction have it started within 45 minutes of the initial 999 call?** (new)
- Standard: NICE NG39 Major trauma: assessment and initial management, rec 1.2.3 (2016): "Aim to perform RSI as soon as possible and within 45 minutes of the initial call to the emergency services, preferably at the scene of the incident." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng39/chapter/Recommendations
- Pass: Time from the initial 999 call to RSI drug administration (scene or en route) is 45 minutes or less. Target: ≥85% within 45 minutes. Sample: 20 consecutive pre-hospital RSIs over 3 months (or all cases if fewer, given expected low volume)
- Change: Feed back individual case timelines to the regional critical care/HEMS desk at the monthly trauma governance meeting, with a standard 'time to RSI' field added to the electronic patient report form so delays are flagged automatically.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-485.csv`
- Pitfalls: 999 call time and drug administration time are recorded on different systems → agree the linkage method with the ambulance trust before cycle 1; Small numbers because pre-hospital RSI is rare → pool data across a longer period or across the regional network; Case-mix varies (rural versus urban scenes) → record scene location type to interpret outliers; Crews may feel individually blamed for system delays → present aggregated, anonymised timelines only; Improvement is not sustained after staff turnover on the critical care desk → build the RSI-time review into the desk's standard handover
- Pearls: Agree data-sharing with the ambulance/critical care service before starting, since most of the data sits outside the hospital; Recruit the regional trauma network's pre-hospital lead as co-owner of the audit; Use the existing trauma governance meeting to close the loop; Keep case numbers pooled across the network if a single trust's volume is too small to interpret alone

**NNA-486. What proportion of adults with active pre-hospital haemorrhage who receive intravenous fluid are given crystalloid only when blood components are not available?** (new)
- Standard: NICE NG39 Major trauma: assessment and initial management, rec 1.5.22 (2016): "In pre-hospital settings only use crystalloids to replace fluid volume in patients with active bleeding if blood components are not available." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng39/chapter/Recommendations
- Pass: Crystalloid is given to a bleeding trauma patient only when the ambulance/HEMS crew records that blood components were not carried or not available at the time. Target: ≥90% appropriate. Sample: 30 consecutive pre-hospital trauma patients with active bleeding who received IV fluid, over 3 months
- Change: Add a mandatory 'blood available: yes/no, reason for crystalloid' field to the ambulance/HEMS electronic patient report form fluid section, and reinforce the crystalloid-avoidance message in the trauma network's annual pre-hospital update training.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-486.csv`
- Pitfalls: Free-text fluid records make coding inconsistent → agree a coding key with the ambulance trust before cycle 1; Blood component availability varies by crew type, confounding comparisons → record crew type for every case; Small numbers if pre-hospital blood is well established locally → pool across the network; Crews may see this as second-guessing a scene decision → frame feedback as system learning, not individual performance; Gains fade if new crews are not told about the change → add to annual mandatory pre-hospital training
- Pearls: Involve the ambulance trust's clinical governance lead from the start; Use the trauma network's existing pre-hospital blood programme meeting to close the loop; Keep the same fluid-choice coding key for both cycles; Share results with crews as a learning bulletin, not a performance table

**NNA-487. What proportion of adults with a head injury and a GCS of 12 or less, and no suspected extracranial bleeding, receive tranexamic acid within 2 hours of injury?** (new)
- Standard: NICE NG232 Head injury: assessment and early management, rec 1.3.17 (2023): "For people with a head injury and a GCS score of 12 or less who are not thought to have active extracranial bleeding, consider: a 2 g intravenous bolus injection of tranexamic acid for people 16 and over ... Give the tranexamic acid as soon as possible within 2 hours of the injury, in the pre-hospital or hospital setting and before imaging." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng232/chapter/Recommendations
- Pass: TXA 2 g IV bolus is given, or a documented reason for not giving it is recorded, within 2 hours of injury. Target: ≥85%. Sample: 30 consecutive eligible adults over 6 months (or all cases if fewer)
- Change: Add TXA as a default prompt on both the ambulance head injury pathway card and the ED trauma order set whenever GCS 12 or less is entered without a bleeding flag, with the 2-hour deadline shown on the prompt.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-487.csv`
- Pitfalls: Time of injury is often uncertain → exclude or flag cases with an estimated rather than witnessed injury time; Ambulance and ED records are on separate systems → agree a single audit form covering both before cycle 1; Small numbers in a district general hospital → extend the collection period to 6-12 months; Clinicians may worry about giving TXA before imaging excludes a contraindication → reinforce the NICE wording ('before imaging') in training; Gains fade if the prompt is switched off during a system upgrade → check it after any EPR update
- Pearls: Agree with the ambulance trust which record system will supply the injury-time and TXA-time fields before starting; Recruit a trauma nurse coordinator to flag eligible cases prospectively as a data-collection aid; Present pooled ambulance and hospital data together so both services see the whole pathway; Keep the same eligibility criteria (GCS ≤12, no extracranial bleeding) across cycles

**NNA-488. What proportion of ambulance patient report forms for head-injured children and adults record a Glasgow Coma Scale score using the correct adult or paediatric version?** (new)
- Standard: NICE NG232 Head injury: assessment and early management, rec 1.3.15 (2003): "Ambulance crews and paramedics should be fully trained in the use of the adult and paediatric versions of the GCS and its derived score." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng232/chapter/Recommendations
- Pass: A GCS score (eye, verbal, motor and total) is recorded on the ambulance patient report form, using the paediatric GCS for children under 5 and the standard GCS for everyone else. Target: ≥95% fully and correctly recorded. Sample: 40 consecutive ambulance-conveyed head injury patients over 2 weeks
- Change: Feed back examples of incomplete or wrong-version GCS recording to the ambulance trust's clinical education team for inclusion in the next mandatory update training cycle, and add a hard-stop prompt for the paediatric GCS version in the electronic patient report form for patients under 5.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-488.csv`
- Pitfalls: Ambulance and hospital notes may be scored differently by different reviewers → use one trained reviewer for the whole audit; Paediatric cases are infrequent, giving small numbers → extend the sampling period for the under-5 subgroup; Ambulance crews may feel individually singled out → report results in aggregate only; Definitions of 'correct version' can be disputed at the 5-year-old boundary → agree the cut-off with the ambulance trust in advance; Improvement is not sustained after a change of electronic patient record supplier → re-check the prompt after any system change
