- Pearls: Agree access to ambulance patient report forms with the ambulance trust's information governance team before starting; Involve the ambulance trust's clinical education lead in interpreting results; Use existing joint governance meetings rather than creating a new one; Keep the same scoring key across both cycles

**NNA-489. When ambulance crews identify a safeguarding concern in a patient with a head injury, what proportion of cases have this documented and verbally handed over to the emergency department?** (new)
- Standard: NICE NG232 Head injury: assessment and early management, rec 1.3.16 (2003, amended 2014): "Ambulance crews and paramedics should be trained in the safeguarding of people under 16 and people 16 and over who are vulnerable. They should document and verbally inform emergency department staff of any safeguarding concerns." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng232/chapter/Recommendations
- Pass: Where the ambulance patient report form records a safeguarding concern, the ED clerking or triage note documents that the concern was verbally handed over and an ED safeguarding action was taken (referral, discussion with named nurse, or documented reason not to act). Target: 100% of flagged cases have a documented ED safeguarding decision. Sample: 20 consecutive flagged cases over 3 months (or all cases if fewer, given expected low volume)
- Change: Add a mandatory 'ambulance safeguarding flag received: yes/no, action taken' field to the ED triage template, so a flagged case cannot be booked in without an ED safeguarding decision being recorded.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-489.csv`
- Pitfalls: Safeguarding flags on ambulance forms are often free text and easy to miss at triage → make the field mandatory rather than free text; Small numbers given expected low case volume → extend the collection period to 6 months; Information governance restrictions on accessing ambulance safeguarding data → agree data-sharing with the ambulance trust's safeguarding lead first; Staff may under-report to avoid extra paperwork → make the field quick (drop-down, not free text); Loop closure stalls if the safeguarding committee meets infrequently → agree a fixed re-audit slot on the agenda in advance
- Pearls: Involve both trusts' safeguarding leads from the outset, since this is a cross-organisational pathway; Use the existing safeguarding committee to close the loop rather than a new meeting; Keep the case definition (types of flag counted) identical across cycles; Share anonymised case learning, not identifiable feedback, with individual crews

**NNA-490. What proportion of adults with suspected acute stroke conveyed by ambulance are admitted directly to a specialist acute stroke unit without first going to a general emergency department bay?** (new)
- Standard: NICE NG128 Stroke and transient ischaemic attack in over 16s, rec 1.3.1 (2008): "Admit everyone with suspected stroke directly to a specialist acute stroke unit after initial assessment, from either the community, the emergency department, or outpatient clinics." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng128/chapter/Recommendations
- Pass: The patient's first inpatient bed after ambulance arrival is the acute/hyperacute stroke unit, or a documented reason is recorded for going elsewhere (for example, needing immediate resuscitation). Target: ≥80% direct conveyance. Sample: 30 consecutive FAST-positive ambulance conveyances over 4 weeks
- Change: Agree a direct-conveyance protocol with the ambulance trust so a FAST-positive pre-alert triggers the stroke unit bed to be held and the patient taken straight there (bypassing the general ED cubicle) unless immediate resuscitation is needed.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-490.csv`
- Pitfalls: Bed availability on the stroke unit may block direct conveyance regardless of the pathway → record bed availability as a separate field; Small numbers in a unit without a hyperacute stroke service → adjust the pathway definition to the local model of care; FAST-positive pre-alerts may be over- or under-called → cross check against the final stroke/TIA/stroke-mimic diagnosis; ED staff may resist bypassing initial ED assessment → involve ED consultants in agreeing exceptions (e.g. unstable airway) in advance; Gains fade if the stroke unit's bed-holding process is not maintained → review bed-holding capacity at the re-audit
- Pearls: Agree the direct-conveyance protocol jointly with ambulance, ED and stroke medicine before cycle 1; Use the stroke operational delivery network meeting, which already exists, to close the loop; Track bed availability as a confounder so failures to bypass are not all attributed to the pathway; Keep the FAST-positive definition identical across both cycles

**NNA-491. What proportion of adults with an ambulance-diagnosed ST-elevation myocardial infarction receive a 300 mg aspirin loading dose before hospital arrival?** (new)
- Standard: NICE NG185 Acute coronary syndromes, rec 1.1.4 (2010): "Offer people with acute STEMI a single loading dose of 300 mg aspirin as soon as possible unless there is clear evidence that they are allergic to it." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng185/chapter/Recommendations
- Pass: 300 mg aspirin is given by the ambulance crew (or already taken and confirmed) before hospital arrival, or a documented allergy/contraindication is recorded. Target: ≥95%. Sample: 30 consecutive ambulance-diagnosed STEMI patients over 3 months (or all cases if fewer)
- Change: Feed back cases where aspirin was omitted or delayed to the ambulance trust's cardiac clinical lead, and add a mandatory 'aspirin given: dose/time or reason not given' field to the ambulance STEMI pathway record.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-491.csv`
- Pitfalls: Patients who self-medicate with aspirin before the ambulance arrives may be miscounted → record 'already taken' as a separate category; Small numbers of pre-hospital STEMI diagnoses in a smaller ambulance sector → pool data across the cardiac network; Allergy documentation is sometimes missing rather than a true contraindication → distinguish 'documented allergy' from 'not recorded'; Crews may feel blamed for a system-level cath lab bottleneck → keep the audit focused on the aspirin step only; Gains fade if the mandatory field is removed in a system update → recheck after any ambulance ePR change
- Pearls: Agree data access with the ambulance trust's cardiac clinical lead before starting; Use the cardiac network's existing primary PCI governance meeting to close the loop; Keep the STEMI diagnosis definition (ambulance 12-lead ECG criteria) identical across cycles; Share results as a learning bulletin for crews, not a named performance table

**NNA-492. What proportion of adults who achieve return of spontaneous circulation after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest have their oxygen saturation titrated to 94-98% by the time of ED handover?** (new)
- Standard: Resuscitation Council UK, Post-resuscitation care guidelines (2021, updated July 2023): "After ROSC, once SpO2 can be measured reliably or arterial blood gas values are obtained, titrate the inspired oxygen to achieve an arterial oxygen saturation of 94-98% ... Avoid hypoxaemia ... Avoid hyperoxaemia following ROSC." https://www.resus.org.uk/library/2021-resuscitation-guidelines/post-resuscitation-care-guidelines
- Pass: The last recorded SpO2 before ED handover is 94-98%, or a documented reason for a different target is recorded (for example, known chronic respiratory disease with a lower target). Target: ≥80% within target range at handover. Sample: 20 consecutive ROSC patients over 6 months (or all cases if fewer, given expected low volume)
- Change: Add a 'post-ROSC oxygen target 94-98%' prompt to the ambulance cardiac arrest care bundle card and the post-ROSC section of the electronic patient report form, so oxygen is actively titrated down once saturations are reliably measured.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-492.csv`
- Pitfalls: Pulse oximetry can be unreliable in a cold, shut-down post-arrest patient → record whether the SpO2 reading was judged reliable; Small numbers given expected low ROSC volume → extend the collection period or pool with a neighbouring ambulance sector; Crews may keep FiO2 high out of caution → reinforce the harm of hyperoxaemia in training, not just hypoxaemia; Definitions of 'reliable SpO2' vary → agree a working definition with the ambulance trust before cycle 1; Gains fade without refresher training after the initial rollout → add to the annual post-resuscitation care update
- Pearls: Link the audit to the trust's existing out-of-hospital cardiac arrest outcomes review meeting; Recruit a resuscitation officer from both the ambulance trust and the ED as joint audit leads; Keep the SpO2 target and 'reliable reading' definitions identical for both cycles; Feed results back through the ambulance trust's cardiac arrest governance process, which already exists

**NNA-493. What proportion of adults with return of spontaneous circulation after cardiac arrest of presumed cardiac cause are transported directly to a hospital with 24/7 primary PCI capability?** (new)
- Standard: Resuscitation Council UK, Post-resuscitation care guidelines (2021, updated July 2023): "Adult patients with a cardiac arrest of presumed cardiac aetiology should be transported directly to a hospital with 24/7 coronary angiography capability." https://www.resus.org.uk/library/2021-resuscitation-guidelines/post-resuscitation-care-guidelines
- Pass: The patient is taken directly to a 24/7 primary PCI centre, or a documented reason for going elsewhere is recorded (for example, airway instability requiring the nearest ED). Target: ≥80% direct conveyance where clinically appropriate. Sample: 20 consecutive eligible ROSC patients over 6 months (or all cases if fewer)
- Change: Agree a documented destination-decision algorithm with the ambulance trust's cardiac arrest desk so presumed-cardiac ROSC cases bypass the nearest general ED and go directly to the network's 24/7 PCI centre unless airway or scene factors prevent it.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-493.csv`
- Pitfalls: Presumed cardiac cause is a judgement call and can be coded inconsistently → agree the coding criteria with ambulance clinicians before cycle 1; Rural areas may have long transfer times to the PCI centre → record transfer distance as a confounder; Small numbers given expected low ROSC volume → pool data across the network if a single ambulance sector is too small; Onward inter-hospital transfers add delay and risk if the algorithm is not followed → track onward transfers as a secondary outcome; Improvement is not sustained if the algorithm is not built into ambulance dispatch software → make it a system default rather than a memory-based decision
- Pearls: Agree the destination algorithm jointly between the ambulance trust and the cardiac network before starting; Use the existing out-of-hospital cardiac arrest outcomes governance meeting to close the loop; Keep the 'presumed cardiac cause' definition identical across both cycles; Track time from ROSC to cath lab as well as destination choice, since it is the outcome that matters clinically

**NNA-494. What proportion of adults with return of spontaneous circulation who remain comatose have active fever prevention (temperature kept below 37.7°C) documented for the first 72 hours?** (new)
- Standard: Resuscitation Council UK, Post-resuscitation care guidelines (2021, updated July 2023): "Continuously monitor the core temperature in patients who remain comatose after ROSC. Actively prevent fever (defined as a temperature > 37.7°C) for at least 72 h in post-cardiac arrest patients who remain comatose." https://www.resus.org.uk/library/2021-resuscitation-guidelines/post-resuscitation-care-guidelines
- Pass: Core temperature is continuously monitored and stays below 37.7°C throughout the first 72 hours, or an active fever-prevention intervention (antipyretic, cooling device) is documented whenever it rises above that threshold. Target: ≥90%. Sample: 20 consecutive comatose post-ROSC patients over 6 months (or all cases if fewer)
- Change: Add a 'post-ROSC fever prevention (target <37.7°C for 72 hours)' order set to the critical care admission bundle, with a nurse-initiated antipyretic protocol that fires automatically when temperature crosses the threshold.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-494.csv`
- Pitfalls: Continuous core temperature monitoring devices are not always available → record the monitoring method used (core probe, bladder, tympanic); Small numbers because comatose ROSC admissions are infrequent → extend the collection period to 6-12 months; Staff may treat fever reactively rather than proactively → make the order set nurse-initiated so no medical review delay is needed; Definitions of 'active prevention' vary between units → agree what counts (paracetamol, cooling blanket, ice packs) before cycle 1; Gains fade after critical care nursing rotation → include in critical care induction training
- Pearls: Recruit the critical care outreach or resuscitation officer team to help identify eligible cases prospectively; Use an existing critical care mortality and morbidity or resuscitation governance meeting to close the loop; Keep the 37.7°C threshold and monitoring definitions identical across cycles; Track antipyretic administration alongside temperature trend, not temperature alone

**NNA-495. What proportion of adults aged 65 and over attended by an ambulance after a fall, but not conveyed to hospital, are referred for a comprehensive falls assessment?** (new)
- Standard: NICE NG249 Falls: assessment and prevention in older people and in people 50 and over at higher risk, rec 1.1.3 (2025): "Offer a comprehensive falls assessment and comprehensive falls management ... for people who ... have fallen and cannot get up without help, or ... have had 2 or more falls in the last 12 months." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng249/chapter/Recommendations
- Pass: A referral to a community falls service (or GP with a falls-specific request) is made and documented at the time of the ambulance 'see and treat, not conveyed' episode for a patient meeting the assessment criteria. Target: ≥85%. Sample: 30 consecutive non-conveyed fall attendances over 4 weeks
- Change: Add a mandatory 'falls service referral: yes/no, reason' field to the ambulance non-conveyance falls pathway, with a direct electronic referral route to the local falls service built into the ambulance ePR.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-495.csv`
- Pitfalls: Non-conveyed falls attendances are not always well documented → agree a minimum dataset with the ambulance trust before cycle 1; Falls services vary in how they accept ambulance referrals → confirm the referral route works before auditing uptake; Small numbers if 'not conveyed' coding is inconsistent → review ambulance coding practice first; Ambulance crews under time pressure may skip the referral step → make it a single click in the ePR rather than a phone call; Gains fade if the falls service cannot cope with increased referrals → agree capacity with the falls service before scaling up
- Pearls: Involve the community falls service lead and the ambulance trust's falls lead together from the start; Use the trust's existing falls prevention steering group to close the loop; Keep the NG249 referral criteria identical across both cycles; Track whether referrals are actually acted on by the falls service, not just made

**NNA-496. What proportion of ED patients on a time-critical medication (Parkinson's, insulin, anti-epileptic, immunosuppressant, or long-term steroid) receive their next scheduled dose at the usual time while waiting in the department?** (new)
- Standard: RCEM Safety Flash: Time Critical Medication (November 2023): "All patients should have time critical medications prescribed and administered at their usual time whilst in the ED." https://rcem.ac.uk/wp-content/uploads/2023/11/Time-Critical-Medication-Safety-Flash-V8-Final-1.pdf
- Pass: The patient's time-critical medication due while in the ED is prescribed and administered within 30 minutes of its usual time, or a documented clinical reason for delay/omission is recorded. Target: ≥90%. Sample: 40 consecutive eligible patients over 4 weeks
- Change: Display the UKCPA patient-facing poster at reception/triage so patients can flag their own time-critical medicines, add a mandatory 'time-critical medication' triage field that creates a timed EPMA task, and confirm ED pharmacy cover for medicines availability.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-496.csv`
- Pitfalls: Patients may not know or disclose that a medicine is time-critical → use the UKCPA poster to prompt disclosure; Triage staff may not recognise all time-critical drug classes → use the MISSED mnemonic (movement, immunomodulators, sugar, steroids, epilepsy, DOACs) in training; Small numbers if flagging is inconsistent → audit the flagging rate itself as a secondary measure; ED pharmacy may not have 24/7 cover → record time of day to see if out-of-hours delays predominate; Improvement fades once the initial safety flash awareness fades → repeat the poster and training at 6-monthly intervals
- Pearls: Display the RCEM/UKCPA poster at triage before starting data collection; Recruit the ED pharmacist as a co-lead, since medicines availability is part of the standard; Use the trust medication safety group, which already exists, to close the loop; Keep the same list of time-critical drug classes (the MISSED categories) across both cycles

**NNA-497. What proportion of adults on long-term steroid therapy who present with signs of possible adrenal crisis receive hydrocortisone promptly?** (new)
- Standard: RCEM Safety Flash: Cortico-Steroid Dependency (December 2023): "Patients on long term steroid therapy (by any route) are at risk of an adrenal crisis if they miss their medication or have intercurrent illness/injury. ... Start steroids promptly in patients at risk of an adrenal crisis. ... Severe intercurrent illness ... Hydrocortisone 100mg IM or IV." https://rcem.ac.uk/wp-content/uploads/2023/12/Cortico_Steroid_Dependancy_Safety_Flash_v8.pdf
- Pass: Hydrocortisone 100 mg IM or IV is given within 30 minutes of triage/first assessment in a steroid-dependent patient with severe intercurrent illness (persistent vomiting, acute trauma, sepsis or surgery). Target: ≥90%. Sample: 20 consecutive eligible presentations over 6 months (or all cases if fewer, given expected low volume)
- Change: Add a mandatory 'steroid card/medic alert seen: yes/no' question to the ED triage template, stock pre-drawn hydrocortisone 100 mg in the resus room drug cupboard, and add an adrenal crisis order set to the ED EPR.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-497.csv`
- Pitfalls: Adrenal crisis presentations are non-specific and easily missed → use the RCEM safety flash's red-flag list (nausea/vomiting, abdominal pain, confusion, syncope, unexplained fever, long-lie) as the case-finding filter; Small numbers given expected low volume → extend the collection period to 12 months if needed; Steroid cards are not always carried → also check EPR medication history and GP summary care record; Hydrocortisone may not be immediately available on the resus trolley → confirm stock location with pharmacy before cycle 1; Gains fade once the safety flash is no longer fresh in staff minds → repeat awareness training at 6-monthly intervals
- Pearls: Display the NHS Steroid Emergency Card image at triage as a visual prompt; Recruit an ED pharmacist to confirm hydrocortisone stocking before starting; Use the ED patient safety meeting, which already exists, to close the loop; Keep the case-finding red-flag list identical across both cycles

**NNA-498. What proportion of children under 16 with a suspected sepsis red flag identified by an ambulance crew have a sepsis pre-alert call made to the receiving emergency department?** (new)
- Standard: NICE NG254 Suspected sepsis in under 16s: recognition, diagnosis and early management, rec 1.7.3 (2025): "Treat the risk of sepsis as an emergency and refer immediately for emergency medical care by the most appropriate means of transport (usually 999 ambulance) if a child or young person with suspected sepsis meets any high risk criteria in table 3." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng254/chapter/Recommendations
- Pass: A structured pre-alert call is made to the receiving ED before arrival, stating that a high-risk sepsis criterion has been identified. Target: ≥85%. Sample: 20 consecutive eligible children over 6 months (or all cases if fewer, given expected low volume)
- Change: Add a paediatric sepsis red-flag prompt to the ambulance clinical decision-support tool that triggers a structured pre-alert message, and set the ED to open the paediatric sepsis order set automatically when a sepsis pre-alert is received.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-498.csv`
- Pitfalls: High-risk criteria may not be explicitly documented by ambulance crews → agree a checklist with the ambulance trust before cycle 1; Small numbers given expected low paediatric sepsis volume → pool across a longer period or with a neighbouring trust; Pre-alert calls may mention 'unwell child' without naming sepsis specifically → record whether the word 'sepsis' or 'high risk' was used; Ambulance crews may feel audited without being consulted → involve the paediatric-trained ambulance clinical lead in the design; Gains fade once the decision-support prompt is switched off in an update → recheck after any ambulance system change
- Pearls: Link the audit to the existing paediatric sepsis quality improvement work already running in the ED; Recruit a paediatric emergency nurse and the ambulance trust's paediatric lead as joint owners; Use the paediatric emergency governance meeting to close the loop; Track time to antibiotics as the outcome that ultimately matters, alongside the process measure of pre-alerting

**NNA-499. What proportion of patients cared for in a corridor or other non-designated clinical space in the ED have a full set of observations recorded at least hourly?** (new)
- Standard: Local standard, based on NICE CG50 Acutely ill patients in hospital, rec 1.3 (2007) principle of physiological track-and-trigger monitoring for all acutely unwell patients regardless of location: "Physiological observations should be monitored at least every 12 hours, unless a decision has been made at a senior level to increase or decrease this frequency for an individual patient." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg50/chapter/Recommendations
- Pass: A full set of observations (respiratory rate, oxygen saturation, blood pressure, pulse, temperature, consciousness level) is recorded at least hourly for every hour spent in a corridor or non-designated space, or a documented senior decision sets a different frequency. Target: ≥90%. Sample: 40 consecutive corridor-care episodes over 2 weeks
- Change: Name a corridor-care safety nurse on each shift with explicit responsibility for hourly observations and NEWS2 escalation, and flag every corridor-care patient on the electronic tracking board with a visible observation-due countdown.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-499.csv`
- Pitfalls: Corridor-care time is not always logged separately from cubicle time → agree a location-logging method before cycle 1; Staff may under-document during periods of extreme pressure, the exact time this audit targets → use direct spot-checks as well as retrospective chart review; Numbers vary hugely by day-of-week surge → sample across several different pressure levels; Staff may see this as adding more paperwork during an already unsafe situation → pair the audit with the safety-nurse role, not extra forms; Improvement is not sustained if the role is dropped once escalation pressure eases → keep it as a standing response to a defined occupancy trigger
- Pearls: Agree with senior nursing and medical leads what counts as 'corridor care' before starting; Use the trust's existing overcrowding/escalation policy meeting to close the loop; Track NEWS2 escalation, not just observation frequency, as the outcome that matters; Keep the same location-logging method for both cycles

**NNA-500. What proportion of adults aged 65 and over attending the ED have a Clinical Frailty Scale score recorded at triage?** (new)
- Standard: NICE NG232 Head injury: assessment and early management, rec 1.4.2 (2023) and BGS Silver Book II principle that frailty assessment should start at first contact: "Consider that older people, or people who are frail, may have a lower threshold for CT scanning after a head injury because of an increased risk of both traumatic intracranial lesions and pre-existing neurological conditions that complicate assessment." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng232/chapter/Recommendations
- Pass: A Clinical Frailty Scale score (1-9) is recorded on the triage assessment for every patient aged 65 and over. Target: ≥90%. Sample: 50 consecutive patients aged 65 and over over 2 weeks
- Change: Make the Clinical Frailty Scale a mandatory field in the ED triage screen for every patient aged 65 and over (cannot complete triage without it), with an automatic prompt to refer to the frailty/same-day emergency care team when the score is 5 or more.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-500.csv`
- Pitfalls: CFS scoring needs a collateral history, which is not always available at triage → allow a 'provisional score, confirm later' option; Staff may not be trained in CFS scoring → provide a laminated CFS reference card at every triage desk; Small numbers if attendance data is not filtered correctly by age → double-check the age filter before sampling; Recording a score without acting on it (no referral) undermines the point → audit the referral step as well as the recording step; Gains fade after new starters join triage → add CFS training to ED induction
- Pearls: Involve the frailty/geriatric medicine team in designing the referral trigger before cycle 1; Use existing frailty service governance meetings to close the loop; Keep the referral threshold (CFS ≥5) identical across both cycles; Display CFS reference cards at every triage station, not just centrally

**NNA-501. What proportion of adults with acute severe hyperkalaemia (potassium 6.5 mmol/L or above, or ECG changes) in the ED receive calcium gluconate or calcium chloride within 15 minutes of the result being available?** (new)
- Standard: UK Kidney Association, Treatment of Acute Hyperkalaemia in Adults clinical practice guideline (2023): "IV calcium gluconate or calcium chloride should be given immediately to patients with severe hyperkalaemia (serum potassium ≥6.5 mmol/L) and/or ECG changes consistent with hyperkalaemia." https://ukkidney.org/sites/renal.org/files/FINAL-Hyperkalaemia-Guideline-June-2023.pdf
- Pass: Calcium gluconate or calcium chloride is given within 15 minutes of the potassium result being available (or of ECG changes being recognised) for patients meeting the severe hyperkalaemia definition. Target: ≥90%. Sample: 20 consecutive eligible patients over 3 months (or all cases if fewer)
- Change: Build a hyperkalaemia order set in the ED EPR that fires automatically when a potassium result of 6.5 mmol/L or above is filed, pre-selecting calcium gluconate 10 ml 10% with a one-click prescribe-and-administer pathway.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-501.csv`
- Pitfalls: Point-of-care and laboratory potassium results may be recorded on different systems → agree a single result-timestamp source before cycle 1; Small numbers given expected low volume of severe hyperkalaemia → extend the collection period to 6-12 months; ECG-change cases without an extreme potassium value are easy to miss in a lab-based search → also screen ED ECGs reported as hyperkalaemic pattern; Nursing may wait for medical review before giving calcium → confirm local policy allows nurse-initiated calcium via a patient group direction or protocol; Gains fade if the automatic order set is switched off in a system update → recheck after any EPR change
- Pearls: Agree the case-finding method (lab result search plus ECG report search) with the laboratory and ED IT teams before starting; Recruit an ED pharmacist to help design the order set; Use the ED patient safety meeting, which already exists, to close the loop; Keep the 6.5 mmol/L and 15-minute definitions identical across both cycles

**NNA-502. What proportion of adults presenting to the ED with suspected carbon monoxide poisoning have a carboxyhaemoglobin level measured before treatment decisions are made?** (new)
- Standard: UK Health Security Agency, Carbon Monoxide Poisoning: Diagnosis and Management (Public Health England/UKHSA toxicological guidance, 2021): "Carboxyhaemoglobin (COHb) concentration should be measured as soon as possible after exposure, either from an arterial or venous blood sample analysed by co-oximetry, to confirm the diagnosis and guide management." https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/carbon-monoxide-toxicological-overview
- Pass: A carboxyhaemoglobin level by co-oximetry is documented before a management decision (oxygen therapy duration, hyperbaric oxygen referral, discharge) is made. Target: ≥90%. Sample: 20 consecutive suspected carbon monoxide poisoning presentations over 6 months (or all cases if fewer)
- Change: Add a 'suspected carbon monoxide exposure' order set to the ED EPR that automatically requests a co-oximetry blood gas and prompts a fire and rescue service/Gas Safe notification and hyperbaric referral consideration.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-502.csv`
- Pitfalls: Mild or vague presentations (headache, flu-like symptoms) may not trigger suspicion → add a seasonal awareness campaign (winter heating season) alongside the audit; Small numbers given expected low local volume → extend the collection period to 12 months; Co-oximetry may not be available on every blood gas analyser → confirm equipment availability before cycle 1; Household/multiple casualties may not all be flagged to the same audit → cross-check ambulance dispatch data for clustered presentations; Gains fade outside the winter season when suspicion is lower → repeat awareness training before each heating season
- Pearls: Recruit ED toxicology/poisons information (TOXBASE) contacts as a resource, not a data source, when designing the order set; Use the ED patient safety meeting to close the loop; Keep the same case-finding method (clerking note search for 'carbon monoxide' or 'CO poisoning') across both cycles; Coordinate with the fire and rescue service so household safety checks follow confirmed cases

**NNA-503. What proportion of children discharged from the ED after a first anaphylaxis episode leave with two adrenaline auto-injectors and a written action plan?** (new)
- Standard: NICE NG258 Assessment and referral after emergency treatment for anaphylaxis, rec 1.1.15 (2026): "Before a person is discharged from hospital after emergency treatment for a suspected or confirmed anaphylactic reaction: provide them (or their family members or carers as appropriate) with 2 adrenaline auto-injectors as an interim measure ... and a written anaphylaxis action plan." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng258/chapter/Recommendations
- Pass: The discharge record confirms 2 adrenaline auto-injectors were supplied (or already owned and confirmed in date) and a written anaphylaxis action plan was given, with training on use documented. Target: ≥90%. Sample: 20 consecutive eligible discharges over 3 months (or all cases if fewer)
- Change: Build a mandatory anaphylaxis discharge bundle in the ED EPR that cannot be completed without ticking 'two auto-injectors supplied/confirmed', 'action plan given' and 'training given', with the auto-injectors and action plan template stocked in every paediatric bay.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-503.csv`
- Pitfalls: Families may already own auto-injectors, making 'supplied' an incomplete measure → record 'supplied or confirmed in-date and carried' as the combined pass criterion; Written action plans are sometimes given verbally only → audit for a physical or electronic copy actually handed over, not just advice given; Small numbers if paediatric anaphylaxis presentations are infrequent → extend the collection period to 6 months; Stock shortages of auto-injector trainer devices can limit training → confirm trainer-device stock with pharmacy before cycle 1; Gains fade if new staff are not shown the mandatory bundle → add to paediatric ED induction
- Pearls: Recruit the paediatric allergy service to help design the action-plan template; Use the paediatric emergency governance meeting to close the loop; Keep the discharge bundle definition identical across both cycles; Stock auto-injectors and action plans directly in paediatric bays to remove a barrier to completion

**NNA-504. What proportion of adults with a suspected ureteric colic who have significant pain in the ED receive their first dose of analgesia within 20 minutes of arrival?** (under-audited)
- Standard: NICE NG118 Renal and ureteric stones: assessment and management, rec 1.2.1 (2019): "Offer people with suspected renal colic a choice of NSAID, paracetamol or opioid if NSAIDs are contraindicated or not giving sufficient pain relief, as first-line treatment for pain relief." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng118/chapter/Recommendations
- Pass: A first dose of NSAID, paracetamol or opioid analgesia is given within 20 minutes of arrival for a patient with a pain score of 4 or more and suspected renal colic. Target: ≥90%. Sample: 30 consecutive eligible patients over 4 weeks
- Change: Introduce a nurse-initiated analgesia patient group direction for suspected renal colic at triage (NSAID unless contraindicated, otherwise paracetamol or opioid), prompted automatically when the triage template flags flank pain with a pain score of 4 or more.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-504.csv`
- Pitfalls: Pain scores are not always recorded at triage → include 'no pain score recorded' as its own category rather than excluding these patients; NSAID contraindications (renal impairment, GI bleed history) may not be checked before an audit reviewer assumes non-compliance → record contraindications explicitly; Small numbers in a lower-volume unit → extend the collection period to 6 weeks; Nursing staff may be reluctant to give analgesia before a doctor review → confirm the patient group direction is signed off by the relevant clinical governance committee before cycle 1; Gains fade if the patient group direction is not refreshed on renewal → set a renewal reminder alongside the re-audit date
- Pearls: Agree the patient group direction with pharmacy and medical leadership before starting; Recruit a triage nurse champion to help embed the new prompt; Use the ED pain management meeting, which already exists for other analgesia audits, to close the loop; Keep the pain-score threshold and analgesia options identical across both cycles

**NNA-505. What proportion of adults given IV opioid analgesia in the ED have their respiratory rate and sedation score checked within 30 minutes of the dose?** (new)
- Standard: Resuscitation Council UK / Royal College of Anaesthetists guidance on opioid safety, summarised in NHS England Patient Safety Alert on opioid medicines (2020) principle: "Patients receiving parenteral opioids should have their respiratory rate, oxygen saturation and sedation score monitored regularly following administration to detect early signs of opioid-induced respiratory depression." https://www.england.nhs.uk/patient-safety/patient-safety-alerts/
- Pass: A respiratory rate and sedation score are both documented within 30 minutes of any IV opioid dose given in the ED. Target: ≥90%. Sample: 30 consecutive IV opioid doses over 2 weeks
- Change: Set the EPMA IV opioid administration step to automatically create a 30-minute 'respiratory rate and sedation score due' nursing task on the tracking board, which cannot be dismissed until both are recorded.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-505.csv`
- Pitfalls: Observations may be recorded as part of routine hourly obs rather than a specific post-opioid check, making them hard to attribute → record the nearest observation time relative to the dose, not just whether one exists in the hour; Sedation scoring tools vary between departments → agree a single sedation scale before cycle 1; Small numbers on quieter shifts → sample across different times of day; Nursing staff already stretched may see this as extra burden → pair with the automatic EPMA task rather than a manual checklist; Gains fade if the EPMA task is removed in an update → recheck after any system change
- Pearls: Agree the sedation scoring tool with anaesthetics/critical care outreach before starting, so it is consistent across the hospital; Recruit an ED pharmacist to help design the EPMA task; Use the ED patient safety meeting to close the loop; Keep the 30-minute window and sedation scale identical across both cycles

**NNA-506. What proportion of adults with suspected sepsis who are discharged from the ED after a period of observation have a documented safety-netting plan given to them in writing?** (new)
- Standard: NICE NG253 Suspected sepsis: recognition, diagnosis and early management, rec 1.10.2 (2025): "Give people being discharged after a suspected sepsis episode (and their family members or carers as appropriate) verbal and written information ... about ... signs and symptoms that should prompt them to seek further medical help." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng253/chapter/Recommendations
- Pass: A written safety-netting leaflet listing red-flag symptoms and when to seek help is documented as given at discharge. Target: ≥90%. Sample: 30 consecutive eligible discharges over 4 weeks
- Change: Add a mandatory 'sepsis safety-netting leaflet given' tick box to the ED discharge template, linked to an automatic print of the leaflet whenever a sepsis screening tool has been used during the attendance.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-506.csv`
- Pitfalls: Verbal advice may be given but not documented → audit only what is written in the record, and note this limitation when presenting results; Leaflet availability may run out during busy shifts → confirm stock levels with the ED matron before cycle 1; Small numbers if sepsis screening is not consistently coded → cross-check against the sepsis screening tool completion rate; Staff may see this as an extra step in an already complex pathway → automate the print rather than relying on staff to remember; Gains fade if the automatic print is switched off in a system change → recheck after any EPR update
- Pearls: Use the existing sepsis steering group to design and own the leaflet trigger; Recruit an ED nurse educator to reinforce safety-netting messaging at induction; Use the ED patient safety meeting, which already exists for other sepsis audits, to close the loop; Keep the definition of 'sepsis screen performed' identical across both cycles

**NNA-507. What proportion of adults presenting to the ED with an acute exacerbation of COPD have their oxygen prescribed with a target saturation range appropriate to their risk of hypercapnia?** (under-audited)
- Standard: BTS/RCP/RCN emergency oxygen guideline, updated NICE NG115 COPD guideline, rec 1.2.9 (2018, updated 2019): "Use a target oxygen saturation range of 88-92% for patients with a history of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease who are at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure, until blood gas results are available." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng115/chapter/Recommendations
- Pass: An oxygen target saturation range of 88-92% is documented on the drug chart/oxygen prescription for a patient with known or suspected hypercapnic risk, before or pending the first blood gas. Target: ≥90%. Sample: 30 consecutive eligible patients over 2 weeks
- Change: Make the oxygen target saturation range a mandatory field on the ED electronic drug chart whenever a COPD diagnosis flag is present, defaulting to 88-92% with an override reason required to change it.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-507.csv`
- Pitfalls: Undiagnosed COPD patients may not be flagged → include 'newly suspected' cases identified from smoking history and examination, not only coded diagnoses; Staff may prescribe 94-98% by habit → make the correct range the system default rather than relying on memory; Small numbers on quieter shifts → sample across a longer period if COPD presentations are infrequent; Definitions of 'at risk of hypercapnia' can be disputed → agree the criteria (known COPD, previous NIV, known CO2 retention) before cycle 1; Gains fade if the default is changed in a system update → recheck after any EPR change
- Pearls: Involve the respiratory team in agreeing the target-range default and override reasons; Recruit an ED pharmacist to help build the mandatory field; Use joint ED-respiratory governance to close the loop; Keep the 88-92% threshold and 'at risk' definition identical across both cycles

**NNA-508. What proportion of adults with a suspected ectopic pregnancy have a formal transvaginal ultrasound or gynaecology review arranged within 24 hours of presenting to the ED?** (new)
- Standard: NICE NG126 Ectopic pregnancy and miscarriage: diagnosis and initial management, rec 1.2.4 (2019, updated 2021): "Refer women and pregnant people to an early pregnancy assessment service if they are more than 6 weeks pregnant, or if the gestation is uncertain and they have pain and/or bleeding, or other complications ... to confirm the location and viability of the pregnancy." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng126/chapter/Recommendations
- Pass: A referral to the early pregnancy assessment service (or a transvaginal ultrasound/gynaecology review if the service is closed) is made and actioned within 24 hours of ED presentation. Target: ≥90%. Sample: 30 consecutive eligible attendances over 4 weeks
- Change: Add a direct electronic referral route from the ED clerking template to the early pregnancy assessment unit, with a weekend/out-of-hours pathway to on-call gynaecology so referrals made overnight are still seen within 24 hours.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-508.csv`
- Pitfalls: Weekend and overnight presentations are the most likely to breach 24 hours → analyse weekday versus weekend/overnight separately; Haemodynamically unstable patients go straight to theatre and should be analysed separately, not counted as a breach → exclude or flag them; Small numbers in a unit with a low volume of early pregnancy attendances → extend the collection period to 6 weeks; Referral may be made but the appointment not actually booked → audit the actual scan/review time, not just referral completion; Gains fade if weekend gynaecology cover is not sustained → confirm the out-of-hours pathway is resourced before scaling up
- Pearls: Agree the out-of-hours pathway with gynaecology before starting data collection; Recruit the early pregnancy assessment unit lead as a co-owner of the audit; Use the joint ED-gynaecology governance meeting to close the loop; Keep the referral criteria and 24-hour definition identical across both cycles

**NNA-509. What proportion of adults with suspected acute limb ischaemia in the ED are discussed with the vascular surgery on-call team within 30 minutes of the diagnosis being suspected?** (new)
- Standard: Vascular Society of Great Britain and Ireland, Quality Improvement Framework for Acute Limb Ischaemia (2020): "Patients with suspected acute limb ischaemia should be discussed with a vascular surgeon immediately, and those with an ischaemic limb should be assessed by a vascular surgeon within 30 minutes of referral." https://www.vascularsociety.org.uk/_userfiles/pages/files/Resources/VSGBI%20Acute%20Limb%20Ischaemia%20QI%20Framework.pdf
- Pass: The vascular surgery on-call team is contacted (call time documented) within 30 minutes of a clinician first documenting suspected acute limb ischaemia. Target: ≥90%. Sample: 15 consecutive eligible presentations over 6 months (or all cases if fewer, given expected low volume)
- Change: Add an 'acute limb ischaemia' one-click referral button to the ED EPR that pages the vascular on-call team directly and time-stamps the call automatically, bypassing switchboard.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-509.csv`
- Pitfalls: Suspicion is not always explicitly time-stamped in free-text notes → train staff to write the time of suspicion as a discrete entry; Small numbers given the expected low volume of this presentation → collect over 6-12 months or pool across a vascular network; Switchboard/bleep delays may be outside ED control → record whether the delay was in ED referral or in reaching the vascular team; Anticoagulation may be delayed while awaiting vascular advice → audit this as a secondary process measure; Gains fade if the one-click referral button is removed in an EPR update → recheck after any system change
- Pearls: Agree the case-finding method (clerking note text search for limb ischaemia symptoms) with ED and vascular leads before starting; Recruit the vascular surgery on-call rota lead as a co-owner of the audit; Use the joint ED-vascular governance meeting to close the loop; Keep the 30-minute definition and referral method identical across both cycles

**NNA-510. What proportion of adults triaged as category 2 (very urgent) in the ED are seen by a clinician within 10 minutes of triage?** (new)
- Standard: Manchester Triage Group / RCEM Triage position statement, summarised in RCEM Best Practice Guideline: Triage (2017, reviewed): "Patients triaged as 'very urgent' (category 2) should be seen by a clinician within 10 minutes of arrival at triage." https://rcem.ac.uk/wp-content/uploads/2021/10/Triage_Guideline.pdf
- Pass: Time from triage completion to first clinician (doctor, ACP or ENP) contact is 10 minutes or less for a category 2 patient. Target: ≥90%. Sample: 40 consecutive category 2 triage episodes over 2 weeks
- Change: Add a category 2 visual flag and 10-minute countdown to the ED tracking board, with a nurse-in-charge escalation if the countdown expires before a clinician has been assigned.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-510.csv`
- Pitfalls: Tracking system timestamps can be inaccurate if staff log in retrospectively → spot-check a sample against direct observation; Occupancy pressure is the main driver of delay and is outside the audit's control → record occupancy as a confounder, not an excuse to exclude cases; Small numbers on quiet shifts → sample across day, evening and night shifts; Staff may feel individually blamed for system-level overcrowding → present results as a department-level flow measure, not a named performance table; Gains fade once escalation fatigue sets in during sustained high occupancy → review escalation triggers at the re-audit
- Pearls: Agree the triage-category definitions with the ED triage lead before starting; Use the department's existing flow/safety huddle to close the loop; Keep the 10-minute definition and category 2 criteria identical across both cycles; Track occupancy alongside compliance so the effect of flow pressure is visible, not hidden

**NNA-511. What proportion of adults discharged from the ED with a new diagnosis of atrial fibrillation have anticoagulation risk (CHA2DS2-VASc) formally assessed before discharge?** (new)
- Standard: NICE NG196 Atrial fibrillation: diagnosis and management, rec 1.4.1 (2021): "Use the CHA2DS2-VASc score to assess stroke risk in people with any of the following: symptomatic or asymptomatic paroxysmal, persistent or permanent atrial fibrillation ... atrial flutter ... a continuing risk of arrhythmia recurrence after cardioversion back to sinus rhythm." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng196/chapter/Recommendations
- Pass: A CHA2DS2-VASc score is calculated and documented, with an anticoagulation decision (start, defer to GP/cardiology, or not indicated) recorded before ED discharge. Target: ≥90%. Sample: 30 consecutive eligible discharges over 4 weeks
- Change: Add a mandatory CHA2DS2-VASc calculator field to the ED discharge template whenever an AF/flutter diagnosis code is entered, which must be completed (with an anticoagulation decision) before the discharge letter can be printed.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-511.csv`
- Pitfalls: New AF is sometimes coded under a general 'palpitations' diagnosis → search discharge diagnoses broadly, not just the exact AF code; Score components (hypertension, diabetes, vascular disease history) may be incompletely documented → record 'unable to calculate, missing data' as its own category; Small numbers in a lower-volume unit → extend the collection period to 6 weeks; Clinicians may defer the decision to the GP without a formal score → count 'deferred with reason' as a partial pass only if the score itself is still documented; Gains fade if the mandatory field is bypassed by overriding it → monitor override rates at the re-audit
- Pearls: Agree the discharge coding search terms with the ED coding/informatics team before starting; Recruit a cardiology liaison clinician to help design the mandatory field and anticoagulation guidance; Use the joint ED-cardiology governance meeting to close the loop; Keep the CHA2DS2-VASc calculation method and pass definition identical across both cycles

**NNA-512. When ambulance crews attend a person who has self-harmed but does not need urgent physical care, what proportion have a documented discussion of the person's care/safety plan and this information passed on if not conveyed?** (new)
- Standard: NICE NG225 Self-harm: assessment, management and preventing recurrence, rec 1.7.9 (2022): "When attending a person who has self-harmed but who does not need urgent physical care, ambulance staff and paramedics should: discuss with the person the best way that the ambulance service can help them; follow the person's care plan and safety plan if available; seek advice from mental health professionals, where necessary; record relevant information ... and pass this information to staff if the person is conveyed, or share it with other relevant people involved in the person's ongoing care if the person is not being conveyed." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng225/chapter/Recommendations
- Pass: The ambulance record documents that the person's existing care/safety plan was checked and followed (or that none existed), and that relevant information was shared with the person's ongoing care team if not conveyed. Target: ≥85%. Sample: 20 consecutive eligible non-conveyance episodes over 3 months (or all cases if fewer)
- Change: Add a structured self-harm non-conveyance section to the ambulance electronic patient record with mandatory fields for care/safety plan check, mental health advice sought, and information sharing, linked to a direct referral route to the crisis/home treatment team.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-512.csv`
- Pitfalls: Non-conveyed episodes are not always separately coded from other 'not conveyed' outcomes → agree a coding filter with the ambulance trust before cycle 1; Care and safety plans may exist in mental health records the ambulance crew cannot access in real time → record whether the crew had access to the plan, not just whether one existed; Small numbers given how this presentation is coded → extend the collection period to 6 months; Crews may under-document sensitive conversations → keep the audit tool short and focused on the specific NG225 items; Gains fade if the crisis team referral route is not resourced → confirm capacity with the crisis team before scaling up
- Pearls: Involve the ambulance trust's mental health lead and the local crisis team from the start; Use an existing joint mental health/ambulance governance meeting to close the loop; Keep the coding filter for 'self-harm, not conveyed' identical across both cycles; Track whether alternative services were actually accessed, not just discussed, as a secondary outcome

**NNA-513. What proportion of pre-hospital chest decompressions for suspected tension pneumothorax are performed only in patients with documented haemodynamic instability or severe respiratory compromise?** (new)
- Standard: NICE NG39 Major trauma: assessment and initial management, rec 1.3.4 (2016): "Only perform chest decompression in a patient with suspected tension pneumothorax if there is haemodynamic instability or severe respiratory compromise." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng39/chapter/Recommendations
- Pass: The pre-hospital record documents haemodynamic instability (hypotension, shock) or severe respiratory compromise immediately before chest decompression was performed. Target: ≥90%. Sample: 15 consecutive pre-hospital chest decompressions over 6 months (or all cases if fewer, given expected low volume)
- Change: Add a mandatory 'indication for decompression: haemodynamic instability / severe respiratory compromise' field to the ambulance/HEMS chest trauma pathway, and reinforce the NG39 threshold in the trauma network's annual pre-hospital training update.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-513.csv`
- Pitfalls: Very low case numbers make single-trust audit under-powered → pool data across the regional trauma network; Retrospective documentation may under-record the clinical picture at the time of decision → use direct crew debrief where possible, in addition to the written record; Post-decompression observation for recurrence is a separate but related safety step → record this alongside indication appropriateness; Crews may feel individually scrutinised for a rare, high-stakes decision → present findings in aggregate, with a focus on system learning; Gains fade without regular case-based teaching → use real (anonymised) cases in the annual training update
- Pearls: Agree with the regional trauma network's pre-hospital lead to pool data across the network before starting; Recruit a HEMS/critical care paramedic clinical lead as co-owner of the audit; Use the trauma governance meeting, which already exists, to close the loop; Keep the indication definitions (haemodynamic instability, severe respiratory compromise) identical across both cycles

**NNA-514. What proportion of adults on warfarin with a head injury and CT-confirmed intracranial haemorrhage receive prothrombin complex concentrate within 1 hour of the scan result?** (under-audited)
- Standard: NICE NG232 Head injury: assessment and early management, rec 1.5.13 (2023), cross-referring to NICE's guideline on blood transfusion: "For advice on reversing vitamin K antagonists for people with traumatic intracranial haemorrhage, see the section on prothrombin complex concentrate in NICE's guideline on blood transfusion." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng232/chapter/Recommendations
- Pass: Prothrombin complex concentrate is prescribed and administered within 1 hour of the CT report confirming intracranial haemorrhage in a patient taking a vitamin K antagonist. Target: ≥90%. Sample: 15 consecutive eligible patients over 6 months (or all cases if fewer, given expected low volume)
- Change: Build a 'warfarin-associated intracranial haemorrhage' order set in the ED EPR that fires automatically when a CT report containing both 'intracranial haemorrhage' and an anticoagulant flag is filed, pre-selecting weight-based prothrombin complex concentrate and vitamin K.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-514.csv`
- Pitfalls: Small numbers given expected low volume of warfarin-associated intracranial haemorrhage → extend the collection period to 12 months; PCC may be delayed by blood bank turnaround time rather than a clinical decision delay → record the time PCC was requested as well as when it was given; INR results may lag behind the clinical decision to reverse → do not delay treatment purely for INR confirmation, in line with the guideline's intent, and audit accordingly; DOAC-treated patients need a different reversal agent and should not be mixed into this sample → keep the two anticoagulant types in separate audits; Gains fade if the order set is switched off in an EPR update → recheck after any system change
- Pearls: Agree the order set design with haematology and pharmacy before starting; Recruit an ED pharmacist to identify eligible cases prospectively as a data-collection aid; Use the ED-haematology joint governance meeting, which already exists, to close the loop; Keep the same reversal-timing definition (from CT report to administration) across both cycles

**NNA-515. What proportion of adults with an ambulance-diagnosed STEMI, when the primary PCI centre is not the nearest hospital, are taken directly to the primary PCI centre rather than the nearest emergency department?** (new)
- Standard: NICE NG185 Acute coronary syndromes, rec 1.1.6 (2013): "Offer coronary angiography, with follow-on primary PCI if indicated, as the preferred coronary reperfusion strategy for people with acute STEMI, if: presentation is within 12 hours of onset of symptoms and primary PCI can be delivered within 120 minutes of the time when fibrinolysis could have been given." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng185/chapter/Recommendations
- Pass: The patient is taken directly to the primary PCI centre (bypassing the nearest non-PCI ED), or a documented reason for going to the nearest ED first is recorded (for example, cardiac arrest requiring immediate resuscitation, or the calculated travel time exceeding the network's bypass threshold). Target: ≥90% direct conveyance where within the network's agreed bypass threshold. Sample: 20 consecutive eligible patients over 6 months (or all cases if fewer)
- Change: Agree a documented bypass-distance threshold with the ambulance trust and cardiac network so any ambulance-diagnosed STEMI within the threshold travel time bypasses the nearest ED automatically, with the cath lab activated directly from the ambulance ECG transmission.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-515.csv`
- Pitfalls: Rural geography may mean bypass is not always feasible within the 120-minute window → record travel time and distance as confounders; Small numbers in a smaller ambulance sector → pool data across the cardiac network; Ambulance ECG transmission failures can force a default to the nearest ED → record technical failures as a separate reason category; Crews may default to the nearest ED out of habit → reinforce the bypass threshold in annual cardiac pathway training; Gains fade if cath lab activation from the ambulance ECG is not reliably actioned → audit cath lab response time alongside conveyance decision
- Pearls: Agree the bypass-distance threshold jointly with the ambulance trust and cardiac network before starting; Use the existing primary PCI governance meeting to close the loop; Keep the 12-hour symptom-onset window and destination definitions identical across both cycles; Track call-to-balloon time as the ultimate outcome, alongside the process measure of direct conveyance

**NNA-516. What proportion of children assessed by an ambulance crew with a NICE 'red' (high-risk) fever feature are conveyed immediately by emergency ambulance rather than left for a delayed or alternative assessment?** (new)
- Standard: NICE NG143 Fever in under 5s: assessment and initial management, rec 1.3.2 (2007): "Children with 'red' features ... should be referred immediately for emergency medical care by the most appropriate means of transport (usually 999 ambulance)." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng143/chapter/Recommendations
- Pass: A child with a documented NICE 'red' fever feature is conveyed by emergency ambulance immediately (not left at home or referred to a delayed pathway), or a documented clinical reason for an alternative pathway is recorded. Target: ≥95%. Sample: 20 consecutive eligible children over 6 months (or all cases if fewer, given expected low volume)
- Change: Build the NICE traffic light system into the ambulance paediatric assessment screen so a 'red' feature triggers a mandatory conveyance recommendation and a paediatric pre-alert prompt, with an override reason required to deviate.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-516.csv`
- Pitfalls: Traffic light features may be assessed inconsistently by non-paediatric-trained crews → provide a laminated traffic-light reference card on every vehicle; Small numbers given expected low volume of red-flag paediatric fever calls → extend the collection period to 12 months; Parents may decline conveyance despite advice → record 'declined against advice' as its own category, not a system failure; Ambulance and hospital records may use different fever assessment tools → agree a shared traffic-light tool with the paediatric department; Gains fade without refresher training → add to the ambulance trust's annual paediatric update
- Pearls: Agree the traffic-light assessment tool jointly with the paediatric emergency department before starting; Recruit the ambulance trust's paediatric clinical lead as a co-owner of the audit; Use the paediatric emergency governance meeting, which already exists, to close the loop; Keep the 'red feature' definition identical to the one used in the ED for continuity across the pathway

**NNA-517. What proportion of people with sudden-onset neurological symptoms assessed by an ambulance crew have a validated FAST (Face Arm Speech Test) screen documented before hypoglycaemia is excluded and a stroke pre-alert decision is made?** (new)
- Standard: NICE NG128 Stroke and transient ischaemic attack in over 16s, recs 1.1.1 and 1.1.2 (2008): "Use a validated tool, such as FAST (Face Arm Speech Test), outside hospital to screen people with sudden onset of neurological symptoms for a diagnosis of stroke or transient ischaemic attack (TIA). Exclude hypoglycaemia in people with sudden onset of neurological symptoms as the cause of these symptoms." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng128/chapter/Recommendations
- Pass: Both a documented FAST score and a documented capillary blood glucose (excluding hypoglycaemia) are recorded on the ambulance patient report form before the stroke pathway decision is made. Target: ≥95%. Sample: 30 consecutive eligible ambulance assessments over 2 weeks
- Change: Make both the FAST score and capillary glucose mandatory fields on the ambulance electronic patient report form before the stroke pre-alert option can be selected, so the sequence cannot be skipped.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-517.csv`
- Pitfalls: Capillary glucose may be checked but not documented in the neurological assessment section → search the whole ambulance record, not just the stroke-specific field; FAST scoring can be inconsistently applied by less experienced crews → provide a laminated FAST reference card on every vehicle; Small numbers if stroke-call coding is inconsistent → cross-check against the stroke pre-alert log as well as the neurological assessment field; Crews under time pressure may prioritise conveyance speed over full documentation → keep the mandatory fields quick (tick-box, not free text); Gains fade without refresher training → add to the ambulance trust's annual stroke pathway update
- Pearls: Agree the mandatory field design with the ambulance trust's stroke clinical lead before starting; Use the stroke operational delivery network meeting, which already exists, to close the loop; Keep the FAST tool and glucose threshold definitions identical across both cycles; Track pre-alert accuracy (stroke mimics versus confirmed stroke) as a secondary measure of the pathway's overall quality

**NNA-518. What proportion of adults with major trauma and active or suspected bleeding who are taking an anticoagulant have a documented decision about reversal made with, or by, a haematologist?** (new)
- Standard: NICE NG39 Major trauma: assessment and initial management, rec 1.5.11-1.5.12 (2016): "Do not reverse anticoagulation in patients who do not have active or suspected bleeding. For advice on reversing direct-acting oral anticoagulants (DOACs), see the MHRA safety advice on DOACs for a list of reversal agents." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng39/chapter/Recommendations
- Pass: For a bleeding trauma patient on an anticoagulant, the trauma record documents a reversal decision (agent given, or reversal not indicated) made with haematology input; anticoagulation is not reversed in a patient without active or suspected bleeding. Target: ≥90%. Sample: 20 consecutive eligible patients over 6 months (or all cases if fewer, given expected low volume)
- Change: Add a mandatory 'anticoagulant reversal decision: haematology contacted, agent/reason' field to the trauma team clerking proforma whenever an anticoagulant is flagged in the drug history.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-518.csv`
- Pitfalls: Anticoagulant use may not be reliably known at first assessment → cross-check with the GP summary care record and pharmacy medicines reconciliation; Small numbers given expected low volume of anticoagulated major trauma → extend the collection period to 12 months; Out-of-hours haematology advice may be by telephone and not always documented → agree a documentation standard for telephone advice before cycle 1; Reversal may be started before haematology is reached in a genuine emergency, which is appropriate → audit for a subsequent haematology discussion, not necessarily a prior one, in the most urgent cases; Gains fade if the mandatory field is not maintained after an EPR update → recheck after any system change
- Pearls: Agree the reversal pathway and documentation standard with haematology before starting; Recruit the trauma coordinator to flag eligible cases prospectively; Use the joint trauma-haematology governance meeting to close the loop; Keep the definitions of 'active or suspected bleeding' and 'reversal indicated' identical across both cycles

**NNA-519. What proportion of adults triaged in the ED with a pain score of 7 or more (severe pain) receive their first analgesia within 20 minutes of triage?** (under-audited)
- Standard: Local standard, based on the pain-severity thresholds used in RCEM's Pain in Children quality improvement programme (2021/22) extended to adults: "Patients in severe pain (pain score 7 or more out of 10) should receive their first dose of analgesia within 20 minutes of a pain score being recorded." https://rcem.ac.uk/wp-content/uploads/2022/02/Pain_in_Children_QIP_Info_Pack_2021-22_v4.pdf
- Pass: A first dose of analgesia (any route) is given within 20 minutes of a pain score of 7 or more being recorded at triage. Target: ≥90%. Sample: 30 consecutive eligible patients over 2 weeks
- Change: Introduce a nurse-initiated analgesia protocol at triage for any adult scoring 7 or more, covering oral and intranasal options that do not need a doctor's prescription first.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-519.csv`
- Pitfalls: Pain scores are not always recorded consistently by all triage staff → audit the recording rate itself as a secondary measure; Nurse-initiated analgesia protocols need pharmacy and governance sign-off before use → secure this before cycle 1; Small numbers on quieter shifts → sample across different shift types; Some patients decline analgesia or have a contraindication, which should not count as a breach → record these separately, not as failures; Gains fade if the protocol lapses on renewal → set a renewal reminder alongside the re-audit date
- Pearls: Agree the nurse-initiated analgesia protocol with pharmacy and medical leadership before starting; Recruit a triage nurse champion to help embed the change; Use the ED pain management meeting, which already exists for other analgesia audits, to close the loop; Keep the pain-score threshold (≥7) and time window identical across both cycles

**NNA-520. What proportion of patients whose ambulance handover is delayed beyond 60 minutes have a full set of vital sign observations recorded by ambulance or ED staff at least every 30 minutes while still in the ambulance or queue?** (new)
- Standard: AACE, Delayed Hospital Handovers: Impact Assessment of Patient Harm (November 2021), summarised on the AACE Hospital Handovers webpage (accessed 2026): "Over eight in ten of those whose 'handover' (from ambulance clinician to hospital clinician) was delayed beyond 60 minutes were assessed as having potentially experienced some level of harm; 53% low harm, 23% moderate harm and 9% (one patient in ten) could have been said to have experienced severe harm." https://aace.org.uk/hospital-handovers/
- Pass: A full set of vital sign observations is recorded at least every 30 minutes for every patient whose handover exceeds 60 minutes, with escalation to a senior clinician if NEWS2 rises. Target: ≥90%. Sample: 20 consecutive handovers exceeding 60 minutes over 4 weeks (or all cases if fewer)
- Change: Introduce a joint ambulance-ED 'queue safety officer' role during any period when more than 2 ambulances are waiting, responsible for cycling through queued patients to check and escalate observations every 30 minutes.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-520.csv`
- Pitfalls: Responsibility for observations during a handover delay can be unclear between ambulance and ED staff → agree ownership explicitly before cycle 1; Small numbers if 60-minute-plus delays are rare (a good sign operationally, but limits audit power) → extend the collection period; Ambulance staff may be tied up with other calls during a queue → record which service (ambulance or ED) took each observation; Staff may see this as adding a role during an already unsafe situation → frame it as protecting patients, not adding paperwork; Gains fade once escalation pressure passes and the role is dropped informally → tie the role to a defined occupancy/queue-length trigger, not to memory
- Pearls: Use the trust's existing ambulance handover delay escalation policy meeting to close the loop; Recruit both an ED matron and an ambulance operations manager as joint audit owners; Keep the 60-minute delay threshold and 30-minute observation interval identical across both cycles; Track NEWS2 escalation events as the safety outcome that matters most, not just the observation count

## Obstetrics, gynaecology and sexual health

**NNA-521. In women on continuous CTG monitoring in labour, what proportion of hourly fetal heart rate assessments had an in-person 'fresh eyes' review by a second clinician documented before the next hourly assessment?** (new)
- Standard: NICE NG229 Fetal monitoring in labour, rec 1.3.6 (2022): "Obtain an in-person review of every hourly assessment (see recommendation 1.3.5) by another clinician ("fresh eyes") for women on CTG, to be completed before the next assessment takes place." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng229/chapter/Recommendations
- Pass: The hourly CTG assessment has a documented fresh-eyes review (name/role and time) by a second clinician, completed before the next hourly assessment is due. Target: ≥90%. Sample: 40 consecutive women on continuous CTG monitoring in labour over the last 4 weeks, one CTG episode of at least 3 hours per woman
- Change: Add a timed 'fresh eyes review due at __:__' prompt to the CTG trace and electronic labour record that is generated automatically at each hourly assessment and must be signed by a second clinician before it can be marked complete.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-521.csv`
- Pitfalls: Paper CTG annotations are often illegible or missing a time → agree a single place (trace margin or e-record) and a minimum data set with the labour ward before cycle 1; Small numbers if the unit has few continuous-CTG labours in the sample window → extend the collection period rather than lowering the sample; Staff may see the fresh-eyes prompt as another tick-box → involve labour ward coordinators in designing the prompt and explain the Each Baby Counts rationale; Definition of 'in-person' review may be interpreted loosely (a verbal comment vs a documented review) → fix the definition and a single documentation location before data collection starts; Gains fade once the audit team rotates → make the fresh-eyes field mandatory in the EPR build rather than relying on a poster reminder
- Pearls: Recruit a labour ward co-ordinator and a supervisor of midwives/PMA as co-investigators so the change has authority on the ward; Agree the exact fresh-eyes documentation field and audit definition with labour ward before cycle 1 starts; Time the audit to include day and night shifts, as fresh-eyes reviews are more often missed at night; Share individual near-miss examples (anonymised) at the labour ward forum to build buy-in before the second cycle; Keep the re-audit sample the same size and season to allow fair comparison

**NNA-522. In women with a low risk of complications having intermittent auscultation in established first stage of labour, what proportion of documented auscultations were performed at least once every 15 minutes?** (new)
- Standard: NICE NG229 Fetal monitoring in labour, rec 1.2.9 (2017, amended 2026): "Offer women with a low risk of complications, fetal heart rate monitoring with intermittent auscultation when in established first stage of labour. Do this as follows: ... carry out intermittent auscultation immediately after a palpated contraction for at least 1 minute, repeated at least once every 15 minutes, and record it as a single rate." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng229/chapter/Recommendations
- Pass: For a woman on intermittent auscultation in established first stage, the interval between two consecutive documented auscultations does not exceed 15 minutes. Target: ≥90%. Sample: 40 consecutive low-risk women having intermittent auscultation in established first stage over the last 4 weeks
- Change: Build a 15-minute auscultation timer into the electronic partogram that flags amber when 12 minutes have elapsed since the last entry and red at 15 minutes, visible on the ward dashboard.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-522.csv`
- Pitfalls: Paper partograms with gaps in recording → exclude labours with more than 20% missing entries and note the exclusion rate; Busy labour ward staffing may make 15-minute auscultation genuinely difficult → review staffing ratios alongside the audit, not instead of the process change; Definition of 'established first stage' varies between recorders → agree the definition (4 cm plus regular contractions) with the labour ward before data collection; One midwife's caseload dominating the sample → sample across shifts and midwives; Improvement fading after the audit team moves on → make the electronic timer the permanent default rather than a temporary poster
- Pearls: Recruit a practice development midwife to co-lead so the change is owned by the ward, not just the audit team; Pilot the electronic timer on one bay before full roll-out to iron out false alarms; Use real (anonymised) examples of delayed auscultation from incident reports to explain the 'why' at launch; Cross-reference with the labour ward's Each Baby Counts and MBRRACE-UK action plan so this audit is not seen as a duplicate task; Feed results back to individual midwives confidentially as well as to the team, to support learning

**NNA-523. Once a woman has signs of, or is in confirmed second stage of labour, what proportion of documented intermittent auscultations were performed at least once every 5 minutes?** (new)
- Standard: NICE NG229 Fetal monitoring in labour, rec 1.2.10 (2007, amended 2026): "Once the woman has signs of, or is in confirmed second stage of labour: perform intermittent auscultation immediately after a palpated contraction for at least 1 minute, repeated at least once every 5 minutes and record it as a single rate." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng229/chapter/Recommendations
- Pass: In second stage, the interval between two consecutive documented auscultations does not exceed 5 minutes. Target: ≥90%. Sample: 40 consecutive women who laboured with intermittent auscultation and reached second stage over the last 4 weeks
- Change: Add a distinct 'second stage' mode to the electronic partogram auscultation timer that shortens the alert interval from 15 to 5 minutes as soon as second stage is confirmed.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-523.csv`
- Pitfalls: Ambiguity about the exact moment second stage starts → use the documented time of full dilatation or bearing-down urge as the trigger, agreed in advance; Very short second stages give few data points → record the number of auscultations expected as well as achieved; Staff may confuse this with the separate first-stage 15-minute standard → make the EPR mode change explicit and visible; Retrospective note review may miss verbal-only auscultations → accept only documented entries as per protocol; Losing momentum after go-live → include the second-stage timer in new starter induction
- Pearls: Pair this audit with the first-stage auscultation audit so both cycles share the same data collection visit; Get labour ward coordinator sign-off on the definition of second stage onset before starting; Use huddle boards to display real-time compliance during the embedding phase; Link learning to the unit's Each Baby Counts action plan; Keep sample size and season consistent at re-audit

**NNA-524. In women starting induction of labour, what proportion had a Bishop score and antenatal cardiotocography documented before the first method of induction was started?** (new)
- Standard: NICE NG207 Inducing labour, rec 1.5.1 (2008, amended 2021): "Ensure the position of the baby and the woman's condition are suitable for induction by: abdominally assessing the level and stability of the fetal head in the lower part of the uterus at or near the pelvic brim ... assessing and recording the Bishop score, confirming a normal fetal heart rate pattern using antenatal cardiotocography interpretation, confirming the absence of significant uterine contractions (not Braxton-Hicks) using cardiotocography." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng207/chapter/Recommendations
- Pass: A Bishop score and a CTG confirming a normal fetal heart rate pattern are both documented in the notes before the first induction method (sweep excluded) is administered. Target: ≥95%. Sample: 40 consecutive women started on induction of labour over the last 6-8 weeks
- Change: Redesign the induction of labour proforma so the Bishop score box and a mandatory pre-induction CTG result field must both be completed before the first prostaglandin, balloon or amniotomy step can be signed for.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-524.csv`
- Pitfalls: Bishop score sometimes recorded narratively rather than as a number → accept only a numeric or component score as compliant; CTG performed but not formally reported before induction starts → require a documented category (normal/suspicious/pathological), not just a trace reference; Staff shortages leading to skipped pre-induction CTG on busy days → escalate persistent gaps to the labour ward matron; Retrospective note-finding may undercount compliance if records are split between paper and EPR → check both systems for each case; Definition drift between cycles (e.g. accepting an antenatal CTG from earlier in the day as 'pre-induction') → fix the definition (within 4 hours of starting) before cycle 1
