- Pitfalls: Training certificates are held by individual staff members rather than centrally by the employer, failing the regulation's requirement → require submission of a copy to the central record as a condition of the training counting.; New starters and locums are not added to the training record promptly → build training-record creation into the pre-employment/induction checklist.; Records show that training happened but not what it covered, failing the 'nature of training' requirement → require a brief description or course title, not just a date.; Staff who have moved role (e.g. from operator to also acting as practitioner) are not flagged for additional training → cross-check role changes against training records annually.; Gains fade after a learning management system migration loses historical records → export and archive records before any system change.
- Pearls: Recruit the radiation protection supervisor and trust education/learning management system administrator together.; Use this audit to also identify any staff whose training has lapsed and needs urgent renewal.; Report the audit result to the trust's statutory and mandatory training compliance dashboard, since it likely already has a reporting mechanism.; Keep a simple named list of practitioners and operators, updated whenever the rota changes, to make future audits quick.

**NNA-591. For planned (non-emergency) interventional radiology procedures, what proportion of patients have their informed consent confirmed at a separate discussion with the radiologist actually performing the procedure, distinct from the initial information-giving discussion?** (new)
- Standard: Royal College of Radiologists, Standards for patient consent particular to radiology, second edition: "Interventional or invasive radiological procedures require particular attention in obtaining the express consent of the patient. In a planned procedure, the patient should receive information, verbally or in writing, in sufficient time before the procedure to consider it and to consult others if they so wish. The patient should have their informed consent confirmed at a separate discussion with the radiologist performing the procedure." https://www.bsgar.org/media/BFCR(12)8_consent.pdf
- Pass: The notes record two distinct consent-related contacts: an initial information-giving discussion in advance of the procedure, and a separate confirmation of consent with the performing radiologist, both documented with dates.. Target: ≥90%. Sample: 40 consecutive planned procedures over the last 2-3 months, from the interventional radiology booking system.
- Change: Add a mandatory 'consent confirmed by performing radiologist' field, with date, time and location, to the interventional radiology electronic procedure record, separate from the initial information-giving documentation.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-591.csv`
- Pitfalls: The 'separate discussion' happens in the procedure room immediately before sedation, which the standard specifically discourages → record the physical location, not just that a discussion happened.; Same-day add-on cases blur the distinction between initial information and confirmation → apply the emergency/unplanned exclusion strictly rather than stretching it to cover convenience add-ons.; A generic consent form is signed without evidence of a genuine second discussion → look for narrative evidence of the discussion, not just a signature.; Patients seen only briefly by a different radiologist than the one performing the procedure may not meet the standard's intent → record whether the confirming radiologist was the same person who performed the procedure.; Gains fade once the mandatory field becomes a box ticked without a real discussion → spot-check a sample against patient-reported experience where feasible.
- Pearls: Recruit the interventional radiology lead and a specialist nurse who runs pre-procedure clinics.; Use existing pre-assessment clinic letters as the source for the 'initial information' half of the audit.; Present findings alongside patient experience feedback on how well-prepared they felt for the procedure.; Keep this as a standing item in the interventional radiology multidisciplinary team meeting, not just a one-off project.

**NNA-592. What proportion of interventional radiology procedures classified locally as complex or carrying significant risk have written consent (a signed consent form), rather than verbal consent alone, documented before the procedure?** (new)
- Standard: Royal College of Radiologists, Standards for patient consent particular to radiology, second edition, citing General Medical Council guidance: "The General Medical Council (GMC) suggests that written consent should be taken in cases where: the treatment or procedure is complex and involves significant risk and/or side-effects... With planned procedures, consideration should be given to asking the patient to sign a written consent form for those examinations and procedures which are recognised to be more complex to undertake or which potentially carry a more serious risk of complication." https://www.bsgar.org/media/BFCR(12)8_consent.pdf
- Pass: For every procedure on the department's locally agreed 'complex/significant risk' list, a signed written consent form is present in the record before the procedure starts.. Target: 100%. Sample: 40 consecutive eligible procedures over the last 2-3 months, from the interventional radiology log.
- Change: Publish an agreed department list of procedures requiring written consent (built from the GMC/RCR criteria) and introduce procedure-specific consent forms for the highest-volume complex procedures, since the corpus shows procedure-specific forms are the fix that reliably works for consent completeness.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-592.csv`
- Pitfalls: Staff disagree on which procedures count as 'complex' without a published list → agree and publish the list with radiology leadership before cycle 1.; A generic hospital consent form is used instead of a procedure-specific one, missing procedure-relevant risks → track use of the correct, procedure-specific form as a separate data point.; Verbal consent is documented in detail but no form is signed, technically failing the standard despite good practice → count only signed forms as meeting 'written consent' for this audit.; Emergency conversions from a planned to an urgent procedure blur the consent pathway → record these separately rather than excluding them silently.; Gains plateau below 100% once the list is published but not enforced → build the list into the booking system so a procedure on it cannot be booked without a linked consent form.
- Pearls: Recruit the interventional radiology lead and a specialist nurse or consent lead as co-authors.; Reuse procedure-specific consent form templates from surgical specialties as a starting point where suitable.; Present the audit alongside the corpus's own consent-documentation learning (procedure-specific forms work; teaching alone does not) to justify the chosen fix.; Track patient understanding of risks as a longer-term follow-on measure once form completeness is achieved.

**NNA-593. What proportion of interventional radiology procedures have a completed Sign In, Time Out and Sign Out safety checklist, adapted from the WHO Surgical Safety Checklist for radiological interventions, on file before, during and after the procedure?** (new)
- Standard: Royal College of Radiologists, WHO Surgical Safety Checklist: for Radiological Interventions Only (adapted from the WHO Surgical Safety Checklist): "The Royal College of Radiologists adapted the checklist of Safe Surgery from the World Health Organization for use in radiological interventions in England and Wales, entitled 'WHO Surgical Safety Checklist: for Radiological Interventions ONLY', with the three phases of Sign In, Team Time Out and Sign Out." https://www.rcr.ac.uk/our-services/all-our-publications/standards/
- Pass: All three phases of the checklist (Sign In, Time Out, Sign Out) are completed and filed in the procedure record for the case.. Target: ≥95%. Sample: 40 consecutive procedures over the last month, from the interventional radiology log.
- Change: Designate a named 'checklist champion' for each interventional radiology session, responsible for leading and confirming all three checklist phases out loud, with the checklist itself made a mandatory field in the electronic procedure record rather than a paper form that can be left incomplete.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-593.csv`
- Pitfalls: The checklist is completed retrospectively rather than in real time, defeating its safety purpose → spot-check timing against the procedure start time where the electronic system logs it.; Staff view the checklist as a barrier for 'quick' procedures and skip it → apply it to all procedures on the interventional list regardless of expected duration.; A paper checklist is easily lost or left blank → prefer an electronic mandatory field that blocks progression to the next step.; The general anaesthetic section, largely irrelevant to most interventional cases, causes staff to disengage with the whole checklist → confirm the department is using the RCR-adapted version, not the unmodified surgical version.; Champions rotate without a clear handover, and the role lapses → build champion allocation into the weekly interventional list planning.
- Pearls: Recruit an interventional radiology consultant and the lead interventional radiology nurse/radiographer together.; Designate a champion for each list as recommended in published implementation experience with this checklist.; Use a clipboard or fixed location for the checklist so it is always available at the point of use.; Report near-miss catches attributed to the checklist (e.g. wrong side identified at Time Out) as a powerful qualitative measure alongside completion rates.

**NNA-594. What proportion of patients undergoing an intimate radiological examination or procedure (for example transrectal or transvaginal procedures) have express consent and the offer of a chaperone documented before the examination?** (new)
- Standard: Royal College of Radiologists, Standards for patient consent particular to radiology, second edition: "Intimate examinations require particular attention and understanding to establish trust and mutual confidence between patient and doctor... Express consent, either verbally or in writing, should be obtained for intimate examinations and serious consideration should be given to the need to provide a chaperone." https://www.bsgar.org/media/BFCR(12)8_consent.pdf
- Pass: The record shows express consent obtained (verbally or in writing) and documented consideration of a chaperone (offered and accepted, offered and declined, or not applicable with reason) before the examination.. Target: 100%. Sample: 30-40 consecutive eligible examinations over the last 2-3 months, from the department booking system.
- Change: Add a mandatory 'chaperone offered: outcome' field, alongside the express consent field, to the booking or procedure checklist for all examinations coded as intimate, so the step cannot be skipped or forgotten.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-594.csv`
- Pitfalls: Staff assume a chaperone is 'obviously' not needed for certain examinations and skip documenting the offer → require the field to be completed for every examination on the intimate-examination list, with 'not applicable' as an explicit, reasoned option rather than a blank.; Patients decline a chaperone and this is not distinguished from 'not offered' → give both options explicitly in the template.; Locum or visiting staff are unaware which examinations are classified as intimate locally → publish and circulate the local list.; The field exists on paper but not in the electronic system used for most bookings → prioritise adding it to whichever system captures the majority of these examinations.; Gains are not sustained after a staff rotation → include the requirement in departmental induction for new radiographers, sonographers and radiologists.
- Pearls: Recruit a radiographer or sonographer who regularly performs these examinations as co-author.; Publish a simple, agreed list of which examinations count as 'intimate' locally to reduce ambiguity.; Present alongside patient experience feedback, since chaperone offer is a well-recognised patient dignity marker.; Keep the audit brief and focused, since this is a quick, high-value dignity-of-care check rather than a complex clinical audit.

**NNA-595. For planned interventional radiology procedures, what proportion of patients are given written, procedure-specific information in sufficient time before the procedure to consider it and consult others if they wish?** (new)
- Standard: Royal College of Radiologists, Standards for patient consent particular to radiology, second edition: "In a planned procedure, the patient should receive information, verbally or in writing, in sufficient time before the procedure to consider it and to consult others if they so wish." https://www.bsgar.org/media/BFCR(12)8_consent.pdf
- Pass: The patient record shows written, procedure-specific information was given (posted, emailed or handed over in clinic) at least 24 hours before a planned interventional radiology procedure, excluding same-day emergency or urgent add-on cases.. Target: ≥90%. Sample: 40 consecutive eligible planned procedures over the last 2-3 months, from the interventional radiology booking system.
- Change: Create a library of procedure-specific written information leaflets for the department's highest-volume interventional procedures, sent automatically (by post or patient portal) as soon as the procedure is booked, rather than being handed over only on the day.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-595.csv`
- Pitfalls: A generic hospital leaflet is sent instead of a procedure-specific one, technically meeting a loose definition of 'written information' but not its intent → require the leaflet to name the specific procedure and its specific risks.; Late-booked planned procedures (booked less than 48 hours ahead) are wrongly included and unfairly counted as failures → apply the inclusion criterion strictly.; Patients report not receiving or not reading the leaflet despite a record that one was sent → consider a simple patient-reported cross-check for a subset of cases.; Leaflets are only available in English, disadvantaging patients needing another language or an accessible format → record whether an alternative format was needed and provided.; Gains fade once the automatic dispatch process is not checked after an IT system change → re-verify the automation after any booking system update.
- Pearls: Recruit a interventional radiology specialist nurse who manages pre-procedure information as co-author.; Start with the two or three highest-volume procedures to build the leaflet library quickly, then expand.; Ask patients directly (a brief survey) whether they felt they had enough information and time to decide, as a complementary patient experience measure.; Share the leaflet library with the pre-assessment or referring team so information can be given even earlier, at the point of referral.

## Allied health professions

**NNA-596. What proportion of adults with a hip fracture have a physiotherapy assessment and are mobilised the day after surgery, unless medically or surgically contraindicated?** (under-audited)
- Standard: NICE CG124 Hip fracture: management, recommendation 1.7.1 (2011): "Offer people a physiotherapy assessment and, unless medically or surgically contraindicated, mobilisation on the day after surgery." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg124/chapter/Recommendations
- Pass: Physiotherapy assessment documented and mobilisation attempted on the calendar day after surgery, or a documented medical/surgical contraindication recorded that day. Target: ≥90%. Sample: 40 consecutive adults having hip fracture surgery over the last 2-3 months, from the hip fracture register/NHFD extract
- Change: Add a mandatory 'day-1 physiotherapy assessment and mobilisation attempt: yes/no, reason if no' field to the hip fracture pathway proforma, and extend weekend physiotherapy cover to match the day-of-week distribution of surgery.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-596.csv`
- Pitfalls: Weekend and bank holiday surgery has no physiotherapy cover → negotiate 7-day therapy rotas with the therapy lead before cycle 1; Contraindications are recorded inconsistently or not at all → add a mandatory free-text reason field so 'not mobilised' always has an explanation; Small numbers if only complete NHFD-linked cases are used → include all operated hip fractures, not just those with full NHFD data; Definitions of 'mobilised' vary between a sit-out and a walk → agree and print one operational definition before data collection starts; Gains fade once weekend cover reverts → make the rota change permanent in the therapy job plan, not a temporary trial
- Pearls: Recruit a physiotherapy team lead and the orthogeriatrician as joint audit leads so the change survives staff rotation; Agree the operational definition of 'mobilised' (sit to stand, transfer, or walk) with therapy staff before collecting data; Use the existing NHFD extract to identify the sample quickly rather than searching EPR from scratch; Feed results back to individual consultants and therapy shifts, not just as a trust-wide average, to drive local ownership

**NNA-597. What proportion of hip fracture inpatients are mobilised at least once a day with regular physiotherapy review throughout their acute stay?** (new)
- Standard: NICE CG124 Hip fracture: management, recommendation 1.7.2 (2011): "Offer people mobilisation at least once a day and ensure regular physiotherapy review." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg124/chapter/Recommendations
- Pass: Documented mobilisation attempt on every day of the acute admission and at least 3 physiotherapy reviews per week until discharge or rehabilitation-ready. Target: ≥85%. Sample: 40 consecutive hip fracture inpatients with a length of stay of 5 days or more over the last 3 months
- Change: Add a daily 'mobilised today: yes/no, reason if no' task to the hip fracture ward's electronic therapy list so a missed day is visible on the ward board round, and set a weekend physiotherapy rota matched to the ward's bed numbers.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-597.csv`
- Pitfalls: Weekend staffing gaps are the commonest cause of missed days → confirm weekend rotas before starting; Patients who become medically unwell mid-stay may appropriately miss a day → record a reason rather than counting every miss as a failure; Documentation of 'seen but not mobilised' is easy to miss in free-text notes → use a structured daily tick box, not narrative notes, for data extraction; Staff may see this as a workload-driven target rather than a patient outcome → present length-of-stay and discharge-destination data alongside mobilisation rates; Long lengths of stay reduce the eligible sample → extend the collection window if fewer than 40 eligible patients are found in 3 months
- Pearls: Link this audit to the existing hip fracture pathway audit so both cycles use the same case list; Ask ward physiotherapists to flag missed days themselves during data collection rather than relying on retrospective note review; Present results by day of week to show where gaps cluster; Keep the daily task list active after the project team disbands by building it into the ward's standard operating procedure

**NNA-598. What proportion of COPD inpatients with excessive sputum production are taught active cycle of breathing techniques or positive expiratory pressure device use by a physiotherapist?** (new)
- Standard: NICE NG115 Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease in over 16s, recommendation 1.2.101 (2004, amended 2018): "If people have excessive sputum, they should be taught: how to use positive expiratory pressure devices, active cycle of breathing techniques." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng115/chapter/Recommendations
- Pass: Documented physiotherapy teaching of active cycle of breathing techniques and/or a positive expiratory pressure device before discharge, for a patient with recorded excessive sputum. Target: ≥85%. Sample: 40 consecutive COPD exacerbation admissions with documented excessive sputum over the last 3 months
- Change: Add 'excessive sputum: yes/no' to the COPD admission bundle so a yes automatically generates a same-day respiratory physiotherapy referral, with airway clearance teaching and a PEP device as the default action.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-598.csv`
- Pitfalls: Sputum volume/purulence is not always documented in a structured field → agree a simple nursing prompt ('sputum: none/scant/moderate/copious') before starting; Weekend admissions may wait 2-3 days for physiotherapy review → record the referral-to-teaching interval, not just whether teaching ever happened; Patients too breathless or drowsy to learn a technique are wrongly counted as failures → add an exclusion/deferred category with a reason; Teaching without device issue undermines the fix → audit both teaching and equipment provision separately; Staff may see this as duplicating existing physiotherapy referral practice → show baseline data first to demonstrate the gap
- Pearls: Involve the respiratory physiotherapy team lead in designing the sputum documentation prompt so it fits their existing workflow; Keep a small stock of PEP devices on the respiratory ward so teaching is not delayed by equipment ordering; Use the same COPD admission cohort as any existing pulmonary rehabilitation referral audit to save data collection time; Report results to the wider medical team, since sputum documentation is a doctor and nurse responsibility as much as a physiotherapy one

**NNA-599. What proportion of hospital inpatients assessed as being at risk of falls are encouraged and supported to remain physically active during their admission?** (new)
- Standard: NICE NG249 Falls in older people: assessing risk and prevention, recommendation 1.3.19 (2025): "Encourage people to remain active during their hospital stay by: reassuring them that they can still get up and do not need to restrict their activity (unless they have been advised not to) and helping them to be less sedentary and more active, for example, encouraging them to get out of bed, get dressed and regularly stand up and walk around and for people able to exercise, look for opportunities to encourage physical activity that addresses the person's risk of falls, such as balance, coordination, strength and power." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng249
- Pass: Documented physiotherapy or nursing encouragement of activity (getting up, walking, or an exercise component) on at least 3 of the first 5 inpatient days for a patient identified as at risk of falls. Target: ≥80%. Sample: 40 consecutive falls-risk inpatients over the last 2-3 months
- Change: Add a daily 'up and active today: yes/no, reason if no' box to the ward activity/mobility chart, with a prompt for a balance or strength exercise when appropriate, replacing any blanket 'bed rest for safety' default.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-599.csv`
- Pitfalls: 'Falls risk' documentation is inconsistent across wards → agree a single falls risk flag (for example, a falls risk assessment score) before starting; Staff may equate encouraging activity with increased falls, causing reluctance → share evidence that inactivity, not appropriate mobilisation, drives post-discharge falls and deconditioning; Bed rest reasons are not always documented → make a reason mandatory whenever activity is withheld; Ward staffing pressure limits time for supervised walking → recruit ward-based therapy assistants for regular short mobilisation rounds; Improvement may not be sustained once the audit team stops checking → build the prompt into existing nursing handover checklists
- Pearls: Frame this as a deconditioning-prevention project, which tends to get more staff buy-in than a pure falls-prevention framing; Recruit a ward sister and a physiotherapist as joint champions before cycle 1; Use existing 'sit up, get dressed, keep moving' campaign materials rather than creating new posters from scratch; Track length of stay alongside activity rates, since the intervention is expected to reduce it

**NNA-600. What proportion of stroke patients receive at least 3 hours of needs-based, multidisciplinary rehabilitation therapy on at least 5 days of the week?** (new)
- Standard: NICE NG236 Stroke rehabilitation in adults, recommendation 1.2.16 (2023): "Offer needs-based rehabilitation to people after stroke. This should be for at least 3 hours a day, on at least 5 days of the week, and cover a range of multidisciplinary therapy including physiotherapy, occupational therapy and speech and language therapy." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng236/chapter/Recommendations
- Pass: Total documented therapy time (physiotherapy, occupational therapy and speech and language therapy combined) is at least 3 hours on at least 5 of 7 days during a defined week of the stroke unit stay, or a documented reason recorded when the person is unable or unwilling to participate at that level. Target: ≥70% of days meeting the 3-hour, 5-day standard. Sample: 40 consecutive stroke unit patients with a stay of 7 days or more over the last 3 months
- Change: Introduce a shared electronic therapy timesheet across physiotherapy, occupational therapy and speech and language therapy that automatically totals daily minutes per patient and flags days below the 3-hour target for review at the daily board round.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-600.csv`
- Pitfalls: Each therapy discipline may record time in a different system, making totals hard to combine → agree one shared recording format before starting; Weekend and bank holiday staffing typically falls below weekday levels → report weekday and weekend rates separately; Patients who genuinely cannot tolerate 3 hours (fatigue, reduced consciousness) are miscounted as failures → record a clinical reason field; Recording therapy time without documenting content risks gaming the metric → also spot-check that time reflects active, needs-based rehabilitation, not passive contact; Improvement may fade if extra weekend staffing is temporary → secure a recurring weekend therapy rota, not a short-term trial
- Pearls: Use the stroke unit's existing SSNAP data collection processes to avoid duplicating data entry; Agree the shared timesheet format with all three therapy disciplines before cycle 1 so ownership is shared, not imposed; Present intensity data alongside length of stay and functional outcome scores to show the clinical case for investment; Nominate a stroke unit therapy lead to keep the timesheet running after the initial audit team moves on

**NNA-601. What proportion of patients receiving a structured rehabilitation programme on the ward after critical illness have a functional assessment covering physical, sensory, communication and activities-of-daily-living dimensions completed before hospital discharge?** (under-audited)
- Standard: NICE CG83 Rehabilitation after critical illness in adults, recommendation 1.20 (2009): "Before discharging patients who were receiving the individualised structured rehabilitation programme during ward-based care (recommendation 1.15): perform a functional assessment which should include the following physical and non-physical dimensions... assess the impact of the outcomes from the functional assessment on the patient's activities of daily living and participation; based on the functional assessment, review, update and agree the rehabilitation goals with the patient." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg83/chapter/Recommendations
- Pass: A documented functional assessment covering physical, sensory, communication, and activities-of-daily-living dimensions, completed and the rehabilitation goals reviewed, within 72 hours before discharge from hospital. Target: ≥85%. Sample: 40 consecutive eligible patients discharged from hospital over the last 3-4 months, identified from the critical care outreach or follow-up log
- Change: Add a mandatory pre-discharge functional assessment template (covering physical, sensory, communication and ADL dimensions) to the EPR for any patient flagged as having received ICU-linked ward rehabilitation, which must be completed before the discharge summary can be finalised.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-601.csv`
- Pitfalls: Patients who move wards or hospitals before discharge are hard to track → use the critical care outreach follow-up list as the sampling frame; ADL impact is often assessed informally without documentation → provide a short structured template rather than relying on free text; Busy discharge processes can push the assessment out of the pre-discharge window → set a hard 72-hour trigger on the EPR; Onward referral (community rehabilitation, GP, outpatient follow-up) is easy to omit even when the assessment is done → audit referral completion as a separate field; Staff turnover on rotating ward teams may not know which patients had a critical care stay → flag ICU-linked patients on the ward handover board
- Pearls: Use the critical care follow-up service, where one exists, to help identify the sample and check onward referrals were received; Involve both physiotherapy and occupational therapy in designing the shared functional assessment template so it captures both disciplines' domains; Present findings jointly to critical care and general ward teams, since responsibility is shared between them; Keep the mandatory EPR trigger active permanently rather than as a time-limited pilot

**NNA-602. What proportion of patients at risk of long-term physical or psychological problems after critical illness are offered a structured, supported self-directed rehabilitation manual for at least 6 weeks after critical care discharge?** (new)
- Standard: NICE CG83 Rehabilitation after critical illness in adults, recommendation 1.18 (2009): "Based on clinical judgement and the individual patient's rehabilitation needs, consider offering a structured and supported self-directed rehabilitation manual for at least 6 weeks after discharge from critical care, as part of the individualised, structured rehabilitation programme." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg83/chapter/Recommendations
- Pass: Documented offer of a structured, supported self-directed rehabilitation manual, with a named coordinating healthcare professional, for a patient identified as at risk of physical or non-physical morbidity. Target: ≥70% of at-risk patients. Sample: 30-40 consecutive at-risk patients discharged from critical care over the last 3-4 months
- Change: Add 'self-directed rehabilitation manual offered: yes/no, coordinator named' as a mandatory field on the critical care discharge summary template, with the manual and coordinator contact details included in the discharge pack as standard.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-602.csv`
- Pitfalls: Which patients count as 'at risk' is subjective without a documented short clinical assessment → use table 1 of CG83 as a structured checklist; The manual may be offered but not actually coordinated for 6 weeks → audit both the offer and the presence of a named coordinator; Patients discharged out of area lose follow-up continuity → record discharge destination and adapt the coordination plan accordingly; Staff may not know the manual exists if it has not previously been used locally → confirm a manual is available and staff are briefed before cycle 1; Low baseline awareness can make the first cycle very low, discouraging staff → present it as a baseline-setting exercise, not a failure
- Pearls: Base the manual on a published, validated self-directed rehabilitation programme rather than creating one from scratch; Identify a single named critical care outreach practitioner to coordinate all manual referrals so responsibility does not diffuse; Combine this with the pre-discharge functional assessment audit, since both draw on the same discharge population; Ask patients or carers at the 2-3 month functional reassessment whether they received and used the manual, to check the fix is actually working, not just documented

**NNA-603. What proportion of people having a comprehensive falls assessment have their gait, balance, mobility and muscle strength formally assessed as part of it?** (under-audited)
- Standard: NICE NG249 Falls in older people: assessing risk and prevention, recommendation 1.2.2 (2025): "Include the following assessments and examinations (where appropriate) in the comprehensive falls assessment to identify the person's individual fall risk factors: ...Gait, balance and mobility, and muscle strength assessment..." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng249
- Pass: Documented assessment of gait, balance, mobility and muscle strength (for example, using a timed up-and-go, Berg balance score, or equivalent structured tool) recorded as part of the comprehensive falls assessment. Target: ≥90%. Sample: 40 consecutive comprehensive falls assessments over the last 2-3 months
- Change: Add mandatory gait, balance and muscle strength fields, with a named structured tool, to the comprehensive falls assessment template, and route any assessment lacking physiotherapy input to a physiotherapist before it is signed off as complete.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-603.csv`
- Pitfalls: Non-physiotherapy staff completing the assessment may skip physical domains they feel less confident measuring → provide a simple, validated tool with brief training; Different services may use different tools, making results hard to compare over time → agree one tool trust-wide before cycle 1; Acutely unwell patients cannot safely be assessed for gait or balance → record a deferred/not-yet-safe category rather than a fail; Duplication of effort if physiotherapy and medical teams assess separately without sharing results → use one shared assessment form; Improvement gained during the audit period may lapse without an embedded prompt → build the fields into the permanent electronic template, not a paper checklist
- Pearls: Recruit a falls service physiotherapist as joint audit lead alongside the geriatrician or falls coordinator; Choose a quick, validated tool (for example, timed up-and-go) that non-specialist staff can be trained to use in one session; Present results split by setting (ward versus falls clinic) since completion rates often differ; Use the audit as an opportunity to formalise physiotherapy input into every comprehensive falls assessment pathway, not just document it

**NNA-604. What proportion of adults identified through a comprehensive falls assessment as needing a home hazard assessment have one carried out using a validated tool, by an occupational therapist or a supervised trained assistant?** (new)
- Standard: NICE NG249 Falls in older people: assessing risk and prevention, recommendations 1.3.5-1.3.6 (2025): "Offer a home hazard assessment and intervention using a validated tool. Consider having the home hazard assessment and intervention from recommendation 1.3.5 carried out by an occupational therapist. If an occupational therapist does not carry out the assessment and intervention, it may be done by: an appropriately trained healthcare professional or an appropriately trained therapy assistant or technician, with supervision from an appropriately trained healthcare professional." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng249
- Pass: A home hazard assessment using a named validated tool, completed by an occupational therapist or a supervised trained assistant, with documented intervention where hazards were found. Target: ≥85% completed within 4 weeks of referral. Sample: 40 consecutive adults referred for a home hazard assessment over the last 3 months
- Change: Set a target referral-to-home-visit interval on the occupational therapy caseload system, with an automated overdue flag, and train falls-service therapy assistants to deliver supervised home hazard assessments using a single named validated tool.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-604.csv`
- Pitfalls: Home visits are cancelled if the patient is not in, wasting capacity → confirm appointments by phone the day before; Different therapists may use different or no validated tools → agree and print a single tool before cycle 1; Long waiting lists mean many referrals are still open at audit close → report both completion rate and median waiting time; Assistants delivering the assessment without documented supervision breaches the standard even if the visit happens → make supervision sign-off a mandatory field; Gains from extra capacity may be temporary if funded only for the audit period → seek a recurring establishment change if waiting times improve
- Pearls: Use the falls service's existing caseload system rather than building a new tracking spreadsheet; Agree with occupational therapy leadership which validated tool to standardise on before starting data collection; Recruit a therapy assistant champion, since much of the extra capacity this audit is likely to need will come from supervised assistants; Report waiting time trends monthly to keep momentum after the formal audit report is presented

**NNA-605. What proportion of people in the community who have fallen once in the last year, with a gait or balance impairment but no other risk factor, are offered a home hazard assessment using a validated tool?** (new)
- Standard: NICE NG249 Falls in older people: assessing risk and prevention, recommendations 1.3.13-1.3.14 (2025): "Consider a home hazard assessment and intervention using a validated tool. Consider having the home hazard assessment and intervention from recommendation 1.3.13 carried out by an occupational therapist. If an occupational therapist does not carry out the assessment and intervention, it may be done by: an appropriately trained healthcare professional or an appropriately trained therapy assistant or technician, with supervision from an appropriately trained healthcare professional." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng249
- Pass: Documented offer of a home hazard assessment using a validated tool for a person with a single fall in the last year and a documented gait or balance impairment, who does not otherwise meet comprehensive falls management criteria. Target: ≥70%. Sample: 30-40 consecutive people identified from GP falls searches or community falls service referrals over the last 3-4 months
- Change: Add a 'single fall with gait/balance impairment: home hazard assessment offered?' prompt to the GP falls template so this group is not missed between comprehensive falls management and no action at all.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-605.csv`
- Pitfalls: This population is easy to miss because it falls between 'no action needed' and 'full comprehensive assessment' → make the eligibility criteria explicit on the GP template; GPs may not routinely document gait or balance impairment structurally → provide a simple one-line documentation prompt; Community occupational therapy capacity for lower-priority referrals may be limited → agree a realistic waiting time target with the service before cycle 1; Patients may decline a home visit they see as unnecessary after a single fall → record declines separately from missed offers; Findings may not generalise if only one GP practice is audited → sample from more than one practice within the primary care network
- Pearls: Work with the primary care network falls lead to identify the sample via a coded search rather than manual note review; Keep the referral pathway simple (a single click or form) to make it easy for GPs to use during a routine consultation; Track whether hazards found at these lower-risk assessments still lead to meaningful interventions, not just a completed form; Share results with the practice, since GPs are the ones who need to change referral behaviour

**NNA-606. What proportion of stroke patients with documented communication or cognitive needs have joint occupational therapy, physiotherapy or speech and language therapy sessions arranged, rather than separate uncoordinated therapy contacts?** (new)
- Standard: NICE NG236 Stroke rehabilitation in adults, recommendation 1.2.21 (2023): "Make special arrangements for people after stroke who have communication or cognitive needs (for example, by holding joint speech and language therapy and physiotherapy sessions for those with communication difficulties)." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng236/chapter/Recommendations
- Pass: At least one documented joint therapy session (two or more disciplines present together) recorded in the multidisciplinary notes for a stroke patient with a documented communication or cognitive need. Target: ≥70% of eligible patients having at least one joint session per week. Sample: 30-40 consecutive eligible stroke unit patients over the last 3 months
- Change: Add a weekly 'joint session planned: which disciplines, when' slot to the stroke MDT therapy timetable for every patient flagged with a communication or cognitive need, agreed at the weekly MDT meeting.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-606.csv`
- Pitfalls: Coordinating diaries across three disciplines is logistically difficult → fix a single weekly slot in advance rather than arranging ad hoc; Joint sessions may happen informally without being documented as such → add a specific joint-session tick box to the shared MDT note; Staff shortages in any one discipline can cancel joint sessions first → monitor cancellation reasons separately from non-arrangement; Patients who are too fatigued for a longer joint session may be excluded inappropriately → allow a shorter, still-joint session to count; The fix may lapse once the weekly MDT champion moves on → build the joint-session slot into the standing MDT meeting template
- Pearls: Agree the joint-session slot with all three therapy leads before cycle 1, not just the audit team; Use the stroke unit's existing weekly MDT meeting to plan the following week's joint sessions rather than a separate coordination meeting; Track patient and carer feedback on joint sessions, since this is often the strongest driver of continued staff engagement; Keep the documentation simple (a tick box plus disciplines present) so it does not become a burden that gets skipped

**NNA-607. What proportion of hip fracture patients considered for early supported discharge have their medical stability, mental capacity to participate, and ability to transfer and mobilise short distances formally assessed and documented before the decision is made?** (new)
- Standard: NICE CG124 Hip fracture: management, recommendation 1.8.4 (2011): "Consider early supported discharge as part of the Hip Fracture Programme, provided the Hip Fracture Programme multidisciplinary team remains involved, and the person: is medically stable and has the mental ability to participate in continued rehabilitation and is able to transfer and mobilise short distances and has not yet achieved their full rehabilitation potential, as discussed with the person, carer and family." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg124/chapter/Recommendations
- Pass: All four criteria (medical stability, mental ability to participate, ability to transfer/mobilise short distances, discussion with patient/carer/family) documented as assessed before an early supported discharge decision is recorded. Target: ≥90%. Sample: 30-40 consecutive hip fracture patients discharged via early supported discharge over the last 4-6 months
- Change: Add a mandatory four-item checklist (medical stability, mental capacity, transfer/mobility, discussion) to the early supported discharge decision form, which must be completed by occupational therapy and physiotherapy jointly before the discharge is booked.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-607.csv`
- Pitfalls: Criteria may be genuinely assessed but not documented in one place → create a single decision form rather than relying on scattered entries; Time pressure to free beds can lead to the decision being made before all four criteria are checked → make the checklist a hard stop on the discharge order; Mental capacity to participate in rehabilitation can be confused with formal mental capacity for decision-making → define the term clearly in the checklist; Family discussion may happen by phone and go unrecorded → add a simple 'discussed with: date, method' field; Early supported discharge teams outside the acute trust may not see this audit as their responsibility → involve the community team from the outset
- Pearls: Design the four-item checklist jointly with occupational therapy, physiotherapy and the early supported discharge team so all parties recognise it; Pilot the checklist on a small number of patients before full rollout to iron out practical problems; Use the same case list as any hip fracture length-of-stay or readmission audit to show the checklist does not increase early readmission; Keep the checklist short (one page) so it is completed rather than bypassed under time pressure

**NNA-608. What proportion of patients receiving a pre-discharge functional assessment after critical illness have the impact on their activities of daily living formally assessed as part of it?** (under-audited)
- Standard: NICE CG83 Rehabilitation after critical illness in adults, recommendation 1.20 (2009): "Before discharging patients who were receiving the individualised structured rehabilitation programme during ward-based care...perform a functional assessment...assess the impact of the outcomes from the functional assessment on the patient's activities of daily living and participation." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg83/chapter/Recommendations
- Pass: Documented assessment of the impact on activities of daily living (for example, washing, dressing, cooking, mobility at home) as part of the pre-discharge functional assessment, with any identified need referred on. Target: ≥85%. Sample: 30-40 consecutive eligible patients over the last 3-4 months
- Change: Add a mandatory occupational-therapy-led ADL impact section to the pre-discharge functional assessment template, with a built-in referral pathway for any identified need.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-608.csv`
- Pitfalls: ADL impact may be assumed rather than formally assessed → require a structured tool or checklist, not a general impression; Occupational therapy capacity may be limited on general wards → prioritise ICU-linked patients on the daily occupational therapy referral list; Identified needs may not lead to an actual referral → audit referral completion as a separate outcome, not just assessment completion; Patients discharged to a care home may have needs met differently → record discharge destination to interpret results correctly; A low baseline in the first cycle may discourage staff → present it as identifying an opportunity, not blaming individuals
- Pearls: Combine this audit with the wider CG83 functional assessment audit to avoid double data collection; Involve ward-based occupational therapists directly in designing the ADL section so it matches their normal assessment style; Track discharge destination and any early readmission alongside ADL assessment completion to show the clinical value of the fix; Keep a named occupational therapy lead responsible for the mandatory field after the initial project ends

**NNA-609. What proportion of hospital inpatients diagnosed with delirium have documented reorientation, effective communication and a suitable care environment provided as part of their initial management?** (under-audited)
- Standard: NICE CG103 Delirium: prevention, diagnosis and management, recommendation 1.7.2 (2010): "Ensure effective communication and reorientation (for example explaining where the person is, who they are and what your role is) and provide reassurance for people diagnosed with delirium. Consider involving family, friends and carers to help with this. Provide a suitable care environment." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg103/chapter/Recommendations
- Pass: Documented reorientation and communication measures and a suitable care environment (for example, clear signage, visible clock, consistent staff, reduced noise or a side room where appropriate) recorded within 24 hours of a delirium diagnosis. Target: ≥85%. Sample: 40 consecutive inpatients newly diagnosed with delirium over the last 3 months
- Change: Add a delirium care bundle to the EPR that is triggered automatically by a positive delirium screening tool, with mandatory reorientation, family involvement and environment fields, and a same-day occupational therapy referral option.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-609.csv`
- Pitfalls: Reorientation is often done verbally but never written down → provide a simple tick-box bundle rather than relying on narrative notes; Ward layout and side-room availability may limit what environmental changes are realistically possible → record what was feasible given bed availability; Occupational therapy may not routinely be involved in delirium care on general wards → create a clear referral trigger rather than assuming automatic involvement; Family involvement is harder to document when visiting hours or distance limit contact → record attempts to involve family, not only successful involvement; Care bundle completion can become a box-ticking exercise disconnected from actual care → spot-check a sample against direct observation or family feedback
- Pearls: Build on any existing delirium screening tool already used on the ward rather than introducing a separate process; Involve a ward-based occupational therapist in designing the environment checklist items so they are practical for the ward layout; Present results alongside length of stay and falls data, since delirium management affects both; Nominate delirium link nurses on each ward to keep the care bundle embedded after the audit team's involvement ends

**NNA-610. What proportion of adults at high risk of a heel pressure ulcer have an individualised offloading strategy discussed with them and documented in their care plan?** (new)
- Standard: NICE CG179 Pressure ulcers: prevention and management, recommendation 1.1.15 (2014): "Discuss with adults at high risk of developing a heel pressure ulcer and, where appropriate, their family or carers, a strategy to offload heel pressure, as part of their individualised care plan." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg179/chapter/Recommendations
- Pass: A documented, individualised heel offloading strategy (device named or positioning plan described) in the care plan of an adult identified as high risk of a heel pressure ulcer, with evidence of discussion with the patient or family. Target: ≥85%. Sample: 40 consecutive high-risk adults identified over the last 2-3 months
- Change: Add a mandatory 'heel offloading strategy: device/plan, discussed with patient/family' field to the electronic SSKIN pressure ulcer care plan, triggered automatically when the risk assessment records high risk.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-610.csv`
- Pitfalls: Heel offloading equipment (boots, wedges) may not be readily available on every ward → confirm equipment stock levels before cycle 1; General repositioning may be documented without a heel-specific plan → make heel offloading a distinct field, not implied by general repositioning notes; Patients may decline or remove offloading devices for comfort → record attempts and reasons for non-use rather than counting these as documentation failures; Occupational therapy or tissue viability capacity to review complex cases may be limited → prioritise review for the highest-risk patients first; Improvement may not be sustained if equipment runs out → agree a recurring equipment budget line with the tissue viability service
- Pearls: Involve tissue viability and occupational therapy jointly in designing the offloading field, since both disciplines contribute to equipment decisions; Use ward equipment champions to check heel-offloading device availability alongside data collection; Present pressure ulcer incidence data alongside documentation rates to show the clinical case for the change; Keep a simple picture-based guide at the bedside showing correct heel offloading positioning to support consistent practice

**NNA-611. What proportion of people having a comprehensive falls assessment have their footwear and foot condition assessed, with referral to podiatry when a problem is found?** (new)
- Standard: NICE NG249 Falls in older people: assessing risk and prevention, recommendation 1.2.2 (2025): "Include the following assessments and examinations (where appropriate) in the comprehensive falls assessment to identify the person's individual fall risk factors: ...Footwear and foot condition..." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng249
- Pass: Documented assessment of footwear and foot condition as part of the comprehensive falls assessment, with a podiatry referral made when a problem is identified. Target: ≥85%. Sample: 40 consecutive comprehensive falls assessments over the last 2-3 months
- Change: Add a mandatory footwear and foot condition field, with a direct one-click podiatry referral option, to the comprehensive falls assessment template.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-611.csv`
- Pitfalls: Staff without podiatry training may feel unqualified to assess foot condition → provide a simple visual checklist (skin, nails, deformity, ulceration) rather than requiring specialist skills; Footwear may be assessed but not foot condition, or vice versa → record both as separate fields; Podiatry referral pathways may be unclear to non-podiatry staff → build a direct referral link into the assessment template; Referrals made may not be tracked to completion → add a follow-up field for whether the podiatry appointment happened; Low staff confidence in the first cycle may underestimate true completion → pair the audit with a short training session on the checklist
- Pearls: Ask the podiatry service to help design the simple foot-condition checklist so referrals are appropriately targeted; Combine this with the physiotherapy-led gait/balance/muscle strength audit, since both use the same comprehensive falls assessment template; Track how many referrals lead to a completed podiatry appointment, not just how many are made; Keep the referral link visible and easy to use so it survives staff turnover

**NNA-612. What proportion of patients admitted to hospital with a stroke have their swallowing function screened before any oral food, fluid or medication is given, with action taken if a problem is identified?** (under-audited)
- Standard: NICE NG236 Stroke rehabilitation in adults, recommendation 1.2.1 (2013): "When a person is admitted to hospital after stroke, screen for the following and, if problems are identified, take action as soon as possible to ensure their safety and comfort: signs of disorientation, how they should be positioned, swallowing function, how they move (for example, from a bed to a chair), pressure area risk, their continence, their communication, including their ability to understand and follow instructions and to convey their needs and wishes, their nutritional status and hydration." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng236/chapter/Recommendations
- Pass: Documented swallow screen completed before any oral food, fluid or oral medication is given, and, if the screen is abnormal, a documented action (nil by mouth, modified diet, or referral for a specialist swallow assessment) recorded the same day. Target: ≥95%. Sample: 40 consecutive stroke admissions over the last 2-3 months
- Change: Make swallow screening a mandatory hard stop on the stroke admission order set, so no oral food, fluid or medication can be prescribed as 'oral' until the screen result is entered, with an automatic alert to speech and language therapy for any abnormal result.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-612.csv`
- Pitfalls: Out-of-hours admissions may lack trained staff to perform the screen promptly → ensure all admitting nursing staff, not just stroke-unit staff, are trained in the screening tool; Medication is sometimes given orally before food or fluid screening is considered, and gets missed from data collection → explicitly define 'oral intake' to include medicines; A pass on a validated screening tool is not the same as a full speech and language therapy assessment → audit the screen, and separately track specialist assessment for those who fail; Staff may screen but delay recording the result, making timing hard to verify → use time-stamped electronic entries rather than paper charts where possible; Compliance may fall out of hours or at weekends → report weekday/weekend and in-hours/out-of-hours rates separately
- Pearls: Recruit the stroke unit matron and a speech and language therapist as joint audit leads; Use the trust's existing validated swallow screening tool rather than introducing a new one; Build the screening prompt into the same admission bundle used for other early stroke standards (glucose, positioning) to reduce duplication of effort; Report results at the same MDT meeting that reviews SSNAP performance so the audit becomes part of routine stroke unit governance

**NNA-613. What proportion of stroke patients are screened for communication difficulties within 72 hours of the onset of stroke symptoms?** (new)
- Standard: NICE NG236 Stroke rehabilitation in adults, recommendation 1.12.1 (2013): "Screen people for communication difficulties within 72 hours of onset of stroke symptoms." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng236/chapter/Recommendations
- Pass: A documented communication screen, using the stroke service's standardised protocol, completed within 72 hours of the recorded onset of stroke symptoms. Target: ≥90%. Sample: 40 consecutive stroke admissions with a documented onset time over the last 2-3 months
- Change: Add a 72-hour 'communication screen due' automated reminder to the stroke unit's electronic task list, triggered from the recorded onset time, with the screen built into the standard admission proforma.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-613.csv`
- Pitfalls: Onset time is often estimated or unwitnessed, complicating the 72-hour calculation → record onset time precision (exact, estimated, unknown) as a separate field; Speech and language therapy weekend cover may be limited → report weekday versus weekend screening rates separately; Communication screening may be recorded informally in ward round notes rather than the standardised protocol → audit for use of the named protocol specifically, not any communication comment; Patients with severe dysphasia may be hard to screen definitively → record 'screen attempted, inconclusive' as a distinct category rather than a straightforward pass or fail; The 72-hour deadline can be missed simply through delayed transfer to the stroke unit → track time from onset to stroke unit arrival as well as to screening
- Pearls: Use the same stroke admission cohort as the swallow screening audit to minimise duplicate data collection; Agree a single standardised communication screening protocol with speech and language therapy before starting; Display the 72-hour deadline visibly on the stroke unit's patient board so nursing staff can prompt therapy teams; Report results alongside SSNAP communication indicators so the audit reinforces existing national reporting

**NNA-614. What proportion of stroke patients with dysphagia who are having modified food or fluids are regularly monitored and reassessed by a speech and language therapist until they are clinically stable?** (new)
- Standard: NICE NG236 Stroke rehabilitation in adults, recommendation 1.11.9 (2013): "Healthcare professionals with relevant skills and training in the diagnosis, assessment and management of swallowing disorders should regularly monitor and reassess people with dysphagia after stroke who are having modified food and liquid until they are stable." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng236/chapter/Recommendations
- Pass: At least one documented speech and language therapy reassessment per week for a patient on modified food or fluids, continuing until the diet is upgraded or the patient is discharged. Target: ≥85%. Sample: 30-40 consecutive eligible patients over the last 3-4 months
- Change: Add an automatic weekly speech and language therapy reassessment task to the stroke unit's electronic caseload for any patient on a modified diet, visible on the unit's therapy whiteboard until discontinued.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-614.csv`
- Pitfalls: Patients transferred to a rehabilitation ward may lose continuity of speech and language therapy follow-up → include a handover trigger for modified-diet patients on transfer; Staff shortages can deprioritise reassessment in favour of new patient screening → protect reassessment capacity as a distinct caseload category; 'Stable' is not clearly defined, so reassessment may stop prematurely → agree a working definition (for example, no diet change for 2 consecutive reviews) before cycle 1; Weekly reassessment may be recorded informally without a clear date → use a structured, dated reassessment note; Long lengths of stay create a large caseload that can overwhelm capacity → monitor caseload size alongside compliance to identify staffing gaps
- Pearls: Use the stroke unit's existing dietary chart as a simple prompt for when reassessment is due; Agree a shared definition of 'stable' with the speech and language therapy team before starting data collection; Present caseload numbers alongside compliance rates to support any staffing business case that follows the audit; Track diet upgrades as a positive outcome measure, showing the reassessment process is clinically meaningful, not just procedural

**NNA-615. What proportion of people with head and neck cancer having radiotherapy are offered a swallowing-exercise programme?** (new)
- Standard: NICE NG36 Cancer of the upper aerodigestive tract: assessment and management, recommendation 1.8.3 (2016): "Consider swallowing-exercise programmes for people having radiotherapy." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng36/chapter/Recommendations
- Pass: Documented offer of a swallowing-exercise programme by speech and language therapy, made before or at the start of radiotherapy. Target: ≥90%. Sample: 30-40 consecutive patients starting head and neck radiotherapy over the last 4-6 months
- Change: Add a mandatory 'pre-radiotherapy swallowing exercise programme offered: yes/no' field to the head and neck MDT outcome form, completed by the MDT speech and language therapist before the radiotherapy planning appointment.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-615.csv`
- Pitfalls: Referral may happen but the exercise programme itself may not start before treatment begins → audit programme start date against radiotherapy start date, not referral alone; Patients may decline the programme due to treatment burden → record declines separately from the service failing to offer it; Speech and language therapy capacity in oncology services may be limited → identify capacity gaps as part of the audit's pitfalls, not just documentation gaps; MDT outcome forms may not have a dedicated field, making the offer hard to trace retrospectively → create the field before, not after, data collection begins; Patients treated at a different centre for radiotherapy may fall outside local documentation → clarify pathway responsibility for shared-care patients
- Pearls: Work with the head and neck cancer nurse specialist to identify the patient cohort quickly from MDT records; Time the swallowing-exercise programme offer to coincide with the pre-treatment dental and nutrition assessments already built into the pathway; Present long-term dysphagia outcome data alongside offer rates to strengthen the case for embedding the change; Keep a simple patient information leaflet ready so the offer can be made and accepted at the same appointment

**NNA-616. What proportion of people with head and neck cancer whose voice has changed because of treatment are offered voice therapy?** (new)
- Standard: NICE NG36 Cancer of the upper aerodigestive tract: assessment and management, recommendation 1.8.5 (2016): "Consider voice therapy for people whose voice has changed because of their treatment." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng36/chapter/Recommendations
- Pass: Documented assessment of voice change at the post-treatment follow-up appointment, with voice therapy offered when a change is identified. Target: ≥85%. Sample: 30-40 consecutive patients at their first post-treatment follow-up over the last 4-6 months
- Change: Add a mandatory 'voice change: yes/no, therapy offered' field to the post-treatment follow-up clinic letter template, with a direct speech and language therapy referral link.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-616.csv`
- Pitfalls: Voice change may not be actively asked about unless prompted → use a direct question in the follow-up template rather than relying on the patient to raise it; Patients may not recognise a gradual voice change as treatment-related → provide a simple patient-facing prompt or questionnaire before the appointment; Voice therapy referral pathways may differ between ENT and oncology-led follow-up → clarify a single referral route before cycle 1; Some voice change may be expected and temporary, leading staff to under-refer → offer therapy for persistent change beyond an agreed time point (for example, 3 months); Low clinic time may limit thorough voice assessment → consider a brief validated voice-related quality-of-life screening tool
- Pearls: Use a short, validated voice-related quality-of-life question set to standardise assessment across clinicians; Involve the ENT and oncology follow-up clinic teams jointly, since patients may attend either; Track referral-to-first-appointment time for voice therapy as a secondary outcome; Keep the referral link in the clinic letter template so it survives staff rotation

**NNA-617. What proportion of patients with communication difficulties suspected after stroke are referred to a speech and language therapist for detailed assessment?** (new)
- Standard: NICE NG236 Stroke rehabilitation in adults, recommendation 1.12.3 (2013): "Refer people with suspected communication difficulties after stroke to a speech and language therapist for detailed analysis of any impairments and assessment of their impact." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng236/chapter/Recommendations
- Pass: A documented speech and language therapy referral made within 24 hours of a suspected communication difficulty being recorded. Target: ≥90%. Sample: 40 consecutive stroke patients with a documented suspected communication difficulty over the last 3 months
- Change: Link the stroke unit's communication screening tool directly to an automatic speech and language therapy referral in the EPR whenever a suspected difficulty is recorded, removing the need for a separate manual referral step.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-617.csv`
- Pitfalls: A suspicion noted informally in ward round notes may not be recognised as needing referral → tie referral directly to the structured screening tool result, not free-text impressions; Weekend suspicion may wait until Monday for referral → report weekday/weekend referral timing separately; Referral may be made but the detailed assessment delayed by caseload pressure → audit both referral and completed assessment as separate steps; Mild or fluctuating symptoms may be under-recognised by non-specialist staff → provide brief training on recognising subtle communication difficulties; Duplicate referrals from multiple staff members may distort the true referral rate → count time-to-first-referral, not total referrals
- Pearls: Build the automatic referral into the same screening tool used for the 72-hour communication screening audit; Agree an escalation route for referrals not actioned within 24 hours with the speech and language therapy team lead; Report referral-to-assessment interval as well as referral rate to show the whole pathway working; Use ward-based posters or prompts to help non-specialist staff recognise subtle communication difficulties

**NNA-618. What proportion of stroke patients with severe communication difficulties are assessed by a speech and language therapist for their potential to benefit from a communication aid or technology?** (new)
- Standard: NICE NG236 Stroke rehabilitation in adults, recommendation 1.12.7 (2013): "Speech and language therapists should assess people experiencing severe communication difficulties after stroke to see if they could benefit from using a communication aid or other technologies (for example, home-based computer therapies or mobile apps)." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng236/chapter/Recommendations
- Pass: A documented speech and language therapy assessment for communication aid or technology suitability, completed within 4 weeks of a severe communication difficulty being confirmed. Target: ≥80%. Sample: 30-40 consecutive eligible patients over the last 4-6 months
- Change: Add a 'communication aid assessment due' flag to the speech and language therapy caseload system for any patient coded with severe aphasia or dysarthria, reviewed weekly at the therapy team meeting.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-618.csv`
- Pitfalls: Severity of aphasia or dysarthria may not be consistently graded, making the eligible population hard to define → agree a clear severity threshold or tool before cycle 1; Assessment may be deprioritised in favour of more immediate rehabilitation goals → build a caseload flag so it is not forgotten, not competing informally for attention; Aids assessed as suitable may not be provided promptly due to funding or equipment delays → audit provision as well as assessment; Patients discharged to community speech and language therapy may lose continuity → include a handover field confirming the assessment need is passed on; Family or carer engagement is often needed for technology use, and its absence can be mistaken for the patient's inability to benefit → record carer involvement separately
- Pearls: Agree a shared definition of 'severe' communication difficulty with the whole speech and language therapy team before starting; Use the caseload flag system already in place for other therapy follow-up tasks rather than creating a new one; Track aid uptake and use at follow-up, not just assessment completion, to show the change is meaningful; Involve community speech and language therapy early so continuity is maintained after hospital discharge

**NNA-619. What proportion of stroke patients with dysphagia who cannot, or find it difficult to, follow a mouth care regimen have a suitably trained healthcare professional, family member or carer delivering or supervising their mouth care?** (new)
- Standard: NICE NG236 Stroke rehabilitation in adults, recommendation 1.10.3 (2023): "Ensure that a suitably trained healthcare professional, family member or carer delivers or supervises mouth care for people after stroke who cannot, or find it difficult to, follow a mouth care regimen." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng236/chapter/Recommendations
- Pass: Documented mouth care delivered or supervised at least twice daily by a named trained healthcare professional, family member or carer, for a patient with dysphagia unable to independently follow a mouth care regimen. Target: ≥85%. Sample: 30-40 consecutive eligible patients over the last 3 months
- Change: Add a structured mouth care chart to the dysphagia management plan, naming the trained staff member or family/carer responsible for each shift, with speech and language therapy providing brief training as part of the initial dysphagia assessment.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-619.csv`
- Pitfalls: Mouth care is often delegated informally without checking staff training → build a simple training checklist into ward induction for stroke unit staff; Family involvement can be inconsistent if visiting hours are limited → record attempts to involve family separately from successful involvement; Mouth care charts may exist but not be completed consistently → use a structured chart requiring a signature at each episode; Patients who resist mouth care because of reduced consciousness or agitation are miscounted as failures → record refusals and adapted approaches as a distinct category; Aspiration pneumonia rates may have multiple causes, complicating outcome attribution → present mouth care compliance as a process measure alongside, not instead of, pneumonia rates
- Pearls: Ask speech and language therapy to provide a short, standard mouth care training session for ward staff as part of stroke unit induction; Use a simple laminated mouth care chart at the bedside rather than relying on the general nursing care plan; Track aspiration pneumonia rates over the audit period as a secondary outcome to strengthen the clinical case; Involve family members proactively by giving them a simple mouth care information leaflet on admission

**NNA-620. What proportion of adult inpatients are screened for the risk of malnutrition using a validated screening tool within 24 hours of admission?** (under-audited)
- Standard: NICE Quality standard QS24, Nutrition support in adults, statement 1 (2012): "All hospital inpatients on admission and all outpatients at their first clinic appointment should be screened. Screening should be repeated weekly for inpatients and for outpatients if there is clinical concern." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/qs24/chapter/quality-statement-1-screening-for-the-risk-of-malnutrition
- Pass: A documented MUST (or other validated tool) screening score completed within 24 hours of hospital admission. Target: ≥95%. Sample: 40 consecutive adult admissions across 2-3 general medical and surgical wards over the last 2-3 months
- Change: Make MUST screening a mandatory field in the electronic nursing admission assessment that cannot be saved as complete until entered, with an overdue alert visible on the ward safety board after 24 hours.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-620.csv`
- Pitfalls: Screening may be attempted but not fully completed (for example, weight recorded but height missing) → count only fully completed, scoreable screens as a pass; Patients unable to be weighed (bed-bound, confused) may be recorded as 'not screened' when an alternative method should be used → record use of alternative MUST methods (ulna length, mid-upper arm circumference) as a valid pass; Night admissions may be screened just after the 24-hour window due to shift patterns → report the distribution of screening times, not just a pass/fail cut-off; Screening completed but not scored or acted on undermines the purpose → pair this audit with monitoring of action taken on high-risk scores; Improvement may not be sustained without an EPR hard stop → avoid relying on a paper reminder alone
- Pearls: Use the trust's existing MUST screening field in the EPR rather than creating a new one; Recruit ward-based nutrition link nurses to champion the mandatory field change; Present results by ward and by day of week to identify where gaps cluster; Feed screening completion rates into the same dashboard used for other admission-bundle metrics so it becomes part of routine ward governance

**NNA-621. What proportion of adult inpatients with a MUST score indicating high risk have a dietitian referral, or another defined local nutrition action, made on the same day as the screen?** (under-audited)
- Standard: BAPEN MUST (Malnutrition Universal Screening Tool): "Refer to dietitian, Nutritional Support Team or implement local policy. Set goals, improve and increase overall nutritional intake. Monitor and review care plan." https://www.bapen.org.uk/must-and-self-screening/must-calculator/
- Pass: A documented dietitian referral or defined local nutrition action taken on the same day as a MUST score of 2 or more is recorded. Target: ≥85%. Sample: 40 consecutive adults with a MUST score of 2 or more over the last 2-3 months
- Change: Set the EPR to automatically generate a dietitian referral and pre-populate a basic local nutrition action plan whenever a MUST score of 2 or more is entered.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-621.csv`
- Pitfalls: High-scoring patients may be seen by the dietitian eventually but not on the same day → record the exact interval, not just whether action ever happened; Weekend screening may have no same-day dietetic cover → report weekday versus weekend rates separately and consider a nursing-led interim action for weekends; Some wards may have an informal local policy (for example, fortified diet menu) that is not documented as a formal action → make 'local policy action' an explicit, codeable option; Automatic referrals may generate an unmanageable volume for the dietetic service → monitor referral volume and dietetic capacity alongside compliance; Duplicate referrals for patients already known to dietetics may inflate apparent non-compliance → exclude patients already under active review
- Pearls: Agree the same-day interim nursing action (for example, starting food record charts and fortified diet) with dietetics before the automatic referral is built; Use the existing MUST screening EPR field as the trigger point rather than creating a parallel system; Track dietetic referral volume weekly during the pilot to catch capacity problems early; Report same-day action rates to ward sisters as well as dietetics, since nursing staff often make the first move

**NNA-622. What proportion of adults identified as high risk of refeeding syndrome have nutrition support introduced at no more than 50% of their estimated requirements for the first 2 days?** (under-audited)
- Standard: NICE CG32 Nutrition support for adults, recommendation 1.4.5 (2006): "People who have eaten little or nothing for more than 5 days should have nutrition support introduced at no more than 50% of requirements for the first 2 days, before increasing feed rates to meet full needs if clinical and biochemical monitoring reveals no refeeding problems." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg32/chapter/Recommendations
- Pass: Documented nutrition support prescription at no more than 50% of estimated requirements for the first 2 days in a patient meeting the high-refeeding-risk criteria, with biochemical monitoring recorded. Target: ≥90%. Sample: 30-40 consecutive high-refeeding-risk patients starting nutrition support over the last 4-6 months
- Change: Add a mandatory refeeding risk box to the enteral and parenteral nutrition prescription form that, when ticked, pre-sets the feed rate to no more than 50% of requirements for the first 2 days and prompts daily biochemical monitoring.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-622.csv`
