- Pitfalls: High-risk criteria may not be systematically checked before feeding starts → build a structured criteria checklist into the dietetic assessment; Estimated requirements may be calculated inconsistently between staff → use a standard calculation method agreed with dietetics; Out-of-hours feeding may start before dietetic review, at full rate by default → provide a simple out-of-hours prescribing guide for medical and nursing staff; Biochemical monitoring may be requested but results not reviewed promptly → audit both request and same-day review of results; Feed rate may be recorded on a nursing chart but not cross-checked against the prescription → use one shared, agreed feeding rate record
- Pearls: Provide a quick-reference refeeding risk card for out-of-hours medical staff, since risk is often first identified outside normal dietetic hours; Agree the standard requirement calculation and prescribing defaults with the nutrition support team and pharmacy together; Track biochemical abnormalities and complications as a secondary outcome to demonstrate the safety benefit of compliance; Keep a small dietetic on-call or telephone advice service, where feasible, to support out-of-hours refeeding decisions

**NNA-623. What proportion of adults screened for malnutrition risk have their screening result and any nutrition support goals documented and communicated in writing within and between care settings?** (new)
- Standard: NICE Quality standard QS24, Nutrition support in adults, statement 3 (2012): "All people who are screened for the risk of malnutrition have their screening results and nutrition support goals (if applicable), documented and communicated in writing within and between settings." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/qs24/chapter/quality-statement-3-documentation-and-communication-of-results-and-nutrition-support-goals
- Pass: The most recent MUST score and any nutrition support goals are documented in the discharge summary or transfer letter for a patient moving between wards, hospitals, or to community/primary care. Target: ≥90%. Sample: 40 consecutive discharges or transfers with a prior MUST screen over the last 2-3 months
- Change: Add a mandatory 'most recent MUST score and nutrition support goals' field to the electronic discharge summary and transfer letter templates, auto-populated from the current MUST record.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-623.csv`
- Pitfalls: Screening results may be documented in the EPR but not carried into the discharge letter, which is what primary care and care homes actually see → audit the discharge letter specifically, not the EPR record alone; Nutrition goals may be informal (for example, verbal advice) and not written down → require a structured goals field, not free text alone; Auto-population may fail if the discharge letter is generated before the final MUST score is entered → sequence the discharge workflow so nutrition data is finalised first; Community and care home recipients may not act on the information even when it is communicated → consider tracking whether GP or care home nutrition action follows, as a stretch outcome; High volume of standard discharge letters may make manual auditing slow → use a coded search for the mandatory field once implemented
- Pearls: Work with the IT/EPR team to auto-populate the discharge letter from the existing MUST record rather than requiring manual entry; Include this as a checklist item in the trust's standard discharge safety checklist; Present results alongside readmission data, since unclear nutrition handover is a recognised contributor to early readmission; Share results with community dietetics and care home liaison teams, who are the ultimate recipients of this information

**NNA-624. What proportion of new outpatients are screened for the risk of malnutrition using a validated tool at their first clinic appointment?** (new)
- Standard: NICE Quality standard QS24, Nutrition support in adults, statement 1 (2012): "All hospital inpatients on admission and all outpatients at their first clinic appointment should be screened. Screening should be repeated weekly for inpatients and for outpatients if there is clinical concern." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/qs24/chapter/quality-statement-1-screening-for-the-risk-of-malnutrition
- Pass: A documented MUST or other validated malnutrition screening score recorded at the patient's first attendance at the clinic. Target: ≥80%. Sample: 40 consecutive new outpatient attendances at 1-2 clinics over the last 2-3 months
- Change: Add a MUST screening step (weight, height or alternative measure, and unintentional weight loss question) to the pre-clinic nursing check-in for new outpatient appointments in the selected specialties, feeding directly into the clinic letter.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-624.csv`
- Pitfalls: Outpatient clinics often lack scales or a private space to weigh patients → confirm basic equipment is available before cycle 1; Nursing or clinic support staff capacity to add a new screening step may be limited → pilot in 1-2 high-yield clinics first, not trust-wide; Patients attending by telephone or video cannot be physically screened → exclude these from the denominator or use a self-reported alternative; A positive screen may not lead to a dietitian referral if no clear pathway exists in outpatients → agree the outpatient referral route before starting data collection; Clinics with high patient turnover may see screening as adding unacceptable time → use the shortest validated tool and involve clinic staff in timing it before rollout
- Pearls: Start with a clinic where malnutrition risk is clinically plausible and staff are receptive (for example, oncology or gastroenterology) to build a strong case study; Provide a simple self-completion weight-loss question card that patients can fill in the waiting room to save clinic time; Agree the outpatient dietitian referral pathway with the dietetic service before starting, so a positive screen has somewhere to go; Report time-per-patient added by screening, to reassure clinic managers ahead of wider rollout

**NNA-625. What proportion of adults at high risk of refeeding problems are cared for by staff with documented expert knowledge of nutritional requirements and nutrition support?** (new)
- Standard: NICE CG32 Nutrition support for adults, recommendation 1.4.7 (2006): "People at high risk of developing refeeding problems (box 1) should be cared for by healthcare professionals who are appropriately skilled and trained and have expert knowledge of nutritional requirements and nutrition support." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg32/chapter/Recommendations
- Pass: Documented dietitian or nutrition support team involvement in the care of a high-refeeding-risk patient from the point of identification until they are stable. Target: ≥85%. Sample: 30-40 consecutive high-risk patients over the last 4-6 months
- Change: Add an automatic same-day dietitian and nutrition support team referral trigger to the EPR whenever high refeeding risk criteria are documented, with a weekend on-call dietetic advice line for urgent queries.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-625.csv`
- Pitfalls: High risk may be identified out of hours when specialist dietetic cover is unavailable → provide a documented on-call or telephone advice route; General ward staff may feel confident managing 'mild' malnutrition without recognising true refeeding risk → provide brief training on the box 1 high-risk criteria; Specialist involvement may be a single initial review without ongoing follow-up until stability → audit ongoing review, not just the first contact; Locum or rotating junior medical staff may be unfamiliar with the referral pathway → include it in induction materials; Nutrition support team capacity may be limited, especially out of hours → monitor referral volume and capacity as part of the fix, not just compliance
- Pearls: Provide a simple laminated card of the box 1 high-risk criteria for admission areas and out-of-hours teams; Agree an on-call dietetic advice arrangement (even a telephone rota) before rolling out the automatic referral trigger; Track biochemical complications as a secondary outcome to show the safety value of specialist involvement; Include the referral pathway in trust induction for new medical and nursing staff so knowledge does not depend on individual experience

**NNA-626. What proportion of patients receiving complex enteral or parenteral nutrition support are reviewed by the multidisciplinary nutrition support team?** (new)
- Standard: NICE CG32 Nutrition support for adults (2006): "All acute hospital trusts should have a multidisciplinary nutrition support team, which may include: doctors...dietitians, a specialist nutrition nurse, other nurses, pharmacists, biochemistry and microbiology laboratory support staff, and other allied healthcare professionals." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg32/chapter/Recommendations
- Pass: Documented review by the multidisciplinary nutrition support team (or, where a formal team does not exist, joint documented input from a dietitian, doctor and pharmacist) within 3 working days of starting parenteral nutrition or complex enteral feeding. Target: ≥90%. Sample: 30-40 consecutive eligible patients over the last 4-6 months
- Change: Set an automatic nutrition support team referral whenever parenteral nutrition or a complex enteral feeding tube is prescribed, with a standing weekly nutrition support team ward round to review all open referrals.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-626.csv`
- Pitfalls: Some trusts may not have a formally constituted nutrition support team, making 'review' hard to define → agree a minimum joint-input definition (dietitian, doctor, pharmacist) before starting where no formal team exists; Parenteral nutrition may be started out of hours before the team can review → audit the interval to first review, not same-day review alone; Referral may happen without a documented outcome → require a written review note, not just a referral entry; Complex feeding started on a surgical ward may not be flagged to the nutrition support team if ownership is unclear → clarify referral responsibility with surgical teams before cycle 1; Capacity of the nutrition support team may limit how many reviews can happen within 3 working days → monitor team capacity alongside compliance
- Pearls: Use parenteral nutrition prescribing records as the simplest way to identify the sample; Agree the automatic referral trigger with pharmacy, since parenteral nutrition prescriptions usually pass through pharmacy first; Present line-related and metabolic complication rates alongside review compliance to show the clinical value of the change; Keep the weekly nutrition support team ward round visible on the hospital's clinical governance calendar so it does not quietly lapse

**NNA-627. What proportion of patients discharged home on enteral tube feeding have a coordinated community multidisciplinary follow-up plan, including a named dietitian, GP and district nursing contact, arranged before discharge?** (new)
- Standard: NICE CG32 Nutrition support for adults (2006): "All people in the community having enteral tube feeding should be supported by a coordinated multidisciplinary team, which includes dietitians, district, care home or homecare company nurses, GPs, community pharmacists and other allied healthcare professionals... Close liaison between the multidisciplinary team and patients and carers regarding diagnoses, prescription, arrangements and potential problems is essential." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg32/chapter/Recommendations
- Pass: A documented discharge plan naming a community dietitian, GP and district/homecare nursing contact for ongoing enteral feeding support, completed before the patient leaves hospital. Target: ≥90%. Sample: 30-40 consecutive patients discharged on home enteral tube feeding over the last 4-6 months
- Change: Add a mandatory home enteral feeding discharge checklist to the EPR, requiring named community dietitian, GP and district/homecare nursing contacts before the discharge summary can be finalised.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-627.csv`
- Pitfalls: Community dietetic and homecare services may vary in how referrals are received, causing delays → map the local referral routes before cycle 1; Discharge may be expedited under bed pressure before all community contacts are confirmed → make the checklist a hard stop on the discharge summary; GP notification may happen via a generic discharge letter without a specific enteral feeding flag → add an explicit enteral feeding section to the discharge letter template; Care home residents may have different notification pathways than those discharged to their own home → record discharge destination and adapt accordingly; Patients or carers may not retain the contact details given → provide a printed, single-page 'who to contact' card in addition to the discharge letter
- Pearls: Work with the homecare feeding company (where one is used) to build a standard discharge checklist together; Involve the community dietetic service in designing the checklist so referrals arrive in the format they need; Give patients and carers a simple laminated contact card, not just a paragraph buried in a longer discharge letter; Track unplanned readmissions related to feeding problems as a secondary outcome to show the value of coordinated discharge

**NNA-628. What proportion of adults with diabetes and a new active (non-limb-threatening) foot problem are referred to the multidisciplinary foot care service or foot protection service within 1 working day, with triage completed within 1 further working day?** (new)
- Standard: NICE NG19 Diabetic foot problems: prevention and management, recommendation 1.4.2 (2015): "For all other active diabetic foot problems, refer the person within 1 working day to the multidisciplinary foot care service or foot protection service (according to local protocols and pathways...) for triage within 1 further working day." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng19/chapter/Recommendations
- Pass: Documented referral to the multidisciplinary foot care service or foot protection service within 1 working day of a new active (non-limb-threatening) diabetic foot problem being identified, with triage recorded within 1 further working day. Target: ≥85%. Sample: 30-40 consecutive new active diabetic foot problems identified over the last 4-6 months
- Change: Create a single, well-publicised electronic referral route (fax-free, one form) to the multidisciplinary foot care service accessible from primary care, community podiatry and the emergency department, with a same-day triage response built into the podiatry team's daily workflow.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-628.csv`
- Pitfalls: Referrers outside the acute trust (GPs, community podiatrists) may not know the correct referral route → publicise a single, simple referral pathway across primary and community care; Weekend or bank holiday presentations may miss the 1-working-day target through no fault of the referrer → report working-day compliance rather than calendar-day compliance; Referral date may be recorded as the date the letter is typed rather than the date the problem was identified → clarify the start point as clinical identification, not paperwork; Triage delay may occur even when referral is prompt, if the foot service is under-resourced → audit referral and triage timeliness as separate steps; Different definitions of 'active' foot problem may be applied inconsistently → use the NG19 risk stratification definitions explicitly in the audit template
- Pearls: Agree a single, shared referral form and route with primary care, the emergency department and community podiatry before starting data collection; Recruit a podiatry team lead and a GP with an interest in diabetes as joint audit leads to bridge primary and secondary care; Track referral source to identify where delays cluster and target the fix accordingly; Report results to the local diabetes network, not just the acute trust, since most referrals originate outside hospital

**NNA-629. What proportion of adults with diabetes have their risk of developing a foot problem formally assessed at diagnosis and at least annually thereafter?** (new)
- Standard: NICE NG19 Diabetic foot problems: prevention and management, recommendation 1.3.3 (2015): "For adults with diabetes, assess their risk of developing a diabetic foot problem at the following times: When diabetes is diagnosed, and at least annually thereafter..." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng19/chapter/Recommendations
- Pass: A documented foot risk assessment (both feet examined, risk stratified as low, moderate, high or active) recorded within the last 12 months for a patient with an established diagnosis of diabetes. Target: ≥90%. Sample: 40 consecutive adults with diabetes due an annual review over the last 3 months
- Change: Add an automated 12-monthly recall to the practice or diabetes service's electronic register that flags any patient overdue a foot risk assessment, generating a reminder letter or text message.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-629.csv`
- Pitfalls: Patients who do not attend routine diabetes reviews are systematically missed → track non-attendance rates and consider opportunistic assessment at any contact; Foot risk assessment may be recorded without formal risk stratification, making the record hard to audit → require the risk category as a discrete, codeable field; Care home residents or housebound patients may be excluded from clinic-based recall systems → arrange domiciliary foot assessment as an alternative pathway; Multiple providers (GP, diabetes clinic, podiatry) may each believe the other completed the assessment → agree a single named responsible service; A high proportion of 'not recorded' risk categories can mask assessments that were actually done but poorly documented → review free-text notes as well as coded fields where discrepancies arise
- Pearls: Use the practice's existing diabetes register and recall system rather than building a new one from scratch; Agree a single coded risk-category field with the clinical system supplier so the data is auditable going forward; Prioritise recall for patients not seen in the last 15 months to catch those falling furthest behind; Report results back to individual GP practices within the network to drive local ownership

**NNA-630. What proportion of adults newly referred to the foot protection service are assessed within the recommended timeframe for their risk category: 2 to 4 weeks for high risk and 6 to 8 weeks for moderate risk?** (new)
- Standard: NICE NG19 Diabetic foot problems: prevention and management, recommendation 1.3.9 (2015): "The foot protection service should assess newly referred people as follows: Within 2 to 4 weeks for people who are at high risk of developing a diabetic foot problem. Within 6 to 8 weeks for people who are at moderate risk of developing a diabetic foot problem." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng19/chapter/Recommendations
- Pass: First foot protection service assessment completed within 4 weeks of referral for high-risk patients, or within 8 weeks for moderate-risk patients. Target: ≥85% of referrals meeting the timeframe for their risk category. Sample: 40 consecutive new foot protection service referrals over the last 3-4 months
- Change: Introduce risk-stratified booking slots in the podiatry appointment system, so high-risk referrals are automatically offered an appointment within 4 weeks and moderate-risk referrals within 8 weeks, with a waiting list review meeting if targets are at risk of being breached.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-630.csv`
- Pitfalls: Risk category may not be clearly stated on the referral, defaulting patients to a lower-priority slot → make risk category a mandatory referral field; Capacity constraints may mean the whole service is over target, not just poorly prioritised → report absolute waiting times alongside risk-stratified compliance to distinguish the two problems; Patients may cancel or rearrange their first appointment, extending the apparent wait → record patient-caused delays separately from service delays; Referrals from different sources (GP, hospital, self-referral) may use inconsistent risk terminology → provide a simple risk-category reference for all referrers; Improvement gained by re-prioritising existing capacity may simply shift delays to lower-risk patients → monitor low-risk waiting times too, to avoid an unintended consequence
- Pearls: Use the podiatry booking system's existing data fields to build the risk-stratified reporting rather than a manual log; Share risk-category definitions with all major referrers (GP practices, diabetes clinics, hospital wards) before making risk category mandatory; Present waiting time data by risk category monthly to the podiatry team so slippage is caught early, not only at re-audit; Use the audit to support any business case for additional podiatry capacity if absolute waiting times, not just prioritisation, are the underlying problem

**NNA-631. What proportion of adults known to the foot protection service are reassessed at the interval appropriate to their risk category (annually for low risk, every 3-6 months for moderate risk, every 1-2 months for high risk)?** (new)
- Standard: NICE NG19 Diabetic foot problems: prevention and management, recommendation 1.3.11 (2015, updated 2023): "Depending on the person's risk of developing a diabetic foot problem, carry out reassessments at the following intervals: Annually for people who are at low risk, as part of their annual diabetes review. Frequently (for example, every 3 to 6 months) for people who are at moderate risk. More frequently (for example, every 1 to 2 months) for people who are at high risk, if there is no immediate concern." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng19/chapter/Recommendations
- Pass: The interval between the two most recent foot risk reassessments is within the recommended range for the patient's documented risk category at the earlier assessment. Target: ≥85%. Sample: 30-40 consecutive moderate- or high-risk patients with two recent assessments over the last 6 months
- Change: Add an automated recall reminder to the podiatry caseload system that flags patients approaching or exceeding their risk-appropriate reassessment interval, reviewed weekly by the administrative team.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-631.csv`
- Pitfalls: Risk category can change between assessments, complicating which interval applies → use the risk category recorded at the earlier of the two assessments; Patients who miss or cancel appointments extend the interval through no fault of the service → record patient non-attendance separately from service delay; High-risk patients needing very frequent review (every 1-2 months) generate a large recall workload → ensure administrative capacity matches the recall volume before rollout; Recall systems may not distinguish moderate from high risk automatically → build risk category into the recall system as a discrete field, not a free-text note; Patients discharged and re-referred may show an artificially long interval → exclude re-referred patients or flag them separately
- Pearls: Build the recall system on the podiatry service's existing caseload database rather than a standalone spreadsheet; Agree recall administrative responsibility explicitly, since this task is easy to lose between clinical and administrative staff; Report interval compliance by risk category separately, since high-risk patients are most vulnerable to slippage; Use missed and rearranged appointment data to identify patients who may need a different reminder method (text message, phone call)

**NNA-632. What proportion of hospital inpatients at moderate or high risk of a diabetic foot problem are given a pressure redistribution device to offload heel pressure, and referred or notified to the foot protection service on discharge?** (new)
- Standard: NICE NG19 Diabetic foot problems: prevention and management, recommendation 1.3.12 (2015): "People in hospital who are at moderate or high risk of developing a diabetic foot problem should be given a pressure redistribution device to offload heel pressure. On discharge they should be referred or notified to the foot protection service." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng19/chapter/Recommendations
- Pass: Documented provision of a heel pressure redistribution device during the admission, and a documented referral or notification to the foot protection service recorded in the discharge summary. Target: ≥85%. Sample: 30-40 consecutive eligible inpatients over the last 4-6 months
- Change: Add a 'diabetic foot risk: moderate/high → heel offloading device provided, FPS notified on discharge' prompt to the diabetes inpatient nursing bundle and the electronic discharge summary template.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-632.csv`
- Pitfalls: Heel offloading devices may not be readily stocked on general wards → confirm equipment availability with tissue viability before cycle 1; Foot risk category may not be documented for inpatients unless specifically prompted → link this audit to any existing inpatient foot risk assessment process; Discharge summaries may mention diabetes generally without a specific foot protection service notification → require an explicit, separate field; Patients transferred between wards may lose their heel offloading device without it being reordered → include a ward-transfer equipment check; Notification to the foot protection service may happen verbally or informally and go unrecorded → require a written notification, ideally electronic
- Pearls: Combine this with any existing inpatient diabetic foot risk assessment audit to use the same case list; Work with tissue viability to ensure heel offloading equipment is readily available on wards with high numbers of diabetes admissions; Build the foot protection service notification into the same discharge workflow as other community referrals, rather than a separate process; Track heel pressure ulcer incidence in this population as a secondary outcome to demonstrate impact

**NNA-633. When diabetic foot ulcer debridement is carried out in hospital, is it done only by a healthcare professional from the multidisciplinary foot care service?** (new)
- Standard: NICE NG19 Diabetic foot problems: prevention and management, recommendation 1.5.7 (2015): "When treating diabetic foot ulcers, debridement in hospital should only be done by healthcare professionals from the multidisciplinary foot care service, using the technique that best matches their specialist expertise and clinical experience, the site of the diabetic foot ulcer and the person's preference." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng19/chapter/Recommendations
- Pass: Documented record that every debridement episode for a diabetic foot ulcer during the hospital stay was performed by a named member of the multidisciplinary foot care service. Target: 100% of debridement episodes performed by multidisciplinary foot care service staff. Sample: 30 consecutive inpatient diabetic foot ulcer debridement episodes over the last 4-6 months
- Change: Add a mandatory 'debridement performed by' field, restricted to named multidisciplinary foot care service staff, to the wound care documentation for diabetic foot ulcers, with an alert if a non-specialist attempts to document a debridement episode.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-633.csv`
- Pitfalls: Ward nursing staff may perform minor debridement as part of routine dressing changes without recognising this as 'debridement' → define debridement clearly (sharp, mechanical, larval, enzymatic) in staff training; Out-of-hours or weekend gaps in multidisciplinary foot care service cover may lead to non-specialist staff stepping in → establish an on-call or escalation pathway for urgent debridement needs; Surgical debridement under a formal operative plan may be wrongly flagged as non-compliant → exclude debridement performed by the surgical team as part of an agreed multidisciplinary foot care service plan; Documentation may record 'wound cleaned' without specifying who did what, obscuring true practice → require role and technique to be recorded explicitly; Staff may be unaware of the restriction if it has not previously been enforced locally → communicate the standard clearly before starting data collection, to avoid appearing punitive
- Pearls: Provide brief training to ward nursing staff on recognising debridement and escalating to the multidisciplinary foot care service rather than proceeding themselves; Agree an urgent escalation or on-call route for debridement needs identified out of hours; Use wound photography, where available, alongside documentation to support quality review of debridement episodes; Present results supportively, focusing on system gaps (access to the specialist service) rather than individual blame

**NNA-634. What proportion of people with suspected acute Charcot arthropathy are referred within 1 working day to the multidisciplinary foot care service for triage within 1 further working day, with non-weight-bearing treatment offered in the meantime?** (new)
- Standard: NICE NG19 Diabetic foot problems: prevention and management, recommendation 1.7.3 (2015): "To confirm the diagnosis of acute Charcot arthropathy, refer the person within 1 working day to the multidisciplinary foot care service for triage within 1 further working day. Offer non-weight-bearing treatment until definitive treatment can be started by the multidisciplinary foot care service." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng19/chapter/Recommendations
- Pass: Documented referral to the multidisciplinary foot care service within 1 working day of suspected acute Charcot arthropathy being identified, triage within 1 further working day, and non-weight-bearing advice or a device offered from the point of suspicion. Target: ≥85%. Sample: 20-30 consecutive suspected acute Charcot presentations over the last 6-12 months (a low-volume but high-harm presentation)
- Change: Add a 'suspected acute Charcot foot' pathway alert to the emergency department and diabetes clinic systems that triggers an immediate non-weight-bearing advice sheet and a same-day fast-track referral to the multidisciplinary foot care service.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-634.csv`
- Pitfalls: Acute Charcot arthropathy is rare, making a 2-week sample impossible → extend the collection window to 6-12 months to reach a meaningful sample; The condition is commonly misdiagnosed as cellulitis or a sprain at first presentation, delaying the referral clock → audit time from first presentation with red flag features, not only from confirmed diagnosis; Non-weight-bearing advice may be given verbally without being documented → provide a printed advice sheet that is given and filed as evidence; Emergency department staff may be unfamiliar with the condition → provide a simple red-flag recognition card for diabetic foot presentations; Small numbers mean a single delayed case has a large effect on the reported percentage → present individual case narratives alongside the overall rate
- Pearls: Use a multi-year or multi-site case series if the local trust sees very few cases in a short window; Provide emergency department and GP education on the classic 'hot, swollen, red foot with intact skin' presentation of acute Charcot arthropathy; Keep printed non-weight-bearing advice sheets and offloading devices readily available in the emergency department; Review every case as an individual learning event with the diabetic foot multidisciplinary team, given how rare and high-harm delayed diagnosis is

**NNA-635. What proportion of people with a foot deformity resulting from previous Charcot arthropathy are under ongoing care with the foot protection service?** (new)
- Standard: NICE NG19 Diabetic foot problems: prevention and management, recommendation 1.7.8 (2015): "People who have a foot deformity that may be the result of a previous Charcot arthropathy are at high risk of ulceration and should be cared for by the foot protection service." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng19/chapter/Recommendations
- Pass: Documented current, active registration with the foot protection service at high-risk review frequency for a patient with a known previous Charcot deformity. Target: 100% of patients with a previous Charcot deformity remaining on active foot protection service review. Sample: 20-30 patients with a coded history of Charcot arthropathy identified from podiatry or orthopaedic records over the last 12 months
- Change: Flag every confirmed Charcot arthropathy diagnosis with a permanent 'high-risk, do not discharge from foot protection service' marker on the podiatry caseload system.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-635.csv`
- Pitfalls: Patients may be discharged from acute Charcot follow-up once the episode resolves, without recognising ongoing high risk → make the high-risk marker permanent, distinct from acute-phase follow-up; Coding of 'Charcot arthropathy' may be inconsistent across systems, making the population hard to identify → cross-check podiatry, orthopaedic and diabetes clinic records; Patients who move house or transfer care may fall out of the local foot protection service without formal discharge being recorded → record transfer of care as a distinct category from discharge; Long time since the acute episode may mean deformity is under-recognised as Charcot-related by newer staff → ensure the permanent marker carries a clear diagnostic note; Small numbers make the percentage sensitive to a single lost-to-follow-up case → review each case individually rather than relying on the percentage alone
- Pearls: Use a permanent, clearly labelled flag in the podiatry electronic record rather than relying on staff memory of individual cases; Cross-reference orthopaedic, diabetes and podiatry records when building the initial case list, since Charcot patients may be seen by any of these services; Review flagged patients annually at a diabetic foot multidisciplinary team meeting to confirm ongoing appropriate review; Communicate the permanent high-risk status clearly in any discharge or transfer letter if the patient does move areas

## Gastroenterology, hepatology, renal and diabetes

**NNA-636. What proportion of adults with cirrhosis without hepatitis B have an ultrasound (with or without alpha-fetoprotein) for hepatocellular carcinoma surveillance at least every 6 months?** (new)
- Standard: NICE NG50 rec 1.3.1 (2016): "Offer ultrasound (with or without measurement of serum alpha-fetoprotein) every 6 months as surveillance for hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) for people with cirrhosis who do not have hepatitis B virus infection." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng50/chapter/Monitoring
- Pass: The interval between the patient's last two surveillance ultrasound scans is 6 months or less (allowing up to 8 weeks' slippage), and this is documented in the hepatology follow-up record.. Target: ≥90%. Sample: 40 consecutive adults with cirrhosis on the hepatology HCC surveillance list, looking at their last 2 scheduled scans.
- Change: Put every eligible patient on a single electronic 6-monthly HCC surveillance recall list (radiology or hepatology database) that books the next scan automatically when one is reported, instead of relying on the clinician to remember to re-request.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-636.csv`
- Pitfalls: Scans done elsewhere (private, another trust) are missed on PACS search: cross-check with the patient at clinic.; Small numbers if the surveillance list is short: pool 2-3 clinics.; Definition of 'on surveillance' can drift between cycles: fix the inclusion list before cycle 1.; Patients who died or transplanted in the interval should be excluded, not counted as failures.; A recall list only helps if someone actions the alert: name an owner.
- Pearls: Ask the hepatology secretary or specialist nurse to hold the surveillance list; they are often the best placed to run the recall.; Agree the definition of 'surveillance patient' (cirrhosis, not palliative, no transplant) with the consultant before starting.; Link AFP requesting to the same recall so both come as one task.; Re-audit before the surveillance list changes hands with rotation, and write the SOP into the department induction pack.

**NNA-637. What proportion of adults newly diagnosed with cirrhosis are offered an upper GI endoscopy to look for oesophageal varices, unless already planned on carvedilol or propranolol?** (new)
- Standard: NICE NG50 rec 1.4.1 (2016, amended 2023): "After a diagnosis of cirrhosis, offer the person an upper gastrointestinal endoscopy to detect oesophageal varices unless they are planning to take carvedilol or propranolol to prevent decompensation." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng50/chapter/Monitoring
- Pass: Within 6 months of a new cirrhosis diagnosis, the patient either has an upper GI endoscopy looking for varices, or a documented decision to start carvedilol/propranolol instead.. Target: ≥85%. Sample: 40 consecutive adults with a new cirrhosis diagnosis over the last 6-12 months.
- Change: Add a 'variceal screen or beta-blocker' prompt to the new-cirrhosis MDT outcome template, which auto-generates either an endoscopy referral or a carvedilol-initiation plan before the patient leaves the meeting.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-637.csv`
- Pitfalls: Patients diagnosed with cirrhosis incidentally (e.g. on imaging for another reason) can be missed from the hepatology new-patient list: cross-check radiology reports too.; Endoscopy waiting lists can push the true 6-month window out: record the referral date as well as the scan date.; Counting a beta-blocker started for another reason (e.g. hypertension) as meeting the standard is a common error: it must be started for this indication.; Losing patients to follow-up before the scan is done should be recorded, not silently excluded.
- Pearls: Agree with endoscopy in advance that new-cirrhosis referrals get a 'surveillance' priority code so they are not queued behind routine OGDs.; Have the MDT coordinator flag every new cirrhosis diagnosis in real time rather than searching retrospectively.; Present early results to the endoscopy unit, since they control the main bottleneck.; Keep the same 6-month reporting window across cycles so trends are comparable.

**NNA-638. Of adults having a surveillance upper GI endoscopy for cirrhosis in whom medium or large oesophageal varices are found, what proportion have endoscopic variceal band ligation performed at the same procedure?** (new)
- Standard: NICE NG50 rec 1.4.3 (2023): "Consider simultaneous endoscopic variceal band ligation if medium or large varices are detected during upper gastrointestinal endoscopy." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng50/chapter/Monitoring
- Pass: If medium or large varices are found at a surveillance OGD, band ligation is performed in the same procedure, or a documented reason is given for not doing so (for example, no trained endoscopist available).. Target: ≥80% of eligible cases. Sample: All surveillance OGDs with medium/large varices found over 3-6 months (expect 15-30 cases in most endoscopy units).
- Change: List which endoscopists are trained in variceal band ligation on the surveillance-list booking screen, so surveillance OGDs for cirrhosis are only booked with a banding-trained endoscopist, or with rescue banding equipment and a second operator on standby.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-638.csv`
- Pitfalls: Numbers will be small in a single centre; consider a longer collection window or combining with a neighbouring unit.; Endoscopist availability for banding is a genuine, recordable constraint, not a data-collection failure: capture it as a reason, not a blank.; Distinguish surveillance procedures from emergency bleeds, which follow a different pathway and should not be pooled.; A drop in banding rates after a trained endoscopist leaves or retires needs a rota fix, not just re-teaching.
- Pearls: Agree the criteria for 'trained in banding' with the endoscopy lead before cycle 1.; Build the booking rule into the endoscopy referral form so it happens automatically rather than depending on memory.; Track which endoscopists most often defer banding, to target support rather than blanket teaching.; Keep the beta-blocker-instead option visible in the template, since NICE treats banding and beta-blockade as alternatives, not banding as mandatory.

**NNA-639. What proportion of adults with cirrhosis and clinically significant portal hypertension (medium/large varices or ascites) are offered carvedilol or propranolol to prevent decompensation?** (new)
- Standard: NICE NG50 rec 1.6.1 (2023): "For people who have cirrhosis and confirmed, or suspected, clinically significant portal hypertension (for example, as indicated by a hepatic venous pressure gradient of more than 10 mmHg or the presence of oesophageal varices), consider the following options for the primary prevention of decompensation: carvedilol as the first-choice treatment ... or propranolol as the second-choice treatment, if carvedilol is contraindicated." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng50/chapter/Managing-complications
- Pass: Carvedilol (first choice) or propranolol (if carvedilol contraindicated) is prescribed, or a documented reason is given for not offering either, in patients with cirrhosis and evidence of clinically significant portal hypertension.. Target: ≥70%. Sample: 40 consecutive adults with cirrhosis and varices or ascites seen in hepatology outpatients.
- Change: Add a 'clinically significant portal hypertension: carvedilol/propranolol offered? yes/no/why not' field to the hepatology clinic template, triggered whenever varices or ascites are coded in the notes.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-639.csv`
- Pitfalls: This is a 2023 recommendation: some clinicians may not yet know it applies beyond variceal bleeding prevention, so expect a low baseline and plan teaching alongside the template.; Carvedilol needs caution in severe hepatic impairment (see the related safe-prescribing audit): don't count inappropriate starts as passes.; Distinguishing 'clinically significant' portal hypertension from cirrhosis in general needs a clear, agreed definition before data collection starts.; Heart rate/blood pressure intolerance stopping the drug should be recorded as a valid reason, not a failure.
- Pearls: Pair this audit with the safe-prescribing check (avoid carvedilol in severe hepatic impairment) so the same data collection covers both.; Brief the hepatology team on the 2023 change before cycle 1 so the low baseline reflects true practice, not confusion about the recommendation.; Use a pharmacist to help identify eligible patients from the clinic list in advance.; Track discontinuation rates at re-audit, since tolerability is the main barrier.

**NNA-640. What proportion of adults with compensated cirrhosis under hepatology follow-up have a MELD score calculated at least every 6 months?** (new)
- Standard: NICE NG50 rec 1.2.2 (2016): "Calculate the Model for End-Stage Liver Disease (MELD) score every 6 months for people with compensated cirrhosis." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng50/chapter/Monitoring
- Pass: A MELD score is documented in the clinic letter or EPR at least once in each 6-month period for the last 12 months of follow-up.. Target: ≥90%. Sample: 40 consecutive adults with compensated cirrhosis with at least 2 hepatology reviews in the last 12 months.
- Change: Add an automatic MELD calculator to the hepatology clinic letter template that pulls the latest bilirubin, creatinine and INR and flags when the last MELD is more than 6 months old.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-640.csv`
- Pitfalls: Bloods done close to, but not attached to, a clinic letter can be missed: search the laboratory system directly, not just letters.; Patients who miss appointments will have gaps that are not the team's fault: record DNA separately from a true miss.; A MELD score without an explicit action plan for a value of 12 or more is a silent gap: capture the 'so what' as well as the number.; Manual MELD calculation is error-prone: check a sample against an online calculator.
- Pearls: An auto-calculating field in the EPR template removes the main source of missed scores.; Ask biochemistry whether the LIMS can flag a MELD-relevant panel automatically for coded cirrhosis patients.; Use the audit to also check that a rising MELD triggers a specific action (more frequent review, transplant discussion), not just a recorded number.; Keep the definition of 'compensated' consistent between cycles to avoid population drift.

**NNA-641. What proportion of adults with cirrhosis and large-volume or refractory ascites who are prescribed a non-selective beta-blocker are prescribed propranolol rather than carvedilol?** (new)
- Standard: NICE NG50 rec 1.5.1 (2023): "carvedilol should be avoided in people with severe hepatic impairment (for example, in those with large-volume or refractory ascites)." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng50/chapter/Managing-complications
- Pass: Patients with large-volume (needing regular paracentesis) or refractory ascites who are on a non-selective beta-blocker are prescribed propranolol, not carvedilol, unless a documented specialist reason is given.. Target: ≥90%. Sample: All patients on the paracentesis/refractory ascites list who are on a beta-blocker (typically 20-40 in a DGH hepatology service over 3-6 months).
- Change: Add an e-prescribing alert that fires when carvedilol is prescribed to a patient coded with large-volume or refractory ascites, prompting a switch to propranolol or a documented reason to continue.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-641.csv`
- Pitfalls: GP-issued prescriptions may lag behind a hospital switch: check the most recent dispensed item, not just the hospital letter.; Some patients are on carvedilol for a genuine cardiac reason agreed with cardiology: exclude these, don't count them as failures.; A single low blood pressure reading is not proof of harm: look for a pattern (hypotension, worsening renal function) alongside the drug choice.; This is a 2023 change: expect resistance from teams used to carvedilol as first-line for variceal prevention generally.
- Pearls: Run the alert past pharmacy before switching it on, since carvedilol/propranolol substitution needs a dose-equivalent plan, not a straight swap.; Use the hepatology specialist nurse to flag ascites severity accurately, since coding alone under-detects refractory ascites.; Combine data collection with the paracentesis/albumin audit, since it is the same patient list.; Re-check blood pressure and renal function trends at re-audit, not just the drug name, to show the change actually protects patients.

**NNA-642. What proportion of adults with severe or moderately severe acute pancreatitis start enteral nutrition within 72 hours of presentation?** (new)
- Standard: NICE NG104 rec 1.2.6 (2018): "Offer enteral nutrition to anyone with severe or moderately severe acute pancreatitis. Start within 72 hours of presentation and aim to meet their nutritional requirements as soon as possible." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng104/chapter/Recommendations
- Pass: Enteral nutrition (oral, nasogastric or nasojejunal) is started within 72 hours of presentation in patients classified as severe or moderately severe acute pancreatitis.. Target: ≥80%. Sample: 30 consecutive adults with severe or moderately severe acute pancreatitis over the last 6-12 months (identify via ITU/HDU admissions and coded pancreatitis with organ support).
- Change: Add a mandatory 'nutrition plan by 72 hours' step to the severe pancreatitis care bundle/ITU admission checklist, with an automatic dietitian referral triggered by the severity score.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-642.csv`
- Pitfalls: Severity classification (moderately severe vs severe) can be applied retrospectively and inconsistently: agree the Atlanta criteria definition with the audit team before starting.; Vomiting or ileus is a valid reason to delay feeding: record it as a reason, not a failure.; ITU and ward notes are often separate systems: check both for the true nutrition start time.; A dietitian referral made is not the same as feed actually starting: capture both timestamps.
- Pearls: Recruit the ITU dietitian to help identify eligible severe cases and confirm start times.; Agree the Atlanta severity definitions with the audit team in writing before collecting data.; Build the 72-hour target into the same proforma as antibiotic and fluid decisions, since these patients are seen together on ward rounds.; Re-audit after any nutrition team staffing change, since dietitian availability is the main driver of delay.

**NNA-643. What proportion of adults with acute pancreatitis without confirmed or suspected infected pancreatic necrosis are NOT started on prophylactic antibiotics?** (new)
- Standard: NICE NG104 rec 1.2.3 (2018): "Do not offer prophylactic antimicrobials to people with acute pancreatitis." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng104/chapter/Recommendations
- Pass: No antibiotic is started in the first 48 hours of admission unless there is a documented indication other than prophylaxis (for example, suspected infected necrosis, cholangitis, or a non-pancreatic infection).. Target: ≥90% appropriate (no unindicated antibiotic). Sample: 40 consecutive adults admitted with acute pancreatitis over the last 3 months.
- Change: Remove 'prophylactic antibiotics' as a default order-set item on the acute pancreatitis admission bundle and require a coded indication (necrosis/cholangitis/other infection) before an antibiotic can be prescribed electronically.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-643.csv`
- Pitfalls: Distinguishing a genuine early infective complication from reflex prophylaxis needs the clinical picture, not just the drug chart: review the indication written at the time.; Antibiotics started for a co-existing infection (e.g. chest, urine) should not count against the standard: capture the stated reason.; A drop in appropriate use after a locum rotation suggests the order-set change needs repeating at induction.; Retrospective note review can under-detect verbal, unwritten justification: flag unclear cases rather than guessing.
- Pearls: Get antimicrobial pharmacy involved early; they usually already track inappropriate starts informally.; Make the order-set change the single fix, since the topic card shows teaching alone reached only 65% risk-stratification gains and no reported re-audit for antibiotics specifically.; Feed results back to the acute take induction so new doctors don't reintroduce reflex prescribing.; Track antibiotic duration as well as whether one was started, since stopping a wrongly-started course late is a second failure mode.

**NNA-644. What proportion of adults who develop necrotic, infective, haemorrhagic or systemic complications of acute pancreatitis have advice sought from a specialist pancreatic centre?** (new)
- Standard: NICE NG104 rec 1.2.14 (2018): "If a person develops necrotic, infective, haemorrhagic or systemic complications of acute pancreatitis: seek advice from a specialist pancreatic centre within the referral network and discuss whether to move the person to the specialist centre for treatment of the complications." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng104/chapter/Recommendations
- Pass: Advice from a specialist pancreatic centre is documented as sought (by phone, MDT or referral letter) within 48 hours of the complication being identified.. Target: ≥90%. Sample: All complicated pancreatitis cases identified over 6-12 months in a non-specialist centre (typically 15-30 cases).
- Change: Add a mandatory 'specialist pancreatic centre discussed: yes/date, or why not' field to the ward round proforma whenever a local complication of pancreatitis is coded, with the regional centre's referral hotline number printed on the form.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-644.csv`
- Pitfalls: Numbers will be small in most DGHs; a longer collection window or combining a few years' cases may be needed.; Verbal advice given informally (consultant-to-consultant phone call) may not be documented: ask staff to write even brief advice calls in the notes.; Retrospective identification of 'complicated' cases relies on coding accuracy: cross-check with the radiology report for necrosis/collections.; Delayed recognition of the complication itself (not just delayed referral) is a separate problem worth flagging separately.
- Pearls: Agree the regional referral pathway and contact route with the specialist centre before starting, so 'discussed' has one clear definition.; Use the upper GI MDT as a backstop: any complicated case not yet discussed externally should be flagged there.; Keep a shared log of specialist centre discussions so this audit can be repeated quickly from existing records.; Feed learning back to acute surgical take doctors, who are often the first to see these patients out of hours.

**NNA-645. What proportion of adults with chronic pancreatitis have an HbA1c checked at least every 6 months to monitor for type 3c diabetes?** (new)
- Standard: NICE NG104 rec 1.3.25 (2018): "Offer people with chronic pancreatitis monitoring of HbA1c for diabetes at least every 6 months." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng104/chapter/Recommendations
- Pass: An HbA1c result is recorded at least once in each 6-month period over the last 12 months of follow-up.. Target: ≥85%. Sample: 40 consecutive adults with chronic pancreatitis with at least 12 months of follow-up.
- Change: Add chronic pancreatitis to the practice/clinic's recall system for 6-monthly HbA1c, with a letter to the GP specifying the interval if follow-up is shared.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-645.csv`
- Pitfalls: Shared care with the GP means results may sit outside the hospital record: check the GP-shared record, not just hospital letters.; New-onset diabetes diagnosed opportunistically should be recorded and cross-checked against the recommended interval going forward.; A recent hospital admission with unrelated bloods can create a false sense that HbA1c is being monitored: check it is specifically HbA1c, not just glucose.; Patients who move between hospital and GP-only follow-up need the recall responsibility made explicit.
- Pearls: Write the monitoring interval explicitly into the GP discharge/shared-care letter (NICE also expects HbA1c and DEXA frequency communicated to GPs, rec 1.1.7).; Combine this audit's data collection with the bone density audit below, since both come from the same patient list and letters.; A single shared spreadsheet or database recall (hospital or practice-run) is more reliable than depending on individual clinicians remembering.; Re-audit after any change of pancreatico-biliary consultant or specialist nurse, since personal recall systems do not survive rotation.

**NNA-646. What proportion of adults with chronic pancreatitis have a bone density (DEXA) assessment at least every 2 years?** (new)
- Standard: NICE NG104 rec 1.3.21 (2018): "Offer adults with chronic pancreatitis a bone density assessment every 2 years." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng104/chapter/Recommendations
- Pass: A DEXA scan report is dated within the last 2 years for the patient's current period of follow-up.. Target: ≥80%. Sample: 40 consecutive adults with chronic pancreatitis and at least 2 years of follow-up.
- Change: Add chronic pancreatitis patients to a 2-yearly DEXA recall list, requested directly by the pancreatico-biliary team rather than relying on a GP referral.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-646.csv`
- Pitfalls: DEXA scans done at another hospital or via a GP osteoporosis pathway can be missed on hospital PACS: ask the patient and check the national image exchange if available.; A DEXA report without a documented follow-up action for osteopenia/osteoporosis is an incomplete pass: capture both.; Waiting-list delays for DEXA are a system issue, not a data error: record the request date as well as the scan date.; Long gaps between clinic reviews can hide overdue scans: check the DEXA system directly rather than only clinic letters.
- Pearls: A direct hospital-requested DEXA recall avoids the extra step (and drop-off) of asking the GP to refer.; Pair this with the HbA1c audit, since both are follow-up-completeness measures on the same chronic pancreatitis list.; Agree with radiology a standing protocol for chronic pancreatitis DEXA requests so referrals are accepted without individual justification each time.; Feed abnormal results into a bone health pathway (calcium/vitamin D, bisphosphonate referral) so the scan itself changes management.

**NNA-647. What proportion of adults with a positive coeliac serology test are referred to a gastrointestinal specialist for endoscopic biopsy within 6 weeks of the result?** (new)
- Standard: NICE NG20 rec 1.3.1 (2015): "Refer young people and adults with positive serological test results to a gastrointestinal specialist for endoscopic intestinal biopsy to confirm or exclude coeliac disease." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng20/chapter/Recommendations
- Pass: A referral for endoscopic biopsy is made within 6 weeks of a positive coeliac serology result, and the patient is advised to continue eating gluten until the biopsy.. Target: ≥85%. Sample: 40 consecutive adults with a new positive coeliac serology result.
- Change: Set the laboratory system to auto-generate a gastroenterology 2-week-equivalent referral (or a direct-access endoscopy booking) whenever a positive coeliac serology result is authorised, rather than relying on the requesting clinician to refer.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-647.csv`
- Pitfalls: Patients who have already started a gluten-free diet before referral will have unreliable biopsies: flag and exclude or record separately.; GP referrals sent by letter rather than an electronic pathway are harder to trace: agree one referral route before starting.; A weakly positive result needing EMA confirmation (NICE 1.2.2) adds a step that can be mistaken for delay: record the confirmatory test date too.; Waiting-list pressure on endoscopy is a genuine constraint: separate 'referral made' (clinician-controlled) from 'biopsy done' (partly system-controlled) in the results.
- Pearls: An automatic referral trigger from the lab removes the main point of failure (a positive result filed without action).; Brief primary care on the 'keep eating gluten until biopsy' message, since this is a common patient safety-netting gap.; Track both referral and biopsy timeliness so any bottleneck (referral vs endoscopy capacity) is clearly identified.; Share results with the endoscopy unit, since a rise in referrals may need a dedicated slot allocation.

**NNA-648. What proportion of adults with confirmed coeliac disease have a documented annual review that includes weight, symptom review and consideration of dietetic input?** (new)
- Standard: NICE NG20 rec 1.4.3 (2015): "Offer an annual review to people with coeliac disease. During the review: measure weight and height, review symptoms, consider the need for assessment of diet and adherence to the gluten-free diet, consider the need for specialist dietetic and nutritional advice." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng20/chapter/Recommendations
- Pass: In the last 12 months, the patient has a review documenting weight, a symptom review, and a decision about dietetic input.. Target: ≥85%. Sample: 40 consecutive adults with confirmed coeliac disease due, or having had, their annual review.
- Change: Build a structured coeliac annual review template (weight, symptoms, dietetic-input decision, vaccination check) into the GP or gastroenterology system, replacing free-text review notes.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-648.csv`
- Pitfalls: Many coeliac annual reviews happen in general practice, sometimes without a distinct template: check GP records, not just hospital letters.; Weight alone without a comparison to a previous value misses faltering weight gain or loss: record trend, not just a single figure.; 'Considered' dietetic input can be interpreted loosely: agree what counts as documented consideration before starting (for example, an explicit yes/no with reason).; Patients discharged from hospital follow-up to GP-only care can fall out of any recall system: check both settings for the relevant year.
- Pearls: A single shared template usable in both primary and secondary care avoids duplicated or missed reviews.; Use the coeliac patient group/dietitian list, if one exists locally, to identify the full eligible population rather than relying on clinic attendance alone.; Bundle the pneumococcal vaccination check into the same template, since NICE links it to coeliac care specifically.; Re-audit after any change to the GP recall system or dietetic staffing, since these reviews often depend on one named clinician.

**NNA-649. What proportion of adults newly diagnosed with type 1 diabetes have coeliac serology testing at or shortly after diagnosis?** (new)
- Standard: NICE NG20 rec 1.1.1 (2015): "Offer serological testing for coeliac disease to: people with ... type 1 diabetes, at diagnosis." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng20/chapter/Recommendations
- Pass: Coeliac serology (tTG-IgA with total IgA) is requested within 3 months of a new type 1 diabetes diagnosis.. Target: ≥90%. Sample: 40 consecutive adults with a new type 1 diabetes diagnosis.
- Change: Add coeliac serology as a pre-selected item on the new type 1 diabetes diagnosis blood panel in the diabetes clinic order set.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-649.csv`
- Pitfalls: Serology requested by the GP rather than the diabetes team can be missed if only hospital systems are checked.; Symptomatic coeliac disease may have already prompted testing before the diabetes diagnosis: record timing relative to diagnosis, not just whether it was ever done.; A negative result does not exclude future risk: NICE also recommends re-testing if symptoms develop later (rec 1.3.4), which is worth a separate note in results.; New diagnoses made as an inpatient (e.g. with diabetic ketoacidosis) may have this step deprioritised: check both inpatient and outpatient pathways.
- Pearls: Adding the test to the admission/diagnosis order set is far more reliable than relying on individual clinicians to remember an easily-missed association.; Use the paediatric-to-adult transition list as an additional source of newly diagnosed young adults.; Share results with the diabetes specialist nurses, who often run the new-diagnosis pathway day to day.; Track outcome of positive results through to biopsy referral, not just whether the test was requested.

**NNA-650. What proportion of adults started on azathioprine or mercaptopurine for Crohn's disease have thiopurine methyltransferase (TPMT) activity checked before the first dose?** (new)
- Standard: NICE NG129 rec 1.2.8 (2012): "Assess thiopurine methyltransferase (TPMT) activity before offering azathioprine or mercaptopurine. Do not offer azathioprine or mercaptopurine if TPMT activity is deficient (very low or absent). Consider azathioprine or mercaptopurine at a lower dose if TPMT activity is below normal but not deficient." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng129/chapter/Recommendations
- Pass: TPMT activity is checked and the result is available and acted on (standard dose, reduced dose, or drug avoided) before the first dose of azathioprine or mercaptopurine is given.. Target: ≥95%. Sample: 30-40 consecutive adults newly started on azathioprine or mercaptopurine for Crohn's disease.
- Change: Make TPMT a mandatory, hard-stop pre-requisite field on the electronic thiopurine prescription for IBD, so the first dose cannot be authorised without a documented result.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-650.csv`
- Pitfalls: A TPMT sent on the same day as the first prescription, before the result is back, is a common near-miss: define 'before' as result available, not just sample sent.; Urgent starts (for example, at discharge) are the highest-risk point for skipping the check: flag these specifically.; Local laboratory turnaround time affects feasibility: know the turnaround before setting a hard-stop rule.; GP-initiated repeat prescriptions after a hospital start need the same rule applied, or risk restarting without a recent result after a long gap.
- Pearls: A pharmacy-enforced hard stop is more reliable than a reminder, since this is a genuine patient-safety risk, not just a documentation gap.; Agree an urgent same-day TPMT turnaround with the laboratory for planned starts, so timeliness does not become an excuse to skip the check.; Audit alongside the ongoing FBC monitoring measure below, since both come from the same thiopurine-start list.; Flag any deficient result found to the whole team immediately, not just recorded, given the severity of the risk it avoids.

**NNA-651. What proportion of adults on ongoing infliximab or adalimumab for Crohn's disease have a documented reassessment of continued need within the last 12 months?** (new)
- Standard: NICE NG129 rec 1.2.16 (2010): "People who continue treatment with infliximab or adalimumab should have their disease reassessed at least every 12 months to determine whether ongoing treatment is still clinically appropriate." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng129/chapter/Recommendations
- Pass: A documented reassessment of clinical symptoms, biomarkers (for example, faecal calprotectin or CRP) or investigation is recorded within the last 12 months for each patient continuing infliximab or adalimumab.. Target: ≥90%. Sample: 40 consecutive adults on ongoing infliximab or adalimumab for Crohn's disease.
- Change: Add a 12-monthly reassessment alert to the biologics prescribing/homecare system that flags any patient approaching 12 months since their last documented review, before the next prescription is authorised.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-651.csv`
- Pitfalls: Biologics given via homecare can be continued on a repeat-prescription basis with limited direct clinical contact: check the homecare database as well as hospital clinic letters.; A telephone or virtual review counts if it is documented with the required content; define this before starting so virtual clinics are not under- or over-counted.; Faecal calprotectin results sitting in a different IT system from the clinic letter can be missed: search the laboratory system directly.; Patients who are stable and rarely seen in person are at highest risk of an undocumented, assumed 'still working' continuation.
- Pearls: A prescribing-system alert tied to the homecare/biologics pharmacy record catches patients who might otherwise coast without face-to-face review.; Use IBD specialist nurses to run virtual reassessments by phone with a structured symptom and biomarker check, rather than requiring a clinic slot for every patient.; Track the decision made at reassessment (continue/stop/switch), not just whether one happened, to show it changes practice.; Re-audit after any biologics service reconfiguration, since responsibility for review can become unclear during service changes.

**NNA-652. What proportion of adults admitted with acute severe ulcerative colitis have a documented daily assessment of the likelihood of needing surgery, including stool frequency and CRP?** (new)
- Standard: NICE NG130 rec 1.2.26 (2013): "Assess and document on admission, and then daily, the likelihood of needing surgery for people admitted to hospital with acute severe ulcerative colitis." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng130/chapter/Recommendations
- Pass: Stool frequency and CRP (or another documented surgical-likelihood assessment) are recorded at least once every 24 hours from admission until discharge or surgery.. Target: ≥90% of inpatient days complete. Sample: All admissions with acute severe ulcerative colitis over the last 12 months (typically 15-30 cases in a DGH).
- Change: Introduce a dedicated acute severe UC daily monitoring chart (stool frequency, CRP, pulse, temperature, albumin) kept at the bedside or in the EPR, separate from the general observation chart.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-652.csv`
- Pitfalls: Weekend and night documentation is the most likely gap: check whether missed days cluster on weekends before proposing a fix.; Retrospective note review can undercount verbal ward-round assessments not written down: only count what is documented, and say so.; Small numbers are expected; consider a rolling collection over 12 months rather than a fixed short window.; A patient transferred to a tertiary centre mid-admission should have their local-stay days counted, not penalised for the transfer.
- Pearls: A single-page bedside chart used by both medical and nursing staff is easier to complete reliably than relying on free-text ward-round notes.; Involve the IBD clinical nurse specialist, who often already tracks these patients closely.; Pair this with the 72-hour escalation-decision audit below, since both use the same admission cohort and monitoring chart.; Feed missed weekend days back to the acute medical take handover process, not just the gastroenterology team, since cover changes at weekends.

**NNA-653. What proportion of adults admitted with acute severe ulcerative colitis who have little or no improvement after 72 hours of intravenous corticosteroids have a documented escalation decision (rescue therapy or surgery) made at that point?** (new)
- Standard: NICE NG130 rec 1.2.24 (2013): "Consider adding intravenous ciclosporin to intravenous corticosteroids or consider surgery for people: who have little or no improvement within 72 hours of starting intravenous corticosteroids or whose symptoms worsen at any time despite corticosteroid treatment." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng130/chapter/Recommendations
- Pass: For patients not clearly improving by 72 hours of IV corticosteroids, a documented decision (escalate to ciclosporin/biologic rescue therapy, proceed to surgery, or continue with explicit reasoning) is recorded on day 3 of treatment.. Target: ≥90%. Sample: All acute severe UC admissions over 12 months not improving by day 3 (typically 10-20 cases).
- Change: Add a mandatory 'day 3 acute severe colitis decision' prompt to the joint gastroenterology/colorectal ward round proforma, due exactly 72 hours after IV steroids start.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-653.csv`
- Pitfalls: The '72 hours' point can fall on a weekend when senior IBD input is less available: check whether delays cluster there.; A verbal decision to 'wait and see' without written reasoning is a common near-miss: require an explicit written plan even if the plan is to continue watching.; Small numbers are expected; combine data over 12 months rather than a short window.; Distinguish patients who improved (correctly not escalated) from those who did not improve but were still not escalated, since only the latter are failures.
- Pearls: A joint gastroenterology/colorectal ward round on or around day 3 for every acute severe UC admission is the single most effective fix reported for this kind of delay.; Build the 72-hour trigger from the steroid start time recorded in e-prescribing, so the prompt is automatic rather than manually tracked.; Share results with both specialties, since the decision genuinely needs both to be involved (NICE rec 1.2.21).; Track outcomes (colectomy rate, length of stay) at re-audit to show timely escalation is not just paperwork.

**NNA-654. What proportion of adults admitted with acute severe ulcerative colitis have a joint gastroenterology and colorectal surgery review documented within 24 hours of admission?** (new)
- Standard: NICE NG130 rec 1.2.21 (2013): "For people admitted to hospital with acute severe ulcerative colitis: ensure that a gastroenterologist and a colorectal surgeon collaborate to provide treatment and management." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng130/chapter/Recommendations
- Pass: Both a gastroenterologist and a colorectal surgeon document a review (jointly or separately but within the same 24-hour window) within 24 hours of admission with acute severe ulcerative colitis.. Target: ≥90%. Sample: All acute severe UC admissions over 12 months (typically 15-30 cases).
- Change: Set an automatic referral to colorectal surgery, alongside the gastroenterology referral, whenever 'acute severe colitis' is coded on admission, so both specialties are alerted from the outset rather than surgery being added later.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-654.csv`
- Pitfalls: Surgical input may be genuinely not needed in every case: only count 'surgery not involved' as a failure if there is no documented reason it was safe to omit.; Out-of-hours admissions may only reach the on-call medical team initially: check whether delays cluster overnight or at weekends.; A surgical opinion recorded as a brief note rather than a full review still counts if it reflects genuine awareness and input: agree the definition in advance.; This audit works best combined with the daily-assessment and 72-hour-escalation audits, since they share the same patient cohort; avoid re-collecting the same admission list three separate times without coordinating.
- Pearls: A single combined data-collection sheet covering all three acute severe UC audits (this one, daily assessment, and 72-hour escalation) saves duplicate note review.; An automatic dual referral removes reliance on the medical team remembering to involve surgery early.; Use the IBD nurse specialist to flag every acute severe UC admission in real time so both teams are alerted immediately.; Present colectomy rate and length of stay alongside process measures, since joint working is intended to improve these outcomes.

**NNA-655. What proportion of adults newly diagnosed with MASLD (fatty liver on imaging) have an enhanced liver fibrosis (ELF) test done to check for advanced fibrosis?** (new)
- Standard: NICE NG49 recs 1.3.1-1.3.2 (2016, updated 2026): "Offer testing for advanced liver fibrosis to people with MASLD. Consider using the enhanced liver fibrosis (ELF) test in people who have been diagnosed with MASLD to test for advanced liver fibrosis." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng49/chapter/Assessment-for-advanced-liver-fibrosis-in-people-with-MASLD
- Pass: An ELF test (or another advanced fibrosis test used consistently with local pathway) is requested within 6 months of a new MASLD diagnosis being recorded.. Target: ≥70%. Sample: 40 consecutive adults with a new MASLD diagnosis.
- Change: Add an automatic ELF test order (or reflex laboratory pathway) whenever a radiology report codes hepatic steatosis with a coded diagnosis of type 2 diabetes or metabolic syndrome.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-655.csv`
- Pitfalls: MASLD is often diagnosed incidentally on imaging done for another reason (e.g. gallstones): a purely GP-list-based search will miss these cases, so also check radiology reports.; ELF may not be available in every laboratory: confirm local availability and, if using an alternative (e.g. FIB-4), record which test was actually used.; A steatosis report without a documented diagnosis of MASLD in the notes can under-count the true denominator: define inclusion criteria carefully with the audit team.; Following up on an abnormal ELF result (referral to hepatology) is a separate step from testing itself: capture both.
- Pearls: A reflex laboratory pathway (steatosis + diabetes coded → automatic ELF) avoids relying on individual GPs or hospital clinicians remembering the test.; Engage radiology to standardise wording that flags steatosis clearly in reports, since ambiguous wording is a common cause of missed follow-up.; Use this as an opportunity to build a simple MASLD register, which also supports the HCC/cirrhosis surveillance audits above if advanced fibrosis is confirmed.; Track the proportion referred on for advanced fibrosis, not just tested, to show the pathway works end to end.

**NNA-656. What proportion of adults diagnosed with advanced liver fibrosis on ELF testing (score ≥10.51) are referred to a hepatology specialist?** (new)
- Standard: NICE NG49 rec 1.3.5 (2016, updated 2026): "Refer adults and young people diagnosed with advanced liver fibrosis to a relevant specialist in hepatology." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng49/chapter/Assessment-for-advanced-liver-fibrosis-in-people-with-MASLD
- Pass: A referral to a hepatology specialist is made within 3 months of an ELF result of 10.51 or above.. Target: ≥90%. Sample: All patients with an ELF ≥10.51 over the last 12-24 months (likely 15-30 in a typical laboratory catchment).
- Change: Set the laboratory system to flag any ELF result ≥10.51 directly to the ordering clinician and to a hepatology virtual clinic inbox, so an abnormal result cannot be filed without a referral decision.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-656.csv`
- Pitfalls: A raised ELF result filed in primary care without hospital visibility is the main risk: a shared alert to both GP and a hepatology inbox closes this gap.; Local availability of ELF is limited to some laboratories: numbers may be small, so extend the collection period if needed.; A patient who declines referral should be recorded as such, not as a system failure.; Distinguish a new ELF-based diagnosis of advanced fibrosis from a result in a patient already known to hepatology for another reason.
- Pearls: A direct laboratory-to-hepatology inbox alert for abnormal ELF results is more reliable than relying on primary care to always act on an unfamiliar test.; Agree a simple 'MASLD-advanced fibrosis' virtual clinic pathway with hepatology so referrals do not need a lengthy standard outpatient wait.; Combine with the ELF-testing audit above as two stages of the same pathway.; Publicise the ELF threshold and referral pathway to GPs, since MASLD referral criteria are still unfamiliar to many.

**NNA-657. What proportion of adults started on corticosteroids for severe alcohol-related hepatitis (discriminant function ≥32) have active infection and gastrointestinal bleeding excluded or treated first?** (new)
- Standard: NICE CG100 rec 1.3.3.1 (2017): "Offer corticosteroid treatment to people with severe alcohol-related hepatitis and a discriminant function of 32 or more, only after: effectively treating any active infection or gastrointestinal bleeding that may be present, controlling any renal impairment, discussing the potential benefits and risks with the person." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg100/chapter/Recommendations
- Pass: Before the first dose of corticosteroid, there is documented evidence that infection has been screened for and treated (or excluded) and any GI bleeding has been controlled.. Target: ≥90%. Sample: All patients started on corticosteroids for severe alcoholic hepatitis over 12 months (typically 10-25 cases).
- Change: Add a mandatory pre-steroid checklist (blood cultures, ascitic tap if ascites present, chest X-ray, GI bleeding assessment) to the severe alcoholic hepatitis order set, which must be completed before the steroid prescription can be signed.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-657.csv`
