- Pitfalls: Retrospective identification of 'active infection' can be difficult without a systematic screen: define what counts as an adequate screen (cultures, ascitic tap, chest X-ray) before starting.; Numbers are likely to be small: extend the collection period to 12 months or pool across a network.; Steroids sometimes started urgently out of hours before a full screen returns: capture whether the screen was at least sent, even if results were pending.; A documented discussion of risks and benefits with the patient (also required by NICE) is a separate item worth tracking alongside the safety screen.
- Pearls: Build the checklist into the same order set as the discriminant function calculation, so the safety steps and the treatment decision happen together.; Involve microbiology/infection specialists in agreeing what counts as an adequate pre-steroid screen.; Track 3-month and 1-month mortality alongside process measures, since this is the clinical outcome the safety check protects.; Re-audit after any change in the on-call hepatology or gastroenterology rota, since urgent decisions often fall to whoever is on call.

**NNA-658. What proportion of adults with abnormal liver blood tests and a history of harmful or hazardous drinking are referred to a specialist experienced in alcohol-related liver disease to confirm the diagnosis?** (new)
- Standard: NICE CG100 rec 1.3.1.2 (2010): "Refer people to a specialist experienced in the management of alcohol-related liver disease to confirm a clinical diagnosis of alcohol-related liver disease." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg100/chapter/Recommendations
- Pass: A referral to a hepatology or gastroenterology specialist is made within 3 months of abnormal liver blood tests being identified in a person with harmful or hazardous drinking, once other causes have been excluded.. Target: ≥70%. Sample: 40 consecutive adults meeting these criteria.
- Change: Add an automatic prompt to the GP or hospital results system: abnormal LFTs plus a coded harmful/hazardous drinking history triggers a suggested hepatology referral rather than a repeat-and-wait approach.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-658.csv`
- Pitfalls: Alcohol history documentation is often incomplete, making the denominator hard to define: agree a minimum threshold (for example, an AUDIT-C score or explicit units/week) with the audit team.; Repeat LFTs without referral is a common default: distinguish 'LFTs repeated' from 'referred' clearly in the data.; Other causes of abnormal LFTs (viral hepatitis, drugs, MASLD) need to be genuinely excluded, not assumed, before this pathway applies.; Patients who decline referral or engagement should be recorded as such, not as a service failure.
- Pearls: A shared primary care-hepatology pathway document, agreed in advance, avoids ambiguity about who refers and when.; Use the alcohol care team or liaison nurse, where one exists, to support engagement with referral for patients who may be ambivalent about it.; Track outcome of the specialist assessment (confirmed ArLD, alternative diagnosis, fibrosis staging) to show the referral changes management.; Re-audit after any change to community alcohol or liver pathway commissioning, since these referral routes can change.

**NNA-659. What proportion of adults with pain from chronic alcohol-related pancreatitis are referred to a specialist centre for multidisciplinary assessment?** (new)
- Standard: NICE CG100 rec 1.4.2.1 (2010): "Refer people with pain from chronic alcohol-related pancreatitis to a specialist centre for multidisciplinary assessment." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg100/chapter/Recommendations
- Pass: A referral to a specialist pancreatic centre for multidisciplinary assessment is made and documented for patients with ongoing pain from chronic alcohol-related pancreatitis not controlled by simple analgesia.. Target: ≥70%. Sample: 30 consecutive adults with chronic alcohol-related pancreatitis and pain.
- Change: Add a 'persistent pain in chronic pancreatitis: specialist pancreatic centre referral considered' prompt to the gastroenterology clinic template, triggered when pain is coded as ongoing at two consecutive reviews.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-659.csv`
- Pitfalls: Pain management is often escalated informally through primary care analgesia rather than referral: capture what was tried locally before assuming referral was appropriate.; Numbers in a single DGH will be small: extend the collection period or combine with neighbouring units.; Ongoing alcohol use complicates referral acceptance and outcome: record engagement with alcohol support as context, not as a reason to withhold referral.; A referral made but not yet seen (long waiting list) should be recorded as 'referred', with the wait time as a separate issue to escalate.
- Pearls: Agree the regional specialist pancreatic centre referral route and typical waiting time before starting, so expectations are realistic.; Loop in the chronic pain team locally as a bridge while a specialist centre referral is pending.; Track whether alcohol support was also offered alongside pain referral, since ongoing drinking undermines both problems.; Use this audit to also flag whether surgical options (see NICE NG104 on duct obstruction) were considered at the specialist assessment.

**NNA-660. What proportion of adults treated for delirium tremens in hospital are prescribed oral lorazepam as first-line treatment before parenteral treatment?** (new)
- Standard: NICE CG100 rec 1.1.4.1 (2010, amended 2017): "In people with delirium tremens, offer oral lorazepam as first-line treatment. If symptoms persist or oral medication is declined, offer parenteral lorazepam or haloperidol." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg100/chapter/Recommendations
- Pass: Oral lorazepam is tried first, with parenteral treatment reserved for persistent symptoms or where oral medication is declined or not possible.. Target: ≥85%. Sample: 30 consecutive adults with a documented diagnosis of delirium tremens.
- Change: Add delirium tremens as a specific pathway on the alcohol withdrawal order set, with oral lorazepam pre-selected as the default first step and parenteral options only unlocked after a documented reason.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-660.csv`
- Pitfalls: Patients too agitated to safely take oral medication are a genuine reason to start parenteral treatment first: record this as a valid reason, not a failure.; Out-of-hours decisions may default to whatever is easiest to draw up (often parenteral): check whether time of day predicts drug choice.; A general alcohol withdrawal order set without a specific delirium tremens pathway can blur the distinction between routine and DT management: confirm the diagnosis is explicit before including a case.; Reviewing the withdrawal regimen after DT develops (1.1.4.2) is a second, separate standard worth capturing alongside first-line drug choice.
- Pearls: A default order-set option removes the need for staff to recall the correct sequence under pressure.; Loop in liaison psychiatry or an alcohol care team, if one exists, since delirium tremens often triggers a specialist review anyway.; Use ward pharmacy to spot-check compliance in real time, not just retrospectively.; Track whether the withdrawal regimen is actively reviewed after DT develops, since this is often forgotten once acute treatment is given.

**NNA-661. What proportion of adults treated for suspected Wernicke's encephalopathy receive parenteral thiamine for a minimum of 5 days before switching to oral thiamine?** (new)
- Standard: NICE CG100 rec 1.2.1.4 (2010): "Offer parenteral thiamine to people with suspected Wernicke's encephalopathy ... Parenteral treatment should be given for a minimum of 5 days, unless Wernicke's encephalopathy is excluded. Oral thiamine treatment should follow parenteral therapy." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg100/chapter/Recommendations
- Pass: Parenteral thiamine (for example, IV/IM Pabrinex) is continued for at least 5 days, or is stopped earlier only with a documented reason that Wernicke's encephalopathy has been excluded, followed by oral thiamine.. Target: ≥85%. Sample: 30 consecutive adults treated for suspected Wernicke's encephalopathy.
- Change: Add a mandatory 5-day course length to the parenteral thiamine (Pabrinex) prescription for suspected Wernicke's encephalopathy in e-prescribing, requiring a documented reason to stop earlier.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-661.csv`
- Pitfalls: Early discharge is a common reason parenteral thiamine is stopped prematurely: a discharge plan should include continuing IM thiamine or an alternative if inpatient days fall short of 5.; 'Suspected' Wernicke's is subjective: agree a working definition (any one of the triad, or high risk plus a clinical decision to treat) with the audit team.; Drug chart gaps (missed doses) should be distinguished from a deliberate early stop.; A switch straight to oral thiamine without any parenteral treatment at all is a different, more serious failure than stopping parenteral treatment slightly early: capture both separately.
- Pearls: Build a 5-day default course into the e-prescribing order, since manual daily re-prescribing is the main point where doses get missed or stopped early.; Arrange IM thiamine continuation in the community or via an alcohol liaison team for patients who could otherwise be discharged before day 5.; Use this audit's data collection to also spot-check that the correct high dose (BNF upper range) is used, not just that thiamine was given.; Share results with the emergency department and acute medical take, since under-treatment often starts at first presentation, not on the specialist ward.

**NNA-662. What proportion of adults with acute upper GI bleeding have a full Rockall score documented after endoscopy?** (new)
- Standard: NICE CG141 rec 1.1.1 (2012, updated 2016): "Use the following formal risk assessment scores for all patients with acute upper gastrointestinal bleeding: the Blatchford score at first assessment, and the full Rockall score after endoscopy." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg141/chapter/Recommendations
- Pass: A full (post-endoscopy) Rockall score, including endoscopic findings, is calculated and documented in the notes or endoscopy report after the index endoscopy.. Target: ≥90%. Sample: 40 consecutive adults with acute upper GI bleeding who had an endoscopy over the last 3 months.
- Change: Add a mandatory full Rockall score field to the endoscopy reporting system template for all upper GI bleed procedures, calculated from pre-filled clinical and endoscopic findings.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-662.csv`
- Pitfalls: A pre-endoscopy (admission) Rockall score is sometimes recorded instead of the full post-endoscopy score: check the field explicitly includes endoscopic findings.; Patients who have emergency surgery instead of endoscopy should be excluded, not counted as missing data.; Teaching-only interventions have repeatedly shown only partial, non-durable gains in this exact measure [2283]; plan for an electronic or template fix from the outset rather than teaching alone.; Endoscopists working across multiple sites may use different reporting systems: confirm the field is mandatory in all systems used locally.
- Pearls: An electronic action set embedded in the endoscopy reporting system has already been shown to work for this exact measure [5670]; replicate that approach rather than starting from teaching.; Auto-calculate the score from fields already entered (age, comorbidity, shock, diagnosis, stigmata) so completion does not add extra work.; Use the score to also verify safe early discharge of low-risk patients, not just as a box-ticking exercise.; Re-audit promptly after the template change, since electronic fixes in this specific measure have shown fast, large gains.

**NNA-663. What proportion of adults admitted with upper GI bleeding who are taking a regular NSAID (excluding low-dose aspirin) have it stopped during the acute admission?** (new)
- Standard: NICE CG141 rec 1.6.2 (2012, updated 2016): "Stop other non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (including cyclooxygenase-2 [COX-2] inhibitors) during the acute phase in patients presenting with upper gastrointestinal bleeding." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg141/chapter/Recommendations
- Pass: Any regular NSAID or COX-2 inhibitor (other than low-dose aspirin for secondary prevention) is stopped by the time of discharge from the acute admission.. Target: ≥90%. Sample: 30 consecutive adults with upper GI bleeding on a regular NSAID at admission, over the last 6 months.
- Change: Add an automatic e-prescribing alert that flags any regular NSAID or COX-2 inhibitor on the drug chart of a patient coded with upper GI bleeding, prompting the prescriber to stop it or document a reason to continue.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-663.csv`
- Pitfalls: NSAIDs prescribed by a GP but not listed clearly on the hospital drug chart can be missed: check the admission medicines reconciliation carefully.; Distinguishing regular NSAID use from occasional over-the-counter use needs a clear history, which is not always well documented.; The discharge summary is the last safety-net point: a drug stopped on the ward but restarted by default on discharge (because it was on a repeat list) is still a failure.; Alternative analgesia not being offered can drive patients to restart NSAIDs themselves after discharge: consider tracking this too.
- Pearls: An e-prescribing alert linked to the GI bleed diagnosis code is more reliable than expecting every prescriber to remember on a busy take.; Make sure the discharge summary explicitly states the NSAID was stopped and why, so GPs do not restart it on a routine medication review.; Offer a paracetamol/weak-opioid alternative pathway alongside stopping the NSAID, to reduce the temptation to restart it for pain.; Distinguish and separately report low-dose aspirin (which NICE says to continue) so the two messages are not confused by staff.

**NNA-664. What proportion of adults who rebleed after initial endoscopic treatment for upper GI bleeding have a repeat endoscopy offered, with a view to further treatment or surgery?** (new)
- Standard: NICE CG141 rec 1.4.6 (2012, updated 2016): "Offer a repeat endoscopy to patients who re-bleed with a view to further endoscopic treatment or emergency surgery." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg141/chapter/Recommendations
- Pass: A repeat endoscopy is offered (and performed, or a documented reason given for proceeding straight to surgery or interventional radiology) for patients who rebleed after initial endoscopic treatment.. Target: ≥90%. Sample: All confirmed rebleeds after endoscopic treatment over 12 months (typically 10-20 cases in a DGH).
- Change: Add a 'confirmed rebleed' escalation pathway to the GI bleed proforma that automatically prompts an urgent repeat endoscopy request (or direct surgical/interventional radiology referral if endoscopy is not appropriate) rather than a routine re-referral.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-664.csv`
- Pitfalls: Numbers are likely to be small in a single centre; extend the collection period to 12 months.; Rebleeding can be missed or delayed in recognition if nursing observations are not escalated promptly: consider auditing recognition time as well as treatment time.; Out-of-hours rebleeds may default to surgical referral without repeat endoscopy being considered first, which may be appropriate but should be a documented decision, not a default.; Distinguish a genuine rebleed from ongoing slow bleeding not yet controlled, which follows a different initial pathway.
- Pearls: Agree a clear definition of 'rebleed' (for example, further melaena/haematemesis with a haemodynamic change) with the audit team before starting.; A single-page escalation pathway readily available on the acute take and gastroenterology on-call phone line helps out-of-hours decision-making.; Track the interval from rebleed recognition to repeat procedure, not just whether one happened, since speed matters clinically.; Share results with interventional radiology, since they are part of the same escalation pathway for unstable rebleeds.

**NNA-665. What proportion of adults given terlipressin for suspected variceal bleeding have it stopped once definitive haemostasis is achieved, or by 5 days, whichever is sooner?** (new)
- Standard: NICE CG141 rec 1.5.1 (2012, updated 2016): "Offer terlipressin to patients with suspected variceal bleeding at presentation. Stop treatment after definitive haemostasis has been achieved, or after 5 days, unless there is another indication for its use." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg141/chapter/Recommendations
- Pass: Terlipressin is stopped once definitive haemostasis is documented at endoscopy, or by day 5 at the latest, unless another indication (for example, hepatorenal syndrome) is documented.. Target: ≥85%. Sample: 30 consecutive adults started on terlipressin for suspected variceal bleeding.
- Change: Add an automatic 5-day maximum duration and a 'stop if haemostasis confirmed' prompt to the terlipressin prescription in e-prescribing, requiring a documented reason to continue beyond either trigger.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-665.csv`
- Pitfalls: Terlipressin sometimes continues by default on a drug chart after endoscopy has confirmed haemostasis, simply because no one actively stops it: this is the main failure mode to look for.; A small number of patients need terlipressin continued for hepatorenal syndrome, a valid separate indication: exclude or flag these clearly.; Weekend handovers are a common point where a 'stop by day 5' plan is lost: check whether stop delays cluster around weekends.; Ischaemic side effects (digital, cardiac, mesenteric) are a rare but serious outcome worth recording if found, even though numbers will be small.
- Pearls: An e-prescribing hard stop at day 5 is a simple, durable fix that does not depend on staff remembering.; Make the endoscopy report a trigger: a 'terlipressin can stop now' flag when haemostasis is confirmed, linked to the drug chart.; Brief nursing and junior medical staff that terlipressin is not a default 3-5 day course regardless of endoscopy findings.; Track ischaemic adverse events over time as a secondary outcome measure, even if numbers are too small for statistics.

**NNA-666. What proportion of adults started on acid-suppression therapy for stress ulcer prophylaxis in critical care have its ongoing need reviewed when they recover or are discharged from critical care?** (new)
- Standard: NICE CG141 rec 1.7.2 (2012, updated 2016): "Review the ongoing need for acid-suppression drugs for primary prevention of upper gastrointestinal bleeding in acutely ill patients when they recover or are discharged from critical care." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg141/chapter/Recommendations
- Pass: A documented decision to continue or stop acid-suppression prophylaxis is made at the point of critical care discharge (or recovery from the acute illness if remaining on the unit).. Target: ≥85%. Sample: 40 consecutive adults started on acid-suppression prophylaxis in critical care.
- Change: Add a mandatory 'stress ulcer prophylaxis: stop or continue with reason' field to the critical care discharge/step-down checklist, so the decision is made before the patient leaves the unit.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-666.csv`
- Pitfalls: Acid-suppression started for a genuine indication (known peptic ulcer disease, reflux) should be excluded from the denominator, since ongoing treatment is then appropriate rather than a review failure.; Ward teams receiving the patient after critical care discharge may not know the drug was started as prophylaxis rather than for an established indication: make the reason for starting visible on the drug chart from the outset.; The drug can continue unreviewed all the way to hospital discharge and onto a GP repeat prescription: track this endpoint too, not just critical care discharge.; A documented review that concludes 'continue' without a stated reason is a partial pass at best: require an explicit reason.
- Pearls: A structured critical care discharge checklist is the natural place for this review, since it already covers other medicines reconciliation items.; Label the indication ('stress ulcer prophylaxis') clearly on the drug chart at the time of starting, so it is not mistaken for a standing indication later.; Loop in ward pharmacists to review stress ulcer prophylaxis specifically on step-down wards, as a safety net if the critical care checklist is missed.; Track whether the drug is still being taken at hospital discharge and, ideally, at a GP medication review, to close the loop fully.

**NNA-667. What proportion of adults aged 40 and over presenting with jaundice are referred using a suspected cancer pathway referral for pancreatic cancer within 2 working days?** (new)
- Standard: NICE NG12 rec 1.2.4 (2015): "Refer people using a suspected cancer pathway referral for pancreatic cancer if they are aged 40 and over and have jaundice." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng12/chapter/Recommendations-organised-by-site-of-cancer
- Pass: A suspected cancer pathway (2-week-wait) referral for pancreatic cancer is made within 2 working days of jaundice being identified in a patient aged 40 or over, unless an alternative, clearly benign cause is already established.. Target: ≥90%. Sample: 30-40 consecutive adults aged 40+ presenting with new jaundice.
- Change: Add jaundice in a patient aged 40+ as a hard-coded trigger on the GP and ED referral systems that pre-populates a suspected cancer pathway referral for pancreatic (and biliary) cancer, rather than relying on the clinician to remember the age/symptom combination.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-667.csv`
- Pitfalls: Jaundice identified incidentally on blood tests (rather than clinically obvious) can be missed if only clinical documentation is searched: also check bilirubin results directly.; A clear, recently confirmed benign cause (known gallstone disease already under active management) should be excluded from the denominator, but this exclusion needs to be genuinely documented, not assumed.; ED presentations out of hours may default to 'admit and investigate' without an explicit 2-week-wait referral being made in parallel: check both routes.; Referral timeliness is only useful if the pathway itself is fast: also track time from referral to first MDT discussion, as the related audit found this step is also delayed [2287].
- Pearls: A hard-coded age-plus-symptom prompt in the referral system removes reliance on individual clinicians recalling the NICE criterion.; Agree with radiology/hepatobiliary surgery a fast-track imaging slot for suspected pancreatic cancer referrals, since imaging is usually the next rate-limiting step.; Present results to both primary care and the acute take, since jaundice can present in either setting.; Track the full pathway (presentation to referral to first MDT discussion to treatment) over time, since referral speed alone will not fix downstream delays shown in [2287].

**NNA-668. What proportion of adults with cirrhosis given prophylactic intravenous antibiotics for upper GI bleeding have the antibiotic reviewed (continued, switched or stopped) by 72 hours?** (under-audited)
- Standard: NICE NG50 rec 1.9.2 (2016): "Review the use of intravenous antibiotics prescribed for upper gastrointestinal bleeding in line with the section on prescribing intravenous antimicrobials in NICE's guideline on antimicrobial stewardship." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng50/chapter/Managing-complications
- Pass: A documented antimicrobial review (continue, switch to oral, or stop) is recorded within 72 hours of starting IV antibiotics for GI bleeding in a patient with cirrhosis.. Target: ≥90%. Sample: 30 consecutive adults with cirrhosis started on IV antibiotics for GI bleeding.
- Change: Add a 72-hour IV antibiotic review alert (forcing a continue/switch/stop decision) to the e-prescribing system for any antibiotic started under a GI bleed indication code.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-668.csv`
- Pitfalls: An antibiotic continued because the patient develops a new, separate infection should be recorded as an appropriate continuation, not a stewardship failure.; Weekend cover can cause reviews to slip past 72 hours: check whether delays cluster there.; Distinguish antibiotics started specifically for GI bleed prophylaxis from those started for spontaneous bacterial peritonitis or another confirmed infection, which follow different courses.; Retrospective note review can miss brief verbal ward-round decisions: only count what is documented, and note this limitation.
- Pearls: A 72-hour hard-stop-style alert is consistent with the same principle already used successfully for surgical prophylaxis elsewhere; adapt that model.; Involve the antimicrobial pharmacist to review these patients proactively rather than relying on the medical team alone.; Pair data collection with the existing IV-antibiotics-before-endoscopy measure, since both use the same patient list.; Track total antibiotic duration as an outcome measure alongside whether a review happened.

**NNA-669. What proportion of adults with refractory ascites due to cirrhosis have a documented assessment for a transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt (TIPS)?** (new)
- Standard: NICE NG50 rec 1.10.1 (2016): "Consider a TIPS procedure for people with cirrhosis who have refractory ascites." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng50/chapter/Managing-complications
- Pass: A documented decision about TIPS suitability (referred for assessment, or a specific reason why not suitable, for example advanced encephalopathy or severe liver failure) is recorded for patients meeting criteria for refractory ascites.. Target: ≥80%. Sample: All patients meeting refractory ascites criteria over 12 months (typically 15-30 in a DGH hepatology service).
- Change: Add refractory ascites (based on paracentesis frequency) as an automatic flag on the hepatology paracentesis list that prompts a TIPS/transplant suitability discussion at the next MDT.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-669.csv`
- Pitfalls: Some patients are clearly unsuitable for TIPS (severe encephalopathy, advanced heart failure) and this should count as meeting the standard if documented, not as a missed opportunity.; Refractory ascites definitions vary; agree a clear, paracentesis-frequency-based definition with the audit team before starting.; Patients already listed for or having had a liver transplant assessment may reasonably have TIPS deprioritised: capture this context.; Retrospective identification from the paracentesis list may miss patients managed with fewer, larger-volume taps: cross-check with clinic letters too.
- Pearls: Use the paracentesis list itself as the simplest way to identify the eligible population, since these patients are already being tracked for another reason.; Build the TIPS/transplant discussion into an existing regular MDT rather than creating a new meeting.; Loop in interventional radiology early, since they will need to give a technical suitability opinion alongside the hepatology assessment.; Track outcomes (TIPS performed, transplant listed, or neither with reason) at re-audit to show the assessment step leads to a real decision.

**NNA-670. What proportion of adults drinking above the high-risk threshold (men >50, women >35 units/week for several months) have transient elastography offered to check for cirrhosis?** (new)
- Standard: NICE NG50 rec 1.1.3 (2016): "Offer transient elastography to diagnose cirrhosis for: ... men and people registered male at birth who drink over 50 units of alcohol per week and have done so for several months; women and people registered female at birth who drink over 35 units of alcohol per week and have done so for several months; people diagnosed with alcohol-related liver disease." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng50/chapter/Diagnosis
- Pass: Transient elastography is offered (referral made, whether or not the patient attends) within 3 months of a documented drinking history meeting the high-risk threshold.. Target: ≥70%. Sample: 40 consecutive adults meeting the high-risk drinking threshold.
- Change: Add an automatic transient elastography referral prompt to the alcohol liaison and GP alcohol-history template whenever units/week above the NICE threshold are recorded.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-670.csv`
- Pitfalls: A full, quantified drinking history (units/week and duration) is often missing from records, making the denominator hard to define: agree a minimum documentation standard before starting.; Some services already scan all heavy drinkers routinely and this may look like a ceiling effect: check local pathway assumptions before assuming a gap exists.; Elastography referred but not attended should be recorded separately from not offered, since these need different fixes (engagement support versus system prompts).; Patients already known to have cirrhosis do not need this specific test again: exclude them from the denominator.
- Pearls: Use the alcohol care team, where one exists, as the most reliable route to both take a full drinking history and refer for elastography in one contact.; A community-based (rather than hospital-only) scanning service increases uptake for patients reluctant to attend hospital appointments.; Track attendance as well as referral, since engagement is often the bigger barrier in this population.; Feed positive findings into the wider cirrhosis surveillance pathway audited elsewhere in this set.

**NNA-671. What proportion of adults with alcohol-related liver disease, or MASLD with advanced fibrosis, who do not have cirrhosis are retested for cirrhosis at least every 2 years?** (new)
- Standard: NICE NG50 rec 1.1.10 (2016): "Offer retesting for cirrhosis every 2 years for: people diagnosed with alcohol-related liver disease, people with hepatitis C virus infection who have not shown a sustained virological response to antiviral therapy, people with MASLD and advanced liver fibrosis." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng50/chapter/Diagnosis
- Pass: A repeat test for cirrhosis (transient elastography or equivalent) is documented within 2 years of the previous negative test in eligible patients.. Target: ≥80%. Sample: 40 consecutive eligible adults with at least 2 years since their last negative cirrhosis test.
- Change: Add a 2-yearly recall for cirrhosis retesting to the hepatology or GP chronic liver disease register for eligible patients, rather than relying on ad hoc re-referral.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-671.csv`
- Pitfalls: Patients who stop attending follow-up (including due to ongoing alcohol use) are the group most likely to miss retesting, and also the group at highest risk: flag non-attendance rather than silently excluding these patients.; A retest done for another reason (e.g. incidental imaging) may satisfy the standard even if not labelled as a 'retest': check imaging history broadly, not just labelled follow-up scans.; Local availability of transient elastography devices limits capacity: record whether delay reflects service capacity rather than a process failure.; Patients who progress to cirrhosis between scheduled retests should be picked up by symptoms/blood tests, not solely by the fixed interval: note any such cases separately.
- Pearls: A chronic liver disease register with an automatic recall function is the most reliable fix; building this once benefits several of the audits in this set.; Community alcohol and liver clinics can help retain patients who might otherwise disengage from hospital follow-up.; Use this audit as an opportunity to build or refine a shared hepatology-primary care register, since retesting often depends on GP-hospital communication.; Report retesting adherence separately by diagnosis group (ArLD vs MASLD vs HCV), since engagement patterns often differ.

**NNA-672. What proportion of adults with decompensated alcohol-related liver disease, still decompensated after best management and 3 months' abstinence, are referred for assessment for liver transplantation?** (new)
- Standard: NICE CG100 rec 1.3.2.1 (2010, amended 2017): "Refer patients with decompensated liver disease to be considered for assessment for liver transplantation if they: still have decompensated liver disease after best management and 3 months' abstinence from alcohol and are otherwise suitable candidates for liver transplantation." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg100/chapter/Recommendations
- Pass: A referral to a liver transplant centre for assessment is made and documented for patients who remain decompensated after best medical management and 3 months' confirmed abstinence, and who have no other clear contraindication.. Target: ≥85%. Sample: All patients meeting these criteria over 12-24 months (typically 10-20 cases in a DGH hepatology service).
- Change: Add a '3-month abstinence and still decompensated: transplant referral considered' prompt to the hepatology follow-up template, triggered automatically once 3 months of documented abstinence is reached in a decompensated patient.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-672.csv`
- Pitfalls: Confirming '3 months' abstinence' reliably (self-report versus biochemical markers) is itself inconsistent between clinicians: agree a documentation standard before starting.; Some patients are correctly not referred due to other contraindications (severe cardiac or psychiatric comorbidity): capture these as valid reasons, not failures.; Numbers will be small; extend the collection period or audit retrospectively over 24 months.; A patient who relapses during the 3-month period restarts the clock under most local pathways: record this clearly rather than treating it as an audit exclusion only.
- Pearls: A structured alcohol-abstinence tracking field (rather than free text) makes this measurable and repeatable.; Engage the regional transplant centre early to confirm the exact local interpretation of 'suitable candidate' criteria used alongside the NICE recommendation.; Loop in the alcohol liaison or addiction service, since abstinence support is central to whether patients ever reach the 3-month point at all.; Present outcomes of transplant centre assessments (accepted, declined, further tests needed) to close the loop beyond referral alone.

**NNA-673. What proportion of adults on azathioprine or mercaptopurine for Crohn's disease have a full blood count checked at the locally agreed monitoring interval, even when TPMT activity is normal?** (under-audited)
- Standard: NICE NG129 rec 1.2.10 (2012): "Monitor the effects of azathioprine, mercaptopurine and methotrexate as advised in the BNF or BNFC. Consult the monographs of individual drugs for advice on monitoring immunosuppressives. Monitor for neutropenia in people taking azathioprine or mercaptopurine even if they have normal TPMT activity." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng129/chapter/Recommendations
- Pass: A full blood count is checked at the locally agreed interval (typically weekly for the first month, then monthly, per BNF monographs) throughout the audit period, with no gap longer than the agreed interval.. Target: ≥85%. Sample: 40 consecutive adults on ongoing azathioprine or mercaptopurine.
- Change: Set up a shared-care monitoring template (hospital or GP-run) with an automatic reminder when an FBC becomes overdue for any patient on ongoing thiopurine therapy for IBD.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-673.csv`
- Pitfalls: Shared-care monitoring split between GP and hospital can create gaps where each assumes the other is checking: agree and document one named responsible party per patient.; Missed appointments for blood tests are common and should be flagged for active follow-up, not just recorded as a gap.; A late-but-eventually-done blood test still represents a period of unmonitored risk: report both 'ever done' and 'done on time'.; Dose changes reset or alter the expected monitoring frequency; make sure the expected interval used in the audit matches current, not historical, dosing.
- Pearls: Use the exact structure that worked in a related paediatric audit: a shared-care guideline plus a tick-box monitoring proforma with all parameters listed together [2966].; A laboratory-generated automatic reminder is more durable than relying on either GP or hospital memory alone.; Make the responsible party for monitoring (GP vs hospital) explicit in every new thiopurine-start letter.; Track outcomes of any neutropenia detected, to show the monitoring system actually catches and acts on the risk it exists to prevent.

**NNA-674. What proportion of adults newly diagnosed with coeliac disease have a documented discussion about pneumococcal vaccination?** (new)
- Standard: NICE NG20 rec 1.6.5 (2015): "Explain to people with coeliac disease and their family members or carers (as appropriate) that the Department of Health's Green Book recommends immunisation against pneumococcus." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng20/chapter/Recommendations
- Pass: A documented discussion about pneumococcal vaccination is recorded at, or within 3 months of, the diagnosis of coeliac disease.. Target: ≥90%. Sample: 40 consecutive adults with a new diagnosis of coeliac disease.
- Change: Add a 'pneumococcal vaccination discussed' tick box with a pre-written information line to the coeliac disease diagnosis clinic letter template, sent to both the patient and the GP.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-674.csv`
- Pitfalls: The discussion may happen verbally at diagnosis but not be written down: this audit measures documentation, and should say so plainly rather than assuming the conversation never happened.; GPs, not gastroenterology, usually administer the vaccine: the audit should track the discussion (specialist's responsibility) separately from vaccine administration (usually primary care's).; Patients already vaccinated for another indication (for example, age-related pneumococcal vaccination) should still have the coeliac-specific discussion recorded, since guidance and eligibility can differ.; A generic coeliac information leaflet mentioning vaccination in passing is not the same as a documented individual discussion: define the standard clearly before starting.
- Pearls: A single sentence and tick box in the standard diagnosis letter, copied to the GP, is a low-effort fix that also prompts GP action.; Pair the vaccination discussion with the annual review audit above so both draw on the same diagnosis-clinic dataset.; Consider adapting the invitation-letter approach already shown to work in the library [9569] as the mechanism for actually getting patients vaccinated once discussed.; Track vaccine uptake as well as discussion rates at re-audit to confirm discussion translates into action.

**NNA-675. What proportion of adults admitted with acute alcohol-related hepatitis have a documented nutritional assessment, with nutritional support started if indicated?** (new)
- Standard: NICE CG100 rec 1.3.4.1 (2010): "Assess the nutritional requirements of people with acute alcohol-related hepatitis. Offer nutritional support if needed and consider using nasogastric tube feeding." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg100/chapter/Recommendations
- Pass: A nutritional assessment (for example, MUST score or dietitian review) is documented within 48 hours of admission with acute alcohol-related hepatitis, with nutritional support started if indicated.. Target: ≥85%. Sample: 30 consecutive adults admitted with acute alcohol-related hepatitis.
- Change: Add acute alcohol-related hepatitis as a trigger diagnosis for an automatic same-day dietitian referral and MUST scoring on the hepatology/gastroenterology admission bundle.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-675.csv`
- Pitfalls: General ward MUST scoring may be completed routinely but not specifically prompt dietitian input for this high-risk group: check whether a score is acted on, not just recorded.; Nasogastric feeding can be difficult in patients with encephalopathy or agitation: a documented reason not to feed enterally should count as a valid clinical decision, not a failure.; Weekend admissions may have delayed dietitian input due to staffing: check whether delays cluster there.; Poor oral intake due to nausea or ongoing alcohol withdrawal symptoms needs separate management alongside nutrition, and should be recorded as context.
- Pearls: An automatic dietitian referral triggered by the diagnosis code removes reliance on the ward team remembering a nutrition-specific step amid other urgent decisions (steroids, infection screen).; Weekend and out-of-hours dietitian cover (or a clear escalation plan) is often the main practical barrier: check this with dietetics before proposing a fix.; Combine data collection with the pre-steroid infection screening audit above, since both draw from the same acute alcoholic hepatitis admission list.; Track nutritional status trends (weight, albumin) through the admission as an outcome measure at re-audit.

## Acute and specialty medicine

**NNA-676. What proportion of adult inpatients have their drug allergy status recorded using one of the three standard categories (drug allergy / none known / unable to ascertain) before their first drug is prescribed?** (under-audited)
- Standard: NICE CG183 Drug allergy: diagnosis and management, rec 1.2.1 (2014): "Document people's drug allergy status in their medical records using 1 of the following: 'drug allergy' 'none known' 'unable to ascertain' (document it as soon as the information is available)." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg183/chapter/Recommendations
- Pass: One of the three standard categories is recorded in the drug chart or EPR allergy field before the first drug is administered. Target: ≥95%. Sample: 40 consecutive adult admissions over the last 4 weeks
- Change: Make the three-category allergy field mandatory (hard stop) in the EPR admission clerking template, so the first drug order cannot be signed until it is completed.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-676.csv`
- Pitfalls: EPR build changes need informatics sign-off → agree the mandatory-field change with the CCIO before cycle 1 ends, not after; Junior doctors rotate before the fix embeds → nominate a pharmacist as the fixed point of contact; Free-text entries can be miscounted as complete → agree the definition of 'category used' with all data collectors before starting; Small numbers in a single specialty → collect from at least two wards to reach 40 cases
- Pearls: Recruit the admissions unit pharmacist as co-lead; they see the chart first; Agree the three-category wording with informatics before cycle 1 so re-audit uses the same EPR field; Present the before/after screenshots of the EPR field change at handover teaching; Keep the data collection tool to a single tick-box sheet so FY1s can complete it in under a minute per patient

**NNA-677. What proportion of adults treated in hospital for suspected anaphylaxis are offered a referral to a specialist allergy service before discharge?** (new)
- Standard: NICE NG258 Anaphylaxis: assessment and referral after emergency treatment, rec 1.1.12 (2011, updated 2026, replaces CG134): "After emergency treatment for suspected anaphylaxis, offer the adult, young person or child a referral to a specialist allergy service (age-appropriate, where possible) consisting of healthcare professionals with the skills and competencies necessary to accurately investigate, diagnose, monitor and provide ongoing management of, and patient education about, anaphylaxis." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng258/chapter/Referral-to-a-specialist-allergy-service
- Pass: A referral to a specialist allergy service is documented as offered (accepted or declined) in the discharge letter. Target: ≥90%. Sample: 30 consecutive adults over the last 6 months (from anaphylaxis coding or adrenaline administration records)
- Change: Add a mandatory 'specialist allergy referral offered: yes/no/declined' field to the ED and ward anaphylaxis discharge template, linked to a one-click referral.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-677.csv`
- Pitfalls: Cases are hard to identify from coding alone → cross-check against adrenaline dispensing or resuscitation trolley records; Allergy clinic capacity may not match referral volume → agree an interim GP-led pathway with commissioners before cycle 1; Referral marked 'offered' without evidence in the letter → require the referral letter itself as the evidence source, not staff recall; Locum staff unaware of the pathway → include the referral step in ED induction
- Pearls: Identify a named allergy clinic contact before starting so the referral has somewhere real to go; Use the same anaphylaxis case list as any tryptase or auto-injector audit already running, to avoid re-searching notes; Show the ED consultant body the presenting numbers first, since they set the pathway; Keep the referral field as a single tick-box so it does not add time to a busy discharge

**NNA-678. What proportion of adults discharged after emergency treatment for suspected anaphylaxis receive a brand-specific demonstration of their adrenaline auto-injector before they leave?** (new)
- Standard: NICE NG258 Anaphylaxis: assessment and referral after emergency treatment, rec 1.1.14 (2011, updated 2026, replaces CG134): "a brand-specific demonstration of the correct use of the adrenaline auto-injector and when to use it, including advice that the person should lie down after using the injector (or sit up if they are struggling to breathe) and should not stand up or change position suddenly, even if they feel better" https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng258/chapter/Discharge-from-AE-or-inpatient-care
- Pass: A brand-specific auto-injector demonstration, including the lie-down/sit-up advice, is documented as given before discharge. Target: ≥90%. Sample: 30 consecutive discharges over the last 6 months
- Change: Stock a trainer device for each auto-injector brand at the ED discharge desk and add a 'training given (brand, trainer device used)' tick-box to the discharge checklist.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-678.csv`
- Pitfalls: Trainer devices go missing or expire → assign restocking to a named nurse each month; Training documented as 'device explained' without naming the brand → define 'brand-specific' clearly for data collectors before cycle 1; Night shifts may lack trainer devices → check stock across all shifts, not just daytime; Patients too unwell at discharge to retain training → offer a follow-up call or allergy clinic re-demonstration
- Pearls: Get free trainer devices from the manufacturers' websites before cycle 1, at no cost; Recruit the ED discharge nurses as co-auditors; they already do the training; Link the audit to the two-auto-injector prescribing audit so the same case list serves both; Laminate a one-page technique card per brand for the discharge desk

**NNA-679. What proportion of adults discharged after emergency treatment for suspected anaphylaxis are given written information about the risk of a biphasic reaction?** (new)
- Standard: NICE NG258 Anaphylaxis: assessment and referral after emergency treatment, rec 1.1.14 (2011, updated 2026, replaces CG134): "information about the risk of a biphasic reaction" https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng258/chapter/Discharge-from-AE-or-inpatient-care
- Pass: Written information about the risk of a biphasic reaction is documented as given at discharge. Target: ≥90%. Sample: 30 consecutive discharges over the last 6 months
- Change: Build a single anaphylaxis discharge leaflet that already contains the biphasic reaction warning, printed automatically from the ED discharge template.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-679.csv`
- Pitfalls: Verbal advice given but not documented → require a tick-box, not free text, for this item; Leaflet given but not the anaphylaxis-specific one → check the leaflet code, not just 'leaflet given: yes'; Patients who leave against advice are missed → exclude self-discharges from the denominator with a documented reason; Paediatric and adult leaflets get mixed up in a shared ED → colour-code them
- Pearls: Print the leaflet directly from the discharge template so giving it is the path of least resistance; Ask the allergy clinic to review the leaflet wording before cycle 1; Combine this data collection round with the auto-injector training audit to save time; Keep a spare stock check as part of the daily ED safety huddle

**NNA-680. What proportion of adults treated for anaphylaxis who receive a single dose of adrenaline with a good response are observed for at least 2 hours before discharge, and what proportion needing two or more doses are observed for at least 6 hours?** (new)
- Standard: NICE NG258 Anaphylaxis: assessment and referral after emergency treatment, recs 1.1.7 and 1.1.8 (2026): "A suitably qualified and experienced healthcare professional should consider discharging the adult, young person or child after 2 hours of observation... if there was a good response (within 5 to 10 minutes) to a single dose of intramuscular (IM) adrenaline... Observe the adult, young person or child for a minimum of 6 hours after resolution of all symptoms if: 2 doses of intramuscular (IM) adrenaline were needed to treat the anaphylaxis or there is a history of biphasic reaction." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng258/chapter/Period-of-observation
- Pass: Documented observation time meets or exceeds the 2-hour (single good-response dose) or 6-hour (two or more doses, or biphasic history) minimum before discharge. Target: ≥90%. Sample: 30 consecutive cases over the last 6 months
- Change: Add an automatic 'earliest safe discharge time' calculation to the ED anaphylaxis pathway, driven by the number of adrenaline doses given.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-680.csv`
- Pitfalls: Department pressure to discharge quickly → make the earliest-safe-discharge time visible on the tracking board so it is a system prompt, not a request; Symptom resolution time is often not documented precisely → agree a definition (last recorded abnormal observation) before cycle 1; Biphasic reaction history may be missed if old notes are unavailable → check the summary care record as well as ED notes; Small numbers if anaphylaxis presentations are infrequent → extend the sampling period to 6–9 months if needed
- Pearls: Recruit the ED sister in charge of patient flow, who controls the discharge decision; Use the same cases already being collected for the tryptase and referral audits; Present the observation-time calculation change alongside the current tracking board build, so it is one change, not two; Keep a laminated observation-time table at each ED bay as an interim measure while the system change is built

**NNA-681. What proportion of adults on a repeat prescription for an adrenaline auto-injector have documented, device-specific training within the last 12 months?** (new)
- Standard: MHRA Drug Safety Update, 'Adrenaline auto-injectors: updated advice after European review' (August 2017): "ensure that people with allergies and their carers have been trained to use the particular auto-injector that they have been prescribed—technique varies between injectors... You should review with the patient and their carers the instructions and operation of the adrenaline auto-injector." https://www.gov.uk/drug-safety-update/adrenaline-auto-injectors-updated-advice-after-european-review
- Pass: A documented device-specific technique review within the last 12 months for the auto-injector brand currently prescribed. Target: ≥85%. Sample: 40 consecutive patients on the practice's adrenaline auto-injector repeat list
- Change: Add an annual adrenaline auto-injector review recall (coded template) to the practice's chronic disease recall system, run alongside asthma or allergy reviews.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-681.csv`
- Pitfalls: Auto-injector brand changes between reviews (supply issues) → check the brand on each review, not just that a review happened; Recall letters go unanswered → combine the review with an existing annual review (asthma, allergy) already attended; Practice nurse time is limited → use a short standardised checklist rather than a full consultation; Patients moving practice are lost to follow-up → check the repeat list is current before each recall round
- Pearls: Use free trainer devices from manufacturers so nurses do not need to buy them; Recruit the practice's allergy or asthma lead nurse to run the recall; Combine the review with the annual flu or asthma clinic to raise attendance; Keep the checklist to under 5 minutes per patient so it is realistic in a nurse clinic

**NNA-682. What proportion of adults with a new genetic diagnosis of familial hypercholesterolaemia are referred to a specialist for confirmation of diagnosis and initiation of cascade testing?** (new)
- Standard: NICE CG71 Familial hypercholesterolaemia: identification and management, rec 1.2.2 (2008): "Healthcare professionals should offer all people with FH a referral to a specialist with expertise in FH for confirmation of diagnosis and initiation of cascade testing." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg71/chapter/Recommendations
- Pass: A referral to an FH specialist for cascade testing is documented within 4 weeks of the diagnosis being made or confirmed. Target: ≥90%. Sample: 30 consecutive new FH diagnoses over the last 12 months
- Change: Add an automatic FH specialist referral prompt to the primary care template that fires when a total cholesterol above the NICE search threshold or a compatible family history is coded.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-682.csv`
- Pitfalls: FH may be diagnosed but not coded consistently → agree a single Read/SNOMED code with the practice before starting; Regional cascade testing services have long waits → record referral made, not seen, as the pass criterion; Patients decline referral → record as a documented decline, not a failure of the process; Small numbers in an individual practice → collect across a PCN if a single practice has too few cases
- Pearls: Agree the FH coding search with the practice's clinical informatics lead before cycle 1; Contact the regional genetics/lipid service to confirm their referral pathway and turnaround; Present the case for automation with real delayed-referral examples from cycle 1; Keep a running FH register so future new diagnoses are captured prospectively, not retrospectively

**NNA-683. Of first- and second-degree relatives of a confirmed familial hypercholesterolaemia index case, what proportion complete DNA cascade testing within 6 months of the index case's genetic diagnosis?** (new)
- Standard: NICE CG71 Familial hypercholesterolaemia: identification and management, rec 1.2.1 (2017): "Carry out cascade testing using DNA testing to identify affected first- and second- and, when possible, third-degree biological relatives of people with a genetic diagnosis of FH." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg71/chapter/Recommendations
- Pass: DNA test result recorded for the relative within 6 months of the index case's genetic diagnosis. Target: ≥70%. Sample: 30 consecutive relatives identified for cascade testing over the last 2 years
- Change: Give the FH clinic a standard cascade testing pack (letter, appointment slot, DNA kit) to send directly to named relatives once consent is given by the index case, rather than relying on the index case to pass on information.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-683.csv`
- Pitfalls: Family communication of risk is inconsistent → offer direct clinic-to-relative contact rather than relying on the index patient alone; Relatives live out of area → agree a shared-care pathway with neighbouring genetics services before cycle 1; Data protection concerns about contacting relatives directly → confirm consent processes with the clinic's information governance lead first; Long lead times for genetic results → record 'test sent' and 'result received' separately
- Pearls: Build the register prospectively from cycle 1 so future cohorts are easy to track; Involve the genetic counsellor early; they already manage family communication; Track by family, not just by relative, to spot families where uptake is systematically low; Share the six-month completion rate with the index patient's GP to prompt local encouragement

**NNA-684. What proportion of newly diagnosed colorectal cancers have mismatch repair (immunohistochemistry) or microsatellite instability testing for Lynch syndrome performed as part of the diagnostic pathway?** (new)
- Standard: NICE HealthTech guidance HTG430 (formerly DG27), Molecular testing strategies for Lynch syndrome in people with colorectal cancer, rec 1.1 (2017, moved to HTG430): "Offer testing to all people with colorectal cancer, when first diagnosed, using immunohistochemistry for mismatch repair proteins or microsatellite instability testing to identify tumours with deficient DNA mismatch repair, and to guide further sequential testing for Lynch syndrome. Do not wait for the results before starting treatment." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/htg430/chapter/1-Recommendations
- Pass: Mismatch repair immunohistochemistry or microsatellite instability testing is recorded on the pathology report for the index colorectal cancer. Target: ≥95%. Sample: 40 consecutive new colorectal cancer diagnoses over the last 6 months
- Change: Make mismatch repair immunohistochemistry a reflex (automatic) test on every colorectal cancer resection and biopsy specimen in the pathology laboratory information system, rather than requiring a separate clinician request.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-684.csv`
- Pitfalls: Reflex testing needs pathology IT and funding agreement → secure sign-off from the trust's cancer alliance before cycle 1; Biopsies with limited tissue may fail testing → record 'test attempted but inadequate sample' separately from 'not tested'; Abnormal results can be missed without a clear referral pathway → build the germline genetics referral into the MDT outcome form; Small numbers in a low-volume unit → extend to 9–12 months of cases if needed
- Pearls: Agree the reflex testing protocol with pathology, genetics and the colorectal MDT together before cycle 1; Use the existing MDT outcome form as the single source of truth for both testing and referral data; Present national uptake figures alongside local data to strengthen the case for reflex testing; Keep a running log of BRAF/MLH1 methylation results, since these determine whether germline testing is needed

**NNA-685. What proportion of newly diagnosed endometrial cancers have mismatch repair immunohistochemistry testing for Lynch syndrome performed?** (new)
- Standard: NICE HealthTech guidance HTG557 (formerly DG42), Testing strategies for Lynch syndrome in people with endometrial cancer, rec 1.1 (2020, moved to HTG557): "Offer testing for Lynch syndrome to people who are diagnosed with endometrial cancer. Use immunohistochemistry (IHC) to identify tumours with mismatch repair (MMR) deficiency." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/htg557/chapter/1-Recommendations
- Pass: Mismatch repair immunohistochemistry testing is recorded on the pathology report for the index endometrial cancer. Target: ≥95%. Sample: 30 consecutive new endometrial cancer diagnoses over the last 6 months
- Change: Make mismatch repair immunohistochemistry a reflex test on every endometrial cancer specimen in the pathology laboratory information system.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-685.csv`
- Pitfalls: Endometrial cancer is sometimes diagnosed on a small biopsy with limited tissue → record inadequate samples separately from untested cases; Genetics referral pathway differs between gynaecology and colorectal teams → agree a single shared pathway before cycle 1; Informing patients about hereditary implications needs trained staff → check rec 1.2 (informed consent and support) is followed alongside testing; Low case numbers in a smaller unit → extend the sampling period if fewer than 30 cases arise in 6 months
- Pearls: Align the endometrial and colorectal reflex testing changes into a single pathology laboratory business case; Involve the clinical geneticist in agreeing the referral trigger criteria before cycle 1; Use the gynae-oncology MDT coordinator as the single point of data collection; Share results with colorectal pathology, since the reflex testing infrastructure can be shared

**NNA-686. What proportion of people referred to a specialist genetics service with a combined BRCA1/BRCA2 mutation carrier probability of 10% or more are offered genetic testing?** (under-audited)
- Standard: NICE CG164 Familial breast cancer, recs 1.5.11 and 1.5.12 (2013): "Offer genetic testing in specialist genetic clinics to a relative with a personal history of breast and/or ovarian cancer if that relative has a combined BRCA1 and BRCA2 mutation carrier probability of 10% or more... Offer genetic testing in specialist genetic clinics to a person with no personal history of breast or ovarian cancer if their combined BRCA1 and BRCA2 mutation carrier probability is 10% or more and an affected relative is unavailable for testing." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg164/chapter/recommendations
- Pass: Genetic testing is documented as offered when the recorded carrier probability is 10% or more. Target: ≥95%. Sample: 40 consecutive referrals over the last 12 months
- Change: Build the carrier probability calculation into the genetics clinic referral template so the score and the testing decision are recorded together, rather than in separate free-text letters.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-686.csv`
- Pitfalls: Different calculators give different probabilities → agree a single approved tool with the genetics service before cycle 1; Older referral letters may not record a numerical probability at all → capture this as 'not recorded' rather than assuming non-compliance; Waiting list pressure may delay the offer beyond the clinic visit being audited → record 'offered' as the pass criterion, not 'tested'; Referrals from multiple specialties (breast, gynae-oncology, primary care) vary in quality → sample across all referral sources
- Pearls: Agree with the genetics service which calculator is their local standard before starting; Use the referral triage log as the single source for identifying cases; Present findings alongside the existing TNBC BRCA audit for a fuller genetics picture; Recruit a genetic counsellor as co-author for credibility with the service

**NNA-687. What proportion of people found to carry a high-risk predisposing gene mutation (for example BRCA1, BRCA2 or TP53) incidentally or on tumour testing are directly referred to a specialist genetics service?** (new)
- Standard: NICE CG164 Familial breast cancer, rec 1.3.6 (2004): "Direct referral to a specialist genetics service should take place where a high-risk predisposing gene mutation has been identified (for example, BRCA1, BRCA2 or TP53)." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg164/chapter/recommendations
- Pass: A direct referral to the specialist genetics service is documented within 4 weeks of the mutation result being reported. Target: ≥95%. Sample: 30 consecutive new high-risk mutation results over the last 12 months
- Change: Add an automatic genetics service alert triggered by the laboratory information system whenever a high-risk predisposing gene result is authorised.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-687.csv`
- Pitfalls: Tumour (somatic) mutation results can be mistaken for germline and missed for referral → clarify in the laboratory report whether germline testing is also needed; Results reported to a non-genetics team who are unfamiliar with the referral pathway → include a referral prompt on the report itself; Patients who die or are lost to follow-up before referral → record as an exclusion with a documented reason; Multiple laboratories report to the same trust → check all reporting routes, not just the main cancer genetics lab
- Pearls: Work with the molecular pathology lab to build the alert directly into result authorisation; Agree with oncology and surgical teams who owns the referral action when a result comes back; Track time from result to referral, not result to genetics appointment, since waiting lists are outside the referring team's control; Share early results with the cancer genetics MDT to build momentum for the system change

**NNA-688. What proportion of adults admitted to hospital with heart failure are offered a referral to a personalised, exercise-based cardiac rehabilitation programme?** (new)
- Standard: NICE NG106 Chronic heart failure in adults: diagnosis and management, rec 1.11.1 (2018, amended 2025): "Offer people with heart failure a personalised, exercise-based cardiac rehabilitation programme. The programme: should be preceded by an assessment to ensure that it is suitable for the person should be provided in a format and setting (at home, in the community or in the hospital) that is easily accessible for the person should include a psychological and educational component." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng106/chapter/recommendations
- Pass: A referral to an exercise-based cardiac rehabilitation programme is documented as offered before or shortly after discharge. Target: ≥90%. Sample: 30 consecutive heart failure admissions over the last 3 months
- Change: Add a mandatory exercise-based cardiac rehabilitation referral field to the heart failure discharge bundle, defaulting to 'referred' with a documented reason required if not.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-688.csv`
- Pitfalls: Cardiac rehabilitation services may be commissioned mainly for post-MI/CABG patients, with heart failure referral pathways less established → confirm the local service accepts heart failure referrals before cycle 1; Frail or very elderly patients may be wrongly assumed unsuitable without a formal assessment → require a documented suitability assessment, not clinician judgement alone; Community or home-based options may not exist locally → record the format offered so gaps in provision are visible; Patients declining rehabilitation should be recorded as offered-declined, not as a system failure
- Pearls: Involve the heart failure specialist nurse, who already coordinates much of this discharge planning; Agree with the cardiac rehabilitation service in advance how they will handle a rise in heart failure referrals; Use the same discharge bundle build as the CABG rehabilitation referral audit already running, for efficiency; Report referral rate by referral format to identify where local provision needs to expand

**NNA-689. What proportion of patients with a new traumatic or non-traumatic spinal cord injury are referred to the linked Spinal Cord Injury Centre within 12 hours of injury via the National Spinal Cord Injury Database, or telephoned within 4 hours where no agreed protocol exists?** (new)
- Standard: NHS England Service Specification, Spinal Cord Injury Services (all ages), 2019: "Referral is made through the National Spinal Cord Injury Database (NSCID) within 12 hours of injury. If agreed protocols do not exist the SCIC should also be telephoned within 4 hours." https://www.england.nhs.uk/wp-content/uploads/2019/04/service-spec-spinal-cord-injury-services-all-ages.pdf
- Pass: Referral is documented via the NSCID within 12 hours of injury, with telephone contact within 4 hours recorded where no agreed local protocol exists. Target: ≥90%. Sample: 20 consecutive new spinal cord injury presentations over the last 12 months (a smaller, targeted sample given expected low case numbers)
- Change: Add an NSCID referral step, timed from presentation, to the trauma team's spinal injury checklist, with a direct telephone number for the linked Spinal Cord Injury Centre displayed on the checklist.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-689.csv`
- Pitfalls: Spinal cord injury presentations are infrequent in a single centre → extend the sampling period to 12–24 months if needed; Non-traumatic cases (for example from compressive pathology) may be referred later, from neurology or spinal surgery rather than the trauma team → include both referral routes; Staff unfamiliar with the NSCID system may default to informal telephone contact only → check both are properly recorded, not just one; Referral timing may be recorded on NSCID but not cross-checked locally → keep a parallel local log during the audit
- Pearls: Contact the linked Spinal Cord Injury Centre to confirm the agreed local referral protocol before cycle 1; Display the NSCID referral pathway and the direct SCIC telephone number in the emergency department trauma bay; Recruit the trauma coordinator or major trauma network rehabilitation lead as audit champion; Present findings to the regional trauma network, since this is a network-wide rather than single-hospital standard

**NNA-690. What proportion of patients admitted to a Spinal Cord Injury Centre have their first documented MDT goal-planning meeting within 3 weeks of mobilisation?** (new)
- Standard: NHS England Service Specification, Spinal Cord Injury Services (all ages), 2019: "documented goal-planning meetings should be held between the MDT staff and the patient. Family and significant others should be encouraged to participate and contribute to goals set. Following acute injury, the first meeting should take place within 3 weeks of mobilisation and subsequent meetings no less often than 4-weekly thereafter." https://www.england.nhs.uk/wp-content/uploads/2019/04/service-spec-spinal-cord-injury-services-all-ages.pdf
- Pass: A documented MDT goal-planning meeting takes place within 3 weeks of mobilisation, with subsequent meetings no more than 4 weeks apart. Target: ≥90%. Sample: 20 consecutive admissions reaching mobilisation over the last 12 months
- Change: Add an automatic goal-planning meeting booking, timed from the mobilisation date recorded in therapy notes, to the SCIC's weekly MDT diary.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-690.csv`
- Pitfalls: Mobilisation date can be recorded inconsistently across therapy disciplines → agree a single definition (first out-of-bed sitting/standing) before cycle 1; Small numbers in a single specialist centre → extend the sampling period if fewer than 20 admissions reach mobilisation in a year; Weekly MDT diary pressure may push meetings later than planned → protect goal-planning meeting slots in the diary rather than fitting them around other business; Family/significant other participation may not be recorded even when the meeting itself happens on time → check both timing and participation
- Pearls: Use the SCIC's own MDT coordinator, who already runs the weekly meeting diary, as audit lead; Cross-check this audit against the referral-timing audit above to build a full picture of the SCI pathway from injury to rehabilitation; Present results alongside UKROC outcome data already collected by the centre; Keep a simple wall planner of mobilisation dates and due goal-planning meetings visible to the MDT

**NNA-691. What proportion of spinal cord injury patients' MDT goal-planning meetings have documented evidence that family or significant others were invited to participate?** (new)
- Standard: NHS England Service Specification, Spinal Cord Injury Services (all ages), 2019: "Family and significant others should be encouraged to participate and contribute to goals set." https://www.england.nhs.uk/wp-content/uploads/2019/04/service-spec-spinal-cord-injury-services-all-ages.pdf
- Pass: The goal-planning meeting record documents that family or significant others were invited, whether or not they were able to attend. Target: ≥90%. Sample: 20 consecutive goal-planning meetings over the last 12 months
- Change: Add a mandatory 'family/significant other invited: yes (who) / no (why not)' field to the goal-planning meeting record template.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-691.csv`
- Pitfalls: Family may live far from the specialist centre, making attendance difficult → accept telephone or video participation as equivalent to invitation and involvement; Patients may decline family involvement, which should be recorded as a valid patient choice rather than non-compliance; Small numbers of meetings in a specialist centre → extend the sampling period if needed; Invitation may happen informally by phone without being logged → require the invitation itself, not just attendance, to be documented
- Pearls: Combine data collection with the goal-planning meeting timing audit, since both use the same meeting records; Offer video-link attendance as standard for family members who cannot travel; Ask the SCIC's clinical psychologist or family liaison worker to help design the invitation record; Share this audit with the trust's patient experience team, since family involvement is closely linked to reported patient experience

**NNA-692. What proportion of adults admitted to a major trauma centre and found to need rehabilitation have their first rehabilitation assessment within 48–72 hours of admission?** (new)
- Standard: NHS England Major Trauma Rehabilitation Prescription 2019, Adult patients (2019 guidance): "A first rehabilitation assessment should take place within 48-72 hours of the patient's admission and the Rehabilitation Prescription (2019) will have to be completed for all major trauma patients who need rehabilitation at discharge." https://www.c4ts.qmul.ac.uk/downloads/mt-rehabilitation-prescription-2019-guidance.pdf
- Pass: A documented first rehabilitation assessment within 48–72 hours of admission for patients identified as needing rehabilitation. Target: ≥90%. Sample: 30 consecutive major trauma patients needing rehabilitation over the last 6 months
- Change: Add an automatic rehabilitation assessment referral, timed from admission, to the major trauma centre's trauma team activation checklist.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-692.csv`
- Pitfalls: Weekend admissions may have reduced therapy staffing → audit weekday versus weekend admissions separately; Patients with fluctuating consciousness may be hard to assess within the window → record a documented reason for delay where clinically necessary; TARN data entry lags behind clinical events → cross-check TARN records against ward notes for accuracy; Multiple specialties (orthopaedics, neurosurgery, general surgery) may each assume another team owns the referral → name a single responsible role in the trauma pathway
- Pearls: Use the existing trauma team activation checklist as the natural place to add the rehabilitation referral trigger; Recruit the trauma rehabilitation coordinator, who already tracks TARN data, as audit lead; Present the audit as part of the annual TARN peer review submission for extra visibility; Keep the assessment threshold simple (48–72 hours) rather than adding local variations that complicate re-audit

**NNA-693. What proportion of major trauma patients with a completed rehabilitation prescription have documented evidence that it was developed with the involvement of the patient and/or their family or carers?** (new)
- Standard: NHS England Major Trauma Rehabilitation Prescription 2019, Adult patients (2019 guidance): "The Rehabilitation Prescription must be developed with the involvement of the patient and/or their family/carers." https://www.c4ts.qmul.ac.uk/downloads/mt-rehabilitation-prescription-2019-guidance.pdf
- Pass: The completed rehabilitation prescription documents patient and/or family/carer involvement in its development. Target: ≥90%. Sample: 30 consecutive completed rehabilitation prescriptions over the last 6 months
- Change: Add a mandatory 'patient/family involvement in developing this prescription: yes (how) / no (why not)' field to the rehabilitation prescription template, so the form cannot be signed off without it.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-693.csv`
- Pitfalls: Involvement may happen verbally at the bedside but go unrecorded → require a specific field, not reliance on general ward round notes; Family may be geographically distant or unavailable → accept telephone or video involvement as documented evidence; Junior staff completing the form may not know who was involved in earlier discussions → make involvement a discussion point at the rehabilitation MDT itself; Patients who decline family involvement should not be marked as non-compliant → record explicit patient choice as a valid reason
- Pearls: Add the involvement field alongside the timing field from the previous audit so both are checked in one form review; Ask the trauma rehabilitation coordinator to prompt involvement documentation at the weekly MDT; Share example wording of a well-documented involvement note with staff before cycle 1; Feed both rehabilitation prescription audits into the same annual TARN peer review submission

**NNA-694. What proportion of grassroots sport participants with a suspected concussion are immediately removed from play, with no same-day return?** (new)
- Standard: UK Concussion Guidelines for Grassroots Sport (Sport and Recreation Alliance, updated November 2024, endorsed across UK sport and government): "As with anyone who suffers a concussion, disabled people who have a suspected concussion must be removed from play. The principles of “If In Doubt Sit Them Out” apply." https://sportandrecreation.org.uk/campaigns-and-policy/concussion/concussion-guidelines-for-grassroots-sport-html-version
- Pass: The player is recorded as removed from play immediately on suspicion of concussion, with no return to play that same session. Target: 100%. Sample: 30 consecutive suspected concussion incidents over the last season (from club first-aid/incident logs)
- Change: Make a documented 'if in doubt, sit them out' incident form a mandatory part of every club's first-aid kit, with copies logged centrally by the club welfare officer.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-694.csv`
- Pitfalls: Incidents are under-reported when there is no injury log at all → introduce a simple paper or app-based log before cycle 1; Coaches and parents may pressure a return to play → back the pitch-side decision-maker with written club policy signed by all coaches; Volunteers may not recognise all concussion signs → provide a short recognition card as part of first-aid kit; Data collection depends on volunteers completing forms consistently → assign a single welfare officer to own the log
- Pearls: Adopt the free downloadable UK Concussion Guidelines pocket card as the pitch-side reference before cycle 1; Recruit the club or league welfare/safeguarding officer as audit lead, since they already handle incident reporting; Run the audit across a whole league or club network rather than a single team, to get a realistic sample; Share the 'if in doubt, sit them out' message at the pre-season coaches' briefing to embed the standard from the start

**NNA-695. What proportion of players with a suspected concussion are assessed by an appropriate healthcare professional before beginning the graduated return to activity and sport programme?** (new)
