- Standard: UK Concussion Guidelines for Grassroots Sport (Sport and Recreation Alliance, updated November 2024): "Return to play should not be permitted until after evaluation by an appropriate Healthcare Professional and the successful completion of a graduated return to activity (education/work) and sport programme." https://sportandrecreation.org.uk/campaigns-and-policy/concussion/concussion-guidelines-for-grassroots-sport-html-version
- Pass: A documented assessment by an appropriate healthcare professional (for example GP, sport and exercise medicine physician or physiotherapist with concussion training) before the graduated return programme begins. Target: ≥90%. Sample: 30 consecutive concussion cases with a return to sport over the last season
- Change: Require a signed healthcare professional clearance form before a player's name can be entered onto the graduated return-to-sport log kept by the club.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-695.csv`
- Pitfalls: Access to a healthcare professional with concussion training can be limited in rural or amateur settings → agree a referral pathway to a local GP or sports medicine clinic in advance; Assessment happens but is not documented in a form the club can check → provide a simple one-page clearance certificate; Financial or time barriers to seeing a healthcare professional → make clubs aware of NHS and GP routes, not only private sports medicine; Players self-declare recovery without assessment → make the clearance form a condition of registration for that fixture
- Pearls: Partner with a local sport and exercise medicine clinic or GP practice willing to provide concussion clearance letters; Use the same incident log built for the removal-from-play audit to identify cases; Publicise the clearance requirement to parents and players, not only coaches, so it is understood league-wide; Keep the clearance form short so it does not become a barrier to a genuinely recovered player returning

**NNA-696. What proportion of players with a confirmed or suspected concussion have no return to a contact/competitive fixture before 21 days from the date of injury?** (new)
- Standard: UK Concussion Guidelines for Grassroots Sport (Sport and Recreation Alliance, updated November 2024): "All concussions should be managed individually, but there should be no return to competition before 21 days from injury." https://sportandrecreation.org.uk/campaigns-and-policy/concussion/concussion-guidelines-for-grassroots-sport-html-version
- Pass: The recorded date of return to competitive/contact fixtures is 21 days or more after the recorded injury date. Target: 100%. Sample: 30 consecutive concussion cases with a documented return to competition over the last season
- Change: Add an automatic 21-day 'earliest eligible return date' calculation to the club's team registration/selection system, blocking selection before that date.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-696.csv`
- Pitfalls: Team sheets are not always retained systematically by amateur clubs → agree with the league to keep a central selection record; Competitive pressure (finals, promotion deciders) may tempt an early return → make the 21-day rule a league regulation, not just guidance, with a stated sanction; Cross-checking injury date against team sheets is time-consuming → digitise team sheet submission where possible; Players who play for multiple teams may return early via a different team → check league-wide registration, not just one club
- Pearls: Ask the league to formally adopt the 21-day rule as a playing regulation, giving the audit real teeth; Use existing fixture and team sheet records already kept for other purposes (discipline, results) to minimise new data collection; Share results with coaches at end-of-season meetings to reinforce the standard for the following season; Combine this audit with the medical-clearance audit above, since both use the same case list

**NNA-697. What proportion of players with concussion symptoms lasting longer than 28 days are referred for assessment by an appropriate healthcare professional such as their GP?** (new)
- Standard: UK Concussion Guidelines for Grassroots Sport (Sport and Recreation Alliance, updated November 2024): "Anyone with symptoms that last longer than 28 days should be assessed and managed by an appropriate Healthcare Professional (e.g. their General Practitioner [GP])." https://sportandrecreation.org.uk/campaigns-and-policy/concussion/concussion-guidelines-for-grassroots-sport-html-version
- Pass: A documented referral for medical assessment is made for players whose symptoms are recorded as still present at 28 days. Target: ≥90%. Sample: 20 consecutive concussion cases with symptoms tracked to 28 days over the last season (a smaller, targeted sample given expected low case numbers)
- Change: Give the club welfare officer a structured 28-day symptom check-in call template, with an automatic prompt to refer to the GP if symptoms persist.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-697.csv`
- Pitfalls: Follow-up beyond the playing season can be lost if the player stops attending training → agree a follow-up method that does not depend on continued attendance (phone call, text); Symptom self-report may be under-reported due to fear of missing further games → reassure players the check-in is about their health, not selection; Small numbers of persistent cases make percentages unstable → report raw numbers alongside the percentage; GPs unfamiliar with sport-specific return-to-play advice → provide GPs with a simple referral information sheet
- Pearls: Give welfare officers a simple three-question symptom check script to use at day 28; Build a relationship with a local sports medicine or GP clinic willing to see referred players promptly; Track persistent symptoms across a season to identify whether any single team or sport has a cluster; Feed this audit into the same welfare committee reporting cycle as the other concussion audits

**NNA-698. What proportion of players advised to rest after a suspected concussion have documentation that they were told to avoid intense exercise, challenging work or sport for the first 24–48 hours?** (new)
- Standard: UK Concussion Guidelines for Grassroots Sport (Sport and Recreation Alliance, updated November 2024): "Anyone with concussion should generally rest for 24-48 hours but can undertake easy activities of daily living and walking, but must avoid intense exercise, challenging work, or sport." https://sportandrecreation.org.uk/campaigns-and-policy/concussion/concussion-guidelines-for-grassroots-sport-html-version
- Pass: Documented advice given at the time of injury includes the 24–48 hour rest period and avoidance of intense exercise, challenging work and sport. Target: ≥95%. Sample: 30 consecutive suspected concussion incidents over the last season
- Change: Stock a standard concussion information card, with the 24–48 hour rest advice pre-printed, in every club first-aid kit alongside the removal-from-play form.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-698.csv`
- Pitfalls: Advice given verbally pitch-side is easily forgotten without a take-home card → make the printed card, not verbal advice alone, the pass criterion; Volunteers may not have the card to hand on the day → check kit stock as part of the pre-season safety check; Under-18s need advice given to both player and parent/carer → record this separately from adult cases; Cards go out of date if guidance is updated → check the card version matches the current national guidance at each audit
- Pearls: Download the free UK Concussion Guidelines information card rather than designing a new one; Combine information-card distribution with the removal-from-play form so both happen at the same pitch-side moment; Ask parents/carers directly (brief survey) whether they received and understood the advice; Refresh first-aid kit stock checks at the start of each new season, not only when an incident occurs

**NNA-699. What proportion of under-18 players with a suspected concussion have their parent or carer informed and involved in the return-to-play decision, alongside the player themselves?** (new)
- Standard: UK Concussion Guidelines for Grassroots Sport (Sport and Recreation Alliance, updated November 2024): "Following a suspected concussion, what's your role? ... Anyone with a suspected concussion should ... [be] removed from play ... the guidance ... is intended for the general public and for individuals participating in all grassroots sports – primary school age and upwards." https://sportandrecreation.org.uk/campaigns-and-policy/concussion/concussion-guidelines-for-grassroots-sport-html-version
- Pass: Documented evidence that the player's parent or carer was informed of the suspected concussion on the day, and involved in the subsequent return-to-play discussion. Target: 100%. Sample: 30 consecutive under-18 suspected concussion incidents over the last season
- Change: Make same-day parental contact a mandatory field on the club's youth incident report form, signed off by the coach before the form is filed.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-699.csv`
- Pitfalls: Contact details for parents/carers may be out of date → verify emergency contact details at the start of each season; Away fixtures make same-day face-to-face contact harder → accept a documented phone call as equivalent; Coaches may assume another adult (a relative at the match) has informed the parent → make the coach personally responsible for confirming this; Player embarrassment may lead to under-reporting to parents → frame the policy as standard practice for every knock, not a special report
- Pearls: Build parental contact into the same incident form used for the removal-from-play audit; Brief parents at the start of the season on what to expect if their child is suspected of a concussion; Use the club's existing safeguarding lead, who already holds emergency contact responsibilities; Share a simple parent-facing information sheet alongside the player-facing concussion card

**NNA-700. What proportion of new healthcare staff who complete a primary course of hepatitis B vaccine have their antibody titre checked 1 to 4 months after completing the course?** (new)
- Standard: UKHSA Green Book chapter 12, Immunisation of healthcare and laboratory staff: "Antibody titres for hepatitis B should be checked one to four months after the completion of a primary course of vaccine. Such information allows appropriate decisions to be made concerning post-exposure prophylaxis following known or suspected exposure to the virus." https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/5a7abc09e5274a319e77a5b9/Green-Book-Chapter-12.pdf
- Pass: An anti-HBs antibody titre result is recorded in the occupational health record 1–4 months after the primary vaccine course is completed. Target: ≥90%. Sample: 40 consecutive staff completing a primary course over the last 12 months
- Change: Add an automatic recall for antibody titre testing to the occupational health vaccination database, triggered at the point the final primary-course dose is recorded.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-700.csv`
- Pitfalls: Staff move between departments or trusts before the check is due → flag the pending check in a shared occupational health system rather than a single department log; Blood test uptake among busy staff is often poor → offer testing at the workplace or during an existing appointment; Non-responder status is not always acted on → link this audit to a booster/re-testing pathway for non-responders; New starters may complete the course at a previous employer → confirm completion dates carefully before including a case
- Pearls: Use the occupational health vaccination database's own recall function rather than a manual spreadsheet; Offer drop-in phlebotomy sessions timed to when most staff are due their check; Report responder/non-responder rates separately, since non-responders need a distinct pathway; Recruit the occupational health nurse manager as audit lead, since they already run the vaccination programme

**NNA-701. What proportion of healthcare staff identified as non-responders to a primary hepatitis B vaccine course have a documented further management plan (for example a second course or confirmation of non-infection status)?** (new)
- Standard: UKHSA Green Book chapter 18, Hepatitis B (updated 5 February 2026): "Reinforcing doses should be considered for people in the following categories: ... healthcare and laboratory workers who have not responded to the primary course (see Testing for evidence of immunity after vaccination)." https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/68385046e0f10eed80aafad9/Hepatitis-B-green_book-chapter-18-06-03-2025.pdf
- Pass: A documented further management plan (repeat course, further testing, or confirmed non-infectious status recorded) exists for each identified non-responder. Target: 100%. Sample: 20 consecutive non-responders identified over the last 2 years (a smaller, targeted sample given expected low case numbers)
- Change: Build a mandatory non-responder pathway into the occupational health database, so a non-responder result cannot be filed without a follow-up plan being recorded at the same time.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-701.csv`
- Pitfalls: Non-responders may be a small, scattered group → collect over 2 years to reach a meaningful sample; Staff may not attend for a repeat course once already vaccinated → explain the individual risk of remaining a non-responder clearly; Some non-responders are never confirmed as HBsAg-negative → include this as an acceptable alternative management outcome; Occupational health records may be split across paper and electronic systems → check both sources before concluding a plan is missing
- Pearls: Base the pathway design on the Green Book's own guidance on further doses and testing; Recruit the occupational health physician for clinical sign-off of the pathway; Track outcomes long-term (does a repeat course convert non-responders?) as a natural extension of this audit; Share anonymised non-responder numbers with the trust's infection prevention team, who share an interest in exposure risk

**NNA-702. What proportion of staff with a significant occupational needlestick injury from a known hepatitis B surface antigen-positive source, in whom hepatitis B immunoglobulin is indicated, receive it within 24 hours of the first vaccine dose?** (new)
- Standard: UKHSA Green Book chapter 18, Hepatitis B (updated 5 February 2026): "If HBIG is also indicated, it should be given as soon as possible, ideally at the same time or within 24 hours of the first dose of vaccine, but not after seven days have elapsed since exposure or vaccine." https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/68385046e0f10eed80aafad9/Hepatitis-B-green_book-chapter-18-06-03-2025.pdf
- Pass: HBIG, when indicated, is given at the same time as or within 24 hours of the first vaccine dose, and always within 7 days of exposure. Target: 100%. Sample: 20 consecutive eligible exposures over the last 2 years (a smaller, targeted sample given expected low case numbers)
- Change: Stock HBIG in the emergency department (rather than only in occupational health, which is often closed out of hours) and add a needlestick post-exposure pathway card to ED triage.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-702.csv`
- Pitfalls: Out-of-hours exposures are the highest-risk group for delay, since occupational health is usually closed → ensure the ED pathway covers all hours; HBIG needs a same-day source patient hepatitis B test where status is unknown → build rapid testing into the pathway; Small numbers of eligible exposures → extend the sampling period to the last 2–3 years; Staff may delay reporting an injury out of embarrassment or workload pressure → reinforce a no-blame reporting culture
- Pearls: Base the local pathway directly on the Green Book's own post-exposure timing wording; Agree HBIG stock-holding and rapid access with pharmacy and the ED lead before cycle 1; Recruit the infection control team, who already investigate needlestick incidents, as co-auditors; Track time-to-first-vaccine-dose as a secondary measure, since this drives the 24-hour HBIG window

**NNA-703. What proportion of staff with a significant occupational exposure to blood or body fluids (for example a needlestick injury) have documented evidence that advice was sought immediately, either from occupational health, the emergency department or the local Health Protection Team?** (new)
- Standard: UKHSA Green Book chapter 18, Hepatitis B (updated 5 February 2026): "Individuals who sustain such exposures should wash the affected area well with soap and warm water and seek medical advice. Advice about prophylaxis after such incidents should be obtained by telephone from the nearest Emergency Department, NHS 111, or from the local Health Protection Team." https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/68385046e0f10eed80aafad9/Hepatitis-B-green_book-chapter-18-06-03-2025.pdf
- Pass: Documented evidence that first aid (washing) was performed and advice was sought on the same day as the exposure. Target: ≥95%. Sample: 30 consecutive reported needlestick/splash injuries over the last 6 months
- Change: Put a laminated needlestick first-response card (wash, seek advice, report) at every clinical area sink and sharps disposal point, with the out-of-hours contact number printed on it.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-703.csv`
- Pitfalls: Incident reporting systems capture what happened but not always when advice was first sought → cross-check with occupational health call logs; Staff may assume a low-risk source means advice is unnecessary → make advice-seeking mandatory regardless of perceived risk; Night-shift staff may not know who to call → ensure the out-of-hours contact is on the card, not only daytime numbers; Under-reporting remains a barrier even with cards in place → reinforce reporting culture alongside the practical change
- Pearls: Involve ward and theatre staff in designing the card so the wording is clear and short; Place cards exactly where sharps injuries happen (sinks, sharps bins), not only in notice boards; Use the same incident case list as the HBIG-timing audit to cover the whole needlestick pathway in one data collection round; Report near-miss data (advice sought quickly even without HBIG) as a positive indicator alongside the compliance rate

**NNA-704. What proportion of new starters with direct patient contact have a pre-employment health assessment that includes a documented review of immunisation needs?** (new)
- Standard: UKHSA Green Book chapter 12, Immunisation of healthcare and laboratory staff: "All new employees should undergo a pre-employment health assessment, which should include a review of immunisation needs." https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/5a7abc09e5274a319e77a5b9/Green-Book-Chapter-12.pdf
- Pass: A documented pre-employment health assessment includes a specific review of immunisation needs, completed before or on the first day of clinical duties. Target: ≥95%. Sample: 30 consecutive new starters over the last 6 months
- Change: Make immunisation needs review a mandatory, separately signed-off section of the electronic pre-employment health questionnaire, rather than a single general health tick-box.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-704.csv`
- Pitfalls: Agency and bank staff may bypass the trust's own pre-employment process → check the pathway covers all staff groups, not only substantive posts; Assessments completed but the immunisation section left blank → treat a blank section as a fail, not an assumed pass; Starting before the assessment is complete under service pressure → agree an escalation process for urgent starts with HR; COSHH risk assessment by role (which pathogens staff are exposed to) needs to inform which immunisations are offered → check this link is made, not assumed
- Pearls: Use the Green Book's own COSHH risk-assessment framework to structure which immunisations are checked by role; Recruit HR/recruitment alongside occupational health, since start dates are set jointly; Present a simple 'before and after' comparison of the questionnaire form to show the change clearly; Track time from job offer to completed assessment as a secondary measure to catch late starts

**NNA-705. What proportion of healthcare workers directly involved in patient care are offered influenza immunisation on an annual basis?** (new)
- Standard: UKHSA Green Book chapter 12, Immunisation of healthcare and laboratory staff: "Influenza vaccination is therefore recommended for healthcare workers directly involved in patient care, who should be offered influenza immunisation on an annual basis." https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/5a7abc09e5274a319e77a5b9/Green-Book-Chapter-12.pdf
- Pass: A documented offer of influenza immunisation (accepted or declined) is recorded for the current season. Target: ≥95% offered (uptake target set locally). Sample: 40 staff sampled from rosters across 3 clinical areas during the current flu season
- Change: Use peer vaccinators to visit every clinical area on the roster during the flu campaign, with a named staff-by-staff checklist so no one is missed, rather than relying on staff to attend a central clinic.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-705.csv`
- Pitfalls: Bank, agency and night staff are often missed by daytime campaigns → schedule peer vaccinator visits across all shifts; Staff who move between departments during the season may be double-counted or missed → use a single trust-wide tracker, not ward-level lists alone; Declining staff should have this recorded, not left blank → treat a blank record as 'not offered', not 'declined'; Campaign timing (early in the season) affects the denominator if staff join partway through → clarify the eligible cohort before cycle 1
- Pearls: Use the trust's existing flu campaign peer vaccinator network as the audit's data collectors; Present ward-by-ward offer rates to identify areas needing extra visits; Report offer rate and uptake rate separately, since this audit is about the offer being made, not just uptake; Time the audit to coincide with the mid-campaign review point so results can still influence that season's efforts

**NNA-706. What proportion of patients on maintenance lithium therapy have a lithium blood level checked at least once every 3 months?** (under-audited)
- Standard: NPSA Patient Safety Alert NPSA/2009/PSA005, Safer lithium therapy (1 December 2009): "one in 10 patients had no documented lithium blood level. (National Institute for Health and Clinical Excellence (NICE) standard: one blood level measurement every three months. Not met for 70 per cent of patients)" https://www.cas.mhra.gov.uk/ViewandAcknowledgment/ViewAttachment.aspx?Attachment_id=101024
- Pass: At least one lithium level result is recorded in the preceding 3 months. Target: ≥90%. Sample: 40 consecutive patients on the lithium monitoring register over the last 3 months
- Change: Add an automatic 3-month lithium level recall to the lithium monitoring register, with a hard stop on repeat prescribing if the level is overdue, as recommended in the original NPSA alert.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-706.csv`
- Pitfalls: Patients under shared care between GP and mental health services can fall between the two → agree who owns the recall before cycle 1; Patients who avoid blood tests are hardest to reach → offer a point-of-care or home phlebotomy option where available; A hard stop on prescribing needs pharmacy system changes → involve pharmacy IT from the outset; Register accuracy depends on all lithium patients being correctly coded → check the register against a full drug search before starting
- Pearls: Base the recall directly on the original NPSA alert's own 3-month standard so the audit maps onto a nationally recognised benchmark; Use the NPSA lithium record book (patient-held) as a low-cost extra safety net alongside the electronic recall; Recruit a mental health pharmacist to lead, since they typically run the lithium register already; Report separately for primary and secondary care patients, since the fix may differ by setting

**NNA-707. What proportion of patients on maintenance lithium therapy have renal and thyroid function checked at least once every 6 months?** (under-audited)
- Standard: NPSA Patient Safety Alert NPSA/2009/PSA005, Safer lithium therapy (1 December 2009): "one in five patients had no renal function tests documented (NICE standard: assessment every six months. Not met for 46 per cent of patients); one in six patients had no thyroid function tests documented (NICE standard: assessment every six months. Not met for 51 per cent of patients)" https://www.cas.mhra.gov.uk/ViewandAcknowledgment/ViewAttachment.aspx?Attachment_id=101024
- Pass: Both a renal function test (U&E/eGFR) and a thyroid function test are recorded within the preceding 6 months. Target: ≥90%. Sample: 40 consecutive patients on the lithium monitoring register over the last 6 months
- Change: Add renal and thyroid function to the same automatic 6-month recall used for the lithium level check, as a single combined blood test request, rather than a separate process.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-707.csv`
- Pitfalls: Renal and thyroid tests are sometimes requested separately from the lithium level, causing extra venepuncture visits → combine them on one request form; Deteriorating renal function may not trigger a dose review → link abnormal results to a documented lithium dose review action; Test results filed but not reviewed by a prescriber → require a clinician sign-off field, not just a filed result; Register may not distinguish patients newly started from established patients → exclude the first 6 months, which has its own more frequent monitoring schedule
- Pearls: Combine data collection with the lithium level audit above, since both use the same register and time period; Ask the laboratory to bundle lithium, renal and thyroid tests under a single 'lithium monitoring panel' order code; Recruit the same mental health pharmacist leading the lithium level audit; Track abnormal results and the action taken as a secondary measure of monitoring quality, not just test completion

**NNA-708. What proportion of patients starting lithium therapy are given a patient information booklet and a record book to track their lithium blood levels and relevant clinical tests?** (new)
- Standard: NPSA Patient Safety Alert NPSA/2009/PSA005, Safer lithium therapy (1 December 2009): "at the start of lithium therapy and throughout their treatment patients receive appropriate ongoing verbal and written information and a record book to track lithium blood levels and relevant clinical tests" https://www.cas.mhra.gov.uk/ViewandAcknowledgment/ViewAttachment.aspx?Attachment_id=101024
- Pass: Documented evidence that a patient information booklet and a record book (or patient-held equivalent) were given at the start of treatment. Target: 100%. Sample: 20 consecutive lithium initiations over the last 12 months (a smaller, targeted sample given expected low volumes of new starts)
- Change: Include the patient information booklet, alert card and record book as a fixed item in the lithium initiation prescribing checklist, so the prescription and the pack are issued together.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-708.csv`
- Pitfalls: Booklets and alert cards can run out of stock → assign restocking responsibility to a named pharmacist; Patients started as inpatients may be discharged before receiving the pack → check discharge as well as initiation records; Record books can be lost by the patient over time → check for a record book at each subsequent review, not just at initiation; Digital patient-held records are increasingly used instead of paper → accept an equivalent digital record as a pass
- Pearls: Order NPSA-format record books/alert cards in bulk so they are always available at initiation; Give the pharmacist dispensing the first lithium prescription responsibility for checking the pack is complete; Ask patients at their first follow-up review whether they still have their record book, as a simple ongoing check; Present this audit alongside the monitoring-frequency audits for a complete picture of the lithium safety pathway

**NNA-709. What proportion of adults with a single acute paracetamol overdose and a plasma-paracetamol concentration on or above the treatment line start acetylcysteine within 8 hours of ingestion?** (new)
- Standard: Oxford University Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust Medicines Information Leaflet, Guideline for the Management of Paracetamol Overdose (March 2024), based on TOXBASE/National Poisons Information Service guidance: "It is most effective if given within 8 hours of paracetamol ingestion, after which effectiveness declines... a plasma-paracetamol concentration on or above the treatment line should be regarded as carrying a serious risk of liver damage." https://ouh.quris.com/media/qw0hejoa/milv11n8.pdf
- Pass: Acetylcysteine is started within 8 hours of the recorded time of ingestion. Target: ≥90%. Sample: 30 consecutive eligible presentations over the last 6 months
- Change: Add an automatic paracetamol overdose pathway to the ED system that calculates the 8-hour treatment deadline from the recorded ingestion time and flags it on the tracking board.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-709.csv`
- Pitfalls: Ingestion time is often uncertain even in 'single acute' presentations → verify with ambulance or collateral history where possible; Laboratory turnaround for the paracetamol level can itself delay treatment → consider point-of-care testing if turnaround exceeds 1 hour; Patients presenting very close to 8 hours may be missed if the level result is delayed → treat empirically if delay risks missing the window, per local policy; Excluding staggered overdoses accurately requires a clear definition agreed with data collectors before cycle 1
- Pearls: Agree with the laboratory a rapid turnaround target for paracetamol levels, since this is often the rate-limiting step; Use the same case-finding method (toxicology coding) as the existing staggered-overdose audit to build a complete paracetamol overdose picture; Recruit the ED pharmacist to review flagged cases in real time during cycle 1; Present findings alongside the NPIS/TOXBASE contact audit below, since both use the same case list

**NNA-710. What proportion of adults treated for paracetamol overdose have documented contact with the National Poisons Information Service (via TOXBASE or telephone) for risk assessment and management advice?** (new)
- Standard: Oxford University Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust Medicines Information Leaflet, Guideline for the Management of Paracetamol Overdose (March 2024), based on TOXBASE/National Poisons Information Service guidance: "This MIL should be used in conjunction with TOXBASE guidance. In all cases of intravenous paracetamol poisoning, clinicians are encouraged to contact the National Poisons Information Service (NPIS) for advice on risk assessment and management." https://ouh.quris.com/media/qw0hejoa/milv11n8.pdf
- Pass: Documented evidence of a TOXBASE search or telephone contact with NPIS for the case. Target: ≥95%. Sample: 30 consecutive paracetamol overdose presentations over the last 3 months
- Change: Add a mandatory 'TOXBASE reference number/NPIS call time' field to the ED paracetamol overdose proforma, so documentation is built into the standard clerking process.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-710.csv`
- Pitfalls: Staff may check TOXBASE but not record having done so → require the reference number, not just a tick-box, as evidence; TOXBASE guidance changes periodically → confirm which version was current at the time of each case if discrepancies arise; Complex or unusual cases may need a telephone call in addition to TOXBASE → capture both contact methods separately; Locum or agency ED staff may be unfamiliar with local access arrangements → include TOXBASE access in induction
- Pearls: Combine this audit with the acetylcysteine-timing audit above, using the same case list; Display the TOXBASE login and NPIS phone number prominently at every ED workstation; Recruit the ED toxicology or pharmacy lead as audit champion; Use real anonymised cases from cycle 1 as teaching examples for induction of new ED staff

**NNA-711. What proportion of valproate-containing medicines dispensed from the pharmacy are supplied in the manufacturer's original full pack, complete with the warning labelling and patient card?** (new)
- Standard: MHRA Drug Safety Update, 'Valproate: dispense full packs of valproate-containing medicines' (31 October 2023): "Unless there are exceptional circumstances, valproate-containing medicines must always be dispensed in the manufacturer's original full pack." https://www.gov.uk/drug-safety-update/valproate-dispense-full-packs-of-valproate-containing-medicines
- Pass: The dispensing record confirms an original full manufacturer's pack was supplied, or documents the exceptional-circumstances risk assessment if not. Target: ≥95%. Sample: 40 consecutive valproate dispensing episodes over the last 4 weeks
- Change: Build a hard stop into the pharmacy dispensing system that requires the dispenser to confirm 'original pack: yes' or record the exceptional-circumstances reason before the label can be printed.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-711.csv`
- Pitfalls: Monitored dosage systems (dosette boxes) are a recognised exception → record these separately, not as non-compliance; Pack sizes may not match the prescribed quantity exactly, tempting repackaging → stock a range of licensed pack sizes to reduce this pressure; Patient cards can run out at the pharmacy → check stock as part of the audit; Dispensing software may not have a field for this at all → this audit's main output may be the business case for adding one
- Pearls: Use this audit to build the business case for a dispensing-system hard stop, even if the first cycle result is poor; Recruit the chief pharmacist and a community pharmacy contractor (if auditing primary care dispensing) as co-leads; Reference the specific MHRA safety update number when briefing dispensing staff, so the requirement is clearly not just local policy; Check patient card stock alongside pack compliance, since one often reveals the other

**NNA-712. What proportion of children, young people and adults newly diagnosed with epilepsy have their MRI scan carried out within 6 weeks of the MRI referral?** (new)
- Standard: NICE NG217 Epilepsies in children, young people and adults, rec 1.3.1 (2022): "Offer an MRI scan to children, young people and adults diagnosed with epilepsy, unless they have idiopathic generalised epilepsy or self-limited epilepsy with centrotemporal spikes. The MRI should be carried out: within 6 weeks of the MRI referral and following regionally agreed epilepsy MRI protocols." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng217/chapter/1-Diagnosis-and-assessment-of-epilepsy
- Pass: The MRI scan is performed within 6 weeks of the date the MRI referral was made. Target: ≥90%. Sample: 30 consecutive epilepsy MRI referrals over the last 6 months
- Change: Create a ring-fenced weekly epilepsy MRI protocol slot in radiology, booked directly from the first-seizure/epilepsy clinic referral rather than joining the general neuroimaging waiting list.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-712.csv`
- Pitfalls: General radiology waiting lists can push epilepsy MRIs beyond 6 weeks → a ring-fenced slot needs radiology capacity agreement, not just a policy statement; Regionally agreed epilepsy MRI protocols may not be locally documented → confirm the protocol exists and is used before starting; Excluded epilepsy syndromes (idiopathic generalised, self-limited with centrotemporal spikes) must be correctly identified to avoid skewing the denominator; Children may need a general anaesthetic for MRI, adding delay → record this as a distinct, expected cause of delay
- Pearls: Agree the ring-fenced slot numbers with radiology using cycle 1 referral volume data; Recruit the epilepsy specialist nurse to track referrals and flag approaching deadlines; Use the same case list as the first-seizure clinic audit to build a complete diagnostic pathway picture; Report scan-to-diagnosis-confirmed time as a secondary measure of overall pathway speed

**NNA-713. What proportion of people newly diagnosed with epilepsy have a documented discussion of the impact of their epilepsy on driving at their first specialist appointment?** (new)
- Standard: NICE NG217 Epilepsies in children, young people and adults, rec 2.1.6 (2022): "Discuss the following issues with them during their first appointment: ... impact on daily activities, including driving ... their epilepsy syndrome or seizure types. The discussion may be reiterated at an information and care-planning session with an epilepsy specialist nurse." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng217/chapter/2-Information-and-support
- Pass: The clinic letter for the first appointment documents that driving was discussed. Target: ≥95%. Sample: 30 consecutive first appointments over the last 6 months
- Change: Add a mandatory 'driving discussed, including DVLA notification' field to the first epilepsy appointment clinic letter template.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-713.csv`
- Pitfalls: Discussion may happen verbally but not be recorded in the letter → require the field to be in the templated letter, not left to free text; Patients below driving age at diagnosis still need future advice → record this as 'deferred, to be discussed before driving age' rather than a straightforward fail; Letters dictated and typed later may lag behind the consultation, delaying documentation → use a same-day templated letter where possible; DVLA rules change periodically → check the letter template references current DVLA guidance at each audit
- Pearls: Build the driving field into the same templated letter build as the care-plan-copy audit below, so both changes happen together; Provide clinicians with a one-line DVLA notification prompt card to use during the consultation; Recruit the epilepsy specialist nurse, who often reiterates this discussion at follow-up; Share DVLA's own patient information leaflet at the same appointment to reinforce the discussion

**NNA-714. What proportion of people with epilepsy are given a copy of their care plan after their first specialist appointment?** (new)
- Standard: NICE NG217 Epilepsies in children, young people and adults, rec 2.1.7 (2022): "Provide the person with epilepsy, and their family or carers if appropriate, with a copy of their care plan, which includes details of their care and support as discussed and agreed with the person, and their family or carers if appropriate." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng217/chapter/2-Information-and-support
- Pass: Documented evidence that a copy of the care plan was given to the patient (and family/carer if appropriate) after the appointment. Target: ≥90%. Sample: 30 consecutive appointments over the last 6 months
- Change: Print the care plan copy automatically at the end of the consultation from the clinic letter template, so it is given at the appointment rather than posted later (or not at all).
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-714.csv`
- Pitfalls: Letters typed and posted after the appointment may never explicitly confirm a copy reached the patient → track 'given at appointment' separately from 'posted later'; Care plans for children may need a version appropriate for the child as well as the parent → check both were considered; Clinic time pressure can make same-visit printing impractical → agree realistic clinic template time with the service before cycle 1; Patients who prefer a digital copy should still be offered one, recorded as an equivalent pass
- Pearls: Combine this audit's data collection with the driving-discussion audit, since both use the same clinic letters; Ask reception or clinic support staff to print and hand over the plan at check-out, taking pressure off clinicians; Offer an electronic copy via the patient portal as an alternative to a paper copy; Use patient feedback (a short survey) to confirm plans given were actually understood, not just handed over

**NNA-715. What proportion of women and girls with epilepsy of childbearing potential have a documented discussion of the risks of their anti-seizure medication in pregnancy within the last 12 months?** (new)
- Standard: NICE NG217 Epilepsies in children, young people and adults, rec 4.3.7 (2022): "Discuss with women and girls with epilepsy who are able to have children (including young girls who are likely to need treatment when they are able to have children), and their families or carers if appropriate, the risks to an unborn child of taking antiseizure medications during pregnancy, such as congenital malformations, neurodevelopmental impairments and fetal growth restriction." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng217/chapter/4-Principles-of-treatment-safety-monitoring-and-withdrawal
- Pass: A documented discussion of pregnancy risks of anti-seizure medication within the last 12 months in the clinic letter. Target: ≥90%. Sample: 30 consecutive women/girls of childbearing potential on the epilepsy clinic caseload
- Change: Add a mandatory annual 'pregnancy risk of current anti-seizure medication discussed' field to the epilepsy clinic letter template for all women and girls of childbearing potential.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-715.csv`
- Pitfalls: This applies to all anti-seizure medications, not only valproate, so existing valproate-specific systems will not fully capture it → build a medication-agnostic field; Young girls not yet needing contraception discussions may still need age-appropriate risk information → include this group explicitly, not just adult women; Discussions at GP-led reviews (rather than specialist clinic) may be missed if only specialist letters are checked → clarify which setting is in scope before cycle 1; Patients seen only by telephone may have shorter, less complete documentation → check both face-to-face and telephone clinic letters
- Pearls: Use the same clinic caseload list as any existing valproate ARAF audit to avoid duplicating case-finding work; Recruit the epilepsy specialist nurse, who often leads these discussions in practice; Provide clinicians with a short structured prompt card covering all anti-seizure medications with teratogenic risk, not only valproate; Report findings by medication class to show where risk communication is strongest and weakest

**NNA-716. What proportion of people of childbearing potential prescribed an enzyme-inducing anti-seizure medication (carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine, phenytoin or topiramate) have documented advice about reduced hormonal contraceptive effectiveness?** (new)
- Standard: NICE NG217 Epilepsies in children, young people and adults, rec 4.3.10 (2022): "Be aware that some antiseizure medications, for example, carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine, phenytoin and topiramate, can impair the effectiveness of hormonal contraceptives. Refer to the summary of product characteristics (SPC) and BNF or BNF for children for individual drug advice on the interactions between antiseizure medications and contraception." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng217/chapter/4-Principles-of-treatment-safety-monitoring-and-withdrawal
- Pass: Documented advice about reduced hormonal contraceptive effectiveness and the need for an alternative or additional method. Target: ≥90%. Sample: 30 consecutive eligible patients on the epilepsy clinic caseload
- Change: Add a drug-interaction alert to the epilepsy prescribing system that fires when one of the four enzyme-inducing medications is prescribed to a person of childbearing potential, prompting a documented contraception discussion.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-716.csv`
- Pitfalls: This standard covers four specific drugs, not all anti-seizure medications, so the alert must be drug-specific to avoid unnecessary prompts; Contraception method may be managed entirely in primary care and not visible to the neurology clinic → check both GP and specialist records; Non-hormonal or copper IUD users need this explicitly recorded as 'not applicable' rather than being marked as a fail; Topiramate's own separate Pregnancy Prevention Programme requirements (already audited) may overlap with this general interaction advice → keep the pass criteria distinct
- Pearls: Coordinate with the existing topiramate Pregnancy Prevention Programme audit to avoid double data collection on the same patients; Provide a simple interaction quick-reference card (drug name, effect on contraception, alternative advice) for clinicians; Recruit a contraception/sexual health lead as an occasional co-reviewer for complex cases; Report by individual drug, since carbamazepine, phenytoin, oxcarbazepine and topiramate caseloads may differ in size

**NNA-717. What proportion of people with epilepsy who continue to have seizures despite treatment are offered an epilepsy specialist nurse session after each emergency department attendance for a seizure?** (new)
- Standard: NICE NG217 Epilepsies in children, young people and adults, rec 11.1.3 (2022): "For people with epilepsy who continue to have seizures, offer epilepsy specialist nurse sessions: at least twice a year and after emergency department visits." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng217/chapter/11-Service-provision-and-transition
- Pass: An epilepsy specialist nurse contact (session, call or clinic appointment) is documented within 2 weeks of the ED attendance. Target: ≥90%. Sample: 30 consecutive epilepsy-related ED attendances over the last 6 months
- Change: Add an automatic epilepsy specialist nurse referral to the ED discharge system, triggered whenever a seizure-related attendance is coded in a patient with known epilepsy.
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-717.csv`
- Pitfalls: ED coding may not clearly distinguish a seizure-related attendance from other reasons → cross-check with the triage complaint as well as the diagnosis code; Epilepsy specialist nurse capacity may not match ED attendance volume → agree a realistic response model (call-back, not always a face-to-face session) with the service before cycle 1; Attendances out of hours or at weekends may be harder to flag for follow-up → build the referral into the discharge process itself, not a manual daily list; Patients who decline contact should be recorded as offered but declined, not as non-compliance
- Pearls: Base the automatic referral trigger on the same seizure-related attendance coding used for existing seizure audits; Recruit the epilepsy specialist nurse team directly, since they are best placed to say what response is realistic; Track whether ED re-attendance rates change over time as a secondary outcome of better specialist nurse contact; Present this alongside the referral-to-first-seizure-clinic audit for a fuller picture of the epilepsy urgent care pathway

## Surgical specialties

**NNA-718. What proportion of adults have a corrected serum calcium checked within 12 hours of thyroidectomy or parathyroidectomy?** (under-audited)
- Standard: BAETS Post-operative Hypocalcaemia Guidance: "POST THYROIDECTOMY / PARATHYROIDECTOMY CORRECTED CALCIUM LEVELS: Check within 12h postoperatively" https://baets.org.uk/wp-content/uploads/2024/07/BAETS-Post-op-Hypocalcaemia-Guidance.pdf
- Pass: Corrected serum calcium result is filed and actioned within 12 hours of the end of surgery. Target: ≥95%. Sample: 40 consecutive adult thyroid or parathyroid operations over the last 4 months
- Change: Build a 'post-thyroid/parathyroid surgery' order set that auto-requests a corrected calcium for 12 hours post-op and displays the BAETS treatment algorithm next to the result
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-718.csv`
- Pitfalls: Sample drawn but result not checked out of hours → build the check into the nursing handover, not just the request; Small numbers at units doing few parathyroidectomies → combine thyroid and parathyroid cases for the denominator; Definition of 'checked' drifts between cycles (requested vs resulted) → fix the definition as 'result available in EPR' before cycle 1; New starters unaware of the algorithm → laminate the algorithm in recovery and on the ward
- Pearls: Recruit the endocrine surgery clinical nurse specialist to check for missed 12-hour bloods each morning; Agree the exact cut-off time (12h from skin closure, not from admission) before cycle 1 starts; Link the order set to the procedure code so it fires automatically; Keep the same nurse-led calcium round after the surgical trainees rotate

**NNA-719. What proportion of adults undergoing thyroidectomy or parathyroidectomy have a documented post-operative laryngoscopy to assess vocal cord movement?** (new)
- Standard: BAETS Consensus, Pre and Post Operative Laryngoscopy in Thyroid and Parathyroid Surgery (FF Palazzo for BAETS, June 2010): "Post-operative laryngoscopy is required as a key quality control measure and should become mandatory." https://baets.org.uk/wp-content/uploads/2024/07/Vocal-cord-check-consenus-document-2010.pdf
- Pass: A fibreoptic or transcutaneous laryngoscopy assessment of vocal cord movement is documented at any point after surgery, up to and including the first outpatient follow-up. Target: ≥90%. Sample: 40 consecutive adult thyroid/parathyroid operations over the last 4 months
- Change: Make a laryngoscopy booking (by the surgical team or ENT) a mandatory step on the electronic discharge checklist for every thyroid/parathyroid operation
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-719.csv`
- Pitfalls: No ENT or voice clinic slots available → negotiate a ring-fenced weekly slot before cycle 1; Refusals not distinguished from omissions → add a separate 'declined' field so the denominator is fair; Surgeons doing their own transcutaneous ultrasound assessment not counted → agree what counts as 'laryngoscopy' before starting; Result not filed back into the surgical record → ask ENT to copy the surgical team into every report
- Pearls: Agree with ENT a same-day or next-day slot before starting the first cycle; Use a transcutaneous laryngeal ultrasound pathway where trained staff exist, to reduce reliance on ENT capacity; Put the laryngoscopy step on the WHO-style discharge checklist so it cannot be missed; Feed back cord palsy rates to the department each year so the mandatory step is not seen as a paperwork exercise

**NNA-720. What proportion of adults with a voice change or suspected/confirmed thyroid malignancy have a documented pre-operative laryngoscopy before thyroid or parathyroid surgery?** (new)
- Standard: BAETS Consensus, Pre and Post Operative Laryngoscopy in Thyroid and Parathyroid Surgery (FF Palazzo for BAETS, June 2010): "Pre-operative laryngoscopy in non-cancer patients with no history of voice change has a low rate of abnormal findings." https://baets.org.uk/wp-content/uploads/2024/07/Vocal-cord-check-consenus-document-2010.pdf
- Pass: A pre-operative laryngoscopy result is documented in the notes before surgery for any patient with a voice change or a cytological/clinical suspicion of malignancy. Target: 100%. Sample: All patients with voice change or suspected malignancy listed for thyroid/parathyroid surgery over the last 6 months (expect 30-40)
- Change: Add a mandatory 'voice change / suspected malignancy → pre-op laryngoscopy booked' field to the thyroid MDT outcome proforma
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-720.csv`
- Pitfalls: Voice change not systematically asked about at clinic → add a standard voice question to the pre-assessment template; Small numbers if malignancy is rare locally → run over 6 months rather than 3; Laryngoscopy done but not documented in the surgical notes → require the ENT report to be filed in the same record; MDT proforma completed retrospectively → complete it in real time at the MDT
- Pearls: Add the voice question to every thyroid nodule clinic template, not just cancer clinics; Use the MDT coordinator to check the field is complete before the case is listed; Share abnormal pre-op findings with the operating surgeon before consent; Keep a log of pre-op abnormal cords to compare with post-op findings

**NNA-721. What proportion of adults with structural persistent thyroid cancer after total or completion thyroidectomy and radioactive iodine are discussed at the thyroid cancer multidisciplinary team meeting?** (new)
- Standard: NICE NG230 Thyroid cancer: assessment and management, rec 1.6.4 (2022): "Discuss at the multidisciplinary team meeting any person who has had a total or completion thyroidectomy and RAI and has evidence of structural persistent disease." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng230/chapter/Recommendations
- Pass: Documented discussion and outcome at the thyroid cancer MDT within 4 weeks of imaging or biochemistry showing structural persistent disease. Target: 100%. Sample: All such patients identified over the last 12 months (expect 20-30 in a regional cancer centre)
- Change: Add an automatic 'structural persistent disease' MDT-list trigger from the radiology reporting system when a report contains that phrase for a coded thyroid cancer patient
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-721.csv`
- Pitfalls: Structural persistence identified in a non-cancer clinic and not flagged → educate all clinicians reviewing thyroid cancer follow-up scans; MDT list overloaded, cases delayed → create a fast-track 'persistent disease' slot; Ambiguity over what counts as 'structural' vs biochemical → agree the definition with radiology and oncology before cycle 1; Retrospective identification bias if reliant on memory → use a coded database search
- Pearls: Ask radiology to use a standard phrase ('structural persistent disease') in reports to enable searching; Give the MDT coordinator a standing search of the radiology system each week; Keep a register of persistent disease cases for continuity when staff rotate; Feed outcomes back to the referring endocrinologist so follow-up plans are updated

**NNA-722. What proportion of fine needle aspiration cytology (FNAC) samples for a thyroid nodule are reported as Thy1 (non-diagnostic/inadequate)?** (new)
- Standard: NICE NG230 Thyroid cancer: assessment and management, rec 1.2.10 (2022): "Consider rapid on-site evaluation of FNAC adequacy rates to improve the diagnostic yield of samples if the Thy1 (inadequate) rate for the centre or individual healthcare professionals is higher than 15% (when Thy1c is excluded)." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng230/chapter/Recommendations
- Pass: Thy1 (excluding Thy1c) rate for the service is 15% or lower over the audit period. Target: Thy1 rate ≤15% (excluding Thy1c). Sample: All thyroid FNAC samples over the last 6 months (expect 40-60)
- Change: Introduce rapid on-site evaluation (ROSE) of FNAC adequacy for ultrasound-guided thyroid biopsies
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-722.csv`
- Pitfalls: ROSE requires a cytotechnologist or pathologist present at every list → negotiate cover before starting the change; Operator-level data seen as punitive → present anonymised operator codes first, agree feedback approach with the team; Thy1c cases wrongly counted as inadequate → use the coded cytology categories, not free text; Small numbers per individual operator → report at service level first, individual level only with consent
- Pearls: Agree with cytology in advance which category counts as 'inadequate' for the audit; Use a dedicated ultrasound-guided FNAC list run by trained operators to improve consistency; Share Thy1 rates quarterly at the endocrine surgery/radiology joint meeting; Track repeat-biopsy rate as a secondary outcome

**NNA-723. What proportion of patients with T1a/T1b or greater differentiated thyroid cancer who have had a hemithyroidectomy or total thyroidectomy without radioactive iodine receive the recommended surveillance ultrasound and annual clinical follow-up?** (new)
- Standard: NICE NG230 Thyroid cancer: assessment and management, rec 1.6.2 (2022): "Consider an ultrasound at 6 to 12 months initially then annual clinical follow-up for up to 5 years for people with T1a (m) or T1b stage or greater thyroid cancer, who have had a hemithyroidectomy or total thyroidectomy without RAI." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng230/chapter/Recommendations
- Pass: An ultrasound is booked or performed 6-12 months after surgery and an annual clinical follow-up appointment is booked for each year up to 5 years. Target: ≥90%. Sample: All such patients treated in the last 18 months (expect 20-30)
- Change: Add an automatic 'low-risk thyroid cancer surveillance' pathway on the cancer follow-up system that books the 6-12 month ultrasound and annual reviews at the point of MDT outcome
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-723.csv`
- Pitfalls: Patients lost to follow-up after discharge from surgical clinic → use a single named follow-up pathway owner; Ultrasound slots not protected for surveillance → agree a standing allocation with radiology; Definition of T1a(m) vs T1a ambiguous to non-specialists → confirm staging with the MDT coordinator for each case; Surveillance stopped early without documented reason → require a reason field if follow-up is curtailed before 5 years
- Pearls: Use the MDT outcome form to auto-generate the follow-up schedule; Give patients a printed follow-up plan at their post-op clinic visit; Audit alongside the cancer MDT's annual outcomes review; Nominate a CNS to track the pathway centrally

**NNA-724. What proportion of adults having cardiac surgery who are not already taking a beta-blocker are offered pharmacological prophylaxis (amiodarone, a standard beta-blocker or a rate-limiting calcium-channel blocker) to reduce the risk of postoperative atrial fibrillation?** (under-audited)
- Standard: NICE NG196 Atrial fibrillation: diagnosis and management, rec 1.10.1 (2021): "In people having cardiothoracic surgery: reduce the risk of postoperative atrial fibrillation by offering 1 of the following: amiodarone a standard beta‑blocker (that is, a beta-blocker other than sotalol) a rate‑limiting calcium‑channel blocker (diltiazem or verapamil) do not offer digoxin." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng196/chapter/Recommendations
- Pass: One of amiodarone, a standard beta-blocker or a rate-limiting calcium-channel blocker is prescribed for AF prophylaxis by the end of the first postoperative day, and digoxin is not used for this purpose. Target: ≥90%. Sample: 40 consecutive beta-blocker-naive adult cardiac surgery patients over the last 4 months
- Change: Add a default 'AF prophylaxis: amiodarone / beta-blocker / calcium-channel blocker (tick one) or contraindicated (reason)' line to the post-cardiac surgery ICU order set
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-724.csv`
- Pitfalls: Digoxin still used from habit → remove it as an option from the order set; Bradycardia or hypotension used as a blanket reason to omit prophylaxis without considering alternatives → require the alternative agent to be considered first; AF occurring after ICU discharge missed by the audit → extend data collection to hospital discharge; Anaesthetists and surgeons prescribing inconsistently → agree a single default order set for both teams
- Pearls: Build the three options into a single tick-box so an active choice is required; Involve pharmacy in checking interactions before amiodarone loading; Review the order set uptake weekly during the first cycle; Keep the postoperative AF rate as a linked outcome measure

**NNA-725. What proportion of patients started on a rhythm-control strategy for new-onset postoperative atrial fibrillation after cardiac surgery have their need for continued antiarrhythmic treatment reassessed at around 6 weeks?** (new)
- Standard: NICE NG196 Atrial fibrillation: diagnosis and management, rec 1.10.6 (2021): "If a rhythm‑control strategy is chosen, reassess the need for antiarrhythmic drug treatment at a suitable time point (usually at around 6 weeks)." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng196/chapter/Recommendations
- Pass: A documented reassessment of the need for continued antiarrhythmic treatment occurs between 4 and 8 weeks after starting rhythm control. Target: ≥90%. Sample: All patients started on rhythm control for postoperative AF in the last 6 months (expect 20-30)
- Change: Add a mandatory 6-week antiarrhythmic review task to the discharge summary for any patient discharged on antiarrhythmic treatment for postoperative AF
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-725.csv`
- Pitfalls: Patients discharged to GP follow-up only, with no cardiology review booked → give GPs a clear stop/review date on the discharge letter; Reassessment done but not documented in a retrievable place → use a coded discharge summary field; Loss to follow-up if patients move between services → name a single team responsible for the review; Antiarrhythmics continued indefinitely 'to be safe' → present the evidence for time-limited use at teaching sessions
- Pearls: Give a clear stop/review date on every antiarrhythmic prescription at discharge; Use the cardiac surgery nurse specialist to track outstanding reviews; Feed reassessment outcomes back to the prescribing team; Align the review with an existing 6-week post-cardiac-surgery follow-up appointment where possible

**NNA-726. What proportion of adults having cardiac surgery who are already taking a statin have it continued after surgery?** (new)
- Standard: NICE NG196 Atrial fibrillation: diagnosis and management, rec 1.10.4 (2021): "In people having cardiothoracic surgery who are already on statins, continue this treatment." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng196/chapter/Recommendations
- Pass: A pre-existing statin is represented on the post-operative drug chart by the end of the first postoperative day, or a documented reason for stopping it is recorded. Target: ≥95%. Sample: 40 consecutive adult cardiac surgery patients known to be on a statin pre-operatively, over the last 4 months
- Change: Add pre-existing statins to the medicines reconciliation prompt that appears automatically when writing the post-cardiac-surgery drug chart
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-726.csv`
- Pitfalls: Statin omitted because the patient is nil by mouth and not represented once feeding resumes → add a re-check step once oral intake restarts; Reconciliation done by a junior doctor without pharmacy cross-check → involve pharmacy in every post-op reconciliation; Statin stopped for a genuine reason (e.g. rhabdomyolysis risk) but not documented → require a reason field; Discharge summary omits the statin even though it was continued in hospital → check the discharge letter as well as the inpatient chart
- Pearls: Use the electronic medicines reconciliation list as the single source of truth for pre-op medicines; Ask pharmacy to review post-cardiac-surgery drug charts within 24 hours; Flag any statin omission for consultant sign-off; Repeat the check at discharge as well as on the ward

**NNA-727. What proportion of adults having cardiac surgery receive mechanical VTE prophylaxis from admission and, where indicated, pharmacological prophylaxis for a minimum of 7 days?** (new)
- Standard: NICE NG89 Venous thromboembolism in over 16s, recs 1.15.1 and 1.15.2 (2018): "1.15.1 Consider mechanical VTE prophylaxis on admission for people who are undergoing cardiac surgery who are at increased risk of VTE. 1.15.2 Consider adding pharmacological VTE prophylaxis for a minimum of 7 days for people who are undergoing cardiac surgery and are not having other anticoagulation therapy: Use LMWH as first-line treatment." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng89/chapter/Recommendations
- Pass: Mechanical VTE prophylaxis is documented from admission, and pharmacological prophylaxis with LMWH is prescribed for at least 7 days in patients not otherwise anticoagulated. Target: ≥90%. Sample: 40 consecutive adult cardiac surgery patients over the last 4 months
- Change: Add a cardiac-surgery-specific VTE prophylaxis bundle (mechanical from admission plus a 7-day LMWH course) to the admission and post-op order sets
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-727.csv`
- Pitfalls: Mechanical prophylaxis omitted because of leg swelling or drains → give clear guidance on device choice around chest drains and vein harvest sites; LMWH delayed because of concern about bleeding after cardiopulmonary bypass → agree a standard start day with the surgical team before cycle 1; 7-day course not completed because of early discharge → include a discharge prescription for the remaining days; VTE risk assessment completed but not linked to a prescribing action → link the assessment directly to the order set
- Pearls: Build both mechanical and pharmacological prophylaxis into a single order-set bundle; Agree the LMWH start time with cardiac surgery and anaesthesia in advance; Audit alongside existing VTE risk-assessment compliance data; Keep a discharge checklist item for completing the 7-day course

**NNA-728. What proportion of adults with an undiagnosed or symptomatic pleural effusion who need a pleural procedure have it within 5 days of the decision being made?** (new)
- Standard: BTS Quality Standard for Pleural Disease, quality statement on access to pleural services: "For symptomatic or undiagnosed pleural effusion, where a pleural procedure is clinically indicated, it should be offered within five days of the decision being made, unless the patient's symptoms or evidence of infection makes a more urgent procedure necessary." https://www.brit-thoracic.org.uk/media/r15gl1kk/bts-quality-standard-for-pleural-disease-for-consultation.pdf
- Pass: The pleural procedure is performed within 5 calendar days of the documented decision to proceed, or sooner if urgent. Target: ≥90% within 5 days. Sample: 40 consecutive referrals for pleural procedures over the last 3 months
- Change: Set up a weekly protected pleural procedure list with direct electronic referral from the point of decision
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-728.csv`
- Pitfalls: 'Decision made' not consistently documented, making the start point unclear → agree a single documentation point (referral form date) before cycle 1; Procedure delayed by lack of ultrasound-trained operators → identify capacity gaps early; Urgent cases wrongly counted against the 5-day target → add an explicit urgent-indication field; Referrals lost between teams → use a single electronic referral pathway
- Pearls: Use a single electronic referral form that timestamps the decision; Protect a weekly list specifically for non-urgent pleural procedures; Involve the pleural nurse specialist in tracking waiting referrals; Review the waiting list weekly at the pleural MDT

**NNA-729. What proportion of patients are given information and advice about how to recognise a surgical site infection and who to contact, documented before discharge after cardiac surgery?** (new)
- Standard: NICE NG125 Surgical site infections: prevention and treatment, rec 1.1.3 (2019): "Offer patients and carers information and advice about how to recognise a surgical site infection and who to contact if they are concerned." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng125/chapter/Recommendations
- Pass: The discharge summary or a discrete leaflet documents that wound infection safety-netting advice (signs to watch for and a contact number) was given. Target: 100%. Sample: 40 consecutive cardiac surgery discharges over the last 3 months
- Change: Add a mandatory 'sternal wound infection advice and contact number given' tick box to the cardiac surgery discharge summary template, linked to a standard leaflet
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-729.csv`
- Pitfalls: Advice given verbally but not documented → make documentation itself, not just the conversation, the pass criterion; Leaflet given but generic (not sternal-wound specific) → develop a cardiac-surgery-specific leaflet; Patients discharged out of hours without the usual checklist → audit weekend/evening discharges separately; Field ticked as a default without the conversation happening → spot-check with post-discharge phone calls
- Pearls: Make the leaflet part of the standard cardiac surgery discharge pack; Give the same information to family/carers where the patient has reduced capacity; Include the sternal wound infection bundle as an agenda item at governance meetings; Track re-presentation rates for wound infection as a linked outcome

**NNA-730. What proportion of children undergoing scrotal exploration for suspected testicular torsion reach theatre within 3 hours of the decision to operate?** (new)
- Standard: NHS England (Midlands) Commissioning Guide for the Management of Paediatric Testicular Torsion: "Timely intervention: Percentage of explorations within 3 hours of decision to operate (NCEPOD 2) (excluding those with co-morbidities) 100%" https://www.england.nhs.uk/mids-east/wp-content/uploads/sites/7/2018/03/torsion-commissioning-guide.pdf
- Pass: Time from documented decision to operate to skin incision is 3 hours or less. Target: 100%. Sample: All scrotal explorations for suspected torsion over the last 12 months (expect 20-40)
- Change: Create a 'suspected testicular torsion' theatre booking category that bypasses the routine emergency list queue and alerts theatre coordination directly
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-730.csv`
- Pitfalls: Decision-to-operate time not documented consistently → agree a single trigger point (consultant/registrar decision documented in notes) before cycle 1; Theatre unavailable out of hours → confirm the emergency theatre escalation pathway covers torsion explicitly; Low case numbers per quarter → collect over 12 months to get a meaningful sample; Fasting status used to justify delay despite clinical urgency → reiterate that assessment should not be delayed by fasting status
- Pearls: Agree the torsion pathway with emergency medicine, theatres and anaesthesia before starting; Use a single-page torsion pathway sheet that timestamps each step; Review every case with a time over 3 hours at the morbidity and mortality meeting; Track testicular salvage rate as the outcome that matters to families

**NNA-731. What proportion of children presenting to a secondary care hospital with suspected testicular torsion are explored locally rather than transferred to a tertiary paediatric surgery centre?** (new)
- Standard: NHS England (Midlands) Commissioning Guide for the Management of Paediatric Testicular Torsion: "Transfer of a boy with a suspicion of torsion from a Secondary Care Institution to a Tertiary Care Centre should therefore be an exceptional occurrence (e.g. medical comorbidities)." https://www.england.nhs.uk/mids-east/wp-content/uploads/sites/7/2018/03/torsion-commissioning-guide.pdf
- Pass: The child is explored at the presenting secondary care hospital unless a documented medical co-morbidity or other exceptional reason requires transfer. Target: ≥90% explored locally (excluding documented exceptions). Sample: All secondary care presentations with suspected torsion over the last 12 months (expect 15-30)
- Change: Agree and circulate a local on-call rota and skills sign-off so that a competent surgeon and anaesthetist are always available locally for suspected torsion, with transfer requiring consultant-to-consultant agreement
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-731.csv`
- Pitfalls: Transfer driven by lack of confidence rather than genuine need → provide simulation training for on-call teams; Reasons for transfer not documented → make a reason field mandatory in the transfer request; Network guidance not known to on-call staff → include the pathway in induction; Transfer perceived as 'safer' despite adding delay → present time-to-theatre and salvage outcome data alongside transfer rates
- Pearls: Use network-level data sharing so all sites can benchmark; Keep an up-to-date on-call competency list for out-of-hours cover; Debrief every transferred case at the regional network meeting; Track testicular salvage rate for transferred versus locally-managed cases

**NNA-732. What proportion of boys referred with physiological phimosis are managed with reassurance, education and (where appropriate) a trial of topical steroid rather than referral for circumcision?** (new)
- Standard: RCS/BAPU/BAPS Commissioning guide: Foreskin conditions (2016): "When physiological phimosis is diagnosed in a primary care assessment of foreskin condition, consultation should focus on reassurance and education of parents and child." https://www.rcseng.ac.uk/-/media/files/rcs/standards-and-research/commissioning/revised-foreskin-conditions-commissioning-guide-republished.pdf
- Pass: Boys with physiological (non-scarred) phimosis and no pathological features have a documented plan of reassurance/education, with or without a topical steroid trial, before any referral for circumcision. Target: ≥90% managed conservatively first. Sample: 40 consecutive new foreskin condition referrals over the last 6 months
- Change: Send GPs a standard foreskin-conditions leaflet and referral proforma that documents whether physiological phimosis has already had reassurance/education and a steroid trial before referral is accepted
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-732.csv`
- Pitfalls: Parental expectation of surgery at first visit → provide written information explaining the conservative-first approach; GP referrals arriving without a trial of conservative management → use the proforma to triage these back with advice; Diagnosis of 'physiological' vs 'pathological' inconsistent between clinicians → agree diagnostic criteria before cycle 1; Steroid trial started but not followed up to assess response → build in a documented review
- Pearls: Give GPs a simple traffic-light referral form so conservative options are tried first; Use a patient information leaflet to manage parental expectations before the clinic visit; Audit alongside circumcision rates for physiological phimosis as an outcome measure; Keep the pathway visible in the electronic referral system

**NNA-733. What proportion of boys with pathological phimosis have a documented trial of a topical steroid before being listed for circumcision?** (new)
- Standard: RCS/BAPU/BAPS Commissioning guide: Foreskin conditions (2016): "Topical steroids may be considered and appear to be a safe, less invasive treatment option and a prescription of this would not normally exceed three months... A topical steroid such as Betamethasone (0.05%) is commonly prescribed for approximately 4 weeks." https://www.rcseng.ac.uk/-/media/files/rcs/standards-and-research/commissioning/revised-foreskin-conditions-commissioning-guide-republished.pdf
- Pass: A topical steroid trial of up to 4-12 weeks is documented and completed (or a documented contraindication is recorded) before circumcision is listed. Target: ≥90%. Sample: All boys listed for circumcision for pathological phimosis over the last 6 months (expect 25-40)
- Change: Add a mandatory 'topical steroid trial: dates and response, or contraindication' field to the outpatient clinic template before circumcision can be listed electronically
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-733.csv`
- Pitfalls: Steroid prescribed by GP but response not fed back to secondary care → ask GPs to document response on the referral back to clinic; Trial too short to assess benefit → specify the recommended 4-week minimum course in the template; Steroid cream not available or not prescribed correctly (wrong strength) → provide a standard prescription card; Circumcision listed 'just in case' before the steroid trial completes → make the field a hard stop on the listing form
- Pearls: Give parents written instructions on how to apply the steroid and for how long; Ask the GP to review response after 4 weeks rather than waiting for the next hospital appointment; Track circumcision avoidance rate as a secondary outcome; Review any listing without a documented trial at the departmental meeting

**NNA-734. What proportion of children having elective day-case surgery are permitted clear fluids up to 1 hour before anaesthesia, rather than being fasted for longer?** (new)
- Standard: APAGBI/ESPA/ADARPEF Consensus statement on clear fluids fasting for elective paediatric general anaesthesia (Thomas et al., Pediatric Anesthesia 2018): "based on the current evidence base, unless there is a clear contraindication, it is safe and recommended for all children able to take clear fluids, to be allowed and encouraged to have them up to 1 hour before elective general anesthesia." https://e-lactancia.org/media/papers/AyunasPreoperatorioBF-PedAnaest2018.pdf
- Pass: The documented last clear fluid intake is within 1-2 hours of anaesthetic induction, with no unexplained longer fast. Target: ≥90% within the 1-2 hour standard. Sample: 40 consecutive elective paediatric day cases over the last 4 weeks
- Change: Reissue pre-admission fasting instructions and ward whiteboards to state '1 hour for clear fluids' explicitly, with clear fluids actively offered on the morning of surgery
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-734.csv`
- Pitfalls: List order changes on the day, leaving children over-fasted despite correct initial instructions → actively offer fluids to children further down the list; Ward staff defaulting to traditional 'nil by mouth from midnight' habits → retrain ward and pre-admission staff; Parents fasting children for longer than instructed out of caution → explain the rationale clearly in pre-admission information; Fluid type not actually 'clear' (e.g. milk given) → define clear fluids explicitly in patient information
- Pearls: Actively offer clear fluids on the ward rather than relying on parents to remember; Update pre-admission letters and phone calls to state the 1-hour rule clearly; Reorder theatre lists to minimise fasting time for younger children; Audit fasting times alongside cancellation rates for over-fasted children

**NNA-735. What proportion of children having elective day-case surgery are fasted from solid food and formula milk for no more than 6 hours, and from breast milk for no more than 4 hours?** (new)
- Standard: APAGBI/ESPA/ADARPEF Consensus statement on clear fluids fasting for elective paediatric general anaesthesia (Thomas et al., Pediatric Anesthesia 2018), Table 1: "Preoperative fasting for elective procedures in children, Age (y) 0-16: Solid food, Formula milk 6h; Breast milk 4h; Clear fluids 1h." https://e-lactancia.org/media/papers/AyunasPreoperatorioBF-PedAnaest2018.pdf
- Pass: Documented fasting time for solids/formula is no more than 6 hours and for breast milk no more than 4 hours before induction, without unexplained excess. Target: ≥90% within recommended maximum times. Sample: 40 consecutive elective paediatric day cases over the last 4 weeks
- Change: Add feed-type-specific maximum fasting times (6h solids/formula, 4h breast milk, 1h clear fluids) to the pre-admission fasting letter and the ward fasting whiteboard
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-735.csv`
- Pitfalls: Breastfeeding mothers given the same 6-hour instruction as formula feeders → make the distinction explicit in written information; List order changes causing unplanned prolonged fasting → build a fallback offer of a snack/feed if delay is expected; Fasting times recorded inconsistently (last 'meal' vs last 'snack') → define clearly what counts as a solid feed; Ward staff unaware of the different breast milk time → include in induction training
