- Pearls: Print the age-specific fasting table on ward information boards; Give parents a written personalised fasting time on the day-before phone call; Prioritise younger children and breastfed infants earlier on the list; Review any case with fasting over 8 hours as an outlier

**NNA-736. What proportion of adult kidney transplant recipients have a clinic blood pressure below 140/90 mmHg (or 130/80 mmHg if significant proteinuria) recorded at their most recent follow-up visit?** (new)
- Standard: Renal Association Clinical Practice Guideline, Post-Operative Care in the Kidney Transplant Recipient (February 2017): "Clinic blood pressure should be <140/90 mmHg in clinic (130/80 mmHg if PCR >50 or ACR >35) (2C)" https://www.ukkidney.org/sites/renal.org/files/FINAL-Post-Operative-Care-Guideline-1.pdf
- Pass: The most recent recorded clinic blood pressure meets the applicable target (<140/90, or <130/80 with significant proteinuria). Target: ≥70% at target. Sample: 40 consecutive transplant follow-up clinic attendances over the last 2 months
- Change: Add a blood pressure target flag to the transplant clinic template that highlights the applicable target based on the patient's most recent proteinuria result
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-736.csv`
- Pitfalls: Home blood pressure readings not considered when clinic readings are borderline → offer home/ambulatory monitoring where available; Proteinuria result out of date, leading to the wrong target being applied → require an annual protein:creatinine ratio; Single reading used rather than an average → standardise to the documented clinic reading process; Target-focused prescribing without checking calcineurin inhibitor levels → review nephrotoxic drug levels alongside blood pressure
- Pearls: Display the applicable target automatically in the clinic template based on the latest proteinuria result; Offer home blood pressure monitoring kits to patients with white-coat effect; Review antihypertensive regimens at every visit, not only when out of target; Feed results back to referring GPs so shared care is aligned

**NNA-737. What proportion of adult kidney transplant recipients due an annual review are assessed in an annual review clinic within the expected time frame?** (new)
- Standard: Renal Association Clinical Practice Guideline, Post-Operative Care in the Kidney Transplant Recipient (February 2017): "Audit Measure: Percentage of total patients assessed in an annual review clinic" https://www.ukkidney.org/sites/renal.org/files/FINAL-Post-Operative-Care-Guideline-1.pdf
- Pass: The patient has a documented annual review clinic assessment within 13 months of their previous one. Target: ≥90%. Sample: 40 consecutive transplant recipients due an annual review over the last 3 months
- Change: Create an automated recall list from the transplant database that flags patients due an annual review 6 weeks in advance
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-737.csv`
- Pitfalls: Patients lost to follow-up after moving GP or address → confirm contact details are updated at every clinic visit; Annual review conflated with a routine transplant clinic visit without the full review content → define what the annual review must include; DNA rates not tracked → record and follow up non-attenders; Recall list not maintained centrally → assign a named administrator
- Pearls: Use a single database to track annual review due dates across the service; Combine the annual review with existing blood test visits to reduce patient burden; Record DNA reasons to target support at high-risk patients; Feed annual review outcomes to GPs for shared-care patients

**NNA-738. What proportion of adult kidney transplant recipients have a documented skin surveillance review at the recommended frequency (at least twice yearly up to 5 years post-transplant, then annually)?** (new)
- Standard: Renal Association Clinical Practice Guideline, Post-Operative Care in the Kidney Transplant Recipient (February 2017): "We suggest that self-examination should be encouraged with guidance provided. This should be supplemented by at least biannual review by a trained healthcare professional up to 5 years post-transplant and annual review from 5 years (2C)" https://www.ukkidney.org/sites/renal.org/files/FINAL-Post-Operative-Care-Guideline-1.pdf
- Pass: A documented skin review by a trained healthcare professional has occurred within the last 6 months (if ≤5 years post-transplant) or 12 months (if >5 years post-transplant). Target: ≥80%. Sample: 40 consecutive transplant follow-up attendances over the last 3 months
- Change: Add a skin surveillance due-date field to the transplant follow-up database that flags overdue reviews and prompts referral to a dermatology or transplant skin clinic
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-738.csv`
- Pitfalls: No dedicated skin surveillance clinic, relying on ad hoc opportunistic checks → set up a named transplant skin surveillance clinic or pathway; Self-examination advice given once at transplant and not reinforced → repeat advice at each annual review; Patients living far from the transplant centre missing reviews → arrange shared care with local dermatology where possible; Frequency requirement not distinguished by years post-transplant → build the changing frequency into the recall system
- Pearls: Combine skin checks with the annual review visit to improve attendance; Give patients a self-examination guide and photograph diary; Refer early for any suspicious lesion rather than waiting for the next scheduled review; Audit alongside skin cancer incidence in the transplant cohort

**NNA-739. What proportion of kidney transplant recipients treated for a presumed acute rejection episode have a transplant biopsy carried out before treatment is started?** (new)
- Standard: Renal Association Clinical Practice Guideline, Post-Operative Care in the Kidney Transplant Recipient (February 2017): "We recommend that a transplant renal biopsy should be carried out before treating an acute rejection episode unless this will substantially delay treatment or pose a significant risk to the patient (1C)" https://www.ukkidney.org/sites/renal.org/files/FINAL-Post-Operative-Care-Guideline-1.pdf
- Pass: A transplant biopsy result is available before treatment for rejection is started, or a documented reason (delay risk/patient risk) is recorded when treatment precedes biopsy. Target: ≥90%. Sample: All rejection episodes treated over the last 12 months (expect 15-30)
- Change: Add a mandatory 'biopsy result before treatment, or documented reason for treating first' field to the rejection treatment order in EPMA
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-739.csv`
- Pitfalls: Biopsy delayed by radiology or histopathology capacity, forcing empirical treatment → agree a rapid-access biopsy slot for suspected rejection; Reason for treating before biopsy not documented → make the reason field mandatory; Coagulopathy or single-kidney risk used inconsistently to justify treating first → agree criteria in advance with the MDT; Biopsy performed but result not available before treatment starts → track turnaround time separately
- Pearls: Negotiate a same-day or next-day biopsy slot with interventional radiology for suspected rejection; Fast-track histopathology reporting for transplant biopsies; Review every case where treatment preceded biopsy at the transplant MDT; Track biopsy turnaround time as a linked process measure

**NNA-740. What proportion of adult kidney transplant recipients receive an annual influenza vaccination unless contraindicated?** (new)
- Standard: Renal Association Clinical Practice Guideline, Post-Operative Care in the Kidney Transplant Recipient (February 2017), Guideline 8.1.1: "Should receive annual influenza vaccination unless contraindicated (1C)" https://www.ukkidney.org/sites/renal.org/files/FINAL-Post-Operative-Care-Guideline-1.pdf
- Pass: Documented receipt of influenza vaccination in the current influenza season, or a documented contraindication. Target: ≥85%. Sample: 40 consecutive transplant follow-up attendances during influenza season
- Change: Add an influenza vaccination status field to the transplant clinic template, checked and acted on at every autumn clinic visit, with on-site vaccination offered if not yet done
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-740.csv`
- Pitfalls: Vaccination assumed to be the GP's responsibility and not checked in clinic → make status-checking part of every autumn transplant clinic visit; No record-sharing between GP and transplant centre → ask patients to bring or confirm vaccination status; Live vaccines incorrectly given to immunosuppressed patients → ensure only inactivated influenza vaccine is used; Vaccination status not re-checked each season → build an annual reminder into the recall system
- Pearls: Offer on-site vaccination during the autumn transplant clinic to remove the barrier of a separate GP visit; Give patients written confirmation of vaccination for their records; Coordinate with GP practices to avoid duplicate or missed vaccination; Audit alongside pneumococcal vaccination and booster status

**NNA-741. What proportion of adult kidney transplant recipients have their hepatitis B surface antibody (HBsAb) level rechecked annually, with revaccination given if titres fall below 10 mIU/mL?** (new)
- Standard: Renal Association Clinical Practice Guideline, Post-Operative Care in the Kidney Transplant Recipient (February 2017), Guideline 8.1.2: "Should have hepatitis B surface antibody (HBsAb) levels rechecked annually and be revaccinated if antibody titres fall below 10 mIU/mL (2D)" https://www.ukkidney.org/sites/renal.org/files/FINAL-Post-Operative-Care-Guideline-1.pdf
- Pass: An HBsAb level is checked within the last 12 months, with revaccination given if the result is below 10 mIU/mL. Target: ≥85%. Sample: 40 consecutive transplant follow-up attendances over the last 3 months
- Change: Add an annual HBsAb check to the standard transplant follow-up blood test panel, with an automatic flag to prompt revaccination when the result is below 10 mIU/mL
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-741.csv`
- Pitfalls: HBsAb not included in the routine annual blood panel → add it as a standing annual test; Low result identified but revaccination not actioned → build an automatic alert into the results system; Patients revaccinated elsewhere (e.g. by GP) without the result being shared → ask patients to confirm at each visit; Turnaround time for the result delays action → track result-to-action time
- Pearls: Bundle the HBsAb check with the existing annual review blood tests; Use an automated laboratory flag for results below 10 mIU/mL; Keep a vaccination record accessible to both transplant and primary care teams; Review results alongside other post-transplant infection surveillance data

**NNA-742. What proportion of patients with a new, surgically significant abnormality on head injury imaging have their care discussed with a neurosurgeon?** (new)
- Standard: NICE NG232 Head injury: assessment and early management, rec 1.4.15 (2023): "Discuss with a neurosurgeon the care of anyone with new and surgically significant abnormalities on imaging." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng232/chapter/Recommendations
- Pass: A documented discussion with a neurosurgeon occurs within 1 hour of the imaging report identifying a new, surgically significant abnormality. Target: ≥90%. Sample: 40 consecutive head injury CT scans reported as showing a new significant abnormality over the last 4 months
- Change: Introduce a direct electronic 'significant finding' alert from radiology to the referring team and neurosurgical registrar as soon as the report is authorised
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-742.csv`
- Pitfalls: 'Surgically significant' not defined locally, causing inconsistent referral → agree a local definition with the neuroscience unit before cycle 1; Discussion happens but is not documented in a retrievable place → require a coded referral log entry; Out-of-hours reporting delays discussion → audit day and night separately; Referring team unaware imaging has been reported → use an automated alert rather than relying on staff checking results
- Pearls: Agree the local definition of 'surgically significant' with the neuroscience unit in advance; Use a single logged referral pathway (phone plus electronic record) for every discussion; Review any delay over 1 hour at the trauma governance meeting; Keep the audit simple by using the radiology report timestamp as the start point

**NNA-743. What proportion of patients with a severe head injury (GCS 8 or less) requiring transfer to a neuroscience unit are transferred in line with local, agreed transfer guidelines?** (new)
- Standard: NICE NG232 Head injury: assessment and early management, rec 1.8.1 (2023): "Ensure local guidelines on the transfer of people with a severe traumatic brain injury are drawn up between the referring hospital trusts, the neuroscience unit and the local ambulance service, and recognise that: transfer would benefit anyone with serious head injuries (a GCS score of 8 or less), irrespective of the need for neurosurgery." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng232/chapter/Recommendations
- Pass: Transfer of a patient with GCS 8 or less follows the documented local transfer guideline (designated referring/receiving consultants, escort standards and communication during transfer). Target: ≥90%. Sample: All such transfers over the last 12 months (expect 15-30)
- Change: Refresh and redistribute the network head injury transfer guideline, with a transfer checklist built into the ambulance handover documentation
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-743.csv`
- Pitfalls: Local guideline out of date or not known to junior staff → include the transfer pathway in trauma induction; Escort training not verified before transfer → use a standard escort competency checklist; Unstable patients transferred without adequate resuscitation → reinforce the requirement to stabilise before transfer; Transfer delayed by bed availability, not process → record reasons for any delay separately
- Pearls: Review the transfer guideline jointly with the ambulance service and neuroscience unit annually; Use a standard transfer checklist that mirrors the NICE recommendations; Debrief any transfer that deviates from the guideline; Track transfer times alongside guideline adherence

**NNA-744. What proportion of adults undergoing cranial surgery receive mechanical VTE prophylaxis from the time of admission?** (new)
- Standard: NICE NG89 Venous thromboembolism in over 16s, rec 1.12.5 (2018): "Consider mechanical VTE prophylaxis for people undergoing cranial surgery, start it on admission. Choose either: anti-embolism stockings or intermittent pneumatic compression." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng89/chapter/Recommendations
- Pass: Anti-embolism stockings or intermittent pneumatic compression are documented as started on the day of admission. Target: ≥90%. Sample: 40 consecutive cranial surgery admissions over the last 3 months
- Change: Add mechanical VTE prophylaxis as a default nursing admission task for every cranial surgery admission, triggered by the admission diagnosis code
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-744.csv`
- Pitfalls: Emergency admissions bypassing the standard admission checklist → build the prompt into the emergency neurosurgical admission proforma as well; Correct stocking size not available → stock a full range of sizes on the ward; Device removed for imaging/theatre and not restarted → include a restart check in the post-procedure checklist; Documentation of 'prophylaxis given' without specifying which device or when → require the specific device and start time
- Pearls: Make mechanical prophylaxis a same-day nursing task linked to the admission diagnosis; Audit alongside VTE risk assessment completion rates; Keep spare stockings and compression sleeves readily available on the ward; Review any gaps at the weekly ward safety huddle

**NNA-745. What proportion of adults undergoing cranial surgery whose VTE risk outweighs their bleeding risk are started on pharmacological VTE prophylaxis with LMWH 24 to 48 hours after surgery?** (new)
- Standard: NICE NG89 Venous thromboembolism in over 16s, rec 1.12.8 (2018): "Consider adding pharmacological VTE prophylaxis with LMWH, starting 24 to 48 hours after surgery for people undergoing cranial surgery whose risk of VTE outweighs their risk of bleeding." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng89/chapter/Recommendations
- Pass: LMWH is started between 24 and 48 hours postoperatively in patients assessed as having VTE risk outweighing bleeding risk, or a documented reason is given for a different timing. Target: ≥85%. Sample: 40 consecutive cranial surgery patients meeting this risk profile over the last 4 months
- Change: Add a mandatory 48-hour post-cranial-surgery VTE prophylaxis decision to the ward round checklist, with a prompt to start LMWH if not already documented
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-745.csv`
- Pitfalls: Decision deferred repeatedly without documentation → require an explicit decision at each ward round after 24 hours; Post-operative CT not repeated to confirm no bleeding before starting LMWH → agree a standard imaging check where required locally; Different consultants applying different thresholds → agree a single departmental risk-assessment tool; LMWH started but not documented as being for VTE prophylaxis specifically → use a coded prescription indication
- Pearls: Build the 24-48 hour decision point into the standard post-operative ward round proforma; Agree a single risk-assessment tool across the department before cycle 1; Review any prolonged delay at the morbidity and mortality meeting; Track post-operative VTE and bleeding events as balancing measures

**NNA-746. What proportion of adults on anticoagulant or antiplatelet therapy who present with a chronic subdural haematoma have a documented multidisciplinary decision on when to stop and, if appropriate, restart the drug?** (new)
- Standard: Protocol for the development of a multidisciplinary clinical practice guideline for the care of patients with chronic subdural haematoma (British Journal of Neurosurgery guideline programme): "Perioperative care pathway • Management of anticoagulation/antiplatelet agents • Optimal anaesthetic technique • Location and timing of optimization • Acute post-operative medical management" https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10905132/
- Pass: A documented decision on stopping and restarting anticoagulant/antiplatelet therapy, made with input from neurosurgery and the prescribing specialty (e.g. cardiology, stroke, haematology), is present in the notes. Target: ≥90%. Sample: All such patients presenting over the last 6 months (expect 20-30)
- Change: Add a mandatory 'anticoagulation/antiplatelet plan' field to the chronic subdural haematoma admission and discharge proforma, requiring a documented joint decision
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-746.csv`
- Pitfalls: Restart decision left to the GP without a clear plan from secondary care → give an explicit restart date or review trigger on the discharge letter; No clear ownership between neurosurgery and the prescribing specialty → name the responsible team on the proforma; Decision documented but rationale not recorded → require a brief rationale field; Practice varies between consultants → agree a departmental default pathway while awaiting the full national guideline
- Pearls: Involve stroke medicine, cardiology or haematology early for complex anticoagulation decisions; Give a clear restart date (or review trigger) on every discharge summary; Review outcomes (rebleeding vs thromboembolism) at the morbidity and mortality meeting; Update local practice once the full multidisciplinary national guideline is published

**NNA-747. Is the external ventricular drain (EVD) infection rate reported as infections per 1000 EVD-days rather than as a simple percentage of patients with an EVD?** (new)
- Standard: Humphreys H et al., Surveillance of infection associated with external ventricular drains: proposed methodology and results from a multicentre study, Journal of Hospital Infection (Healthcare Infection Society), 2017: "The use of denominators that account for the duration of the device are preferable (e.g. per 1000 EVD-days) as the risk of infection increases the longer the EVD is in situ." https://www.his.org.uk/media/1068/z-download2.pdf
- Pass: The unit's EVD infection surveillance report expresses the infection rate per 1000 EVD-days, alongside the total number of EVD-days and number of infections. Target: 100% of surveillance reports expressed per 1000 EVD-days. Sample: All EVDs inserted over the last 6 months (expect 30-60)
- Change: Change the unit's EVD infection prevention dashboard to calculate and display the rate per 1000 EVD-days as the primary metric
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-747.csv`
- Pitfalls: EVD removal dates not consistently recorded → make removal date a mandatory nursing record field; Multiple EVDs in one patient counted inconsistently → agree that a replaced EVD counts as a new device, per the published methodology; Case definitions for infection vary between reviewers → adopt a single published case definition; Denominator data collected but not fed into a usable dashboard → assign a named person to update the dashboard monthly
- Pearls: Use a single infection prevention and control dashboard updated monthly; Adopt a standard published case definition for EVD-associated ventriculitis; Present rates per 1000 EVD-days alongside duration and manipulation frequency data; Compare rates over time to check the effect of any care bundle changes

**NNA-748. What proportion of patients with a flexor tendon laceration of the hand are seen at the next available soft tissue hand clinic within 24 hours of referral?** (new)
- Standard: BSSH Standards of Care in Hand Trauma: Lacerations with flexor tendon involvement: "Referral category green – The patient should be seen at the next available soft tissue hand clinic (ideally within 24 hours)." https://www.bssh.ac.uk/_userfiles/pages/files/professionals/Trauma%20standards/3%20Flexor%20tendon%20final.pdf
- Pass: The patient is seen in the soft tissue hand clinic within 24 hours of the referral being made. Target: ≥90%. Sample: 40 consecutive flexor tendon referrals over the last 3 months
- Change: Set up a daily protected soft tissue hand clinic slot with direct electronic referral from the emergency department hand injury pathway
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-748.csv`
- Pitfalls: No hand clinic capacity at weekends → agree a weekend cover arrangement or extend the 24-hour window definition consistently; Referrals miscategorised as a lower priority → use the BSSH hand injury triage app or equivalent local tool for grading; Clinic booking delays because of incomplete referral information → use a structured referral proforma; Referral time not recorded accurately → timestamp referrals electronically
- Pearls: Use the BSSH Hand Injury Triage guidelines/app for consistent categorisation; Protect a daily hand clinic slot specifically for green-category referrals; Review any breach of 24 hours at the weekly hand trauma meeting; Keep referral and booking data in one system to make audit straightforward

**NNA-749. What proportion of patients undergoing operative repair of a flexor tendon injury of the hand have surgery within 4 days of injury?** (new)
- Standard: BSSH Standards of Care in Hand Trauma: Lacerations with flexor tendon involvement: "Operative management requirements Timing • Within 4 days." https://www.bssh.ac.uk/_userfiles/pages/files/professionals/Trauma%20standards/3%20Flexor%20tendon%20final.pdf
- Pass: Operative flexor tendon repair is performed within 4 days (96 hours) of the injury. Target: ≥90%. Sample: 40 consecutive flexor tendon repairs over the last 4 months
- Change: Create a ring-fenced weekly hand trauma theatre list with flexor tendon repairs given priority booking within the 4-day window
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-749.csv`
- Pitfalls: Hand trauma list regularly cancelled or reduced by emergency general theatre demand → secure formal protection of the list with theatre management; Delay caused by late referral from the emergency department, not theatre capacity → audit referral-to-listing time separately; Reasons for delay not recorded → make a delay-reason field mandatory; Patients unfit for surgery (e.g. intoxication, other injuries) skewing results → record and exclude these with a documented reason
- Pearls: Protect a specific weekly hand trauma list with agreed access rules; Track referral-to-theatre time in stages (referral to clinic, clinic to theatre) to find the real bottleneck; Review breaches monthly at the hand trauma governance meeting; Feed outcomes back to the emergency department to reinforce early referral

**NNA-750. What proportion of patients with a burn covering more than 20% total body surface area (TBSA) are nursed in a single-bedded, thermally controlled cubicle?** (new)
- Standard: British Burn Association National Standards for burn care services (2023-24): "Compliance: All burns over 20%TBSA have access to a single-bedded thermally controlled cubicle" https://www.uhnm.nhs.uk/media/vtnhswke/20240708-burn-care-standards-foi-ref-182-2425-2-of-2.pdf
- Pass: The patient is nursed in a single-bedded, thermally controlled cubicle from admission (or as soon as a bed becomes available, with any delay documented). Target: 100%. Sample: All such admissions over the last 12 months (expect 10-20 in a regional burn service)
- Change: Reserve a designated single-bedded thermally controlled cubicle for major burns within the bed management escalation policy, so it cannot be allocated to another patient without director-of-nursing sign-off
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-750.csv`
- Pitfalls: Low case numbers make month-to-month interpretation unreliable → audit over 12 months; Cubicle used for another patient at the time of a major burn admission → build an explicit escalation and de-escalation policy; Delay not recorded when the standard is not met → make the delay-reason field mandatory; Facility exists but is not thermally controlled to specification → verify against network self-assessment criteria (BBA Standards F.06.A/B)
- Pearls: Include the single-room requirement explicitly in the bed management escalation policy; Use the twice-daily bed utilisation data already submitted to the national Directory of Services as a data source; Review any breach at the next Burn Care Network board meeting; Align this audit with the service's biennial self-assessment against national Burn Care standards

**NNA-751. What proportion of burns inpatients have a documented multidisciplinary plan of care that includes psychological therapy needs?** (new)
- Standard: British Burn Association National Standards for burn care services (2023-24): "Plans for therapeutic interventions and rehabilitation, including physical, nutritional and psychological therapies" https://www.uhnm.nhs.uk/media/vtnhswke/20240708-burn-care-standards-foi-ref-182-2425-2-of-2.pdf
- Pass: The documented MDT plan of care explicitly addresses psychological therapy needs (input given, planned, or assessed as not currently required). Target: ≥90%. Sample: 40 consecutive burns inpatient admissions over the last 4 months
- Change: Add a mandatory 'psychological needs' field to the burns MDT plan of care template that must be completed (input given/planned/not currently required) before the plan can be saved
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-751.csv`
- Pitfalls: Psychological input assumed to be 'not needed' by default without assessment → require an active choice rather than a blank field; Psychology team capacity insufficient to see all patients → use a tiered psychological care model with staff training for lower-tier support; Plan completed once on admission but not updated as needs change → review the psychological needs field at each MDT update; Field completed as a tick-box without genuine assessment → spot-check with patient and family feedback
- Pearls: Use a tiered psychological care model so ward staff can provide first-line support while specialist psychology sees the highest-need patients; Make the psychological needs field a required part of every MDT plan review, not just at admission; Involve psychology in burns MDT meetings routinely, not only on request; Track psychology referral-to-review time as a linked process measure

**NNA-752. What proportion of patients whose wide local excision for stage 0 (in situ) melanoma does not achieve an adequate histological margin have their further management discussed with the specialist skin cancer multidisciplinary team?** (new)
- Standard: NICE NG14 Melanoma: assessment and management, rec 1.5.2 (2022): "If excision for stage 0 melanoma does not achieve an adequate histological margin, discuss further management with the specialist skin cancer multidisciplinary team." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng14/chapter/Recommendations
- Pass: A documented discussion at the specialist skin cancer MDT occurs within 4 weeks of the histology report confirming an inadequate margin. Target: 100%. Sample: All such cases identified over the last 12 months (expect 10-20)
- Change: Add an automatic MDT-list trigger from the histopathology reporting system whenever a melanoma excision margin is coded as inadequate
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-752.csv`
- Pitfalls: Inadequate margin identified by a non-specialist pathologist without automatic MDT flagging → use a coded histology field to trigger listing; Re-excision performed before MDT discussion out of habit → require discussion first unless there is a clinical urgency; Low case numbers → audit over 12 months; Patient not informed of the plan promptly → require a documented patient communication step
- Pearls: Use a coded histology margin field to enable automatic MDT list triggering; Keep a register of incomplete excisions for continuity across staff rotations; Feed outcomes back to referring dermatology/GP services; Review turnaround time from histology to MDT discussion

**NNA-753. What proportion of patients with melanoma of Breslow thickness greater than 1.0 mm have sentinel lymph node biopsy (SLNB) considered and documented?** (new)
- Standard: NICE NG14 Melanoma: assessment and management, rec 1.4.4 (2022): "Consider SLNB for people who have melanoma with a Breslow thickness greater than 1.0 mm." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng14/chapter/Recommendations
- Pass: A documented discussion of SLNB (offered, declined, or not suitable with reason) is recorded in the MDT outcome or clinic letter for melanoma with Breslow thickness over 1.0 mm. Target: ≥90%. Sample: All such patients diagnosed over the last 12 months (expect 20-30)
- Change: Add a mandatory 'SLNB considered: yes/no and outcome' field to the melanoma MDT outcome proforma for every case with Breslow thickness over 1.0 mm
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-753.csv`
- Pitfalls: Breslow thickness not clearly stated in the histology report used for triage → require a coded thickness field from pathology; SLNB capacity/waiting times limit ability to offer it promptly → identify capacity constraints early; Patient preference not documented when SLNB is declined → require a reason field; Cases discussed at MDT before full histology is available, causing the step to be missed → build a re-check step once full histology is back
- Pearls: Use a coded Breslow thickness field from pathology to auto-populate the MDT list with an SLNB prompt; Give patients written information on SLNB to support shared decision-making; Audit SLNB uptake alongside re-excision rates as a package of melanoma care measures; Review any case where SLNB was omitted without documented reason at the MDT

**NNA-754. What proportion of adults under surveillance for an asymptomatic abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA) are rescanned at the same frequency as the NHS AAA screening programme?** (new)
- Standard: NICE NG156 Abdominal aortic aneurysm: diagnosis and management, rec 1.2.3 (2020): "Offer surveillance with aortic ultrasound to people with an asymptomatic AAA. Use the same surveillance frequency as the NHS AAA screening programme." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng156/chapter/Recommendations
- Pass: The next surveillance ultrasound is booked/performed at the interval used by the NHS AAA screening programme for the patient's aortic diameter band (annual for 3.0-4.4cm, 3-monthly for 4.5-5.4cm). Target: ≥95%. Sample: 40 consecutive patients under AAA surveillance over the last 3 months
- Change: Move all non-screening-detected AAA surveillance patients onto the same recall system used by the NHS AAA screening programme so intervals are applied automatically
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-754.csv`
- Pitfalls: Clinic-diagnosed AAA surveillance run on a separate, less robust system than the screening programme → merge onto a single recall database; Surveillance interval changed inconsistently as the aneurysm grows → automate the interval based on the latest measurement; Patients lost to follow-up after discharge from vascular clinic → use an opt-out recall system rather than relying on re-referral; Ultrasound capacity insufficient to meet 3-monthly recalls for medium AAA → identify capacity gaps before committing to the target
- Pearls: Use the same IT recall system as the national screening programme wherever possible; Automate interval calculation from the latest scan result; Audit alongside the screening programme's own quality assurance data; Review any patient overdue by more than 4 weeks at a monthly recall meeting

**NNA-755. What proportion of adults with a diabetic foot problem referred to the vascular/diabetic foot service are seen and triaged within the recommended timeframe (immediately if limb- or life-threatening, otherwise referred within 1 working day and triaged within a further working day)?** (new)
- Standard: NICE NG19 Diabetic foot problems: prevention and management, recs 1.4.1 and 1.4.2 (2015, updated 2019): "1.4.1 If a person has a limb-threatening or life-threatening diabetic foot problem, refer them immediately to acute services and inform the multidisciplinary foot care service... 1.4.2 For all other active diabetic foot problems, refer the person within 1 working day to the multidisciplinary foot care service or foot protection service... for triage within 1 further working day." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng19/chapter/Recommendations
- Pass: Limb/life-threatening problems are referred immediately; all other active diabetic foot problems are referred within 1 working day and triaged within a further working day. Target: ≥90%. Sample: 40 consecutive diabetic foot referrals over the last 3 months
- Change: Create a single electronic 'diabetic foot problem' referral form with built-in severity triage that routes limb/life-threatening cases directly to same-day assessment and all others to a 1-working-day queue with automatic triage reminders
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-755.csv`
- Pitfalls: Referrals sent by fax or letter with no timestamp → move to a timestamped electronic referral; Severity misclassified at the point of referral → provide clear referral criteria and examples; Weekend/bank holiday referrals miscounted against working-day targets → define 'working day' clearly in the template; Triage capacity insufficient for a 1-day turnaround → identify staffing gaps before committing to the change
- Pearls: Use a single, mandatory electronic referral form with built-in severity flagging; Set up an automatic reminder if a referral is untriaged after 1 working day; Audit alongside the National Diabetes Foot Care Audit dataset where the unit participates; Review any breach at the weekly diabetic foot MDT

**NNA-756. What proportion of adults with recent stable non-disabling stroke or TIA and 50-99% (NASCET) or 70-99% (ECST) symptomatic carotid stenosis are assessed and referred urgently for carotid endarterectomy?** (new)
- Standard: NICE NG128 Stroke and transient ischaemic attack in over 16s, rec 1.2.4 (2008, amended 2019): "Ensure that people with stable neurological symptoms from acute non-disabling stroke or TIA who have symptomatic carotid stenosis of 50% to 99% according to the NASCET... criteria, or 70% to 99% according to the ECST... criteria: are assessed and referred urgently for carotid endarterectomy to a service following current national standards." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng128/chapter/recommendations
- Pass: Urgent referral to vascular surgery for carotid endarterectomy is documented on the same day as the carotid imaging result confirming qualifying stenosis, with surgery performed in line with the National Stroke Service Model. Target: ≥90%. Sample: All qualifying patients identified over the last 12 months (expect 15-25)
- Change: Set up a direct, same-day electronic referral pathway from the TIA/stroke clinic and carotid imaging report straight to the vascular surgery urgent carotid list
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-756.csv`
- Pitfalls: Referral delayed pending a formal MDT slot rather than being sent immediately → allow direct urgent referral outside the routine MDT cycle; Carotid imaging reported out of hours with no same-day action → agree an out-of-hours escalation route; Low case numbers per unit → audit over 12 months; Best medical therapy delayed while awaiting surgery → audit medical therapy start date as a secondary measure
- Pearls: Agree a direct, single-phone-call referral route between stroke medicine and vascular surgery; Track total time from symptom onset to surgery, not just referral to surgery; Review every case exceeding the target pathway time at the joint governance meeting; Feed outcomes into the national Sentinel Stroke National Audit Programme (SSNAP) submission

**NNA-757. What proportion of patients with Rutherford IIb acute limb ischaemia are treated by specialist staff within six hours of their symptoms appearing?** (new)
- Standard: NCEPOD, Risking Life and Limb: acute limb ischaemia national report: "In severe cases (Rutherford IIb), patients need to be treated by specialist staff within six hours of their symptoms appearing." https://www.ncepod.org.uk/2025ali/Risking%20Life%20and%20Limb_Extended%20report.pdf
- Pass: Revascularisation (surgical or endovascular) by specialist staff is achieved within six hours of documented symptom onset for Rutherford IIb limb ischaemia. Target: ≥70% within 6 hours (with continuous improvement). Sample: All Rutherford IIb presentations over the last 12 months (expect 15-25 in a vascular hub)
- Change: Introduce a standard acute limb ischaemia pathway with mandatory Rutherford classification at triage and direct ambulance conveyance/transfer to the vascular hub, bypassing local emergency departments where already agreed in the network
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-757.csv`
- Pitfalls: Rutherford classification rarely used outside vascular hubs → train spoke hospital emergency teams to classify and flag IIb cases; Patients directed to a spoke hospital first, adding avoidable transfer time → agree direct ambulance conveyance to the hub for suspected IIb ischaemia; Symptom onset time poorly documented → standardise how this is elicited and recorded; No national/local data collection system in place → set up a simple local log as an interim measure
- Pearls: Train ambulance and ED staff to recognise and flag suspected Rutherford IIb limb ischaemia for direct hub conveyance; Use the '6Ps' assessment consistently and document each element; Review every case exceeding six hours at the vascular morbidity and mortality meeting; Share pathway performance data across the network to drive improvement

**NNA-758. What proportion of patients undergoing major lower limb amputation have a documented discussion of their treatment options with the lower limb multidisciplinary team before the decision to amputate?** (new)
- Standard: VSGBI Best Practice Clinical Care Pathway for Peripheral Arterial Disease, Quality Improvement Framework (2022): "Patients should have adequate opportunities to discuss treatment with members of the lower limb MDT." https://jvsgbi.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/04/PAD-QIF-2022-update-1.1.pdf
- Pass: A documented lower limb MDT discussion, including the patient's views, occurs before the decision to proceed to major amputation (except in a genuine emergency, e.g. overwhelming sepsis). Target: ≥90% (excluding documented emergencies). Sample: 40 consecutive major lower limb amputations over the last 4 months
- Change: Make lower limb MDT discussion a mandatory pre-requisite field on the electronic theatre booking form for elective/urgent major amputation, with an emergency override that requires consultant sign-off
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-758.csv`
- Pitfalls: Amputation booked directly by the on-call team without MDT input → build the pre-requisite field into the booking form itself; MDT discussion documented in generic terms without evidence of shared decision-making → require a specific 'patient views' field; Genuine emergencies wrongly used to bypass MDT discussion → require consultant sign-off for any emergency override; Frail or end-of-life patients not offered a broader discussion including palliative options → include amputation counsellor/palliative care input where relevant
- Pearls: Include the amputation counsellor and rehabilitation team in the MDT discussion, not only surgeons; Use a structured MDT proforma capturing revascularisation options considered and patient preference; Review every emergency-override case at the vascular governance meeting; Track amputation counselling and rehabilitation referral rates as linked outcomes

**NNA-759. What proportion of adults undergoing major lower limb amputation whose risk of VTE outweighs their risk of bleeding receive pharmacological VTE prophylaxis with LMWH for a minimum of 7 days?** (new)
- Standard: NICE NG89 Venous thromboembolism in over 16s, rec 1.15.5 (2018): "Consider pharmacological VTE prophylaxis with LMWH for a minimum of 7 days for people who are undergoing lower limb amputation whose risk of VTE outweighs their risk of bleeding." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng89/chapter/Recommendations
- Pass: LMWH is prescribed and given for at least 7 days postoperatively in patients whose VTE risk outweighs bleeding risk, with mechanical prophylaxis to the contralateral leg where pharmacological prophylaxis is contraindicated. Target: ≥90%. Sample: 40 consecutive major lower limb amputations over the last 4 months
- Change: Add a 7-day minimum LMWH course as the default in the post-amputation order set, with a discharge prescription for any remaining days and a mechanical prophylaxis option built in for contraindicated cases
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-759.csv`
- Pitfalls: Course stopped early at discharge because the discharge prescription is overlooked → build the remaining LMWH days into the discharge prescription automatically; Bleeding risk assessment not documented, making it unclear whether the recommendation applies → make risk assessment a mandatory pre-op step; Mechanical prophylaxis omitted on the amputated/residual limb without considering the contralateral leg → clarify in the order set that intermittent pneumatic compression is used on the remaining leg; Early discharge to rehabilitation interrupting the course → communicate the remaining course clearly in the transfer letter
- Pearls: Build the full 7-day course, including any discharge supply, into a single order set; Communicate VTE prophylaxis plans clearly in transfer letters to rehabilitation units; Audit alongside post-amputation VTE and bleeding event rates as balancing measures; Review any early discontinuation at the vascular governance meeting

## Psychiatry

**NNA-760. What proportion of children and young people assessed by CAMHS or crisis services after self-harm are referred to an age-appropriate crisis response service (or equivalent specialist mental health professional) for a psychosocial assessment as soon as possible after arrival?** (under-audited)
- Standard: NICE NG225 Self-harm: assessment, management and preventing recurrence, rec 1.7.13 (September 2022): "When a person attends the emergency department or minor injury unit following an episode of self-harm, offer referral to age-appropriate liaison psychiatry services, or for children and young people, crisis response service (or an equivalent specialist mental health service or a suitably skilled mental health professional) as soon as possible after arrival, for a psychosocial assessment ... and support and assistance alongside physical healthcare." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng225/chapter/Recommendations
- Pass: Referral to the crisis response service (or equivalent) is documented as made, with the time of referral recorded, for every under-18 self-harm attendance. Target: 100%. Sample: 30 consecutive under-18 self-harm attendances to the emergency department over the last 3 months, identified from the ED self-harm coding list
- Change: Add a mandatory 'crisis response/CAMHS referral made: time' field to the ED self-harm triage template, which cannot be closed without either a referral time or a documented reason none was needed
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-760.csv`
- Pitfalls: Referral may happen by phone/bleep with no written record: agree with the crisis team in advance that every referral is also logged electronically; Patients who abscond before triage or assessment are not comparable: exclude them explicitly and report the number excluded; Staff may push back that 'we always refer everyone': collect a baseline before assuming this, since local card CR-3174/3392 show gaps even where staff believe compliance is high; A single term for the crisis service may not match every trust's naming: agree the exact service name with the ED and CAMHS leads before data collection starts; Out-of-hours attendances may use a different on-call pathway: capture time of day so out-of-hours performance can be reported separately
- Pearls: Recruit an ED consultant and a CAMHS/crisis team consultant as joint audit leads so the fix can be built into both systems; Agree before cycle 1 exactly what counts as 'referral made' (a bleep call, an electronic referral, or both); Use the ED's existing self-harm coding list to identify the sample quickly rather than manually screening all attendances; Present the baseline to both teams together so the fix is owned jointly, not seen as an ED-only or CAMHS-only problem; Hand the audit and the mandatory-field build to the incoming CAMHS liaison trainee at rotation, with the re-audit date fixed in the departmental audit calendar

**NNA-761. What proportion of children and young people are seen and spoken to by an age-appropriate liaison psychiatry professional or a suitably skilled mental health professional at every attendance to the emergency department following an episode of self-harm?** (under-audited)
- Standard: NICE NG225 Self-harm: assessment, management and preventing recurrence, rec 1.7.14 (September 2022): "An age-appropriate liaison psychiatry professional or a suitably skilled mental health professional should see and speak to the person at every attendance after an episode of self-harm." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng225/chapter/Recommendations
- Pass: A note from an age-appropriate liaison psychiatry professional or suitably skilled mental health professional is present for that specific attendance. Target: 100%. Sample: All under-18 patients with 2 or more self-harm attendances in the last 6 months (typically 30-40 attendances across a district general hospital), identified from the ED self-harm coding list
- Change: Add an automatic flag on the ED tracking board for any patient with a previous self-harm attendance in the last 6 months, prompting mandatory liaison review even if the presentation looks minor
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-761.csv`
- Pitfalls: Repeat attenders may be seen by different professionals each time, fragmenting the record: search by patient identifier across all attendances, not by single episode; 'Suitably skilled mental health professional' is not defined locally: agree a short list of qualifying roles with CAMHS before data collection; Attendances that end in the young person leaving before assessment will look like a 'fail' for reasons outside the team's control: record and report separately; Staff may see repeat self-harm as 'attention seeking' and be less thorough: present the data without individual blame and focus on the system flag; Six months may be too short to find repeat attenders in a small unit: extend the window rather than lowering the sample size
- Pearls: Ask the ED data team to run the repeat-attendance search electronically rather than manually cross-referencing notes; Recruit the CAMHS lead nurse to help define 'suitably skilled' before cycle 1 so there is no dispute at analysis; Share the individual (anonymised) attendance timelines with the team, not just the percentage, as this is the most persuasive way to show gaps; Agree with IT in advance whether the repeat-attendance flag can be built as an automatic alert, since this is what worked in comparable services; Keep the audit with the liaison team rather than a rotating CAMHS trainee, since continuity of care is the point being measured

**NNA-762. What proportion of children and young people assessed by mental health services after self-harm have a written safety plan for future episodes, developed and agreed with them, documented before they leave the assessment?** (under-audited)
- Standard: NICE NG225 Self-harm: assessment, management and preventing recurrence, rec 1.5.14 (September 2022): "developing a safety plan for future episodes of self-harm, which should be written with and agreed by the person who self-harms." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng225/chapter/Recommendations
- Pass: A safety plan document exists in the record for that assessment, is dated, and states it was agreed with the young person. Target: ≥90%. Sample: 30 consecutive completed self-harm psychosocial assessments in under-18s over the last 3 months
- Change: Replace the free-text 'plan' box in the self-harm assessment template with a structured safety plan template (warning signs, coping strategies, contacts, means restriction) that must be completed and printed or shared with the young person before the assessment can be closed
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-762.csv`
- Pitfalls: A generic 'risk management plan' may be wrongly counted as a safety plan: define the required elements (triggers, coping strategies, contacts) in the data collection tool; Assessments completed out of hours by a duty worker may use a paper safety plan that is not scanned into the electronic record: check both paper and electronic sources; Families may decline to be involved: record this as a valid reason rather than a failure of the young person's own agreement; Clinicians may feel a template is too rigid for individual presentations: pilot the template with two or three clinicians and gather feedback before full rollout; Improvement may fade once the pilot team's enthusiasm wears off: build the template into the mandatory record rather than relying on a reminder poster
- Pearls: Base the template on an existing published safety-planning tool (e.g. a suicide safety plan format) rather than designing one from scratch; Involve a young person or family representative in reviewing the template wording before rollout; Agree with reception/admin that the safety plan can be printed on the spot so families leave with a physical copy; Present both the completion rate and a couple of anonymised examples of good versus poor plans to help clinicians see what 'good' looks like; Hand ownership of the re-audit to the CAMHS or crisis team's own quality improvement lead rather than a single trainee, since teams rotate

**NNA-763. What proportion of children and young people on ADHD medication have their height and weight measured at the intervals specified by NICE (height every 6 months; weight every 3 months if aged 10 or under, or at 3 and 6 months then every 6 months if older)?** (under-audited)
- Standard: NICE NG87 Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder: diagnosis and management, rec 1.8.5 (2018): "For people taking medication for ADHD: measure height every 6 months in children and young people measure weight every 3 months in children 10 years and under measure weight at 3 and 6 months after starting treatment in children over 10 years and young people, and every 6 months thereafter, or more often if concerns arise ... plot height and weight of children and young people on a growth chart and ensure review by the healthcare professional responsible for treatment." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng87/chapter/Recommendations
- Pass: Height and weight are both recorded at the NICE-specified interval for the child's age and plotted on a growth chart. Target: ≥90%. Sample: 40 consecutive children and young people on ADHD medication for at least 6 months, from the CAMHS/paediatric ADHD clinic caseload
- Change: Build an automatic reminder into the ADHD clinic appointment system that flags when height or weight is due, and require the growth chart to auto-populate from the recorded measurements
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-763.csv`
- Pitfalls: Height and weight recorded at a GP or school nurse visit outside the ADHD clinic may be missed: agree a single source of truth for measurements before starting; A telephone or video review cannot include physical measurements: record whether the appointment was face-to-face and exclude remote reviews from the numerator; The interval differs by age band (under 10 vs over 10): pre-sort the sample by age so the correct schedule is applied to each patient; Teaching alone rarely moves this measure, as the library shows an electronic record change is needed to convert centiles automatically; Non-attendance at review appointments will look like a monitoring gap: record DNAs separately from measurements not taken at an attended appointment
- Pearls: Recruit the ADHD clinic administrator to help build the automatic reminder, since they control the appointment system; Agree the exact NICE interval definitions with the clinic team before data collection to avoid disputes at analysis; Use the growth chart itself (not just a text entry) as the source of truth, since a plotted point is easy to verify; Share the topic card's finding that a dedicated clinic model (not teaching) achieved the biggest gains, to set expectations for the fix; Timetable the re-audit for after the reminder system has been running for a full monitoring cycle (6 months), not sooner

**NNA-764. What proportion of children, young people and adults on ADHD medication have their heart rate and blood pressure measured and compared with the normal range for age before and after each dose change, and at least every 6 months?** (under-audited)
- Standard: NICE NG87 Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder: diagnosis and management, rec 1.8.9 (2018): "Monitor heart rate and blood pressure and compare with the normal range for age before and after each dose change and every 6 months." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng87/chapter/Recommendations
- Pass: Heart rate and blood pressure are recorded and compared with the normal range for age, both at the most recent dose change and at the most recent 6-monthly review. Target: ≥90%. Sample: 40 consecutive patients on ADHD medication with a dose change in the last 12 months, from the ADHD clinic caseload (CAMHS, adult ADHD service or shared care)
- Change: Link the ADHD e-prescribing dose-change order to a mandatory observation set, so the prescription cannot be finalised without a recorded heart rate and blood pressure compared against the age-normal range
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-764.csv`
- Pitfalls: Recording a raw heart rate/BP without comparing to the age-normal range should not count as a pass: define 'compared' as an explicit centile or normal/abnormal statement in the data tool; Dose changes made by a shared-care GP may not be visible to the specialist service: include a data-sharing check with primary care before starting; The library shows posters and teaching failed here because the electronic system could not calculate centiles: budget for an IT change, not just an education session; Patients who decline monitoring should be recorded as a specific category, not counted as a system failure; Multiple small dose titrations in a short period could be double-counted: use the most recent dose change in the audit period as the index event
- Pearls: Involve the electronic prescribing/IT team from the outset, since the library shows a system fix (not teaching) is what worked elsewhere; Use an age-appropriate blood pressure centile calculator built into or linked from the record, rather than a paper chart; Present the topic card evidence (teaching failed, system change worked) to secure sign-off for an IT change request; Pilot the mandatory link with one prescriber before rolling out trust-wide, to catch workflow problems early; Fix the re-audit date at 6 months so at least one full monitoring cycle has passed since the change

**NNA-765. What proportion of children and young people on ADHD medication whose blood pressure is consistently above the 95th centile for age and height are referred to a paediatric hypertension specialist before medication is continued?** (new)
- Standard: NICE NG87 Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder: diagnosis and management, rec 1.7.6 (2018): "Refer to a paediatric hypertension specialist before starting medication for ADHD if blood pressure is consistently above the 95th centile for age and height for children and young people." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng87/chapter/Recommendations
- Pass: A referral to a paediatric hypertension specialist is documented within 4 weeks of the blood pressure being confirmed as consistently above the 95th centile. Target: 100%. Sample: All identified cases in the last 12 months from the ADHD clinic caseload (expect approximately 15-25 cases in a typical CAMHS/paediatric ADHD service, given the low rate of BP centile use found elsewhere in the corpus)
- Change: Add an automatic alert in the electronic record that fires when a blood pressure centile is entered above the 95th centile for an ADHD patient, prompting an immediate referral order
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-765.csv`
- Pitfalls: If BP centiles are rarely calculated in the first place (as the library shows), the true denominator of 'confirmed high BP' may be undercounted: report the number of patients with any BP centile recorded alongside the audit result; A single high reading without repeat measurement should not count towards the denominator: require a second confirmatory reading before counting a case; Referral pathways to paediatric hypertension services vary between trusts: confirm the correct local referral route before data collection; Cases may be too few for a stable percentage: report as a proportion with the raw numerator and denominator, not just a percentage; Prescribers may continue medication while awaiting referral without recording a reason: capture this explicitly rather than assuming an oversight
- Pearls: Work with the ADHD clinic's admin team to search the record for any BP centile entries above the 95th centile, since these cases are rare and easy to miss manually; Agree the referral pathway and target response time with paediatric cardiology/hypertension before cycle 1; Because numbers will be small, present individual case summaries (anonymised) alongside the percentage to make the point clearly; Build the alert as a hard stop or strong prompt in the electronic record, since a soft reminder is unlikely to succeed given how rarely centiles are used; Keep this audit running continuously (rather than a single cycle) since new high-BP cases will appear slowly over time

**NNA-766. What proportion of adults with a learning disability newly started on a psychotropic medication for behaviour that challenges have a documented plan for reducing or stopping the medication, with a target timescale?** (under-audited)
- Standard: NICE NG11 Challenging behaviour and learning disabilities, rec 1.8.5 (2015): "Ensure that the following are documented: a rationale for medication (explained to the person with a learning disability and everyone involved in their care, including their family members and carers) how long the medication should be taken for a strategy for reviewing the prescription and stopping the medication." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng11/chapter/Recommendations
- Pass: The record states how long the medication should be taken for and a strategy for reviewing and stopping it, with a specific target date or trigger. Target: ≥90%. Sample: 30 consecutive adults with a learning disability newly started on a psychotropic for behaviour that challenges in the last 12 months, from the community learning disability team or STOMP register
- Change: Add a mandatory 'planned duration and stopping strategy' field to the STOMP medication initiation template, which must be completed before the prescription can be signed
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-766.csv`
- Pitfalls: A generic 'review in clinic' note without a specific date or trigger should not count as a pass: define this precisely in the data tool; New starters may be prescribed by an out-of-area or private provider whose notes are not available: exclude and record these separately; Staff may see stopping plans as unrealistic for long-standing behaviour: present the audit as measuring documentation of intent, not a requirement to actually stop; The library shows side-effect discussion fell after criteria changed between cycles in one service [3416]: keep the same criteria across both cycles; Family or paid carers may not be present at review to discuss stopping: record whether they were consulted, as this affects the quality of the plan
- Pearls: Base the mandatory field on the exact NG11 1.8.5 wording so there is no ambiguity about what counts as a strategy; Recruit the learning disability pharmacist to help design and monitor the field, since they typically run the STOMP register; Share the topic card's consultant advice (count actual dose reductions, not just plans) directly with the team to set the improvement target; Time the re-audit to align with the annual STOMP reporting cycle already required by NHS England, so data collection is not duplicated; Keep the audit register with the learning disability team pharmacist rather than a rotating psychiatry trainee, for continuity

**NNA-767. Of adults with a learning disability prescribed an antipsychotic for behaviour that challenges with a documented review of effectiveness, what proportion with no indication of response by 6 weeks have the medication actually stopped or the decision to continue explicitly justified in writing?** (under-audited)
- Standard: NICE NG11 Challenging behaviour and learning disabilities, rec 1.8.4 (2015): "stop the medication if there is no indication of a response at 6 weeks, reassess the behaviour that challenges and consider further psychological or environmental interventions." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng11/chapter/Recommendations
- Pass: The medication is stopped by 6 weeks if there is no indication of response, or, if continued, a specific written justification for continuing is present in the notes. Target: ≥90%. Sample: 30 consecutive adults with a learning disability on antipsychotics for behaviour that challenges who have passed their 6-week review point, from the community learning disability team caseload
- Change: Add a hard-stop prompt in the electronic prescribing system at the 6-week point for any antipsychotic coded as 'for behaviour that challenges', requiring either a stop order or a written justification before the prescription can be continued
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-767.csv`
- Pitfalls: 'No clear response' may be under-recorded because staff default to continuing rather than actively reassessing: define the audit to flag any review note lacking an explicit response statement as a fail; Environmental or psychological interventions may be tried without being recorded as linked to the medication review: cross-check care plans as well as prescription notes; Carers and care home staff may resist stopping medication they believe is working: record any documented carer view as part of the justification, not as an automatic pass; A change of prescriber partway through the period could mean the 6-week review was never formally handed over: check for a gap in responsibility; Numbers may be small in a single team: consider a longer collection window or pooling across neighbouring learning disability teams
- Pearls: Use the exact NG11 wording ('no indication of a response at 6 weeks') as the pass/fail definition to avoid subjective judgement calls; Involve a learning disability nurse or support worker who knows the person well in the review, since they can describe real behavioural change; Present the finding alongside the topic card's headline gap (50.6% with no clear indication [3584]) to show this is a known, high-harm, fixable problem; Agree the pharmacy hard-stop build with IT and pharmacy governance before cycle 1 so the change can go live immediately after presentation; Track actual dose reductions and stops at re-audit, not just documentation, as this is what the topic card identifies as missing from every existing audit

**NNA-768. What proportion of adults with a learning disability have an annual health check that includes a review of mental health problems?** (new)
- Standard: NICE QS142 Learning disability: identifying and managing mental health problems, quality statement 1 (10 January 2017): "Young people and adults with a learning disability have an annual health check that includes a review of mental health problems." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/qs142/chapter/quality-statements
- Pass: The annual health check record includes an explicit mental health review (a question, screening tool result, or narrative comment on mental state), not just physical health items. Target: ≥90%. Sample: 40 consecutive annual health checks completed in the last 12 months, from the GP learning disability register at one or two participating practices
- Change: Add a mandatory mental health review section to the GP annual health check template (already used for the learning disability DES), which cannot be marked complete without an entry
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-768.csv`
- Pitfalls: Annual health checks are often nurse-led using a template that may not prompt for mental health explicitly: check the template itself as well as individual entries; A tick-box 'mental health: normal' with no detail may be too weak to count as a real review: agree with the primary care team what counts as adequate detail before data collection; People who decline or do not attend are excluded from this audit but should be tracked separately, since non-attendance is itself a known access problem; GP data systems vary (EMIS, SystmOne): the exact template location for annual health checks will differ between practices; A learning disability nurse or GP may feel this adds to an already long consultation: build the change into the existing template rather than adding a separate step
- Pearls: Work with the practice's learning disability register lead, who already runs the annual health check DES, to make this change with minimal extra burden; Use a short, validated question (for example, a simple mood and behaviour change screen) rather than a lengthy new tool; Present the audit to the primary care network learning disability lead, since a template change there can spread across several practices at once; Agree in advance how referral for a mental health concern found at the check will be actioned (to the community learning disability team), so the change closes a real loop; Fix the re-audit to the next annual health check cycle so the same patients can be tracked over time

**NNA-769. What proportion of adults with a learning disability referred for a mental health assessment are seen by a professional with specific expertise in mental health problems in people with a learning disability?** (new)
- Standard: NICE QS142 Learning disability: identifying and managing mental health problems, quality statement 2 (10 January 2017): "People with a learning disability who need a mental health assessment are referred to a professional with expertise in mental health problems in people with learning disabilities." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/qs142/chapter/quality-statements
- Pass: The assessing clinician is a psychiatrist, nurse or psychologist with a learning disability specialism (community learning disability team, or a generic mental health service with documented learning disability liaison input). Target: ≥90%. Sample: 30 consecutive learning disability mental health referrals in the last 12 months, from the community learning disability team or generic community mental health team referral log
- Change: Add an automatic flag on the community mental health team referral system that redirects any referral coded 'learning disability' to the specialist learning disability team, or requires documented learning disability liaison input if seen elsewhere
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-769.csv`
- Pitfalls: A generic community mental health team may see the person without recognising the learning disability, especially if mild: check the referral coding as well as the outcome; Rural or smaller services may have no dedicated learning disability specialist and rely on liaison input: define what counts as adequate liaison before data collection; Referral letters may not state the person has a learning disability if it is not the presenting reason: cross-check against the GP learning disability register; Waiting times to a specialist team may be longer than to a generic team, creating pressure to bypass the specialist route: record time to assessment for both; Historic referrals may predate a service reorganisation: use only referrals from the last 12 months to reflect current pathways
- Pearls: Cross-reference the referral list against the GP learning disability register to make sure no relevant referral is missed; Agree a single definition of 'learning disability expertise' with both teams before starting, to avoid disputes over borderline cases; Recruit a joint audit lead from both the learning disability and generic mental health teams so the fix is owned by both; Use the audit findings to support a business case for a formal liaison arrangement if none currently exists; Keep the referral log query script so the re-audit can be run quickly by whoever holds the audit next

**NNA-770. What proportion of adults with a learning disability and a serious mental illness have a named key worker recorded in their care plan to coordinate their care?** (new)
- Standard: NICE QS142 Learning disability: identifying and managing mental health problems, quality statement 3 (10 January 2017): "People with a learning disability and a serious mental illness have a key worker to coordinate their care." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/qs142/chapter/quality-statements
- Pass: A single named key worker is documented in the current care plan, with their role and contact details. Target: ≥90%. Sample: 30 consecutive adults with a learning disability and serious mental illness on the current community learning disability/mental health caseload
- Change: Add a mandatory 'named key worker' field to the community learning disability team's care plan template, which must be completed and updated at every care plan review
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-770.csv`
- Pitfalls: A team may be named as 'key worker' rather than an individual, which does not meet the intent of the standard: define 'named' as a specific person in the data tool; Key workers may change with staff turnover without the care plan being updated: check the last care plan review date alongside the named worker; People open to both a community learning disability team and a separate community mental health team may have two different named workers, causing confusion: record and flag this as a fail; Caseload lists may be out of date: verify the current caseload with the team manager before sampling; Care plans stored only on paper in some services will need manual review alongside the electronic record
- Pearls: Agree the definition of 'serious mental illness' (psychosis, bipolar disorder, severe depression) with the team before sampling to keep the population consistent; Ask the team manager for an up-to-date caseload list rather than relying on a historic report; Present the audit alongside the QS142 statement wording so the standard is unambiguous to the team; Build the key worker field into whatever care planning software is already in use, rather than a separate document; Repeat the audit after the next round of staff changes, since key worker continuity is most at risk during turnover

**NNA-771. What proportion of adults with a learning disability who remain on an antipsychotic medication that has not been reduced or stopped have the reasons for continuing it documented at least once in the last 12 months?** (under-audited)
- Standard: NICE QS142 Learning disability: identifying and managing mental health problems, quality statement 5 (10 January 2017): "People with a learning disability who are taking antipsychotic drugs that are not reduced or stopped have annual documentation on reasons for continuing this prescription." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/qs142/chapter/quality-statements
- Pass: A dated entry in the last 12 months explicitly states the reason for continuing the antipsychotic. Target: ≥90%. Sample: 30 consecutive adults with a learning disability on an unchanged antipsychotic dose for more than 12 months, from the community learning disability team or STOMP register
- Change: Add an annual STOMP review reminder to the electronic record for every patient on an unchanged antipsychotic dose, which must be completed with an explicit reason for continuing before it can be dismissed
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-771.csv`
- Pitfalls: A brief 'continue as before' note should not count as a pass: define the required content (specific clinical reason) in the data tool; Patients seen only by a GP on a shared-care basis may not have specialist review documented at all: check both specialist and GP records; Long-stay patients with decades of unchanged prescribing may have no recent documented rationale anywhere: report this finding directly rather than assuming it exists; Staff may resist a formal reminder as bureaucratic if they know the patient well: frame the change as a safeguard against unexamined long-term prescribing, per LeDeR-type learning; A dose reduction attempted and reversed due to relapse should still count as active review, not treated the same as no review at all
- Pearls: Use the STOMP register (already required by NHS England) as the sampling frame so the audit does not duplicate existing data collection; Recruit the learning disability pharmacist to lead the annual reminder build and review the findings; Present the QS142 statement 5 wording directly to prescribers so the annual documentation requirement is unambiguous; Track whether annual review leads to any actual dose changes over time, not just documentation, to show real impact; Align the re-audit date with the trust's existing annual STOMP reporting deadline to avoid duplicate data pulls

**NNA-772. What proportion of women of childbearing potential newly assessed by adult or perinatal mental health services while already prescribed valproate for a mental health condition have a documented discussion of switching to an alternative medication?** (under-audited)
- Standard: NICE CG192 Antenatal and postnatal mental health, rec 1.2.3 (2014, amended 2020): "Do not offer valproate for acute or long-term treatment of a mental health problem in women or girls of childbearing potential (including young girls who are likely to need treatment into their childbearing years), unless other options are ineffective or not tolerated and the pregnancy prevention programme is in place." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg192/chapter/Recommendations
- Pass: The record shows either that valproate was not used, or, if it was continued, a documented trial or consideration of at least one alternative and that the pregnancy prevention programme is in place. Target: ≥90%. Sample: All identified cases in the last 12 months from the mental health service valproate register (typically 15-25 women in a district general hospital catchment)
- Change: Add a mandatory 'alternative treatment considered' field to the mental health service's valproate register review template, which must be completed at every review of a woman of childbearing potential
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-772.csv`
- Pitfalls: Women may already be stable on valproate after multiple failed alternatives, making a switch clinically inappropriate: record this as a documented, reasoned decision rather than a fail; Perinatal and adult mental health teams may hold separate valproate registers: reconcile both before sampling to avoid double counting or missed cases; Small numbers are likely given how few women of childbearing potential remain on valproate once the pregnancy prevention programme is enforced: report raw numbers alongside any percentage; A woman may not disclose she is sexually active or planning pregnancy, affecting the urgency of the discussion: record what was asked, not assumed; Switching medication carries its own relapse risk: frame the change as ensuring the discussion happens, not mandating a switch
- Pearls: Use the mental health pharmacist-held valproate register as the single source of truth for the sampling frame; Involve both perinatal and adult mental health pharmacy leads, since patients often move between these services; Present the topic card's consultant advice directly to the team to justify why this specific angle (switching, not just ARAF completion) is the audit focus; Agree with the team in advance what counts as an acceptable 'alternatives ineffective or not tolerated' justification; Keep the valproate register under pharmacy ownership so the re-audit can be run without waiting for a trainee rotation

**NNA-773. What proportion of women with a current or past severe mental health problem who are planning a pregnancy are referred to a secondary mental health service, preferably a specialist perinatal mental health service, for preconception counselling?** (new)
- Standard: NICE CG192 Antenatal and postnatal mental health, rec 1.4.2 (2014): "Consider referring a woman to a secondary mental health service (preferably a specialist perinatal mental health service) for preconception counselling if she has a current or past severe mental health problem and is planning a pregnancy." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg192/chapter/Recommendations
- Pass: A referral for preconception counselling is documented as made, or offered and declined, when a woman with a current or past severe mental health problem states she is planning a pregnancy.
