Target: ≥90%. Sample: All identified cases in the last 12 months from mental health service records (typically 15-30 women across a community mental health team caseload)
- Change: Add a mandatory prompt to the community mental health team electronic care plan review: 'planning a pregnancy: yes/no', which triggers an automatic preconception counselling referral suggestion when answered yes
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-773.csv`
- Pitfalls: Pregnancy planning may be discussed informally in a routine appointment without a specific documented field: agree with clinicians to actively ask and record this at every relevant review; Women may not disclose pregnancy plans to a mental health worker they see infrequently: report the number of women asked as well as the number referred; Specialist perinatal services may have geographic or capacity limits, making referral to a generic secondary service the only option: record this as a partial pass with the reason given; Retrospective identification of 'planning a pregnancy' entries may be difficult if not coded: consider prospective data collection over a fixed window instead of retrospective search; The record may show a referral made but never actioned by the receiving service: check the perinatal team's own referral log for confirmation, not just the sending note
- Pearls: Recruit the perinatal mental health service lead as a joint audit lead with the adult community mental health team; Use a structured yes/no prompt rather than free text so future searches are reliable; Agree a simple referral pathway and response time standard with the perinatal service before starting, so the change has somewhere to route referrals; Present the finding to the trust's perinatal mental health network (many now exist under the NHS Long Term Plan), which can support scaling the change; Keep prospective data collection running via the new prompt so the re-audit is a simple data pull rather than a fresh manual search

**NNA-774. Do women with sudden onset of symptoms suggesting postpartum psychosis have a documented referral to a secondary mental health service (preferably specialist perinatal) with assessment completed within 4 hours of referral?** (new)
- Standard: NICE CG192 Antenatal and postnatal mental health, rec 1.5.12 (2014): "If a woman has sudden onset of symptoms suggesting postpartum psychosis, refer her to a secondary mental health service (preferably a specialist perinatal mental health service) for immediate assessment (within 4 hours of referral)." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg192/chapter/Recommendations
- Pass: Assessment by a secondary mental health service is documented as completed within 4 hours of the referral being made. Target: 100%. Sample: All identified urgent postpartum psychosis referrals in the last 12 months (typically a small number, 10-20 cases, given the rarity of the presentation; extend the window if fewer than 10 are found)
- Change: Add a mandatory 'suspected postpartum psychosis' flag to the crisis team referral triage system, which starts a 4-hour countdown timer and pages the on-call perinatal or general psychiatry consultant automatically
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-774.csv`
- Pitfalls: Postpartum psychosis is rare, so numbers will be very small: report raw numerators/denominators and consider a rolling collection over 12-24 months rather than a single 3-month window; Out-of-hours referrals may go through a different crisis pathway with less clear time-stamping: check both in-hours and out-of-hours logs; A woman may present to a general adult crisis team unfamiliar with the postpartum psychosis red flags and be triaged as routine: check for missed or delayed recognition, not just delay after correct triage; Referral and assessment times may be recorded inconsistently (referral received vs. referral accepted): agree a single time-stamp definition before starting; A perinatal mental health service may not operate 24/7 in smaller areas, meaning the target route is unavailable out of hours: record and report this system gap
- Pearls: Work with the crisis team and perinatal mental health service together, since the referral usually crosses between them; Use the rarity of the condition as an argument for prospective, continuous data collection via the new flag, rather than a fixed 3-month audit window; Base the change on a simple, recognisable red-flag checklist for postpartum psychosis so referrers do not need specialist perinatal knowledge; Present any near-miss or delayed case (even outside the identified events) as a case study to strengthen the argument for the timer system; Escalate any finding that the specialist perinatal service is unavailable out-of-hours to commissioners, as this is a systemic, not just documentation, gap

**NNA-775. What proportion of women who may need to take psychotropic medication in pregnancy or the postnatal period have a documented discussion of the benefits of breastfeeding and the risks of the specific medication with breastfeeding?** (new)
- Standard: NICE CG192 Antenatal and postnatal mental health, rec 1.4.4 (2014): "Discuss breastfeeding with all women who may need to take psychotropic medication in pregnancy or in the postnatal period. Explain to them the benefits of breastfeeding, the potential risks associated with taking psychotropic medication while breastfeeding..." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg192/chapter/Recommendations
- Pass: A dated note records that breastfeeding and the specific medication's risks/benefits were discussed with the woman. Target: ≥90%. Sample: 30 consecutive women under perinatal mental health services prescribed a psychotropic medication in the last 12 months
- Change: Add a mandatory 'breastfeeding and medication discussed' checkbox with a free-text summary field to the perinatal mental health medication review template
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-775.csv`
- Pitfalls: A discussion may happen verbally without being recorded: agree with the team that this is a documentation standard, and undocumented discussions still count as a fail; Specialist perinatal pharmacy advice (e.g. from UKTIS or a specialist pharmacist) may be sought but not linked in the main note: check pharmacy correspondence as well as the clinical note; Women who are not breastfeeding and have no plans to should be excluded, but this needs to be explicitly documented, not assumed; The discussion needs to be specific to the medication prescribed, not a generic breastfeeding leaflet: define this distinction in the data tool; Views may change over the postnatal period (a woman may start breastfeeding after initially not planning to): capture the date of the woman's current status alongside the discussion date
- Pearls: Recruit the perinatal mental health pharmacist to help build and monitor the mandatory field; Use an established resource (such as a specialist medicines-in-pregnancy/breastfeeding information service) as the reference point for what a 'complete' discussion covers; Present the change as reducing legal and clinical risk from undocumented advice, which helps secure clinical engagement; Time the re-audit for 6 months to capture a full cohort of women moving through pregnancy to the postnatal period; Keep a simple log of specialist pharmacy queries made, as this is a useful secondary marker that the discussion is happening

**NNA-776. What proportion of patients in seclusion have a nursing review recorded at least every 2 hours, undertaken by two registered nurses, at least one of whom was not involved in the decision to seclude?** (under-audited)
- Standard: Mental Health Act 1983 Code of Practice (2015), paragraph 26.134: "Nursing reviews of the secluded patient should take place at least every two hours following the commencement of seclusion. These should be undertaken by two individuals who are registered nurses, and at least one of whom should not have been involved directly in the decision to seclude." https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/code-of-practice-mental-health-act-1983
- Pass: Every 2-hour interval of the seclusion episode has a nursing review recorded by two registered nurses, with at least one independent of the original decision to seclude. Target: ≥90%. Sample: All seclusion episodes of 2 hours or more in the last 3 months (typically 20-40 episodes across a secure or acute inpatient service)
- Change: Add a mandatory seclusion nursing review proforma with a built-in 2-hourly timer and a field confirming the second reviewer's independence, replacing free-text observation entries
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-776.csv`
- Pitfalls: Nursing reviews may be recorded in general nursing notes rather than a dedicated seclusion record, making them hard to find: search both sources; The 'independence' requirement may be poorly understood by staff: provide clear guidance on what counts as involvement in the original decision; Overnight and asleep-patient reviews may follow a modified schedule under local policy: record these separately rather than counting them as missed reviews; A template alone gave only modest gains in one service (75% to 83%) with minimal further change on a statistical process control chart [3552]: plan for ongoing monitoring, not a single fix; Staff may see 2-hourly review as excessive during long seclusion episodes: reinforce the safeguarding rationale in training, not just the form
- Pearls: Base the proforma directly on Mental Health Act Code of Practice paragraph 26.134 wording so staff can see exactly what is required; Use a physical or electronic timer/alert to prompt the 2-hourly review, since the corpus shows structural prompts outperform teaching alone; Recruit a senior ward nurse as the audit lead, since they can identify realistic barriers to documenting independence; Present the topic card's finding that huddles and weekly meetings raised consultant review compliance from under 70% to over 90% [3105], to support a similar nursing huddle model; Track average seclusion duration alongside review compliance, since the corpus shows a huddle model also reduced average seclusion time from 30 to 20 hours [3105]

**NNA-777. Where a patient has been secluded for 8 hours continuously or 12 hours intermittently within a 48-hour period, is an independent multidisciplinary team review carried out promptly, including a doctor, a nurse and other professionals not involved in the incident?** (under-audited)
- Standard: Mental Health Act 1983 Code of Practice (2015), paragraph 26.141: "An independent MDT review should be promptly undertaken where a patient has either been secluded for eight hours consecutively or for 12 hours intermittently during a 48-hour period." https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/code-of-practice-mental-health-act-1983
- Pass: An independent MDT review, with the required minimum membership and none of them involved in the original seclusion decision, is documented as carried out on reaching the 8-hour/12-hour trigger. Target: 100%. Sample: All qualifying episodes in the last 6 months (numbers will be small in most services; extend the window if fewer than 10 are found)
- Change: Add an automatic alert to the seclusion record that fires at the 8-hour continuous or 12-hour intermittent trigger, notifying the site manager to convene the independent MDT review
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-777.csv`
- Pitfalls: Long or intermittent seclusion episodes reaching the 12-hour-in-48-hours trigger may be harder to track than continuous episodes: build a running total into the seclusion record, not a manual calculation; 'Independent' membership may be compromised if the same small on-call team covers both the original decision and the review: record and flag this explicitly; IMHA involvement may not be arranged in time, especially out of hours: track whether the patient has an IMHA and whether they were invited; Numbers will be small: consider extending data collection to 6-12 months and pooling with other wards in the same secure service if needed; A review that happens late may still be recorded as 'done' without the delay being visible: always capture the time from trigger to review, not just yes/no
- Pearls: Build the 8-hour/12-hour trigger calculation into the seclusion record software so staff do not need to calculate it manually; Involve the trust's Mental Health Act administrator, who is well placed to track prolonged seclusion episodes across wards; Use this audit to also check IMHA involvement, since the two safeguards are meant to work together; Present near-miss cases (episodes close to but not reaching the trigger) to show the alert would have helped, even with a small confirmed sample; Since this trigger is rare, keep it as a standing, continuously monitored indicator rather than a one-off audit

**NNA-778. Does the seclusion care plan for every patient in seclusion include, as a minimum, a statement of clinical needs and risks, a plan for meeting needs and de-escalation, and details of bedding, clothing and dietary provision, as required by the Mental Health Act Code of Practice?** (new)
- Standard: Mental Health Act 1983 Code of Practice (2015), paragraph 26.147: "As a minimum the seclusion care plan should include: a statement of clinical needs (including any physical or mental health problems), risks and treatment objectives; a plan as to how needs are to be met, how de-escalation attempts will continue and how risks will be managed; details of bedding and clothing to be provided; details as to how the patient's dietary needs are to be provided for." https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/code-of-practice-mental-health-act-1983
- Pass: All four minimum elements (clinical needs/risks, de-escalation plan, bedding/clothing, dietary needs) are present in the seclusion care plan. Target: ≥90%. Sample: All seclusion episodes over 2 hours in the last 3 months (typically 20-40 episodes)
- Change: Replace the free-text seclusion care plan section with a structured proforma with the four mandatory headings from the Code of Practice, so none can be skipped
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-778.csv`
- Pitfalls: Staff may complete a generic care plan template not specific to seclusion, missing the required elements: check against the exact four headings, not a general impression of completeness; Bedding/clothing and dietary needs may be managed verbally by nursing staff without being written into the plan: this should still count as a fail, since the standard requires documentation; Care plans may be updated as seclusion continues, so audit the most recent version, but also check the plan was in place from early in the episode, not only by the time it ended; A well-intentioned but generic 'as per care plan' note without specific content should not count as a pass; Fatigue during very long seclusion episodes may mean updates lapse over time: sample from both early and later points in longer episodes if resources allow
- Pearls: Base the structured proforma exactly on Code of Practice paragraph 26.147 so nothing required is left to interpretation; Recruit ward matrons/senior nurses to pilot the new proforma before a full rollout, since they complete these plans in practice; Link this audit with the seclusion review audits (nursing/medical/independent) so a single data collection exercise can gather several linked measures; Share examples of complete versus incomplete plans anonymised from the audit findings, to help staff see what 'good' looks like; Keep the proforma under the ward's own clinical documentation folder so it survives staff rotation

**NNA-779. Before section 17 leave is first granted to a detained patient, is a documented risk assessment carried out and any necessary safeguards put in place, as required by the Mental Health Act Code of Practice?** (under-audited)
- Standard: Mental Health Act 1983 Code of Practice (2015), paragraph 27.10: "When considering and planning leave of absence, responsible clinicians should: ... undertake a risk assessment and put in place any necessary safeguards ..." https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/code-of-practice-mental-health-act-1983
- Pass: A documented risk assessment, dated before or on the date leave is first authorised, is present with any safeguards specified. Target: ≥90%. Sample: 30 consecutive first-time section 17 leave authorisations in the last 3 months, across acute and secure/forensic wards
- Change: Add a mandatory risk assessment field to the electronic section 17 leave form, which cannot be submitted for signature without a completed, dated risk assessment attached
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-779.csv`
- Pitfalls: A generic ward risk assessment done on admission may be wrongly counted as the leave-specific risk assessment: require it to be dated at or after the leave decision and to reference the leave itself; Escorted vs unescorted leave carry different risk profiles: record which type of leave was granted, since a blanket risk assessment may not address both; For patients on long-term leave with periodic short extensions, distinguish the first grant (audited here) from routine extensions; Forensic/secure wards may already do this well due to existing MDT risk review processes: report results by ward type to identify where the gap is greatest; A documented risk assessment that is a copy-paste from a previous one without genuine reassessment should not count as a pass
- Pearls: Use the existing library audit [3245] baseline (83% missing) as the starting comparison point to show the scale of the problem; Recruit the Mental Health Act administrator, who processes every section 17 form, to help identify the sample and enforce the mandatory field; Agree with ward consultants in advance what counts as an adequate risk assessment specific to leave (not just a general admission risk assessment); Present the [3505] closed-loop audit's approach as a template for how to structure the re-audit; Fix ownership of the audit with the Mental Health Act office, which has continuous oversight of every section 17 form issued

**NNA-780. In secure or smoke-free mental health units, do patients taking clozapine or olanzapine who stop or significantly reduce smoking have a documented dose review or plasma level check within 1 week of the change in smoking status?** (new)
- Standard: NICE CG178 Psychosis and schizophrenia in adults: prevention and management, rec 1.1.2.3 (2014): "Offer people with psychosis or schizophrenia who smoke help to stop smoking, even if previous attempts have been unsuccessful. Be aware of the potential significant impact of reducing cigarette smoking on the metabolism of other drugs, particularly clozapine and olanzapine." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg178/chapter/Recommendations
- Pass: A dose review (with or without a change) or a clozapine plasma level check is documented within 1 week of a recorded reduction or stop in smoking. Target: 100%. Sample: All identified cases of smoking reduction/cessation on clozapine or olanzapine in the last 12 months across the secure service (numbers will vary; expect roughly 10-25 cases given typical smoke-free unit admission rates)
- Change: Add an automatic alert to the electronic prescribing record that fires when a patient on clozapine or olanzapine is flagged as reducing or stopping smoking (via the smoking cessation service record), prompting an urgent dose review and plasma level request
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-780.csv`
- Pitfalls: Smoking status changes may not be formally recorded outside the smoking cessation service, especially if a patient simply cannot smoke on a secure ward without a documented cessation attempt: cross-check ward observation notes as well; A patient may relapse and restart smoking during a leave period, requiring the reverse adjustment: track both directions of change, not just cessation; Some units may already build in an automatic clozapine level check on admission to a smoke-free ward regardless of prior smoking status: record baseline unit practice before assuming a gap exists; Toxicity symptoms (sedation, hypersalivation, seizures) may be misattributed to other causes: prompt staff to consider the smoking-clozapine interaction explicitly in the proforma; Numbers will be small in a single unit: consider pooling data across a regional secure services network
- Pearls: Involve the secure unit's pharmacist and smoking cessation lead jointly, since this crosses both services; Use national forensic pharmacy network guidance (where available) alongside the CG178 recommendation to design the alert threshold; Present real (anonymised) cases of clozapine toxicity linked to smoking cessation from national safety alerts to support the case for change; Build the alert to also flag e-cigarette or vaping changes, since nicotine (not smoke) is not the enzyme-inducing component, and confusion here is common; Keep monitoring live rather than a single cycle, since a secure ward's smoke-free policy affects every new admission who smokes

**NNA-781. What proportion of patients with an eating disorder admitted to a medical or paediatric ward have a physical risk assessment that includes nutritional status, disordered eating behaviours, physical examination, blood tests and electrocardiography, as recommended by MEED?** (new)
- Standard: Royal College of Psychiatrists CR233 Medical emergencies in eating disorders: guidance on recognition and management, recommendation 3 (2022): "Physical risk assessment in primary and secondary settings should include nutritional status (including current intake), disordered eating behaviours, physical examination, blood tests and electrocardiography." https://www.rcpsych.ac.uk/improving-care/campaigning-for-better-mental-health-policy/college-reports/2022-college-reports/cr233
- Pass: All five elements (nutritional status, disordered eating behaviours, physical examination, blood tests, ECG) are recorded within 24 hours of admission. Target: ≥90%. Sample: 30 consecutive eating disorder-related medical/paediatric admissions over the last 6 months
- Change: Introduce a MEED-based eating disorder admission proforma with all five elements as mandatory fields, triggered automatically by an eating disorder diagnosis code or referral
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-781.csv`
- Pitfalls: Medical and paediatric teams unfamiliar with MEED may not recognise the need for the full bundle if the patient appears clinically well: include awareness training alongside the proforma; ECG may be delayed or deferred if the patient is thought to be 'medically stable': define the audit standard as within 24 hours regardless of apparent stability; Disordered eating behaviours may be under-documented due to patient reluctance to disclose: record what was asked, not just what was found; A generic 'bloods taken' entry without specifying which tests (including phosphate, magnesium) may overstate compliance: specify the required panel in the data tool; Small numbers in a single hospital: consider pooling data across a regional eating disorder network if fewer than 20 cases are found in 6 months
- Pearls: Base the proforma on the CR233 summary sheets (Annexe 1), which are designed as quick-reference guides for non-specialist medical and paediatric staff; Involve the eating disorder service's specialist dietitian and physician in designing the proforma so it fits real ward workflow; Present the CR233 finding that patients can appear well with normal bloods but still be high risk, to build buy-in from medical/paediatric teams who may otherwise underestimate risk; Link the proforma trigger to the eating disorder referral or diagnosis code so it activates automatically rather than relying on staff to remember; Share results with both the medical/paediatric directorate and the eating disorder service, since both need to act on gaps

**NNA-782. What proportion of patients under 18 admitted with an eating disorder have their physical risk assessed using age-adjusted thresholds for BMI and blood pressure, rather than adult reference ranges?** (new)
- Standard: Royal College of Psychiatrists CR233 Medical emergencies in eating disorders: guidance on recognition and management, recommendation 4 (2022): "Assessment measures (such as body mass index [BMI] or blood pressure [BP]) for patients under 18 years must be age-adjusted." https://www.rcpsych.ac.uk/improving-care/campaigning-for-better-mental-health-policy/college-reports/2022-college-reports/cr233
- Pass: BMI is recorded as a centile or percentage of median BMI for age, and blood pressure is compared against an age-adjusted (not adult) reference range. Target: ≥90%. Sample: 30 consecutive under-18 eating disorder admissions over the last 12 months
- Change: Build an automatic BMI centile and age-adjusted blood pressure calculator into the paediatric eating disorder admission proforma, replacing free-text adult BMI entry
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-782.csv`
- Pitfalls: Staff trained primarily in adult eating disorder services may default to adult BMI thresholds out of habit: highlight this explicitly in training; A centile chart may be available on paper but not transferred into the electronic record: check both sources; Growth faltering in younger adolescents can be missed if only a single BMI centile is checked rather than trend over time: consider capturing a growth trajectory as a secondary measure; Some electronic systems may not support automatic centile calculation, requiring a manual chart: budget for this if an IT fix is not immediately available; Transitional-age patients (17-18) moving between CAMHS and adult services may have inconsistent practice: flag these cases separately
- Pearls: Use the RCPCH UK-WHO growth charts (or trust-approved equivalent) as the reference standard for age-adjustment; Involve a paediatrician or paediatric dietitian in building the calculator to ensure clinical accuracy; Present the CR233 rationale (adult thresholds underestimate risk in the young) directly to staff to explain why this matters; Pilot the automatic calculator with one admitting team before wider rollout to catch usability issues; Align the re-audit with the CAMHS eating disorder service's existing annual quality review cycle

**NNA-783. What proportion of patients identified as high risk of refeeding syndrome on eating disorder admission receive thiamine before enteral or oral refeeding begins?** (new)
- Standard: Royal College of Psychiatrists CR233 Medical emergencies in eating disorders: guidance on recognition and management, section 4 Safe refeeding of malnourished patients with restrictive eating disorders (2022): "avoid refeeding syndrome caused by too rapid refeeding ... safely refeed the patient" https://www.rcpsych.ac.uk/improving-care/campaigning-for-better-mental-health-policy/college-reports/2022-college-reports/cr233
- Pass: Thiamine (oral or intravenous, per local protocol) is given before or at the start of refeeding for every patient identified as high risk using the MEED risk factors for refeeding. Target: 100%. Sample: 20-30 consecutive high-refeeding-risk eating disorder admissions over the last 12 months (a longer window may be needed given lower admission volumes for this specific risk group)
- Change: Add a MEED-based refeeding risk grid to the eating disorder admission and drug chart, which pre-selects thiamine on the drug chart automatically when high risk is ticked
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-783.csv`
- Pitfalls: Eating disorder patients may start oral intake gradually without a formal 'refeeding start' order, making the index time unclear: define the start point as the first recorded increase in calorie intake; Risk grading may be done informally by the dietitian without a documented score: require the MEED risk grid to be completed and filed; Community/day-care patients starting a structured meal plan at home are harder to audit than inpatients: restrict this cycle to inpatient admissions only; Thiamine given after feeding has already started should count as a fail even if given the same day: capture the exact timing relative to the first feed; A patient may already be on oral thiamine from a GP for unrelated reasons: check that the dose and timing meet the refeeding-specific protocol, not just any thiamine prescription
- Pearls: Use the MEED refeeding decision tree (CR233 Figure 4) directly as the basis for the risk grid; Involve the eating disorder service dietitian, who typically leads on refeeding risk grading, as a joint audit lead; Present the audit alongside the existing general refeeding syndrome audit findings in the corpus to show the gap is consistent across settings; Build the thiamine pre-selection into the electronic drug chart order set so the fix does not depend on staff memory; Track any refeeding syndrome events (electrolyte derangement) alongside compliance, to show clinical impact at re-audit

**NNA-784. What proportion of patients with an eating disorder taking medication that could compromise cardiac function (including medication that could cause electrolyte imbalance, bradycardia below 40 beats per minute, hypokalaemia, or a prolonged QT interval) are offered ECG monitoring?** (under-audited)
- Standard: NICE NG69 Eating disorders: recognition and treatment, rec 1.8.17 (2017): "Offer electrocardiogram (ECG) monitoring for people with an eating disorder who are taking medication that could compromise cardiac functioning (including medication that could cause electrolyte imbalance, bradycardia below 40 beats per minute, hypokalaemia, or a prolonged QT interval)." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng69/chapter/Recommendations
- Pass: ECG monitoring is documented as offered (and either accepted and performed, or declined) for every patient on a medication with cardiac risk while an eating disorder is active. Target: ≥90%. Sample: 30 consecutive patients with an active eating disorder on a cardiac-risk medication, identified from the eating disorder service caseload over the last 12 months
- Change: Add an automatic ECG-offer prompt to the eating disorder service e-prescribing system, triggered whenever a medication on a defined cardiac-risk list is prescribed to a patient with an active eating disorder
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-784.csv`
- Pitfalls: The defined list of 'cardiac-risk medications' needs pharmacy input, since risk varies by dose and individual patient factors: agree this list before data collection; Patients may decline ECG monitoring, especially if needle- or procedure-anxious: record declines as a distinct category rather than a system failure; A historical ECG from before the medication was started should not count as current monitoring: require the ECG to be after the medication was started or at a defined interval; The corpus shows ECG completion can fall between cycles even after a documented improvement: build monitoring into a permanent system change, not a one-off intervention; Community and day-care patients may need to travel for ECG access, creating a practical barrier: consider community ECG provision as part of the change
- Pearls: Agree the specific cardiac-risk medication list with eating disorder pharmacy and cardiology input before starting; Use the corpus finding that ECG/bloods worsened after an initial improvement [3306] to argue for an automatic system prompt rather than a reminder poster; Recruit the eating disorder service's medical lead to champion the change, since they will need to interpret ECG results; Track the reason for any ECG not performed (declined, access issue, clinical decision) so the fix can be targeted correctly; Repeat the audit at 12 months to check the automatic prompt has not faded in effect, as seen elsewhere in the corpus

**NNA-785. Does the written record of a mental capacity assessment name the specific decision the person is being asked to make, rather than a general statement that the person 'lacks capacity'?** (under-audited)
- Standard: NICE NG108 Decision-making and mental capacity, rec 1.1.28 (2018): "Practitioners should make a written record of the decision-making process, which is proportionate to the decision being made. ... Include: what the person is being asked to decide ... whether on the balance of probabilities a person lacks capacity to make a decision." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng108/chapter/Recommendations
- Pass: The record states the specific decision in question (e.g. 'to consent to insertion of a nasogastric tube', not just 'capacity') and a specific conclusion about capacity for that decision. Target: ≥90%. Sample: 30 consecutive liaison psychiatry mental capacity assessments over the last 3 months
- Change: Replace the free-text capacity assessment note with a structured proforma that requires the specific decision to be typed into a mandatory field before the assessment can be saved
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-785.csv`
- Pitfalls: Clinicians may write 'capacity for discharge' as a decision when the actual decision is narrower (e.g. capacity to consent to a specific treatment): define 'specific' clearly in the data tool with examples; Multiple decisions may be assessed in one encounter (e.g. treatment and discharge): record each decision separately rather than as one combined entry; A well-completed proforma from one liaison clinician does not guarantee trust-wide uptake: monitor variation between individual assessors, not just an overall average; The MCA teaching intervention in the corpus [3531] was not stated to have been re-audited beyond the immediate cycle: build in the mandatory field so gains are not teaching-dependent; Time pressure in acute settings may lead to brief, non-specific entries: consider a very short mandatory field rather than a lengthy form to protect completion rates
- Pearls: Base the mandatory field wording directly on NG108 1.1.28 so there is no ambiguity about what 'specific' means; Recruit the liaison psychiatry service's own quality lead to pilot the proforma before wider rollout; Use the corpus finding that teaching alone raised compliance from 77.5% to 95% [3531] to show the size of gain possible, then aim to lock this in structurally; Present anonymised examples of vague versus specific decision statements in a short teaching session alongside the proforma launch; Track completion by individual assessor at re-audit to identify anyone needing extra support, without naming individuals in the wider report

**NNA-786. Does the written record of a mental capacity assessment include the reasoning for the conclusion under each of the four functional test elements (understand, retain, weigh up, communicate), rather than a bare conclusion?** (under-audited)
- Standard: NICE NG108 Decision-making and mental capacity, rec 1.1.28 (2018): "Practitioners should make a written record of the decision-making process... Include: ... steps taken to help the person make the decision ... key considerations for the person in making the decision ... needs identified as a result of the decision." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng108/chapter/Recommendations
- Pass: Evidence or reasoning is recorded for each of the four functional test elements (understanding, retaining, weighing up, communicating the decision), not just a yes/no conclusion. Target: ≥90%. Sample: 30 consecutive liaison psychiatry mental capacity assessments concluding a lack of capacity, over the last 6 months
- Change: Add four mandatory free-text boxes to the capacity proforma, one per functional test element, each requiring a specific entry (not a repeated tick) before the assessment can be saved
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-786.csv`
- Pitfalls: Clinicians experienced in capacity assessment may feel a four-box structure is unnecessarily rigid for a clear-cut case: pilot with a senior clinician first to refine wording; A single sentence covering all four elements together may be entered into one box: require each box to be completed individually; Assessments done jointly with another specialty (e.g. surgery) may be recorded in a different note format outside liaison psychiatry's own system: check both sources; Retrospective identification of 'lacks capacity' conclusions may need a coded search: agree the search term with the liaison team's data administrator; A well-completed proforma at initiation does not guarantee ongoing quality: monitor a rolling sample rather than a single cycle only
- Pearls: Reuse and adapt the structured MCA template already shown to work in the corpus [3531] rather than designing a new one from scratch; Recruit a liaison psychiatry consultant to co-design the four-box wording so it captures genuine clinical reasoning, not just a repeated tick; Present the 40-50% baseline finding from the topic card to secure buy-in for the change; Track whether the quality improvement is sustained six months after the initial teaching seen in [3531], since teaching effects can fade; Keep an example bank of well-reasoned, anonymised entries to use in ongoing induction for new liaison trainees

**NNA-787. What proportion of liaison psychiatry referrals for acute confusion in general hospital inpatients have a 4AT assessment completed before or as part of the liaison assessment?** (under-audited)
- Standard: NICE CG103 Delirium: prevention, diagnosis and management in hospital and long-term care, rec 1.6.1 (2010, updated 2023): "If indicators of delirium are identified, a health or social care practitioner who is competent to do so should carry out an assessment using the 4AT tool." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg103/chapter/Recommendations
- Pass: A 4AT score is recorded either by the referring ward before liaison psychiatry assessment, or by the liaison psychiatry team at the point of assessment. Target: ≥90%. Sample: 30 consecutive liaison psychiatry referrals for acute confusion over the last 3 months
- Change: Make a 4AT score a mandatory field on the liaison psychiatry referral form, which cannot be submitted without either a score or a documented reason it could not be completed
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-787.csv`
- Pitfalls: This audit targets the liaison referral pathway specifically, not general ward screening: exclude referrals where 4AT was clearly not indicated (e.g. clear acute stroke referral) to avoid repeating the overdone ward-level measure; A 4AT may be completed but not communicated to the liaison team at referral: check both the ward chart and the liaison referral form; The library shows gains from stickers and lanyard cards faded over a few weeks [1781][1875][3442]: plan for a mandatory field, not a passive reminder; Referrals made verbally or by phone before a formal written referral may bypass the mandatory field: agree that all referrals must be confirmed in writing with the field completed; Non-orthopaedic wards vary widely in delirium awareness: report results by ward type to target further work
- Pearls: Frame this specifically as a liaison-referral-pathway audit to avoid duplicating the corpus's already extensive ward-level delirium screening audits; Use the corpus's clear finding that only a compulsory electronic field held gains, to justify a mandatory (not optional) referral field; Recruit the liaison psychiatry team's referral coordinator to monitor and enforce the mandatory field; Present the audit alongside the follow-on diagnosis audit (see the linked liaison audit on final diagnosis) as a two-part quality improvement package; Track whether the referring ward type predicts poor compliance, to target teaching where it is most needed

**NNA-788. Where a liaison psychiatry 4AT assessment score is 4 or more (suggesting delirium), is a final diagnosis of delirium confirmed or excluded by a clinician with the relevant expertise, rather than left recorded only as 'query delirium'?** (under-audited)
- Standard: NICE CG103 Delirium: prevention, diagnosis and management in hospital and long-term care, rec 1.6.2 (2010, updated 2023): "If the assessment described in recommendation 1.6.1 indicates delirium, a healthcare professional with the relevant expertise should make the final diagnosis. This could be the same person who made the assessment." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg103/chapter/Recommendations
- Pass: A final diagnosis (delirium confirmed, delirium excluded, or delirium superimposed on dementia) is documented by a clinician with relevant expertise, and a management plan follows. Target: ≥90%. Sample: All liaison psychiatry assessments with a 4AT score of 4 or more in the last 6 months (typically 20-30 cases in a general hospital with an active liaison service)
- Change: Add a mandatory 'final diagnosis' field to the liaison psychiatry assessment template for any 4AT score of 4 or more, which cannot be left as 'query delirium' without an explicit plan to review and confirm within 48 hours
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-788.csv`
- Pitfalls: 'Query delirium' may persist in the notes even after a clear diagnosis is later made verbally: require the final diagnosis to be a discrete, searchable entry; Delirium superimposed on dementia can be genuinely difficult to distinguish: this audit should record 'delirium superimposed on dementia' as a valid, positive answer, not a fail; A patient discharged or transferred before a final diagnosis is reached should be recorded separately, since resolution may happen elsewhere; Antipsychotic prescribing without a documented diagnosis is a red flag identified in the corpus [1870]: capture this as a linked secondary measure; Liaison psychiatry may see the patient only once and rely on the ward team for follow-up: track who is responsible for confirming the diagnosis if not resolved at first assessment
- Pearls: Pair this audit with the referral-stage 4AT audit above so the full pathway from referral to diagnosis is covered by one data collection exercise; Use the corpus finding on misdiagnosed 'psychosis' [1365] to illustrate the harm of an unresolved 'query delirium' label; Recruit a liaison psychiatry consultant to define what counts as 'relevant expertise' for the final diagnosis in the local service; Track whether an antipsychotic was started without a documented diagnosis, as a secondary safety indicator; Present the two linked audits (referral 4AT and final diagnosis) together to the ward teams so the whole pathway, not just liaison psychiatry, understands its role

**NNA-789. Where a person's presentation makes it difficult to distinguish between delirium, dementia or delirium superimposed on dementia, is the delirium managed first, as required by NICE, rather than management being deferred pending a definitive diagnosis?** (new)
- Standard: NICE CG103 Delirium: prevention, diagnosis and management in hospital and long-term care, rec 1.6.3 (2010): "If there is difficulty distinguishing between the diagnoses of delirium, dementia or delirium superimposed on dementia, manage the delirium first." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg103/chapter/Recommendations
- Pass: Where the notes record diagnostic uncertainty between delirium and dementia, a delirium management plan (addressing reversible causes, environment, medication review) is started without waiting for a definitive diagnosis. Target: ≥90%. Sample: All identified cases of documented diagnostic uncertainty in the last 6 months (typically 15-25 cases in a general hospital with an active liaison service)
- Change: Add a short delirium management checklist (reversible causes, medication review, environment) directly to the liaison psychiatry proforma, triggered automatically whenever 'diagnostic uncertainty' is selected as an outcome
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-789.csv`
- Pitfalls: Diagnostic uncertainty may not be recorded as a discrete, searchable phrase: agree a short list of equivalent phrases (e.g. 'query delirium on dementia', 'difficult to distinguish') with the coding team; Teams may wait for cognitive testing results before starting any management, believing this is safer: reinforce in training that NICE recommends managing delirium first specifically because waiting can cause harm; A delirium management plan may be started informally (e.g. verbally asking to stop a medication) without being documented: this should still count as a fail if not written down; Elderly care and liaison psychiatry may each assume the other team is leading management: clarify ownership in the proforma; Retrospective case-finding for 'uncertainty' will be slower than for a coded diagnosis: budget more time for data collection than for a straightforward yes/no audit
- Pearls: Use the exact NICE wording ('manage the delirium first') as the standard so there is no room for a 'wait and see' interpretation; Recruit a liaison old age psychiatrist and a geriatrician jointly, since this decision typically sits between the two specialties; Frame training around the harm of delay (worsening delirium, falls, increased length of stay) rather than just the documentation requirement; Build the checklist to be quick to complete (a handful of tick boxes) so it does not become a barrier to fast action; Present real (anonymised) cases where delay caused harm, if available locally, to strengthen buy-in

**NNA-790. What proportion of people newly diagnosed with dementia are given oral and written information at diagnosis explaining their dementia subtype, expected changes, and which professionals will be involved in their care and how to contact them?** (new)
- Standard: NICE NG97 Dementia: assessment, management and support for people living with dementia and their carers, rec 1.1.6 (2018): "At diagnosis, offer the person and their family members or carers (as appropriate) oral and written information that explains: what their dementia subtype is and the changes to expect as the condition progresses; which healthcare professionals and social care teams will be involved in their care and how to contact them." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng97/chapter/Recommendations
- Pass: Both oral discussion and a written information resource covering subtype, expected changes and contact details are documented as given at the diagnosis appointment. Target: ≥90%. Sample: 30 consecutive new dementia diagnoses over the last 6 months, from the memory assessment service or old age psychiatry clinic
- Change: Create a standard post-diagnostic information pack (one per dementia subtype) with a named team contact sheet, and make handing it out a mandatory step in the diagnosis appointment template
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-790.csv`
- Pitfalls: A verbal explanation without a written record of what was said or given should not count as a pass: define this clearly in the data tool; Subtype-specific information (e.g. Lewy body versus Alzheimer's) may not be readily available as separate leaflets: check whether generic information was used and whether this meets the standard; Diagnoses given jointly with a GP or via a letter rather than a face-to-face appointment need a different process for delivering information: record the diagnosis method; Family members may be given the information while the patient with reduced capacity is not directly addressed: record who received the information; Contact information may go out of date if staff change: build a review step into how often the pack's contact sheet is updated
- Pearls: Involve the Admiral Nurse or dementia support worker (where available) in designing and distributing the information pack; Use nationally available dementia information resources (e.g. from a recognised dementia charity) rather than creating leaflets from scratch; Present the audit to the memory service's multidisciplinary team so the change is owned by whoever gives the diagnosis, not just doctors; Track whether patients/carers can name their named contact at a follow-up appointment, as a simple outcome check; Repeat the audit after any change of memory service staff or information pack version

**NNA-791. Do people living with dementia have a single named health or social care professional recorded who is responsible for coordinating their care?** (new)
- Standard: NICE NG97 Dementia: assessment, management and support for people living with dementia and their carers, rec 1.3.1 (2018): "Provide people living with dementia with a single named health or social care professional who is responsible for coordinating their care." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng97/chapter/Recommendations
- Pass: A single named individual (not a team name) with a role and contact method is documented as the care coordinator in the current care record. Target: ≥90%. Sample: 30 consecutive patients with dementia currently open to the old age psychiatry/memory service caseload
- Change: Add a mandatory 'named care coordinator' field to the dementia care plan template, updated automatically whenever the case is transferred between workers
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-791.csv`
- Pitfalls: A team name (e.g. 'memory service') rather than an individual should not count as a pass: define 'named' strictly as a specific person; Coordinators may change with staff turnover without a corresponding record update: check the last reviewed date, not just presence of a name; Patients under both a GP and a specialist service may have two different coordinators without either being aware: flag and record this as a fail; Caseload lists may include patients who have moved out of area or died: verify the current caseload with the team manager before sampling; A coordinator listed only on paper records, not the electronic system, may be missed: check both if the service uses hybrid records
- Pearls: Work with the memory service's care coordinator role holders (often community psychiatric nurses) to design the mandatory field; Use a case transfer checklist that requires updating the named coordinator field whenever a case moves between workers; Present the audit alongside the annual health check and key worker audits for learning disability, since the underlying principle (a single accountable named person) is shared; Track patient/carer awareness of who their named coordinator is at a follow-up visit, as a simple outcome check; Repeat the audit after any staffing changes in the service, since this is when coordination is most likely to be lost

**NNA-792. Do adults referred to a memory assessment service have anticholinergic burden from their current medicines documented as part of the reversible-causes work-up before a diagnosis of dementia is confirmed?** (under-audited)
- Standard: NICE NG97 Dementia: assessment, management and support for people living with dementia and their carers, rec 1.2.6 (2018): "...refer them to a specialist dementia diagnostic service (such as a memory clinic or community old age psychiatry service) if: reversible causes of cognitive decline (including delirium, depression, sensory impairment [such as sight or hearing loss] or cognitive impairment from medicines associated with increased anticholinergic burden) have been investigated and dementia is still suspected." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng97/chapter/Recommendations
- Pass: An anticholinergic burden score (or explicit medication review for anticholinergic drugs) is documented before a dementia diagnosis is confirmed. Target: ≥90%. Sample: 30 consecutive new dementia diagnoses over the last 6 months, from the memory assessment service
- Change: Add an automatic anticholinergic burden score calculation to the memory assessment service's pre-diagnosis work-up template, pulling from the current medication list, with a mandatory action field when the score is high
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-792.csv`
- Pitfalls: A high ACB score with no action documented should count as a fail, even if the score itself was calculated: audit the action, not just the calculation, per consultant advice; Some anticholinergic medicines may be prescribed by another specialty (e.g. urology, gastroenterology) and not visible to the memory service: request a full GP medication list, not just psychiatric medicines; Stopping a medicine started for a good clinical reason may not be appropriate: a documented reason for continuing should count as a pass, not just a stop or switch; The library shows the only closed loop for this topic got worse at re-audit [3388]: monitor closely after any change rather than assuming a single intervention will hold; Retrospective identification of anticholinergic burden calculations may be difficult if not consistently coded: consider prospective data collection via the new automatic field instead
- Pearls: Build the ACB calculator directly into the memory assessment pre-diagnosis template so it is not a separate, easily skipped step; Involve a memory service pharmacist to review any high-score cases and recommend action, closing the loop the corpus shows is currently missing; Use the topic card's finding that a previous closed loop got worse at re-audit [3388] to argue for embedding the fix in the system rather than relying on a single education cycle; Present both the ACB score and the resulting action rate together, since scoring alone (without action) is already common practice; Repeat the audit at 6 months specifically to check whether action rates (not just scoring rates) have genuinely improved

**NNA-793. Are adults in acute alcohol withdrawal assessed immediately on admission to hospital by a healthcare professional skilled in the management of alcohol withdrawal?** (under-audited)
- Standard: NICE CG100 Alcohol-use disorders: diagnosis and management of physical complications, rec 1.1.2.3 (2010): "People in acute alcohol withdrawal should be assessed immediately on admission to hospital by a healthcare professional skilled in the management of alcohol withdrawal." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg100/chapter/Recommendations
- Pass: An assessment by a professional documented as skilled in alcohol withdrawal management (e.g. addiction liaison nurse, specialist doctor) is recorded within 4 hours of admission. Target: ≥90%. Sample: 30 consecutive adults admitted with acute alcohol withdrawal risk over the last 3 months
- Change: Add an automatic referral to the alcohol/addiction liaison team triggered by any admission coded with an alcohol withdrawal risk flag, with a target response time built into the referral system
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-793.csv`
- Pitfalls: A generic admitting doctor with no specific alcohol withdrawal training may be wrongly counted as 'skilled': define this role explicitly with the addiction liaison team before data collection; Out-of-hours admissions may have no immediate access to a specialist assessor: record and report out-of-hours performance separately; Alcohol withdrawal risk may not be identified at all on admission if the history is incomplete: this audit should separately note where risk was missed entirely, as a more serious finding; A busy acute medical unit may triage alcohol withdrawal as lower priority than other presentations: highlight the safety rationale (risk of seizures, delirium tremens) in any change; Small numbers in a quieter unit: extend the collection window if fewer than 20 cases are found in 3 months
- Pearls: Use the existing alcohol liaison team's own referral log as a secondary data source to cross-check ward documentation; Present the corpus finding that a ward SOP with training (not just a scoring tool) achieved full compliance [3299], to support investment in a similar local SOP; Recruit an acute medicine consultant alongside the addiction liaison lead, since assessment timing depends on acute take processes; Track out-of-hours versus in-hours compliance separately, since this is likely to reveal the biggest gap; Fix the re-audit date at 3 months to check whether an automatic referral trigger, once built, is being used consistently

**NNA-794. What proportion of adults treated for acute alcohol withdrawal have their withdrawal severity monitored using a structured, validated tool (such as CIWA-Ar or GMAWS), completed and scored at the frequency specified in the local protocol?** (under-audited)
- Standard: NICE CG100 Alcohol-use disorders: diagnosis and management of physical complications, rec 1.1.2.2 (2010): "Follow locally specified protocols to assess and monitor patients in acute alcohol withdrawal. Consider using a tool (such as the Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment - Alcohol, revised [CIWA-Ar] scale) as an adjunct to clinical judgement." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg100/chapter/Recommendations
- Pass: A CIWA-Ar (or locally approved equivalent) score is recorded at the frequency specified in the local protocol for at least the first 48 hours of admission or until withdrawal resolves. Target: ≥90%. Sample: 30 consecutive adults treated for acute alcohol withdrawal on a general medical/surgical ward over the last 3 months
- Change: Replace the free-text withdrawal observation chart with an integrated electronic CIWA-Ar/GMAWS chart that calculates the score automatically from entered items and flags missed or overdue scores
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-794.csv`
- Pitfalls: A withdrawal scoring tool used inconsistently (e.g. only at night) may look complete on a single spot-check: audit the full expected schedule over 48 hours, not a single time point; Incorrect scoring (miscounted items) is common per the library findings: sample a subset for scoring accuracy by an independent reviewer, not just presence of a score; Ward staff turnover and unfamiliarity with the tool contribute to poor completion: pair any electronic chart rollout with brief mandatory training; The library shows repeated re-audits with teaching alone made only small gains: do not repeat a teaching-only cycle without a structural change; Patients transferred to a specialist detox unit partway through admission should have their general ward period audited separately from the specialist unit period
- Pearls: Use the corpus finding that a ward SOP with nurse-administered CIWA-Ar and team training achieved full risk stratification at re-audit [3299] as the template for the local change; Build automatic scoring calculation into the electronic system so nurses do not need to add up items manually, reducing the correct-scoring gap found in the corpus; Recruit ward nursing leads as co-audit leads, since they complete the chart in practice; Present the corpus's repeated-failure finding [3603] to justify prioritising an electronic fix over another teaching cycle; Track whether correct, frequent scoring changes the benzodiazepine dose given (symptom-triggered dosing), linking this audit to safer prescribing

**NNA-795. What proportion of adults with decompensated liver disease being treated for acute alcohol withdrawal have a documented plan agreed with, or advice sought from, a healthcare professional experienced in liver disease?** (new)
- Standard: NICE CG100 Alcohol-use disorders: diagnosis and management of physical complications, rec 1.1.3.2 (2010, amended 2021): "People with decompensated liver disease who are being treated for acute alcohol withdrawal should be offered advice from a healthcare professional experienced in the management of liver disease..." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg100/chapter/Recommendations
- Pass: Advice from, or a joint plan with, a healthcare professional experienced in liver disease (hepatology, gastroenterology or a liver-specialist nurse) is documented within 24 hours of decompensated liver disease being identified during alcohol withdrawal treatment. Target: ≥90%. Sample: All identified cases in the last 12 months (numbers are likely to be small, 10-20 cases, in a district general hospital; extend the window if fewer are found)
- Change: Add an automatic hepatology/gastroenterology referral trigger to the electronic alcohol withdrawal order set whenever decompensated liver disease is coded alongside alcohol withdrawal treatment
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-795.csv`
- Pitfalls: Decompensated liver disease may not be clearly coded, especially if the presentation is dominated by withdrawal symptoms: cross-check liver function tests and clinical notes, not just the coding system; Advice may be given informally by phone without a written record: require the advice or plan to be documented in the notes regardless of how it was obtained; Choice of sedative may need adjustment in liver failure (e.g. shorter-acting benzodiazepines): record whether the medication choice reflects this, as a secondary marker of specialist input; Numbers will be small: consider a 12-month or longer collection window and report raw numbers alongside any percentage; Weekend and out-of-hours presentations may have delayed access to liver specialist advice: record and report time-of-week separately
- Pearls: Recruit a hepatology or gastroenterology liaison consultant as a joint audit lead with addiction liaison psychiatry; Use liver function tests and coding together to build a more complete case-finding search than either alone; Present the audit as protecting a small, very high-risk group, to secure engagement despite the modest case numbers; Build the electronic referral trigger to also suggest a liver-safe benzodiazepine choice, closing two safety gaps at once; Keep this as an ongoing, rolling audit given the low case volume, rather than a single fixed 3-month cycle

**NNA-796. What proportion of patients discharged from inpatient drug treatment services (including specialist community and inpatient detoxification services) after treatment for opioid use are supplied with take-home naloxone, or have a documented reason why not?** (new)
- Standard: GOV.UK Supplying take home naloxone without a prescription (Human Medicines Regulations 2012, regulation 238; guidance updated 12 September 2025): "The types of drug treatment services that can supply naloxone include, but may not be limited to: drug services provided by primary care services; drug services provided by secondary care services (including a range of specialised community and inpatient drug services)..." https://www.gov.uk/guidance/supplying-take-home-naloxone-without-a-prescription
- Pass: A take-home naloxone kit is documented as supplied at discharge, or a specific reason for not supplying it (e.g. already holds a kit, clinically inappropriate, declined) is recorded. Target: ≥90%. Sample: 30 consecutive discharges with a history of opioid use from the inpatient drug treatment or dual diagnosis service over the last 6 months
- Change: Add a mandatory 'naloxone supplied or reason not supplied' field to the inpatient drug treatment discharge checklist, which cannot be completed without an entry, and stock take-home naloxone kits on the ward
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-796.csv`
- Pitfalls: Patients may already hold a naloxone kit from a community drug service: record this as a valid reason for non-supply rather than a fail; Ward staff may be unfamiliar with the legal basis for supplying naloxone without an individual prescription: provide brief training alongside the mandatory field; Family members or carers present at discharge may also need training in use, which is easy to miss if only the patient is addressed; Stock and expiry management of naloxone kits on the ward needs a named responsible person, or supply will lapse; A patient who leaves against medical advice before formal discharge may miss the opportunity for supply: consider a rapid-access naloxone offer earlier in the admission for high-risk patients
- Pearls: Partner with the local community drug and alcohol service, which will already have a naloxone supply protocol that can be adapted for inpatient use; Use the gov.uk guidance's explicit inclusion of inpatient drug services to reassure ward staff of the legal basis for supply without an individual prescription; Build training on naloxone use into existing discharge planning conversations rather than as a separate appointment; Track whether kits supplied are ever used (via ambulance service or community data, where locally available) as a longer-term outcome measure; Keep a standing stock of naloxone kits on the ward with a named pharmacy lead responsible for restocking and expiry checks

**NNA-797. When a multidisciplinary, medical or independent review determines that seclusion is no longer warranted, does the patient leave seclusion without unnecessary delay?** (new)
- Standard: Mental Health Act 1983 Code of Practice (2015), paragraphs 26.144-26.145: "Seclusion should immediately end when a MDT review, a medical review or the independent MDT review determines it is no longer warranted... Seclusion ends when a patient is allowed free and unrestricted access to the normal ward environment or transfers or returns to conditions of long-term segregation." https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/code-of-practice-mental-health-act-1983
- Pass: The time recorded for the end of seclusion is within 30 minutes of the review decision that seclusion is no longer warranted. Target: ≥90%. Sample: All seclusion episodes ended in the last 3 months (typically 20-40 episodes across a secure or acute inpatient service)
- Change: Add a mandatory 'time of review decision' and 'time seclusion ended' pair of fields to the seclusion record, both time-stamped by the system rather than handwritten, so any delay is automatically visible
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-797.csv`
- Pitfalls: Staff may record the review decision time and the ending time as the same moment out of habit, masking a real delay: use system time-stamps rather than staff-entered times where possible; A delay may be clinically justified (e.g. arranging safe staffing to support the patient leaving seclusion): capture the reason for any delay rather than treating all delay as a failure; Night shifts with lower staffing may show longer delays: report results by time of day; Ending seclusion for a toilet or food break should not be confused with a genuine end of seclusion: apply the Code of Practice definition (free and unrestricted access) strictly; A patient may be reviewed as 'no longer warranted' by one professional but a second required reviewer disagrees: record how such disagreements are resolved and timed
- Pearls: Use existing seclusion review audit infrastructure (already common in the corpus) to add these two extra time fields rather than building a new audit from scratch; Recruit ward nursing staff to identify realistic causes of delay (e.g. arranging support) so the fix addresses real barriers, not just recording; Present the corpus finding that a huddle model cut average seclusion duration by a third [3105], to support a similar staffing/planning change here; Track the reason for delay over time to see if a particular cause (e.g. staffing) dominates and needs a separate fix; Keep this as a standing indicator on the ward's seclusion dashboard rather than a single-cycle audit

**NNA-798. Do people living with dementia prescribed an antipsychotic for behaviour and psychological symptoms of dementia have the medication reassessed at least every 6 weeks, with the decision to continue or stop documented at that review?** (under-audited)
- Standard: NICE NG97 Dementia: assessment, management and support for people living with dementia and their carers, rec 1.7.6 (2018): "When using antipsychotics: use the lowest effective dose and use them for the shortest possible time reassess the person at least every 6 weeks, to check whether they still need medication." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng97/chapter/Recommendations
- Pass: A documented reassessment, with an explicit decision to continue or stop, is present at an interval of 6 weeks or less throughout the prescribing period. Target: ≥90%. Sample: 30 consecutive people with dementia on an antipsychotic for behavioural and psychological symptoms, from the old age psychiatry or memory service caseload
- Change: Add an automatic 6-weekly review reminder to the electronic record for every patient coded as being on an antipsychotic for behavioural and psychological symptoms of dementia, which must be actioned with a continue/stop decision before it can be dismissed
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-798.csv`
- Pitfalls: A general medication review note that does not specifically address whether the antipsychotic is still needed should not count as a pass: require an explicit continue/stop statement; Community-dwelling patients seen less frequently than every 6 weeks by a specialist may be reviewed jointly with a GP: check both records for the review; Some patients may be on a long-standing, stable dose with an implicit assumption that stopping is unsafe: this should be recorded as an explicit, reasoned decision to continue, not an omission; This audit should be framed around the reassessment interval and action, not repeat existing physical health monitoring audits, to avoid the corpus's identified overdone territory; A short administrative gap (e.g. patient in hospital) may extend the interval for a valid reason: record and report these separately from true gaps in follow-up
- Pearls: Frame this audit explicitly as measuring the reassessment interval and stop/continue decision, not repeating overdone physical health monitoring measures; Recruit the old age psychiatry pharmacist to help identify the current antipsychotic-for-BPSD caseload and build the reminder system; Use the NICE wording directly ('reassess... to check whether they still need medication') as the pass criterion to keep the standard unambiguous; Track the proportion of reviews resulting in an actual dose reduction or stop over successive re-audits, as the ultimate measure of impact; Align the re-audit timing with the service's existing dementia care review cycle to avoid extra data collection burden

**NNA-799. Do adults with a learning disability prescribed medication for behaviour that challenges receive only a single psychotropic drug at a time, rather than two or more used concurrently for the same target behaviour?** (under-audited)
- Standard: NICE NG11 Challenging behaviour and learning disabilities, rec 1.8.3 (2015): "start with a low dose and use the minimum effective dose needed only prescribe a single drug monitor side effects as recommended in the NICE guidelines on psychosis and schizophrenia..." https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng11/chapter/Recommendations
- Pass: Only one psychotropic drug is prescribed for the target behaviour at any one time, or, where more than one is used, a specific documented clinical reason for combination therapy is present. Target: ≥90%. Sample: 30 consecutive adults with a learning disability on psychotropic medication for behaviour that challenges, from the community learning disability team or STOMP register
- Change: Add an automatic polypharmacy alert to the electronic prescribing system, triggered when a second psychotropic is added for a patient already coded as being treated for behaviour that challenges, prompting a mandatory documented reason
- Template: `new_audits/templates/NNA-799.csv`
- Pitfalls: Distinguishing 'for the same target behaviour' from legitimate separate diagnoses requires careful case-by-case review: use a learning disability psychiatrist to adjudicate ambiguous cases; Historic long-term polypharmacy may be well established and difficult to safely change quickly: record whether a reduction plan exists even where combination therapy continues; PRN (as-needed) medication used occasionally alongside a regular psychotropic should be recorded separately, since NG11 addresses this differently; The library shows this measure resisted improvement even when other measures improved sharply [3268]: expect this to be a harder change and plan a longer improvement timeline; Switching directly from one drug to another (a brief overlap during a cross-taper) should not be wrongly counted as ongoing combination therapy: define a minimum overlap duration before counting as polypharmacy
- Pearls: Use the STOMP register as the sampling frame, since it should already list current psychotropic prescriptions for this population; Present the corpus finding that single drug therapy resisted improvement even where other STOMP measures improved sharply [3268], to justify a dedicated focus on this specific measure; Recruit the learning disability pharmacist to review combination cases and support tapering plans where appropriate; Track the number of patients on 2 or more psychotropics for the same behaviour over successive audits as the key outcome measure, not just documentation of a reason; Keep the audit register with the learning disability pharmacist for continuity across trainee rotations
